then Qín will send messengers with light burdens and heavy bribes
to serve your state."
The Lord of Yìqú said:
"I respectfully receive your word."
After not long,
five states attacked Qín.
Chén Zhěn said to the King of Qín:
"The Lord of Yìqú
is a worthy ruler among the barbarians;
it would be better for Your Majesty to bribe him to appease his heart."
The King of Qín said:
"Very well."
Consequently, he sent a thousand rolls of patterned embroidery
and a hundred beautiful women
to the Lord of Yìqú.
The Lord of Yìqú summoned his ministers to deliberate, saying:
"This is exactly what Gōngsūn Yǎn spoke of."
Thereupon he raised troops and ambushed Qín,
soundly defeating the Qín people at the foot of Lǐbó.
The physician Biǎn Què went to see Qín Wǔ Wáng.
King Wǔ showed him his ailment;
Biǎn Què asked to remove it.
Those close to the King said:
"The Great King’s ailment
is in front of the ear
and below the eye.
Removing it may not necessarily cure it,
and it might cause the ear to lose its hearing
and the eye to lose its clarity."
The King told this to Biǎn Què.
Biǎn Què was enraged and threw down his acupuncture stone:
"Your Majesty deliberates with those who know
but allows those who do not know to ruin it.
If this is how the government of Qín is managed,
Your Majesty would destroy the state in a single move."
King Wǔ of Qín said to Gān Mào:
"I wish to lead my chariots through Sānchuān
to spy upon the House of Zhōu.
If I do so, will my fame not endure after I die?"
Gān Mào replied:
"Please allow me to go to Wèi
and make an agreement to attack Hán."
The King ordered Xiàng Shòu to assist and accompany him.
When Gān Mào reached Wèi,
he said to Xiàng Shòu:
"You return and tell the King:
'Wèi has listened to your servant,
but I hope the King will not attack.'
If the matter succeeds,
I will give all the credit to you."
Xiàng Shòu returned and told the King,
and the King went to meet Gān Mào at Xīrǎng.
When Gān Mào arrived,
the King asked for his reason.
He replied:
"Yíyáng
is a large district.
Shàngdǎng and Nányáng have long amassed resources there;
though it is called a district,
it is in reality a commandery.
Now the King is turning his back on several strategic passes
and traveling a thousand lǐ to attack it;
it will be difficult.
I have heard that Zhāng Yí annexed the lands of Bā and Shǔ in the west,
took the territory beyond the Xīhé in the north,
and took Shàngyōng in the south,
yet the world did not give much credit to Zhāng Yí but rather considered the former kings to be virtuous.
Marquis Wén of Wèi ordered Yuè Yáng to lead an army
to attack Zhōngshān.
After three years he captured it.
When Yuè Yáng returned and spoke of his achievements,
Marquis Wén showed him a trunk full of slanderous letters.
Yuè Yáng bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
'This was not your servant's achievement,
but the power of my lord.'
Now I am but a guest-official.
Chūlǐ Jí and Gōngsūn Yǎn, these two men,
will use the case of Hán to argue against me,
and the King will surely listen to them.
This would mean the King deceives Wèi,
while I receive the resentment of Gōngzhòng Chǐ.
Long ago, when Zēngzǐ lived in Bì,
there was a person in Bì with the same name and clan as Zēngzǐ
who killed someone.
Someone told Zēngzǐ's mother:
'Zēng Shēn has killed a man.'
Zēngzǐ's mother said:
'My son does not kill people.'
She continued weaving as before.
A moment later,
someone again said:
'Zēng Shēn has killed a man.'
His mother still continued weaving as before.
After a short while,
another person told her:
'Zēng Shēn has killed a man.'
His mother became afraid,
threw down her shuttle, climbed over the wall, and fled.
Now, with Zēng Shēn's virtue
and the trust his mother had in him,
yet because three people doubted him,
even a compassionate mother could no longer believe him.
Now my virtue is not equal to that of Zēngzǐ,
and the King's trust in me
is not equal to that of Zēngzǐ's mother.
Those who doubt me
will be more than three people;
I fear the King will throw down his shuttle on my account."
The King said:
"I will not listen to them;
I request to make a covenant with you."
Thereupon, he made a covenant with him at Xīrǎng.
He eventually attacked Yíyáng,
but after five months he could not capture it.
Chūlǐ Jí and Gōngsūn Yǎn were present
and they argued with the King.
The King was about to listen to them,
so he summoned Gān Mào and told him.
Gān Mào replied:
"Xīrǎng is over there."
The King said:
"Indeed it is."
Consequently, he mobilized all his troops,
sent Gān Mào to attack it again,
and finally captured Yíyáng.
During the campaign of Yíyáng,
Féng Zhāng said to the King of Qín:
"If we do not capture Yíyáng,
Hán and Chǔ will take advantage of our exhaustion,
and the state will surely be in danger!
It would be better to promise Hànzhōng to Chǔ to please them.
If Chǔ is pleased and does not advance,
Hán will surely be isolated,
and they will be unable to do anything against Qín!" The King said:
"Excellent."
He indeed sent Féng Zhāng to promise Hànzhōng to Chǔ,
and then he captured Yíyáng.
The King of Chǔ, based on those words, demanded Hànzhōng from Féng Zhāng.
Féng Zhāng said to the King of Qín:
"The King should then exile your servant,
and certainly say to the King of Chǔ:
'I indeed had no land to promise to the King of Chǔ.'"
Gān Mào attacked Yíyáng;
after three signals to advance, the soldiers would not ascend.
An officer of Qín’s Right Army replied:
"If you do not distribute rewards to the army,
you will surely be in great difficulty."
Gān Mào said:
"The reason I, a guest, have been able to serve as the Chancellor of Qín
is because I baited the King with Yíyáng.
Now if I attack Yíyáng and do not capture it,
Gōngsūn Yǎn and Chūlǐ Jí will frustrate me from within,
while Gōngzhòng will exhaust me with Hán from without.
There will never be another day to attack!
I request that if we beat the drums tomorrow and the city still cannot be taken,
I shall use the outer walls of Yíyáng as my tomb."
Thereupon he brought out his private gold
to increase the public rewards.
The next day they beat the drums,
and Yíyáng was captured.
Before Yíyáng was won,
Qín's dead and wounded were numerous,
and Gān Mào wanted to rest the troops.
Zuǒ Chéng said to Gān Mào:
"You are being attacked from within by Chūlǐ Jí and Gōngsūn Yǎn,
and from without you have earned the resentment of Hán Chǐ.
If you now use the army without success,
you will surely be in desperate straits.
It would be better for you to advance the troops and attack Yíyáng;
if Yíyáng is captured,
then your achievements will be many.
This will leave Chūlǐ Jí and Gōngsūn Yǎn with nothing to say,
and the people of Qín will all deeply resent them."
During the campaign of Yíyáng,
Chǔ abandoned Qín and joined with Hán.
The King of Qín was afraid.
Gān Mào said:
"Although Chǔ has joined Hán,
they will not be the first to fight for the Hán clan;
Hán is also afraid to fight
lest Chǔ has a change of heart behind them.
Hán and Chǔ will surely keep a watch on each other.
Chǔ speaks of siding with Hán
yet they harbor no deep resentment against Qín;
this is how I know they are just watching each other."
The King of Qín said to Gān Mào:
"The envoys coming from Chǔ are mostly forceful;
they argue with me,
and I am frequently at a loss for words.
What should be done about this?"
Gān Mào replied:
"The King should not worry!
When their forceful ones come as envoys,
then the King should not listen to their business.
When their weak and hesitant ones come as envoys,
then the King must listen to them.
In this way, the weak and hesitant ones will be employed,
and the forceful ones will not be!
The King can thereby control them."
Gān Mào fled Qín
and was about to go to Qí.
Leaving the pass, he met Sū Zǐ
and said:
"Have you heard of the maidens on the riverbank?"
Sū Zǐ said:
"I have not."
He said:
"Among the maidens on the riverbank,
there was one whose family was poor and had no candles.
The maidens were talking among themselves
and wanted to cast her out.
The one whose family was poor and had no candles was about to leave,
and she said to the maidens:
'Because I have no candle,
I always arrive first,
sweep the room and arrange the mats.
Why do you begrudge the leftover light that shines upon the four walls?
If you are kind enough to grant it to me,
how does it harm you maidens?
I believe I am of benefit to you,
so why drive me away?'"
The maidens spoke to one another
and, considering it to be so, they let him stay.
"Now I, your servant, am unworthy,"
"having been discarded and driven out of Qín and having left the pass,"
"I wish to sweep the rooms and spread the mats for you,"
"and hope that you will not drive me away."
Sū Zǐ said:
"Good."
"I shall make you esteemed in Qí."
Then he went west to persuade the King of Qín, saying:
"Gān Mào
is a man of talent,
not an ordinary scholar."
"He resided in Qín for many generations and was highly regarded;"
"from the Xiáo Sài
to the mountain valleys, he knows all the dangers and ease of the terrain."
"If he uses Qí to form an alliance with Hán and Wèi
and turns around to plot against Qín,
this would not be to Qín's advantage."
The King of Qín said:
"If that is so, what should be done?"
Sū Dài said:
"It is best to increase his ceremonial gifts
and provide him with a generous salary to welcome him back."
"When he comes, place him in Huái Gǔ
and never let him out for the rest of his life;"
"then how could the world plot against Qín through him?"
The King of Qín said:
"Good."
He granted him the rank of Shàng Qīng
and sent an envoy to Qí to welcome him.
Gān Mào declined and would not go.
Sū Qín falsely said to the King:
"Gān Mào
is a man of talent."
"Now Qín has granted him the rank of Shàng Qīng
and sent an envoy to welcome him;"
"Mào is so grateful for Your Majesty's favor
that he refuses to go
and wishes to be Your Majesty's servant."
"How will Your Majesty treat him with ritual now?"
"If Your Majesty does not keep him,
he will certainly not feel grateful to Your Majesty."
"With Gān Mào's talent
and the ability to control the masses of powerful Qín,
it would then be difficult to plot against him!"
The King of Qí said:
"Good."
He granted him the rank of Shàng Qīng
and commanded that he reside there.
Gān Mào served as the Chancellor of Qín.
The King of Qín favored Gōngsūn Yǎn
and, while in private with him, considered appointing him,
thus saying to him:
"I am about to make you Chancellor."
An official of Gān Mào heard this on the road
and told Gān Mào.
Gān Mào then went in to see the King and said:
"Your Majesty has found a worthy chancellor;
I dare to bow twice in congratulation."
The King said:
"I have entrusted the state to you;
where else would I have found a worthy chancellor?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty is about to make Xī Shǒu the Chancellor."
The King said:
"Where did you hear this?"
He replied:
"Xī Shǒu told me."
The King was angry that Xī Shǒu had leaked the matter,
and so he banished him.
Gān Mào made an agreement with Qín and Wèi to attack Chǔ.
Qū Gài, a man of Chǔ serving as Chancellor in Qín,
sought peace for Chǔ from Qín;
Qín opened the pass and listened to the Chǔ envoy.
Gān Mào said to the King of Qín:
"If you are intimidated by Chǔ
and do not let Wèi control the peace settlement,
Chǔ will certainly say
'Qín has sold out Wèi.'"
"Being displeased, they will ally with Chǔ;
once Chǔ and Wèi become one,
I fear the state will be harmed."
"It would be better for Your Majesty to let Wèi control the peace settlement;"
"if Wèi controls the peace settlement, they will surely be pleased."
"If Your Majesty does not earn the ill-will of Wèi,
then the lands entrusted to you will surely be many."
Regarding the matter of Xíng Shān,
Zhào was about to join Qín in attacking Qí.
Qí was afraid
and ordered Tián Zhāng to use Yáng Wǔ to align with Zhào,
and sent Shùn Zǐ as a hostage.
The King of Zhào was pleased;
he then halted his troops and informed Qín, saying:
"Qí has granted Yáng Wǔ to my humble state
and sent Shùn Zǐ to us,
wishing to resolve the attack."
"I dare to inform your subordinates."
The King of Qín sent Gōngzǐ Tā to Zhào
and said to the King of Zhào:
"Qí and your great state were to rescue Wèi but then broke the agreement;
they cannot be trusted or relied upon."
"Your great state was unrighteous,
so you informed my humble state of your previous alliance,
and we granted you the land of two communal altars
to maintain the sacrifices."
"Now you have halted your troops again
and wish to ally with Qí and receive its land;
this is not something I, your servant, understand."
"I request to add forty thousand armored troops;
let your great state decide upon it."
Sū Dài, on behalf of Qí, presented a letter to Ráng Hóu, saying:
"I have heard those who travel to and fro say:
'Qín is about to increase Zhào's armored troops by forty thousand to attack Qí.'"
"I personally asserted to the King of my humble state:
'The King of Qín is enlightened and thorough in his planning,
and Ráng Hóu is wise and experienced in affairs;
they will surely not increase Zhào's armored troops by forty thousand to attack Qí.'"
"Why is this?"
"The alliance of the Sān Jìn
is the mortal enemy of Qín."
"If the Sān Jìn turn their backs on Qín a hundred times
and deceive Qín a hundred times,
it is not considered untrustworthy by them,
nor is it considered conduct without principle."
"Now to destroy Qí to fatten Zhào—
Zhào being the mortal enemy of Qín—
is not beneficial to Qín."
"This is the first reason."
"The strategists of Qín will surely say:
'Destroy Qí and weaken the Jìn states,
and afterward secure victory over the Jìn and Chǔ states.'"
"Now Qí
is an exhausted state;"
"using the whole world to strike it
is like using a crossbow of a thousand-jūn weight to burst an ulcer."
"How then could the King of Qín control Jìn and Chǔ?"
"This is the second reason."
"If Qín sends out few troops,
then Jìn and Chǔ will not believe it;
if it sends out many troops,
then Jìn and Chǔ will be controlled by Qín."
"If Qí is afraid,
then it will certainly not flee to Qín
but will instead flee to Jìn and Chǔ."
"This is the third reason."
"If Qí carves off land to satisfy Jìn and Chǔ,
then Jìn and Chǔ will be at ease."
"If Qí raises its troops
and they become like a blunt sword,
then Qín will conversely receive the attack."
"This is the fourth reason."
"This is for Jìn and Chǔ to use Qín to destroy Qí,
and use Qí to destroy Qín."
"How wise Jìn and Chǔ would be,
and how foolish Qí and Qín would be!"
"This is the fifth reason."
"If Qín obtains Ānyì,
and remains friendly with Qí to keep it at peace,
then surely there will be no trouble."
"If Qín possesses Ānyì,
then Hán and Wèi will certainly not have Shàngdǎng."
"Between taking the 'bowels and stomach' of the Sān Jìn
and sending out troops while fearing they might not return,
which is more beneficial?"
"Therefore, I personally asserted to the King of my humble state:
'The King of Qín is enlightened and thorough in his planning,
and Ráng Hóu is wise and experienced in affairs;
they will surely not increase Zhào's armored troops
by forty thousand
to attack Qí.'"
Xuān Tàihòu of Qín loved Wèi Chǒufū.
When the Dowager Empress was ill and about to die,
she issued an order:
"For my burial,
Master Wèi must be interred with me as a human sacrifice."
Wèi Chǒufū was distressed by this.
Yōng Ruì persuaded the Dowager Empress on behalf of Master Wèi, saying:
"Do you believe that the dead have consciousness?"
The Dowager Empress said:
"They have no consciousness."
He said:
"If your divine spirit, Your Majesty,
clearly knows that the dead have no consciousness,
then why uselessly take one whom you loved in life
and bury him with a dead person who has no consciousness?"
"If the dead do have consciousness,
then the late King's accumulated anger has lasted for a long time;"
"Your Majesty will not even have enough time to compensate for your faults—
what leisure would you have then to dally with Wèi Chǒufū?"
The Dowager Empress said:
"Good."
Then she stopped.
Xuē Gōng, on behalf of Wèi, said to Wèi Rǎn:
"Wén has heard that the King of Qín wants to use Lǚ Lǐ to win over Qí
in order to settle the affairs of the world;
if so, your influence will certainly diminish.
When Qí and Qín join together to overlook the Sān Jìn,
Lǚ Lǐ will certainly serve as Prime Minister to both;
this means you would be winning over Qí
only to increase the importance of Lǚ Lǐ.
If Qí is spared from the armies of the world,
its resentment toward you will certainly be deep.
You would be better off advising the King of Qín to command my humble state to finish the task of attacking Qí.
If Qí is broken,
Wén requests to use the territory gained to enfeoff you.
When Qí is broken and the Jìn states become strong,
the King of Qín will fear the strength of Jìn
and will certainly value you more to win over Jìn.
When Qí yields to Jìn and my humble state
and can no longer support Qín,
Jìn will certainly value you more to serve Qín.
Thus you break Qí to gain merit
and hold Jìn to increase your importance.
By breaking Qí and securing your fief,
both Qín and Jìn will value you.
If Qí is not broken
and Lǚ Lǐ is employed again,
you will certainly be in great distress."
The Qín Guest Minister Zào said to the Ráng Hóu:
"Qín enfeoffed you in Táo,
and has relied on you to manage the world for several years.
If the task of attacking Qí succeeds,
Táo will become a state of ten thousand chariots
and the leader of the small states,
leading them to pay court to the Son of Heaven.
The world will surely listen;
this is the achievement of the Five Hegemons.
If the attack on Qí does not succeed,
Táo will become an object of neighborly concern
with nothing to rely upon.
Therefore, the attack on Qí is, for Táo,
the turning point between survival and ruin."
"If you wish to succeed,
why not send someone to say to the Prime Minister of Yān:
'A sage cannot create an opportunity,
but when the opportunity arrives, he does not lose it.
Though Shùn was virtuous,
if he had not encountered Yáo,
he could not have become the Son of Heaven.
Though Tāng and Wǔ were virtuous,
if they had not encountered Jié and Zhòu, they would not have become kings.
Therefore, despite the virtue of Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ,
without encountering the right time, they could not have become emperors and kings.
Now, the attack on Qí
is indeed your great opportunity.
Use the strength of the world
to attack the enemy state of Qí,
to avenge the shame of Huì Wáng,
to complete the merit of Zhāo Wáng,
and to remove harm for ten thousand generations;
this is the long-term benefit for Yān
and a great name for you.
The *Shū* says:
"In planting virtue, nothing is like making it flourish;
in removing harm, nothing is like being thorough."
Because Wú did not destroy Yuè,
Yuè eventually destroyed Wú.
Because Qí did not destroy Yān,
Yān should now destroy Qí.
Qí being destroyed by Yān,
or Wú being destroyed by Yuè,
these are cases of not removing a disease thoroughly.
If it were not for this time
to achieve your merit
and remove your harm,
if Qín should suddenly have other matters and follow Qí,
and Qí and Zhào unite,
their resentment toward you will certainly be deep.
They will take hold of their resentment against you to punish Yān,
and though you may regret it later,
you will not be able to fix it.
If you mobilize all of Yān's troops and strike quickly,
the world's following you
will be like avenging the feud of a father or son.
If you can truly destroy Qí,
you will be enfeoffed in Hénán,
becoming a state of ten thousand chariots,
with a road reaching to the Central States,
bordering Táo to the south,
and having no worries for generations.
I hope you will focus your will solely on attacking Qí
and have no other concerns.' "
A man of Wèi said to Wèi Rǎn:
"Have you heard the talk from the East?"
He said:
"I have not heard it."
He said:
"Xīn, Zhāng Yáng,
and Wú Zé have persuaded the Wèi Wáng,
Xuē Gōng, and Gōngshū,
saying:
'I shall fight;
I carry the treaties of the allied states to make an agreement with the King,
and there will surely be no trouble.
If there are those who cause failure,
I ask to be beheaded.
However, I have a concern.'
That the King of Chǔ uses his minister to request beheading,
yet I have a concern.
That the King of Chǔ
relies on Wèi Rǎn with his state,
and serves my master—
this is my deep concern.
Now if you go east and rely on words in Chǔ,
this makes Zhāng Yí's words as authoritative as those of Yǔ,
and works to ruin your affairs.
You would be better off returning to your own fief,
showing favor to Chǔ while observing what Xuē Gōng does for you.
Observe what the Three States seek from Qín but cannot obtain,
and request it in the name of the Three States to prove your good faith.
Observe what Zhāng Yí and Wú Zé cannot obtain from Xuē Gōng,
and request it yourself to increase your own importance."
One said to Wèi Rǎn:
"If peace is not achieved,
the army must go out.
Bái Qǐ
will again be the general.
If he wins the battle,
it will certainly exhaust you;
if he does not win,
he will certainly serve Zhào and follow you.
You will again be devalued.
You had better not hesitate much,
but arrive quickly."
One said to the Ráng Hóu:
In planning your fief,
if it were like removing
Sòng's guilt, while increasing
Qí's anger; one must
destroy the chaotic Sòng,
gain favor with strong Qí,
and secure your own enfeoffment.
This is also a once-in-a-hundred-generations opportunity!
One said to Wèi Rǎn:
"If Chǔ breaks Qín,
it cannot balance the scales against Qí.
Qín for three generations has built up prestige over Hán and Wèi,
while Qí's influence is newly added.
If Qí and Qín struggle,
and Hán and Wèi listen to the East,
then Qín will be attacked.
Qí has the territory of the Eastern States,
a thousand leagues square.
Chǔ encompasses the Nine Yí tribes,
also a thousand leagues square,
with the fortress of Fúlí to the south
and the mouth of Gānyú to the north.
If their power hangs over Sòng and Wèi,
then Sòng and Wèi are just like Ā and Zhēn.
Having two areas of benefit a thousand leagues wide,
their wealth dominates the subjects of Yuè.
How can Qín balance the scales against Qí,
or Hán and Wèi, who divide the fertile lands of Fāngchéng to approach Zhèng?
If the troops rest and then rise again,
it is enough to harm Qín,
without having to wait for Qí."
When the five states ceased fighting at Chénggāo,
the King of Qín wanted to seek the prime ministership of Hán and Wèi for Chéngyáng Jūn,
but Hán and
Wèi would not listen.
The Queen Dowager of Qín, on behalf of Wèi Rǎn, said to the King of Qín:
"Because of you, Chéngyáng Jūn
was impoverished and lived in Qí.
Now that you see him successful and try to win him over,
can you truly capture his heart?"
The King said:
"No."
The Queen Dowager said:
"If you did not take him in when he was impoverished,
but reward him when he is successful,
I fear he will not be used by the King;
moreover, by taking in Chéngyáng Jūn,
you lose the way to deal with Hán and Wèi."
Fàn Zǐ, via Wáng Jī, entered Qín
and presented a letter to Zhāowáng, saying:
"I have heard that when an enlightened ruler governs,
those with merit cannot but be rewarded,
and those with ability cannot but be given office;
those whose labor is great have thick salaries,
those whose merit is much have honorable titles,
and those who can govern the masses have high offices.
Therefore, the incompetent do not dare to take up their duties,
and the capable cannot be obscured."
If you consider my words to be acceptable,
then act upon them to further benefit your way;
if you are not going to act upon them,
then keeping me here for a long time serves no purpose.
A proverb says:
'A ruler of men rewards those he loves
and punishes those he hates.
An enlightened ruler is not like this;
rewards must be bestowed upon those with merit,
and punishments must be decided for those with guilt.'
Now my chest is not enough to face the chopping block,
and my waist is not enough to await the axe;
how would I dare to try a doubtful matter with the King?
Even if you consider me lowly
and treat me with contempt and insult,
do you alone not value the one who recommended me,
lest he be seen as inconsistent before the King later!"
"I have heard that Zhōu had the Dǐ'è gem,
Sòng had the Jiélǜ,
Liáng had the Xuánlí,
and Chǔ had the Hépú.
These four treasures
were once discarded by craftsmen,
yet they became famous vessels of the world.
If so, then are those rejected by a sage-king
alone insufficient to enrich a state?"
"I have heard that those good at enriching their families
take from the state;
those good at enriching the state
take from the feudal lords.
When the world has an enlightened ruler,
then the feudal lords cannot enrich themselves arbitrarily.
Why is this?
Because he withers their prosperity.
A good doctor knows the life and death of a patient;
a sage ruler is clear about the matters of success and failure.
If something is beneficial, he does it;
if harmful, he abandons it;
if doubtful, he tries it a little.
Although Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng were to be reborn,
they could not change this!
As for the most profound words, I do not dare to record them in writing;
the shallow ones are not worth hearing.
Perhaps it is
that I am foolish and do not harmonize with the King's heart?
Or is it that the one who spoke of me
is lowly and not worth listening to?
If it is not like this,
then it is my wish
to be granted a brief moment of leisure
to see Your Excellency and present them."
The letter was presented,
and the King of Qín was pleased with it.
He then thanked Wáng Jī for his recommendation
and sent someone with a carriage to summon him.
Fàn Suī arrived in Qín,
and the King met him in the court,
saying to Fàn Suī:
"I should have received your instructions in person long ago.
Recently, the affairs of Yìqú were urgent,
and I daily consulted with the Queen Mother.
Now that the Yìqú matter is over,
I am finally able to receive your commands in person.
I personally feel regretful for my lack of intelligence,
and respectfully observe the etiquette of guest and host."
Fàn Suī declined politely.
On that day he met Fàn Suī,
and among those who saw him, none did not change their expression and demeanor.
The King of Qín dismissed his attendants,
and the palace was empty and without people.
The King of Qín knelt and requested,
"How will the Master fortunately instruct me?"
Fàn Suī said:
"Yes, yes."
After a while,
the King requested again,
Fàn Suī said:
"Yes, yes."
This happened three times.
The King of Qín knelt upright and said:
"Will the Master not fortunately instruct me?"
Fàn Suī apologized, saying:
"It is not that I dare not.
I have heard that when Lǚ Shàng first met Wén Wáng,
he was but a fisherman
fishing on the banks of the Wèi River.
In such a case,
their relationship was distant.
After one talk,
he was appointed Grand Mentor
and rode back in the same carriage,
because his words were profound.
Therefore, Wén Wáng indeed achieved success through Lǚ Shàng,
and eventually held the whole world, establishing himself as an emperor.
If Wén Wáng had treated Lǚ Wàng as distant and not spoken deeply with him,
then Zhōu would have lacked the virtue of a Son of Heaven,
and Wén and Wǔ would have had no one with whom to achieve their kingship.
Now I am a traveling minister,
distant from the King,
and what I wish to present
are all matters of correcting the ruler,
which involve the relations between your flesh and blood.
I wish to present my humble loyalty,
but do not yet know the King's heart;
this is why the King asked three times and I did not answer.
It is not that I have something to fear and dare not speak.
I know that if I speak today before you,
tomorrow I may be executed behind you,
yet I do not dare to be afraid.
If the Great King believes and acts upon my words,
death is not enough to be a concern for me,
exile is not enough to be a worry for me,
painting my body to appear as a leper,
or disheveling my hair to appear as a madman,
is not enough to be a shame for me.
The sagely Five Emperors died,
the benevolent Three Kings died,
the worthy Five Hegemons died,
the strong Wū Huò died,
and the brave Bèn and Yù died.
Death is
what people inevitably cannot avoid.
To be in an inevitable situation
and be able to be of some small help to Qín,
this is my greatest wish;
what have I to worry about?
Wǔ Zǐxū was carried in a sack to pass through Zhāoguān;
he traveled by night and hid by day
until he reached the Lí River;
having nothing to feed himself,
he crawled on all fours
and begged for food in the markets of Wú.
In the end, he made the state of Wú flourish,
and Hélǘ became a hegemon.
If I were allowed to offer plans like Wǔ Zǐxū,
even if I were then imprisoned
and never seen again for the rest of my life,
if my persuasion were acted upon,
what have I to worry about?
Jìzǐ and Jiēyú
painted their bodies as lepers
and disheveled their hair as madmen,
yet they were of no benefit to Yīn or Chǔ.
If I were to act like Jìzǐ and Jiēyú,
but painting my body could help a worthy ruler,
that would be my great honor;
what shame would I have?
What I fear
is only that after my death,
the world will see that I gave my full loyalty yet my life was ruined,
and thus they will keep their mouths shut and wrap their feet,
none being willing to come to Qín.
Your Excellency fears the severity of the Queen Mother above
and is confused by the behavior of treacherous ministers below;
living in the depths of the palace,
never leaving the hands of the tutors and guardians;
if you remain ignorant and confused all your life,
with no one to expose the treachery,
then at most the ancestral temple will be destroyed,
and at least you yourself will be isolated and in danger.
This is what I fear!
As for the matters of hardship and insult
or the disaster of death,
I do not dare to fear them.
If I die and Qín is well-governed,
that is better than living."
The King of Qín knelt upright and said:
"Master, what are you saying!
The state of Qín is remote and secluded,
and I am foolish and unworthy.
That you have fortunately arrived here
is Heaven using me to trouble you, Master,
and to preserve the temple of the former kings.
That I can receive instructions from the Master
is how Heaven favors the former kings and does not abandon their orphan.
Why, Master, do you speak like this!
In matters great or small,
from the Queen Mother above
to the high ministers below,
I wish the Master would teach me all of them
and not doubt me."
Fàn Suī bowed twice,
and the King of Qín also bowed twice.
Fàn Suī said:
"The Great King's state
has Gānquán and Gǔkǒu to the north,
is girded by the Jīng and Wèi rivers to the south,
has Lǒng and Shǔ to the right,
and the Passes and Slopes to the left;
with a thousand chariots
and a million fierce warriors.
With the bravery of Qín soldiers
and the abundance of chariots and cavalry,
to face the feudal lords
is like letting loose the Hánlú hound
to chase a lame rabbit;
the achievement of a hegemon can be attained."
Now, the reason [the gates] are closed and you do not dare to send troops to Shāndōng,
is that Ráng Hóu is disloyal in his plans for the state,
and Your Majesty's strategy is flawed. "
The King said:
"I wish to hear about the flawed strategy. "
Suī said:
"For Your Majesty to bypass Hán and Wèi to attack the powerful Qí
is not a good strategy.
If you send out few troops,
they will be insufficient to harm Qí;
if you send many, it will harm Qín.
I suspect Your Majesty's plan is to send few troops
and rely entirely on the armies of Hán and Wèi, but this would be unrighteous.
Now, seeing that allied states cannot be trusted,
is it feasible to bypass another's country to attack?
This is a negligent strategy!
In the past,
the people of Qí attacked Chǔ,
won the battle,
destroyed the army and killed the generals,
expanding their territory by a thousand lǐ on two occasions,
yet they gained not even a tiny bit of land.
Was it that Qí did not want the land?
Its geographical position made it impossible to possess.
When the feudal lords saw that Qí was exhausted and exposed,
and that the ruler and ministers were not in harmony,
they raised troops and attacked it.
The ruler was disgraced and the army destroyed,
making them the laughingstock of the world.
The reason it was so
was that by attacking Chǔ, they only enriched Hán and Wèi.
This is what is called lending weapons to thieves and providing provisions to robbers.
It would be better for Your Majesty to befriend those distant and attack those near.
An inch gained is Your Majesty's inch;
a foot gained is also Your Majesty's foot.
Now to abandon this and attack far away,
is that not an error?
Furthermore, in the past,
the land of Zhōngshān,
which was five hundred lǐ square,
was taken by Zhào alone.
Success was achieved, fame established, and benefits accrued,
so that no one in the world could harm them.
Now Hán and Wèi
are located in Zhōngguó
and are the pivot of the world.
If Your Majesty wishes to attain hegemony,
you must befriend Zhōngguó
and make it the pivot of the world,
so as to overawe Chǔ and Zhào.
When Zhào is strong, Chǔ will submit;
when Chǔ is strong, Zhào will submit.
When Chǔ and Zhào submit, Qí will surely be afraid.
Being afraid, they will surely use humble words and heavy gifts to serve Qín.
Once Qí submits, Hán and Wèi can be undermined. "
The King said:
"I wish to befriend Wèi,
but Wèi is a country of many changes;
I cannot become close to them.
May I ask how to befriend Wèi? "
Fàn Suī said:
"Use humble words and heavy gifts to serve them.
If that fails,
cede land to bribe them.
If that fails,
raise troops and attack them. "
Thereupon, he raised troops and attacked Xíngqiū.
Xíngqiū was captured,
and Wèi requested to submit.
It was said:
"The terrain of Qín and Hán
is intermingled like embroidery.
For Qín to have Hán
is like a tree having woodworms,
or a person having a disease in the heart and belly.
If there are changes in the world,
none can harm Qín more than Hán.
It would be better for Your Majesty to win over Hán. "
The King said:
"I wish to win over Hán,
but if they do not listen,
what should be done? "
Fàn Suī said:
"Raise troops and attack Xíngyáng,
then the road to Chénggāo will be blocked;
to the north, cut off the road of Tàiháng,
then the troops of Shàngdǎng will not come down.
With one move, attack Róngyáng,
then their state will be severed into three parts.
When Wèi and Hán see they will surely perish,
how can they not listen?
If Hán listens, then the work of hegemony can be completed. "
The King said:
"Good. "
Fàn Suī said:
"When I lived in Shāndōng,
I heard that within Qí there was Tián Dān,
but I did not hear of its king.
I heard that Qín had a Tàihòu, a Ráng Hóu,
a Jīngyáng, and a Huáyáng,
but I did not hear that it had a king.
Now, he who controls the state is called king;
he who can monopolize profit and harm is called king;
he who wields the authority over life and death is called king.
Now the Tàihòu acts arbitrarily without looking back,
Ráng Hóu goes on missions without reporting,
Jīngyáng and Huáyáng make decisions and strikes without restraint.
That a state could have these four nobles and not be in danger
is something that has never happened.
With these four in place,
for those below, it is as if there were no king.
In such a case, how could power not be tilted,
and how could commands issue from the King?
I have heard:
'He who is good at governing a state
consolidates his authority within
and emphasizes his power without.'
Ráng Hóu's envoys wield the King's influence,
dealing with the feudal lords,
granting tallies throughout the world,
attacking enemies and invading states,
and none dare not listen.
When battles are won and lands taken,
the profit returns to Táo;
when the state is exhausted,
it is resisted by the feudal lords;
when battles are lost,
resentment is harbored by the common people,
and disaster falls upon the state altars.
The Shī says:
'When a tree's fruit is too abundant,
it breaks its branches;
those who break the branches harm the core.
He who makes his capitals too large endangers his state;
he who exalts his ministers debases his ruler.'
Nào Chǐ held the power of Qí,
pulled out the tendons of Mǐn Wáng,
hung him from the temple beams,
and he died overnight.
Lǐ Duì held power in Zhào,
reduced the food of the Zhǔfù,
who starved to death after a hundred days.
Now in Qín,
the Tàihòu and Ráng Hóu are in charge,
with Gāolíng and Jīngyáng assisting them;
ultimately, there is no Qín Wáng.
This is just the same as the likes of Nào Chǐ and Lǐ Duì.
I now see Your Majesty standing alone in the court,
and I fear that those who possess the state of Qín in later generations
will not be Your Majesty's descendants. "
The King of Qín was afraid;
thereupon he deposed the Tàihòu,
banished Ráng Hóu,
expelled Gāolíng,
and sent Jīngyáng away beyond Guānwài.
Zhāo Wáng said to Fàn Suī:
"In the past,
Qí Gōng gained Guǎn Zhòng,
and at that time regarded him as Zhòngfù.
Now that I have gained you,
I also regard you as a father. "
Yìng Hóu said to Zhāo Wáng:
"Have you also heard that in Héngsī there is a sacred grove?
In Héngsī there was a bold youth
who asked to gamble with the grove,
saying:
'If I win against the grove,
the grove shall lend me its divinity for three days;
if I do not win against the grove,
the grove may trap me.'
Then with his left hand he threw for the grove,
and with his right hand he threw for himself.
He won against the grove,
and the grove lent him its divinity.
After three days,
the grove went to ask for it back,
but he would not return it.
After five days the grove withered;
after seven days the grove perished.
Now, the state
is Your Majesty's grove;
power
is Your Majesty's divinity.
If you lend this to others,
is it not dangerous?
I have never heard of fingers being larger than the arm,
or the arm being larger than the thigh.
If such a thing exists,
then the illness must be severe indeed.
One hundred people carrying a gourd while rushing
is not as good as one person holding it and running fast.
If one hundred people truly carry a gourd,
the gourd will surely split.
Now in the State of Qín,
Huáyáng governs it,
Ránghóu governs it,
the Queen Mother governs it,
and the King also governs it.
If one does not consider the gourd a vessel,
then so be it;
but since one considers the gourd a vessel,
the state will surely split.
Your servant has heard:
"When a tree's fruit is too heavy, the branches will surely break;
when the branches break, they damage the heart of the tree.
When capital cities are too large, they endanger the state;
when ministers are too powerful, they endanger their lord."
Among those in the districts from the rank of Dǒushí upward,
to the Commandant, the Chamberlain of the Capital, and the King’s inner circle,
is there anyone who is not a man of the Chancellor?
If the state has no troubles,
then so be it;
but if the state has troubles,
your servant will surely hear and see the King standing alone in the court.
Your servant privately fears for the King,
fearing that after ten thousand generations, those who possess the state
will not be the King’s descendants.
"Your servant has heard
that in ancient times, those who were good at governing
maintained their authority within
and extended their support outside;
the administration was orderly in all directions, neither chaotic nor rebellious;
messengers followed the straight path
and did not dare to do wrong.
Now the Queen Mother’s messengers
divide the feudal lords
and spread their tallies throughout the world,
wielding the power of a great state,
forcibly conscripting troops,
and attacking the feudal lords.
When they win battles and seize territory,
the profits all return to Táo;
the state’s wealth and silks
are entirely funneled into the Queen Mother’s house;
the resources within the borders
are diverted to Huáyáng.
What was called in ancient times
'the way to endanger the lord and destroy the state'
must begin from this.
The three nobles exhaust the state to secure themselves;
in that case, how can orders come from the King,
and how can power not be divided?
Thus, my King truly occupies only one-third of the power."
Qín attacked Hán
and besieged Xíng.
Fàn Suī said to King Zhāo of Qín:
"There are those who attack people,
and those who attack land.
The reason Ránghóu attacked Wèi ten times without inflicting damage
was not that Qín was weak and Wèi was strong,
but that what he attacked
was the land.
Land is something
the ruler loves dearly.
For the ruler,
his ministers and subjects are willing to die.
Attacking what the ruler loves
and fighting against those who are willing to die,
therefore, even after ten attacks, one cannot be victorious.
Now the King is about to attack Hán and besiege Xíng;
your servant wishes the King would not only attack its land
but attack its people.
When the King attacks Hán and besieges Xíng,
use Zhāng Yí as the pretext.
If Zhāng Yí’s influence is great,
he will cede land to redeem himself to the King,
and Hán will not be entirely lost despite the ceding of land;
if Zhāng Yí’s influence is small,
then the King should expel Zhāng Yí
and instead deal with someone who is not as capable as Zhāng Yí.
Then what the King seeks from Hán
can be obtained through words."
Yìnghóu said:
"People of Zhèng call unpolished jade 'pú';
people of Zhōu call a rat that has not been dried 'pǔ'.
A man of Zhōu carrying a pǔ passed a merchant of Zhèng and asked:
'Do you want to buy a pǔ?'
The merchant of Zhèng said:
'I want it.'
He produced his pǔ,
and when the merchant looked at it,
it was a rat.
He then declined and did not take it.
Now Lord Píngyuán considers himself worthy and has a prominent name throughout the world,
yet he brought his former lord,
the King's Father, to surrender at Shāqiū and made him a subject.
The kings of the world still respect him;
this shows that the kings of the world
are not as wise as the merchant of Zhèng,
for they are blinded by a name
and do not know the reality."
The scholars of the world
formed a Hézòng alliance and gathered in Zhào,
intending to attack Qín.
The Chancellor of Qín, Yìnghóu, said:
"The King should not worry;
please allow me to cause their failure.
Qín has no grudge against the scholars of the world;
the reason they gather to attack Qín
is merely because they desire wealth and honor for themselves.
Does the King see your Majesty’s dogs?
Those lying down lie down,
those standing up stand up,
those walking walk,
those stopping stop,
and none fight with each other.
But if you throw them a bone,
they quickly rise and bare their teeth at each other.
Why is this?
Because they have the intent to compete."
Thereupon Táng Jū carried musicians,
was given fifty pieces of gold,
and stayed in Wǔ’ān,
holding a grand assembly where they drank together,
saying:
"Who from Hándān will come to take this?"
Thus, those who were plotters certainly could not be given it yet,
but those who could be given it,
he treated them like brothers.
"When you calculate merit for Qín,
do not ask where the gold goes;
those who exhaust the gold have the greatest merit.
Now I will order people to again carry fifty pieces of gold to follow you."
Táng Jū departed,
and when he reached Wǔ’ān,
before he could even distribute three thousand pieces of gold,
the scholars of the world
were fighting greatly among themselves.
Someone said to Yìnghóu:
"Did you capture Mǎfú?"
He said:
"Yes."
"And are you about to besiege Hándān?"
He said:
"Yes."
"If Zhào is destroyed,
the King of Qín will be the supreme ruler,
and Wǔ’ānjūn will become one of the Three Ducal Ministers.
The reason Wǔ’ānjūn has won battles and seized more than seventy cities for Qín,
destroyed Yān, Yǐng, and Hànzhōng in the south,
and captured the army of Mǎfú
without losing a single soldier,
is such that even the merit of Lǚ Wàng of Zhōu
would not surpass this.
If Zhào is destroyed
and the King of Qín becomes the supreme ruler,
and Wǔ’ānjūn becomes one of the Three Ducal Ministers,
can you bear to be beneath him?
Even if you wish not to be beneath him,
it will certainly be unavoidable.
Qín once attacked Xíng in Hán
and was trapped at Shàngdǎng,
for the people of Shàngdǎng all turned back to support Zhào.
It has indeed been a long time since
the people of the world have not been happy to be subjects of Qín.
Now if you attack Zhào,
the northern lands will go to Yān,
the eastern lands will go to Qí,
and the southern lands will go to Chǔ and Wèi;
then what Qín obtains will be very little.
Therefore, it is better to take the opportunity to have them cede land,
and let that be the extent of the merit for Wǔ’ān."
Yìnghóu lost Rǔnán of Hán.
King Zhāo of Qín said to Yìnghóu:
"You have lost a territory;
are you worried about it?"
Yìnghóu said:
"Your servant is not worried."
The King said:
"Why is that?"
It is said:
"Among the people of Liáng, there was a man named Dōngmén Wú.
When his son died, he did not grieve.
His steward said:
'Your love for your son
was unmatched in the world.
Now that your son has died and you do not grieve,
why is this?'
Dōngmén Wú said:
'I once had no son,
and at the time I had no son, I did not grieve.
Now that my son is dead,
it is just the same as when I had no son.
Why should I grieve?'
I also was once a commoner,
and when I was a commoner, I did not grieve.
Now that I have lost Rǔnán,
it is just the same as being a commoner of Liáng again.
Why should I grieve?"
The King of Qín did not think this was so,
and he told Méng Ào:
"Now,
when a single city of mine is besieged,
food loses its sweet taste for me,
and I cannot rest easy on my mat.
Now Yìng Hóu has lost territory,
yet he says he does not grieve.
Is this his true feeling?"
Méng Ào said:
"I request to find out his true feeling."
Méng Ào then went to see Yìng Hóu
and said:
"I, Ào, wish to die."
Yìng Hóu said:
"What do you mean?"
He said:
"The King of Qín treats you as his teacher;
there is no one in the world who has not heard of this,
let alone those in the state of Qín!
Now I, Ào, have attained the position of a general for the King of Qín
and lead his troops. Because Hán is small,
I have brought about a clear reversal of fortune and punishment
and allowed your land to be taken.
How can I, Ào, continue to live?
It is better to die."
Yìng Hóu bowed to Méng Ào and said:
"I wish to entrust this matter to you, Minister."
Méng Ào reported this to King Zhāo.
From that time on,
whenever Yìng Hóu spoke of the affairs of Hán,
the King of Qín would not listen to him,
because he considered him a loser of Rǔnán.
Qín attacked Hándān,
and did not capture it for seventeen months.
Zhuāng said to Wáng Jī:
"Why do you not grant rewards to the military officers?"
Wáng Jī said:
"Between me and the King,
there is no need for the words of others."
Zhuāng said:
"Not so.
Even between a father and a son,
there are orders that will surely be followed
and those that will surely not be followed.
If he says, 'Cast away your noble wife
and sell your beloved concubine,'
this is an order that will surely be followed.
If he then says, 'Do not dare to think of them,'
this is an order that will surely not be followed.
If the woman guarding the village gate says,
'That evening,
such-and-such a weakling let in such-and-such a man,'
the noble wife might already be gone,
and the beloved concubine already sold,
yet his heart is not at ease.
If you wish to instruct them,
the human heart is naturally like this.
Now, although you are favored by the King,
it is no more than the intimacy of a father and son.
Although the military officers are lowly,
they are not more humble than the woman guarding the village gate.
Moreover, you have monopolized the ruler and slighted your subordinates for a long time.
I have heard
'Three people make a tiger,
and ten men can bend a heavy bar.
What many mouths move
will fly even without wings.'
Therefore I say,
it is better to grant rewards to the military officers and treat them with ritual."
Wáng Jī did not listen.
The military officers were pushed to their limits,
and indeed they slandered Wáng Jī and Dù Zhì
as being in revolt.
The King of Qín was greatly enraged
and wished to execute Fàn Suī as well.
Fàn Suī said:
"I
am a lowly person from the eastern borders.
I offended Chǔ and Wèi
and fled here to seek refuge.
I had no support from the feudal lords
nor any old acquaintances.
You raised me up from among the travelers,
assigned me duties,
and the whole world heard of my person and your elevation of me.
Now if I am misguided or of one heart with a criminal,
and you openly execute me,
then your error in elevating me will be manifest to the world,
and you will be criticized by the feudal lords.
I wish to request medicine to be granted death,
and as an act of grace, have your ministers oversee my burial.
Then you will certainly not fail to punish my crime,
and yet you will not have the reputation of having made an erroneous elevation."
The King said:
"There is truth in this."
Consequently, he did not kill him but treated him well.
Cài Zé was driven out from Zhào
and entered Hán and Wèi.
He met with the theft of his cooking pots on the road.
Hearing that Yìng Hóu's appointees, Zhèng Ānpíng
and Wáng Jī,
had both committed capital crimes,
and that Yìng Hóu was inwardly ashamed,
he then went west into Qín.
Intending to see King Zhāo,
he sent someone to declare a message to provoke Yìng Hóu's anger, saying:
"The guest from Yàn, Cài Zé,
is a magnificent hero and a master of grand eloquence.
Once he sees the King of Qín,
the King of Qín will surely make him Chancellor and seize your position."
Yìng Hóu heard this
and sent someone to summon Cài Zé.
When Cài Zé entered,
he only gave a casual bow to Yìng Hóu.
Yìng Hóu was naturally displeased,
and when he met him,
Cài Zé was also arrogant.
Yìng Hóu therefore rebuked him, saying:
"You have frequently declared
that you would replace me as Chancellor of Qín;
did you say such a thing?"
He replied:
"Indeed."
Yìng Hóu said:
"I request to hear your explanation."
Cài Zé said:
"Alas!
How late you have come to see this!
In the order of the four seasons,
those who have achieved success depart.
For a person to have strong limbs,
keen ears and eyes, and sagacious wisdom—
is this not what a gentleman desires?"
Yìng Hóu said:
"Indeed."
Cài Zé said:
"To possess the substance of benevolence and uphold righteousness,
to practice the Way and bestow virtue upon the world
so that the world cherishes, rejoices in, respects, and loves you,
wishing to have you as its ruler—
is this not what the wise look forward to?"
Yìng Hóu said:
"Indeed."
Cài Zé continued:
"To be wealthy, noble, and illustrious,
to bring order to all things
so that each finds its proper place;
to have a long life
and complete one's years without being cut short or harmed;
for the world to continue one's lineage
and preserve one's legacy,
passing it on without end, with name and reality both pure,
with influence flowing through a thousand generations
and praise that never ceases,
lasting as long as the world itself—
is this not the fulfillment of the Way,
and what the sages call a propitious and good thing?"
Yìng Hóu said:
"Indeed."
Cài Zé said:
"Regarding Shāng Jūn of Qín,
Wú Qǐ of Chǔ,
and Dàfū Zhòng of Yuè,
can their deaths also be desired?"
Yìng Hóu knew that Cài Zé wished to corner him with his persuasion,
so he replied:
"Why should they not be?
Gōngsūn Yāng served Xiào Gōng,
dedicating himself without a second thought,
being entirely public-spirited without private interest.
He made rewards and punishments certain to achieve order,
exhausted his wisdom and ability,
showed his true sincerity,
endured resentment and blame,
deceived old acquaintances,
and captured Gōngzǐ Àng of Wèi."
In the end, he captured generals for Qín,
crushed enemy armies,
and expanded territory by a thousand lǐ.
Wú Qǐ served Dào Wáng;
he ensured that private interests did not harm the public good,
slanders did not obscure loyalty,
words did not seek easy agreement,
and actions did not seek easy acceptance.
In practicing righteousness, he was not swayed by praise or blame;
to ensure there would be a hegemon or a strong state,
he did not shrink from calamity or misfortune.
Dàfū Zhǒng served the Yuè Wáng;
when his lord suffered distress and humiliation,
he exerted all his loyalty without slackening.
Even though his lord was ruined and cut off,
he exhausted his abilities and did not leave.
Though he achieved much, he did not boast;
though rich and noble, he was not arrogant or idle.
As for these three men,
they reached the pinnacle of righteousness
and the standard of loyalty.
Therefore, a gentleman sacrifices his life to establish his name.
Where righteousness resides,
even if one dies,
there are no regrets or remorse.
Why should it not be done?"
Cài Zé said:
"When the lord is sage and the ministers are worthy,
it is a blessing for the world.
When the ruler is enlightened and the ministers are loyal,
it is a blessing for the state.
When the father is kind and the son is filial,
when the husband is faithful and the wife is chaste,
it is a blessing for the family.
Thus, Bǐ Gān was loyal,
but he could not preserve Yīn.
Zǐ Xū was wise,
but he could not preserve Wú.
Shēn Shēng was filial,
yet Jìn fell into confusion and disorder.
There were loyal ministers and filial sons,
yet the states were destroyed and in chaos.
Why is this?
It is because there were no enlightened rulers or worthy fathers to listen to them.
Therefore, the world regards their rulers and fathers as shameful
and pities their ministers and sons.
If one must wait for death before one can establish loyalty and a name,
then Wēi Zǐ was not benevolent enough,
Kǒng Zǐ was not sage enough,
and Guǎn Zhòng was not great enough."
At this, Yìng Hóu called it good.
Cài Zé found a brief opening
and consequently said:
"As for Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Dàfū Zhǒng,
in their roles as ministers,
that they exhausted loyalty and achieved merit
was indeed desirable.
Hóng Yāo served Wén Wáng,
and Zhōu Gōng assisted Chéng Wáng;
were they not also loyal?
Comparing them as lords and ministers,
which would one rather be: Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, or Dàfū Zhǒng,
or would one rather be Hóng Yāo
or Zhōu Gōng?"
Yìng Hóu said:
"Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Dàfū Zhǒng
are not as good."
Cài Zé said:
"In that case, regarding your lord—
in his kindness, benevolence, and trust in the loyal,
and in not betraying old friends—
how does he compare with Qín Xiào Gōng, Chǔ Dào Wáng,
or the Yuè Wáng?"
Yìng Hóu said:
"I do not know how he compares."
Cài Zé said:
"Even if the lord is truly close to loyal ministers,
he would not exceed Qín Xiào, the Yuè Wáng, or Chǔ Dào.
As for your service to your lord:
you corrected chaos, fended off disasters, and resolved difficulties;
you expanded territory and increased grain production;
you enriched the state, provided for families, and strengthened the lord;
your prestige covers all within the seas,
and your achievements are manifest beyond ten thousand lǐ.
This does not exceed Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, or Dàfū Zhǒng.
Yet your rank and position are noble and flourishing,
and your private wealth exceeds that of those three men.
If you do not retire now,
I privately fear for your safety.
The saying goes:
'When the sun reaches its zenith, it begins to set;
when the moon is full, it begins to wane.'
That things decline after reaching their peak
is the constant law of Heaven.
Advancing and retreating, filling and shrinking, changing and transforming—
these are the constant ways of the sage.
In the past,
Qí Huán Gōng assembled the feudal lords nine times
and unified the world.
But at the meeting of Kuí Qiū,
he had an air of arrogance,
and nine states rebelled.
Wú Wáng Fū Chāi had no equal in the world;
he slighted the feudal lords
and oppressed Qí and Jìn,
which ultimately led to his death and the destruction of his state.
Xià Yù and Tàishǐ Qǐ could terrify three armies with a shout,
yet they died at the hands of ordinary men.
These all resulted from riding the height of
prosperity without following
the proper principles.
Shāng Jūn, for Xiào Gōng,
leveled the scales,
standardized measures,
adjusted weights,
broke down the field boundaries,
and taught the people farming and warfare.
Thus, when the army moved, territory was expanded;
when the army rested, the state was enriched.
Therefore, Qín had no equal in the world
and established its prestige among the feudal lords.
Once his achievements were complete,
he was eventually torn apart by chariots.
The land of Chǔ held a million halberdiers.
Bái Qǐ led an army of tens of thousands
to battle Chǔ.
In one battle, he took Yān and Yǐng;
in a second battle, he burned Yílíng.
To the south, he annexed Shǔ and Hàn;
he also crossed Hán and Wèi to attack the strong Zhào.
In the north, he buried the Mǎfú army
and slaughtered over four hundred thousand people.
Blood flowed in rivers,
and the sound of boiling cries was like thunder.
He enabled the Qín enterprise to achieve emperorship.
From then on,
Zhào and Chǔ were awestruck and submissive.
That they did not dare attack Qín
was due to Bái Qǐ's power.
He himself conquered
over seventy cities.
His achievements were complete,
yet he was ordered to commit suicide at Dù Yóu.
Wú Qǐ, for Chǔ Dào, dismissed the incompetent,
abolished the useless,
reduced unnecessary offices,
and blocked the requests of private interests.
He unified the customs of the state of Chǔ.
To the south, he attacked Yáng Yuè;
to the north, he annexed Chén and Cài.
He broke the Horizontal Alliance and dispersed the Vertical Alliance,
leaving the traveling orators with no opportunity to open their mouths.
His achievements were complete,
yet he was eventually dismembered.
Dàfū Zhǒng, for the Yuè Wáng,
cleared the wilds and established towns,
opened up lands and grew grain.
He led the scholars from all directions
and coordinated the efforts of those above and below
to capture the powerful Wú
and achieve the work of a hegemon.
In the end, Gōu Jiàn used a club to kill him.
As for these four men,
they achieved success but did not leave,
and thus calamity reached them.
This is what is meant by 'knowing how to stretch but not how to bend,
knowing how to go forward but not how to return.'
Fàn Lǐ understood this;
he transcended and withdrew from the world,
becoming Táo Zhū for a long time.
Do you alone not observe the gamblers?
Some wish to share the large stakes,
and some wish to share the winnings.
These are all things that you clearly know.
Now you are the Prime Minister of Qín.
Your plans do not leave your mat,
and your strategies do not leave the halls of the temple,
yet you control the feudal lords from where you sit.
Benefits are bestowed upon Sān Chuān,
enriching Yíyáng.
You cleared the dangers of Yángcháng,
blocked the pass of Tàiháng,
and cut off the paths of the Fàn and Zhòngháng clans.
You built a thousand lǐ of plank roads in Shǔ and Hàn,
causing the whole world to fear Qín.
Qín's desires have been fulfilled,
and your achievements have reached their peak.
This is also the time for Qín to 'share the winnings'!
If you do not retire now,
then you will follow Shāng Jūn, Bái Gōng,
Wú Qǐ, and Dàfū Zhǒng.
Why do you not take this opportunity to return your prime ministerial seal
and yield to a worthy man, handing it over to him?
You would surely have the integrity of Bó Yí.
You would remain Yìng Hóu for a long time,
with your descendants titled as lords for generations,
and you would enjoy the longevity of Qiáo and Sōng.
How does that compare with ending in calamity!
Where do you stand on this?"
Yìng Hóu said:
"Excellent."
He then invited him in and seated him as an honored guest.
Several days later,
he entered the court
and said to King Zhāo of Qín:
"There is a guest who has recently come from east of the mountains
named Cài Zé.
He is a persuasive rhetorician.
I have seen many people,
but none can equal him;
even I am not as good as he is."
King Zhāo of Qín summoned and granted him an audience,
spoke with him,
and was greatly pleased with him,
appointing him as a Guest Minister.
Yìng Hóu then excused himself on account of illness
and asked to return the seal of the Chancellor.
King Zhāo tried to force Yìng Hóu to stay,
but Yìng Hóu then claimed his illness was severe
and was thus dismissed from the chancellorship.
King Zhāo was recently pleased by Cài Zé's plans,
so he appointed him as the Chancellor of Qín
to take control of the house of Zhōu in the east.
Cài Zé served as Chancellor to the King of Qín for several months.
Someone slandered him;
fearing execution,
he resigned due to illness and returned the seal of the Chancellor,
being titled Lord Gāngchéng.
He remained in Qín for more than ten years,
serving King Zhāo,
King Xiàowén, and King Zhuāngxiāng,
finally serving Shǐ Huángdì.
He served as Qín's envoy to Yàn,
and after three years, Yàn sent Crown Prince Dān to Qín as a hostage.
Qín took Hànzhōng from Chǔ
and fought again at Lántián,
heavily defeating the Chǔ army.
Hán and Wèi heard of Chǔ's distress
and launched a southern raid as far as Dèng;
the King of Chǔ led his troops back.
Later, the three states plotted to attack Chǔ
but feared Qín would rescue it.
Someone persuaded the Lord of Xuē:
"You can send an envoy to tell Chǔ:
'Now the troops of the three states are about to leave Chǔ;
if Chǔ can respond and join in attacking Qín,
even Lántián will not be hard to take!
How much more so for Chǔ's former lands?'
Chǔ doubts that Qín will necessarily rescue them,
and now that the three states speak of leaving,
Chǔ will surely be encouraged to respond.
This means Chǔ and the three states will plot to draw out Qín's troops.
If Qín knows this,
they will certainly not come to the rescue.
The three states can then attack Chǔ swiftly;
Chǔ will surely rush to Qín in urgency.
Qín will be even more afraid to come out,
and thus we isolate Qín while attacking Chǔ;
our troops will surely succeed."
The Lord of Xuē said:
"Excellent."
He then sent a high-ranking envoy to Chǔ,
and Chǔ was indeed encouraged to respond.
Thereupon, the three states combined their forces to attack Chǔ.
Chǔ indeed reported the emergency to Qín,
but Qín consequently did not dare to send troops.
The high officials achieved merit.
The Lord of Xuē entered Wèi
and brought out a woman of Qí.
Hán Chūn said to the King of Qín:
"Why not take her as your wife
and use Qí and Qín to coerce Wèi?
Then Shàngdǎng
will belong to Qín.
Qí and Qín can join together to install Fùchú;
once Fùchú is installed
and his mother is in Qín,
then Wèi will simply be a prefecture of Qín.
Mǐn wants to use Qí and Qín to coerce Wèi and distress the Lord of Xuē;
Zuǒ wants to secure his younger brother.
I ask to handle Mǐn and Zuǒ for Your Majesty.
Wèi will be afraid and restore him;
Fùchú will surely serve Qín with the state of Wèi for the rest of his life.
The woman of Qí will enter Wèi and resent the Lord of Xuē,
and ultimately serve Your Majesty with the support of Qí."
The three states attacked Qín
and entered Hángǔ Pass.
The King of Qín said to Lóu Huǎn:
"The troops of the three states have penetrated deep;
I wish to cede Hédōng and sue for peace."
He replied:
"Ceding Hédōng
is a great cost,
but to be free from the disaster facing the state
is a great benefit.
This is a responsibility for the elders of the royal house.
Why does Your Majesty not summon Prince Chí and ask him?"
The King summoned Prince Chí and asked him.
He replied:
"Suing for peace brings regret;
not suing for peace also brings regret."
The King said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"If Your Majesty cedes Hédōng and sues for peace,
although the three states will leave,
Your Majesty will surely say:
'What a pity!
The three states were about to leave anyway,
and I simply gave them three cities to follow.'
This is the regret of suing for peace.
If Your Majesty does not sue for peace
and the three states enter Hángǔ Pass,
Xiányáng will surely be in danger,
and Your Majesty will again say:
'What a pity!
I cherished three cities and did not sue for peace.'
This is the regret of not suing for peace."
The King said:
"Since the regrets are equal,
I would rather lose three cities and regret it
than endanger Xiányáng and regret it.
I have decided to sue for peace."
He finally sent Prince Chí to sue for peace with the three states using three cities,
and their troops then withdrew.
King Zhāo of Qín said to his attendants:
"Today, Hán and Wèi,
how do they compare to their original strength?"
They replied:
"They are not as strong."
The King said:
"Are the current Rú Ěr and Wèi Qí
as worthy as Mèngcháng
and Máng Mǎo?"
They replied:
"They are not as worthy."
The King said:
"With the worthiness of Mèngcháng and Máng Mǎo
leading the strong troops of Hán and Wèi to attack Qín,
they still could do nothing against me!
Now with the incompetent Rú Ěr and Wèi Qí
leading the weak Hán and Wèi to attack Qín,
that they can do nothing against me
is also clear!"
The attendants all said:
"That is very true."
Zhōng Qī pushed aside his zither and replied:
"Your Majesty's assessment of the world
is mistaken.
In the past, during the time of the six lineages of Jìn,
the Zhì clan was the strongest;
they destroyed the Fàn and Zhōngháng lineages
and led Hán and Wèi to besiege Zhào Xiāngzǐ at Jìnyáng.
They breached the Jìn River to flood Jìnyáng;
the city wall remained above water by only three planks' height.
Zhì Bó went out to inspect the waters,
with Hán Kāngzǐ driving the chariot
and Wèi Huánzǐ as the chariot-aide.
Zhì Bó said:
'At first, I did not know that water could destroy a person's state,
but now I know it.
The Fén River can be used to flood Ānyì,
and the Jiàng River can be used to flood Píngyáng.'
Wèi Huánzǐ nudged Hán Kāngzǐ with his elbow,
and Kāngzǐ stepped on Wèi Huánzǐ's foot,
treading on his heel.
Elbow and foot met upon the chariot,
and the Zhì clan's territory was divided.
Zhì Bó himself died and his state perished,
becoming a laughingstock for the world.
Now the strength of Qín
cannot surpass that of Zhì Bó,
and though Hán and Wèi are weak,
they are still better off than those beneath the walls of Jìnyáng.
This is precisely the time when they will use elbows and feet;
I hope Your Majesty will not treat them lightly."
Chǔ and Wèi fought at Xíngshān.
Wèi promised Shàngluò to Qín
to cut Qín off from Chǔ.
Wèi won the battle,
and Chǔ was defeated at Nányáng.
Qín demanded the promised payment from Wèi,
but Wèi did not give it.
Yíng Qiǎn said to the King of Qín:
"Why does Your Majesty not say to the King of Chǔ:
'Wèi promised me land,
but now that victory is won,
the King of Wèi has gone back on his word to me.'
Why does Your Majesty not meet with the King of Chǔ?
Wèi will fear the alliance of Qín and Chǔ,
and will surely give land to Qín.
This results in Wèi defeating Chǔ but losing land to Qín;
thus the King of Chǔ uses Wèi's land to gain favor with me,
and Qín's support for Chǔ will be substantial.
Wèi is weak;
if they do not produce the land,
then Your Majesty attacks their south,
while I cut off their west,
and Wèi will surely be in danger."
The King of Qín said:
"Good."
He informed Chǔ of this.
The King of Chǔ spread word that he would meet with Qín,
and the King of Wèi heard this and was afraid;
he ceded Shàngluò to Qín.
The Chǔ envoy Jǐng Lǐ was in Qín,
and he accompanied the King of Qín to meet the King of Wèi at the border.
Chǔ was angry at the alliance with Qín,
so Zhōu Zuì said to the King of Chǔ:
"Wèi requested not to meet with Chǔ
but to ally with Qín,
which is why Jǐng Lǐ met with them.
My humble state favored the meeting,
which is why Qí did not join the alliance."
Consequently, the King of Chǔ did not punish Jǐng Lǐ
and felt grateful to Zhōu and Qín.
The King of Chǔ sent Jǐng Lǐ to Qín.
A guest said to the King of Qín:
"Jǐng Lǐ
is a minister much loved by the King of Chǔ.
Your Majesty would do better to detain him to trade for land.
If the King of Chǔ complies,
then you gain land without using troops;
if the King of Chǔ does not comply,
then kill Jǐng Lǐ
and never let him return;
nothing is better than detaining Jǐng Lǐ.
This is a convenient plan."
The King of Qín then detained Jǐng Lǐ.
Jǐng Lǐ sent someone to persuade the King of Qín, saying:
"I see that Your Majesty's power is light in the eyes of the world,
and land cannot be obtained.
When I came as an envoy,
I heard that Qí and Wèi were both about to cede land to serve Qín.
The reason for this
was because Qín and Chǔ are brother states.
Now that Your Majesty has detained me,
it shows the world you are without Chǔ;
why should Qí and Wèi regard an isolated state as important?
Once Chǔ knows Qín is isolated,
it will not give land,
but will instead form external alliances with the lords to plot against you;
then your state will surely be in danger.
It is better to release me."
The King of Qín then released him.
The King of Qín wished to see Dùn Ruò.
Dùn Ruò said:
"My principles do not allow me to perform the ritual bow.
If the King can allow me not to bow,
then it is acceptable.
If not,
then I shall not see him."
The King of Qín granted this.
Thereupon Dùn Zǐ said:
"In the world, there are those
who have the reality but not the name,
those who have the name but not the reality,
and those who have neither the name nor the reality.
Does Your Majesty know of this?"
The King said:
"I do not."
Dùn Zǐ said:
"Those who have the reality but not the name
are the merchants.
They have no power to handle shovels or push hoes,
yet they have the reality of accumulated grain.
These are they who have the reality but not the name.
Those who have the name but not the reality
are the farmers.
They plow when the frost thaws
and weed with their backs exposed to the sun,
yet they do not have the reality of accumulated grain.
These are they who have the name but not the reality.
As for having neither the name nor the reality,
that is Your Majesty.
You have been established as a ruler of ten thousand chariots,
but you do not have the name of filial piety;
you use a thousand li to support her,
but you do not have the reality of filial piety."
The King of Qín flared up in anger.
Dùn Ruò said:
"East of the mountains, there are six warring states.
Your Majesty's awe does not overshadow those east of the mountains,
but instead it overshadows your mother.
I humbly suggest that Your Majesty should not choose this."
The King of Qín said:
"Can the states east of the mountains
be annexed?"
Dùn Zǐ said:
"Hán
is the throat of the world;
Wèi
is the chest and belly of the world.
If Your Majesty provides me with ten thousand pieces of gold
to travel abroad,
and I persuade Hán and Wèi
to send their state ministers into Qín,
then Hán and Wèi will follow.
Once Hán and Wèi follow,
the world can be planned for."
The King of Qín said:
"My state is poor,
and I fear I cannot provide it."
Dùn Zǐ said:
"The world is never without affairs;
if it is not the Vertical Alliance, then it is the Horizontal Alliance.
If the Horizontal Alliance is successful,
then Qín will become Emperor;
if the Vertical Alliance is successful,
then Chǔ will become King.
If Qín becomes Emperor,
then the whole world will reverently support you;
if Chǔ becomes King,
then even if Your Majesty has ten thousand pieces of gold,
you will not be able to keep them for yourself."
The King of Qín said:
"Good."
He then provided ten thousand pieces of gold,
and sent him to travel east to Hán and Wèi,
to win over their generals and ministers.
He traveled north to Yān and Zhào,
and caused Lǐ Mù to be killed.
The King of Qí came to court,
and the four states were bound to follow;
this was due to the persuasion of Dùn Zǐ.
In the twentieth year of Qǐng Xiāng Wáng,
Bái Qǐ of Qín captured Xīlíng in Chǔ,
and then captured Yān, Yǐng, and Yīlíng,
burning the tombs of the former kings.
The King moved to the northeast
and defended the city of Chén.
Chǔ was subsequently weakened
and looked down upon by Qín.
Thereupon Bái Qǐ again led troops to attack.
There was a man of Chǔ named Huáng Xiē,
who was widely traveled and learned.
Xiāng Wáng considered him eloquent,
and thus sent him as an envoy to Qín.
He spoke to Zhāo Wáng, saying:
"None in the world are stronger than Qín and Chǔ.
Now I hear Your Majesty wishes to attack Chǔ;
this is like two tigers fighting
while a weak dog suffers the consequences.
It would be better to be friendly with Chǔ.
I beg to present the explanation for this.
I have heard it said:
'When things reach an extreme, they must reverse,'
just as winter and summer do.
'Reaching the ultimate limit brings peril,'
just as with a stack of Go pieces.
Now your great state's land covers half the world,
and it has two frontiers;
since the birth of the people,
there has never been a land of ten thousand chariots such as this.
From the former emperors Wén Wáng and Zhuāng Wáng,
to Your Majesty's own time,
for three generations your land did not border Qí,
so as to cut off the vital links of the Vertical Alliance.
Now Your Majesty has thrice sent Shèng Qiáo to manage affairs in Hán,
and north of Chéng Qiáo you entered Yān.
Thus Your Majesty, without using armor
or exerting your might,
has obtained a hundred li of land;
Your Majesty can indeed be called capable.
Your Majesty then raised armored troops to attack Wèi,
blocking the gates of Dàliáng,
seizing Hénèi,
and capturing Yàn, Suānzǎo, Xū, and Táorén.
The troops of Chǔ and Yān hover like clouds and dare not contest;
Your Majesty's achievements are indeed many."
The King should let the people rest for two years,
and only then resume his campaigns.
He should then take Pú, Yǎn, and Shǒuyuán,
to bear down on the troops of Rén and Píng.
Xiǎohuáng and Jìyáng will then be shut up within their walls,
and the Wèi clan will submit.
The King should also cede the area north of Pú and Mó to belong to Yān,
cutting off the vital routes of Qí and Qín,
and severing the backbone of Chǔ and Wèi.
Though the world should join in five-fold or six-fold alliances, they would not dare to come to the rescue,
for the King's majesty will be held in awe.
If the King can maintain his achievements and preserve his majesty,
tempering his desire for conquest and strengthening his commitment to the admonitions of benevolence and righteousness,
ensuring no further troubles arise,
then the Three Kings would not be a fourth to him,
nor would the Five Hegemons be a sixth.
"If the King relies on the multitude of his followers
and the strength of his fine weapons and armor,
once he has destroyed the power of the Wèi clan,
if he seeks to use force to make subjects of the world's rulers,
I fear there will be future troubles.
The *Book of Odes* says:
'All have a beginning,
but few can reach the end.'
The *Book of Changes* says:
'The fox gets its tail wet.'
This refers to things being easy at the start,
but difficult at the end.
How do we know this is so?
The Zhì clan saw the advantage in attacking Zhào,
but did not know the disaster awaiting them at Yúci;
Wú saw the convenience in attacking Qí,
but did not know
the defeat awaiting them at Gānsuì.
These two states
were not without great achievements,
but they set their sights on gains in front of them
while treating lightly the troubles that followed.
Wú trusted Yuè
and proceeded to attack Qí;
having defeated the people of Qí at Àilíng,
they returned only to be captured by the King of Yuè at the banks of the Sānjiāng.
The Zhì clan trusted Hán and Wèi
and proceeded to attack Zhào;
they besieged the city of Jìnyáng,
and victory was within days,
but Hán and Wèi turned against them
and killed Zhì Bó Yáo
atop the Zàotái.
Now the King is jealous that Chǔ has not been destroyed,
yet he forgets that destroying Chǔ would strengthen Wèi.
I consider this for the King and do not favor taking such a course.
The *Book of Odes* says:
'The Great Martial power dwells afar and does not cross over.'
From this perspective,
the state of Chǔ
is an ally;
the neighboring states
are the enemies.
The *Book of Odes* says:
'Others have their thoughts,
and I can measure them.
The nimble, crafty hare
meets a dog that captures it.'
Now, if the King midway
trusts that Hán and Wèi are well-disposed toward the King,
this is exactly like Wú trusting Yuè.
I have heard
that an enemy should not be treated lightly
and an opportunity should not be lost.
I fear that Hán and Wèi use humble words to ward off trouble
while actually deceiving your great state.
Why is this?
The King has no generations of virtue
toward Hán and Wèi,
but rather generations of accumulated resentment.
The fathers, sons, and brothers of Hán and Wèi have followed one another's heels
in dying at the hands of Qín
for a hundred generations.
Their home states are ravaged,
their altars of state ruined,
their ancestral temples destroyed;
with bellies ripped open and jaws broken,
heads and bodies separated,
their bones are exposed in the grass and marshes,
and their skulls lie prostrate,
visible to one another across the borders.
The elderly and weak, fathers and sons, are bound as captives,
following one another along the roads.
The ghosts and spirits have no place to feed,
the common people have no means of livelihood,
clans and families are scattered,
and those who have fled to become servants and concubines
fill all within the four seas.
That Hán and Wèi have not yet perished
is a cause for concern for the state of Qín.
Now, for the King to attack Chǔ,
is this not a mistake?
On the day the King attacks Chǔ,
from where will he deploy his troops?
Will the King borrow a path
from his mortal enemies Hán and Wèi?
On the day the troops go out,
the King will worry about them not returning;
this would be the King providing troops
to his mortal enemies Hán and Wèi.
If the King does not borrow a path from his mortal enemies Hán and Wèi,
he must attack Yáng and the right territory.
To pass through Yáng and the right territory,
these are all areas of wide rivers and great waters,
of mountains, forests, and valleys—land that yields no food.
Even if the King possesses it,
it cannot be considered gaining territory.
Thus the King would have the reputation for destroying Chǔ
without the reality of gaining land.
Furthermore, on the day the King attacks Chǔ,
the four states will surely all rise up to respond to the King.
While Qín and Chǔ are entangled and cannot separate,
the Wèi clan will deploy troops to attack Liú,
Fāngyǔ, Zhì, Húlíng,
Dàng, Xiāo, and Xiāng;
thus the former land of Sòng will surely be entirely taken.
The people of Qí will face south,
and the land north of the Sì River will surely be seized.
These are all plains accessible from all directions
and fertile lands,
yet the King allows them alone to attack there.
The King's breaking of Chǔ will thereby fatten Hán and Wèi in the central states and strengthen Qí;
the strength of Hán and Wèi would then be sufficient
to challenge Qín.
Qí will have the Sì River as its border to the south,
face the sea to the east,
and lean on the Yellow River to the north;
having no future troubles,
among the states of the world,
none will be stronger than Qí.
Qí and Wèi will have gained land and preserved their interests,
yet they will feign service as subordinate officials.
After one year,
even if they cannot yet become Emperors,
they will have more than enough
to prevent the King from becoming Emperor.
Now, despite the King's vast territory,
the multitude of his followers,
and the strength of his weapons and armor,
if he raises his hosts at once and pours his resources into Chǔ,
only to submit to the orders of Hán and Wèi
and hand the prestige of the Emperor over to Qí,
then the King has failed in his planning.
"As I plan for the King,
nothing is better than befriending Chǔ.
If Qín and Chǔ unite as one
and bear down on Hán,
Hán must surrender.
With the King holding the strategic passes of Shāndōng
and the advantages of the Héqu river bend,
Hán must become a border guard for the area within the passes.
If this happens,
the King can take Zhèng with complete success,
the Liáng clan will be terrified,
Xǔ and Líng will be besieged within their walls,
and Shàngcài and Zhàolíng will have no communication.
In this way,
Wèi also becomes a border guard within the passes.
Once the King befriends Chǔ,
