and these two lords of ten thousand chariots within the passes focus their efforts on Qí,
the right territory of Qí can be taken with hands folded.
Thus the King's land will border both seas,
cutting off the vital links of the world.
Without Qí and Chǔ, there would be no Yān and Zhào;
without Yān and Zhào, there would be nothing left.
Then he can threaten and move Yān and Zhào
while holding Qí and Chǔ;
these four states
will submit without waiting for a painful blow."
Someone spoke on behalf of the Six States to the King of Qín, saying:
"Vast territory is not enough for security,
and a large population is not enough for strength.
If vast territory brought security
and a large population brought strength,
then the descendants of Jié and Zhòu would still exist.
In the past,
the Zhào clan was also once strong.
If you ask how strong Zhào was:
it raised its left hand to press down Qí,
raised its right hand to press down Wèi,
and weighed down upon states of ten thousand chariots;
those two states
were like the thousand-chariot state of Sòng.
Gāngpíng was built,
Wèi no longer possessed its eastern fields,
and those gathering fodder, herding, or collecting firewood dared not even look toward the East Gate.
At that time,
Wèi was in a state of danger more precarious than piled eggs,
and the scholars of the world conspired together, saying:
"Shall we return our tokens of allegiance
and pay court to the Lord of Hándān?"
Thus, among those in the world who advocated attacking Hándān,
none failed to make their court travel there.
Wèi attacked Hándān,
and subsequently withdrew to hold the meeting at Féngzé,
riding in a Xià-style carriage,
styling himself as the King of Xià,
and acting as the Son of Heaven receiving court,
and the world all followed him.
Tàigōng of Qí heard of this
and raised an army to attack Wèi;
its territory was split in two,
and the state was in great peril.
The King of Liáng personally held the hostage and grasped the jade disc,
requesting to become a subject of the Chén Hóu,
whereupon the world released Liáng.
King Wēiwáng of Yǐng heard of this,
and he could not sleep in his bed,
nor could he eat his fill;
he led the common people of the world
to encounter Shēn Fù at the Sìshuǐ,
and soundly defeated Shēn Fù.
When the people of Zhào heard of this, they reached Zhīsāng;
when the people of Yān heard of this, they reached Gédào.
Gédào became impassable,
and the border at Píngjì was cut off.
Qí was defeated in battle and was not victorious,
its plans did not succeed,
so they sent Chén Máo to lay down his sword and watchman's rattle,
to submit to the south and await punishment,
to the west to persuade Zhào,
to the north to persuade Yān,
while internally enlightening its own common people,
and then the world released Qí.
Thus, what was thin accumulated
to become thick,
and what was small gathered to become much,
so that they spoke in unison about King Wēiwáng of Yǐng
as being in the ranks of Zhòu.
How could I say that King Wēiwáng of Yǐng's governance had declined
or that his plans were chaotic, leading to this result?
Yǐng was strong
and looked down upon the feudal lords of the world,
therefore the world delighted in attacking it!"
Someone spoke to the King of Qín, saying:
"I am privately puzzled by Your Majesty's slighting of Qí and looking down on Chǔ,
while treating Hán as a lowly subordinate.
I have heard that
a king's army should be victorious but not arrogant,
and a hegemonic leader should be restrained and not resentful.
Victorious but not arrogant,
therefore one can subdue the world;
restrained and not resentful,
therefore one can make neighbors follow.
Now Your Majesty extends great favor to Wèi and Zhào,
but lightly loses Qí;
this is arrogance.
You were victorious in the battle of Yíyáng,
yet you do not care for the alliance with Chǔ;
this is resentment.
Arrogance and resentment are not the deeds of a hegemonic leader.
I have privately reflected on this for Your Majesty
and do not approve of it."
"The *Shī* says:
'None do not have a beginning,
but few are able to have an end.'
Therefore, that which the former kings valued
was only the beginning and the end.
How do we know this is so?
Formerly, Zhì Bó Yáo destroyed the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
and besieged and pressured Jìnyáng,
but in the end, he was ridiculed by the Sān Jiā.
King Fūchāi of Wú forced Yuè to take refuge at Kuàijī,
defeated Qí at Àilíng,
held the meeting at Huángchí,
and was disrespectful to Sòng,
but was finally captured by Gōujiàn,
and died at Gānsuì.
The Lord of Liáng attacked Chǔ and defeated Qí,
controlled the armies of Zhào and Hán,
and drove twelve feudal lords to pay court to the Son of Heaven at Mèngjīn,
but later his son died,
and he himself wore a linen cap and was imprisoned in Qín.
These three were not without merit,
but they could begin well and could not end well.
Now Your Majesty has crushed Yíyáng,
devastated Sānchuān,
and made the scholars of the world dare not speak.
You have blocked the states of the world,
shifted the borders of the Liǎng Zhōu,
and the lords of the age dare not cross the passes of Yánghóu.
You took Huángjí,
and the armies of Hán and Chǔ dare not advance.
If Your Majesty can provide an end to this,
then the Three Kings will not be enough to make four,
and the Five Hegemons will not be enough to make six.
If Your Majesty cannot provide an end to this
and there are later troubles,
then I fear that the lords of the states
and the scholars of the Hé and Jì rivers
will regard Your Majesty's affairs as those of Wú or Zhì.
"The *Shī* says:
'Of those who travel a hundred lǐ, ninety is only halfway.'
This speaks of the difficulty of the final stretch.
Now Your Majesty's countenance is entirely arrogant.
Observing from my heart,
as for the affairs of the world,
depending on the hearts of the lords of the age,
if it is not Chǔ that receives an attack,
it must be Qín.
How do I know this is so?
The people of Qín support Wèi to resist Chǔ;
the people of Chǔ support Hán to resist Qín.
The armies of the four states are matched,
and they are not yet able to fight again.
Qí and Sòng are outside the guidelines and serve as the balance of power.
Therefore it is said, those who first obtain Qí and Sòng will attack Qín.
If Qín first obtains Qí and Sòng,
then the Hán clan will be melted away;
if the Hán clan is melted away,
then Chǔ will be isolated and receive the attack.
If Chǔ first obtains Qí,
then the Wèi clan will be melted away;
if the Wèi clan is melted away,
then Qín will be isolated and receive the attack.
If one proceeds according to this plan,
then both states will surely be ridiculed by the world."
The King of Qín had a debate with Zhōng Qī
and did not win.
The King of Qín was greatly enraged,
and Zhōng Qī walked away slowly.
Someone spoke to the King of Qín on behalf of Zhōng Qī, saying:
"He is a fierce man.
It is only because Zhōng Qī happened to encounter an enlightened ruler.
If he had previously encountered Jié or Zhòu,
he would surely have been killed."
Because of this, the King of Qín did not punish him.
Xiàn Zé spoke to Gōngsūn Xiāo, saying:
"Sir,
you are an honored high minister
who has many times attacked and gained merit.
The reason you have not become Prime Minister
is that the Queen Dowager does not favor you.
Xīn Róng
is one whom the Queen Dowager is close to.
He has now fled to Chǔ
and is in Eastern Zhōu.
Why do you not use the weight of Qín and Chǔ
to support him and make him Prime Minister in Zhōu?
Chǔ will certainly find this convenient.
Thus, Xīn Róng will have the weight of Qín and Chǔ,
and the Queen Dowager will certainly be pleased with you;
then your becoming Prime Minister will be certain."
Lóu allied Qín and Wèi,
and the Crown Prince of Wèi became a hostage.
Fēn Qiáng wanted to ruin it.
He said to the Queen Dowager:
"States are things that exchange with each other.
If this ruins Qín and benefits Wèi,
Wèi will certainly betray it.
On the day they betray Qín,
the Crown Prince will be worthless."
The Queen Dowager sat with the King and wept.
The King consequently became suspicious of the Crown Prince
and ordered him to stay at Suānzǎo.
Master Lóu was worried about this.
Zhāo Yǎn went from Zhōu to Liáng,
and Master Lóu told him about it.
Zhāo Yǎn saw the King of Liáng.
The King of Liáng said:
"What have you heard?"
He said:
"I heard that Qín is about to attack Wèi."
The King said:
"Regarding the scheduled time,
It was said:
"Qín is suspicious of Your Majesty's treaty
because the Crown Prince remains in Suānzǎo
and has not gone to Qín.
The King of Qín’s strategy says:
'If Wèi does not make a treaty with me,
they will surely attack me;
rather than remaining here
and waiting to be attacked,
it is better to strike them first.'
With Qín's strength humbling itself to negotiate with other states,
I fear this will bring harm to Dōngzhōu."
Lǚ Bùwéi, a man of Púyáng, was trading in Hándān
when he saw the Qín hostage prince Yìrén.
Returning home, he said to his father:
"How many times is the profit from plowing the fields?"
The father said:
"Ten times."
"How many times is the profit from pearls and jade?"
The father said:
"A hundred times."
"How many times is the profit from
establishing a ruler for a state?"
The father said:
"Incalculable."
Lǚ Bùwéi said:
"Now, even with hard labor in the fields,
one cannot obtain warm clothes and surplus food;
but if one establishes a state and a ruler,
the benefits can be passed down to future generations.
I wish to go and serve him."
Prince Yìrén of Qín was a hostage in Zhào,
residing in the city.
Therefore, Lǚ Bùwéi went to persuade him, saying:
"Zǐxī has the right of succession to the state,
and also has his mother within the court.
Now you have no mother within,
and abroad you are entrusted
to an unpredictable state.
If one day the treaty is broken,
your body will become as dust and mire.
Now, if you listen to my plan,
and seek to return,
you can possess the state of Qín.
I shall act as your envoy to Qín,
and will surely come to request your return."
He then went to persuade the Queen of Qín's brother, Yángquán Jūn, saying:
"Your Lordship's crime is worthy of death;
does Your Lordship know this?
Among Your Lordship's retainers, there are none who do not hold high and honorable positions,
yet among the Crown Prince's retainers, there are no noble ones.
Your Lordship's storehouses are filled with pearls, treasures, and jade,
your fine horses fill the outer stables,
and beautiful women fill the rear courtyards.
The King's years are high;
if one day the mountain and ridge crumble,
and the Crown Prince takes power,
Your Lordship's danger
will be greater than piled-up eggs,
and your life will be shorter than one born in the morning.
I have a proposal that can
make Your Lordship rich and noble for ten million years,
with security like the four pillars of Mount Tài,
and you will surely be without the worry of danger or ruin."
Yángquán Jūn moved off his mat
and asked to hear the proposal.
Lǚ Bùwéi said:
"The King is old,
the Queen has no son,
but Zǐxī has the right of succession to the state,
and Shì Cāng furthermore assists him.
If one day the King passes away,
and Zǐxī is established,
and Shì Cāng takes charge,
then at the Queen's gates,
mugwort and weeds will surely grow.
Prince Yìrén is a man of talent,
but he is cast away in Zhào,
with no mother inside the court.
He cranes his neck looking westward,
wishing for a chance to return.
If the Queen would truly request
to establish him,
then Prince Yìrén will go from having no state to having a state,
and the Queen will go from having no son to having a son."
Yángquán Jūn said:
"Indeed."
He went in to persuade
the Queen,
and the Queen then requested Zhào to return him.
Zhào had not yet sent him back,
so Lǚ Bùwéi persuaded Zhào, saying:
"Prince Yìrén
is a favored son of Qín,
but he has no mother within;
the Queen wishes to take him and make him her son.
If Qín intended to slaughter Zhào,
they would not change their plans for the sake of one son;
thus you would be holding an empty hostage.
If you let Prince Yìrén return and he succeeds in being established,
and Zhào sends him back with generous gifts,
he would not dare betray such virtue or turn his back on such favor;
this would be to establish a bond of virtue for yourselves.
The King of Qín is old;
if one day he passes away,
even if you have Prince Yìrén,
it will not be enough to bind Qín."
Zhào then sent him back.
When Yìrén arrived,
Lǚ Bùwéi had him dress in Chǔ clothing for the audience.
The Queen was pleased with his appearance
and highly valued his wisdom,
saying:
"I am a person of Chǔ."
She made him her son
and changed his name to Zǐchǔ.
The King had the Prince recite,
and the Prince said:
"Having been abandoned abroad while young,
I never had a tutor to teach me,
and am not practiced in recitation."
The King dismissed the matter
and kept him there.
On another occasion, the Prince said:
"Your Majesty once stopped your carriage in Zhào;
of the heroes of Zhào,
those whose names are known to you are many.
Now that Your Majesty has returned to your state,
they all look westward with hope.
Yet Your Majesty has not sent a single envoy to inquire after them;
I fear they all harbor resentment.
This will cause the borders to be closed early and opened late."
The King agreed
and marveled at his plan.
The Queen urged him to establish him.
The King then summoned the Chancellor
and ordered him, saying:
"Among my sons, none are like Zǐchǔ."
He established him as the Crown Prince.
When Zǐchǔ was established,
he made Lǚ Bùwéi the Chancellor,
with the title of Wénxìn Hóu,
and granted him twelve counties in Lántián.
The Queen became Huáyáng Tàihòu,
and the feudal lords all ceded cities to Qín.
Wénxìn Hóu wished to attack Zhào
to expand Héjiān.
He sent Gāngchéng Jūn Cài Zé to serve Yàn
for three years,
after which the Crown Prince of Yàn became a hostage in Qín.
Wénxìn Hóu then requested Zhāng Táng
to be the Chancellor of Yàn,
wishing to attack Zhào together with Yàn
to expand the territory of Héjiān.
Zhāng Táng declined, saying:
"To go to Yàn, one must pass through Zhào;
if the people of Zhào capture me,
they will receive a hundred li of land."
Wénxìn Hóu left, feeling displeased.
His young retainer Gān Luó said:
"Why is Your Lordship so very displeased?"
Wénxìn Hóu said:
"I sent Gāngchéng Jūn Cài Zé to serve Yàn for three years,
and the Crown Prince of Yàn has already entered as a hostage.
Now I personally requested Minister Zhāng to be Chancellor of Yàn,
but he is unwilling to go."
Gān Luó said:
"I will make him go."
Wénxìn Jūn shouted at him to leave, saying:
"I personally requested him and he was unwilling;
how could you make him go?"
Gān Luó said:
"Xiàng Tuó was seven years old
and became the teacher of Kǒngzǐ.
Now I am twelve years old!
Your Lordship should let me try;
why shout so hastily?"
Gān Luó went to see Zhāng Táng and said:
"Between your achievements
and those of Wǔ'ān Jūn, whose are greater?"
Zhāng Táng said:
"Wǔ'ān Jūn won battles and captured lands,
beyond count;
he attacked cities and toppled towns,
beyond count.
My achievements are not equal to those of Wǔ'ān Jūn."
Gān Luó said:
"Do you clearly understand
that your achievements are not equal to those of Wǔ'ān Jūn?"
He said:
"I know it."
"When Yìng Hóu served Qín,
how did he compare to Wénxìn Hóu in having sole authority?"
The reply was:
"Yìng Hóu was not as authoritative as Wénxìn Hóu."
He asked:
"Do you clearly know
why he was not as authoritative as Wénxìn Hóu?"
He said:
"I know it."
Gān Luó said:
"Yìng Hóu wished to attack Zhào,
but Wǔ'ān Jūn made it difficult for him;
only seven lǐ from Xiányáng,
he was strangled and killed.
Now Wénxìn Hóu has personally requested that you serve as Prime Minister in Yān,
yet you are unwilling to go.
I do not know where you will end up meeting your death!"
Táng said:
"I beg to go because of you, young lad!"
He ordered the armory to prepare carriages,
the stables to prepare horses,
the treasury to prepare gifts,
and the date for departure was set.
Gān Luó said to Wénxìn Hóu:
"Lend me five carriages;
I wish to report to Zhào ahead of Zhāng Táng."
He met with the King of Zhào,
and the King of Zhào welcomed him in the outskirts.
He said to the King of Zhào:
"Have you heard of Crown Prince Dān of Yān entering Qín as a hostage?"
He said:
"I have heard of it."
"Have you heard of Zhāng Táng becoming the Prime Minister of Yān?"
He said:
"I have heard of it."
"The Crown Prince of Yān entering Qín
ensures that Yān will not deceive Qín.
Zhāng Táng becoming Prime Minister of Yān
ensures that Qín will not deceive Yān.
If Qín and Yān do not deceive each other,
then the attack on Zhào
will be perilous. The reason Yān and Qín do not deceive each other
is for no other purpose
than wanting to attack Zhào and expand the territory of Héjiān.
Now, if Your Majesty grants me five cities to expand Héjiān,
I shall request the return of the Crown Prince of Yān
and have Zhào join the strong Qín to attack the weak Yān."
The King of Zhào immediately carved off five cities
to expand Héjiān,
and the Crown Prince of Yān was returned.
Zhào then attacked Yān,
obtaining thirty-six counties in Shànggǔ,
and gave one-tenth of them to Qín.
Wénxìn Hóu went into exile
and went to Zhào with Sīkōng Mǎ,
where Zhào appointed him as acting Prime Minister.
Qín mobilized its armor and attacked Zhào.
Sīkōng Mǎ advised the King of Zhào, saying:
"When Wénxìn Hóu was Prime Minister of Qín,
I served him
as a high official
and was familiar with Qín's affairs.
Now Your Majesty has me holding a minor office
while I learn Zhào's affairs.
Please allow me to compare the conflict between Qín and Zhào for Your Majesty,
so you may personally see who would win.
How does Zhào compare to Qín in size?"
He said:
"It is not as large."
"How do its people compare in number?"
He said:
"They are not as numerous."
"How do its gold, currency, and grain compare in wealth?"
He said:
"They are not as wealthy."
"How does the state compare in order?"
He said:
"It is not as well-ordered."
"How does its Prime Minister compare in worthiness?"
He said:
"He is not as worthy."
"How do its generals compare in valor?"
He said:
"They are not as valiant."
"How do its laws and decrees compare in clarity?"
He said:
"They are not as clear." Sīkōng Mǎ said:
"Thus, in Your Majesty's state,
not one of a hundred measures equals Qín,
so Your Majesty's state will perish."
The King of Zhào said:
"You have not distanced yourself from Zhào
and have fully instructed me on national affairs;
I wish to follow your strategy."
Sīkōng Mǎ said:
"If Your Majesty carves off half of Zhào to bribe Qín,
Qín will obtain half of Zhào without clashing blades,
and Qín will surely be pleased.
Internally, they would loathe the effort of attacking Zhào's defenses;
externally, they would fear the rescue of the feudal lords;
Qín will surely accept it.
Once Qín accepts the land and withdraws its troops,
Zhào can defend half the state to preserve itself.
Qín will use the bribe to strengthen itself,
and the lands east of the mountains, Shāndōng, will surely be terrified;
seeing the demise of half of Zhào, they will feel their own danger,
and the feudal lords will surely be afraid.
Being afraid and coming to each other's rescue,
the Vertical Alliance can then be established.
I ask Your Majesty to form this alliance.
If the alliance is successful,
then although Your Majesty nominally loses half of Zhào,
you will actually gain the support of Shāndōng to oppose Qín,
and Qín will not be capable of destroying you."
The King of Zhào said:
"In the past, when Qín mobilized armor to attack Zhào,
Zhào bribed them with twelve counties in Héjiān;
our land was carved away and our troops weakened,
yet in the end we did not escape the calamity of Qín.
Now if we again carve off half of Zhào to strengthen Qín,
our strength will not be enough to preserve ourselves and we will perish because of it.
I wish for you to reconsider your plan."
Sīkōng Mǎ said:
"In my youth I was a scribe in Qín;
I rose from being a head official to holding a minor office,
and have never been a military leader.
I ask Your Majesty to mobilize all of Zhào's troops for me to lead against them."
The King of Zhào could not make him a general.
Sīkōng Mǎ said:
"I have offered my humble strategy,
but Your Majesty does not use it.
This means I have no way to serve Your Majesty,
and I beg to take my leave."
Sīkōng Mǎ left Zhào
and crossed the Píngyuán Ford.
The Magistrate of Píngyuán Ford, Guō Yí, greeted him and asked:
"Qín's troops are descending upon Zhào.
You, honored guest, come from Zhào;
how are Zhào's affairs?"
Sīkōng Mǎ spoke of how he had planned for the King of Zhào
but was not used,
and thus Zhào would surely perish.
The Magistrate of Píngyuán asked:
"Based on your estimation, honored guest,
when will Zhào perish?"
Sīkōng Mǎ said:
"If Zhào's general is Wǔ'ān Jūn,
it will perish in a year;
if they kill Wǔ'ān Jūn,
it will be no more than half a year.
Among the King of Zhào's ministers is one Hán Cāng,
who uses devious ways
to align with the King of Zhào.
Their relationship is very close,
and he is a man who resents the worthy and is jealous of meritorious ministers.
Now that the state is in danger of perishing,
the King will surely use his words,
and Wǔ'ān Jūn will surely die."
Hán Cāng indeed slandered him,
and the King sent someone to replace him.
When Wǔ'ān Jūn arrived,
Hán Cāng was sent to rebuke him, saying:
"The General was victorious in battle,
and the King offered a toast to the General.
When the General offered a toast for the King's longevity in his presence,
he was clutching a dagger;
he should be put to death."
Wǔ'ān Jūn said:
"I, Zuǒ, suffer from a hooked deformity;
my body is large and my arms are short,
so they cannot reach the ground.
When rising or sitting I appear disrespectful,
and I feared a capital offense before the King.
Therefore, I had a craftsman make wooden pieces
to extend my hands.
If His Majesty does not believe this,
I, Zuǒ, ask to bring them out and show them."
He pulled them out from his sleeves
to show Hán Cāng;
they looked like outspread wings,
wrapped in cloth.
"I wish for you, sir,
to go in and clarify this."
Hán Cāng said:
"I have received the command from the King
to bestow death upon the General;
there is no pardon.
I do not dare to speak of it."
Wǔ’ān Jūn faced north, bowed twice, and was granted death.
He drew his sword to execute himself
and said:
“A subject must not commit suicide within the palace.”
He arrived at the Sīkōng Mǎ Gate,
moved very quickly,
and went out through the Chù Gate.
He raised his sword with his right hand to kill himself,
but his arm was too short to reach.
He took the sword in his mouth and braced it against a pillar to pierce himself.
Wǔ’ān Jūn died.
Five months later, Zhào perished.
Whenever the Magistrate of Píngyuán met with various lords,
he would certainly say to them:
“Alas,
Sīkōng Mǎ!”
He also believed that Sīkōng Mǎ was driven out of Qín,
not because he was ignorant;
he left Zhào,
not because he was unworthy.
Zhào got rid of Sīkōng Mǎ and the state perished.
As for a state perishing,
it is not because there are no worthy men,
but because they cannot be employed.
Four states united as one
to attack Qín.
The King of Qín summoned sixty ministers and guests
and questioned them,
saying:
“Four states have united
to plot against Qín.
I am constrained within,
and the common people are exhausted without.
What shall be done about this?”
None of the ministers replied. Yáo Jiǎ replied:
“I, Jiǎ, wish to go as an envoy to the four states.
I will certainly break their plans
and still their troops.”
He was then provided with a hundred chariots
and a thousand pounds of gold.
He was dressed in the King’s robes
and wore the King’s cap and sword.
Yáo Jiǎ took his leave,
broke their plans,
stopped their troops,
and formed alliances with them to report back to Qín.
The King of Qín was greatly pleased.
Jiǎ was enfeoffed with a thousand households
and appointed as a high minister.
Hán Fēi learned of this
and said:
“Jiǎ used pearls and precious treasures
to serve as an envoy south to Jīng and Wú,
and north to the regions of Yàn and Dài
for three years.
The alliances of the four states might not have truly united,
but the pearls and precious treasures were exhausted within.
Thus, Jiǎ used the King’s power
and the state’s treasures
to personally form alliances with the feudal lords abroad.
I hope the King will investigate this.
Furthermore, he is the son of a gatekeeper in Liáng;
he once committed theft in Liáng,
and he served in Zhào and was driven out.
To take the son of a hereditary gatekeeper,
a great thief of Liáng,
and an expelled subject of Zhào,
and allow him to share in the planning for the state
is not the way to encourage the ministers.”
The King summoned Yáo Jiǎ and asked:
“I have heard that you used my wealth
to form alliances with the feudal lords.
Is this true?”
He replied:
“It is true.”
The King said:
“With what face do you dare see me again?”
He replied:
“Zēng Shēn was filial to his parents,
and everyone in the world wished to have him as a son.
Zǐxū was loyal to his lord,
and everyone in the world wished to have him as a minister.
A chaste woman is skilled in her craft,
and everyone in the world wishes to have her as a consort.
Now I, Jiǎ, am loyal to the King, but the King does not know it.
If I do not return to the four states,
where else would I go?
If I were not loyal to my lord,
why would the kings of the four states employ me?
Jié listened to slander and executed his good generals;
Zhòu heard slander and killed his loyal ministers,
leading to their own deaths and the ruin of their states.
If the King now listens to slander,
then there will be no loyal ministers.”
The King said:
“You are the son of a gatekeeper,
a great thief of Liáng,
and an expelled subject of Zhào.”
Yáo Jiǎ said:
“Tàigōng Wàng
was a man driven out of Qí,
a failed butcher in Zhāogē,
an expelled subject of Zǐliáng,
and an unwanted laborer in Jíjīn;
yet Wén Wáng used him and became king.
Guǎn Zhòng
was a merchant from a rustic area,
impoverished and obscure in Nányáng,
and a released prisoner of Lǔ;
yet Huán Gōng used him and became hegemon.
Bǎilǐ Xī
was a beggar from Yú,
sold for the price of five ram skins;
yet Mù Gōng made him chancellor
and made the Xīróng pay court.
Wén Gōng used a thief from Zhōngshān
and triumphed at Chéngpú.
These four men
all had shameful reputations
and were greatly reviled by the world,
yet enlightened rulers used them,
knowing that they could achieve great deeds.
If men like Biàn Suí, Wù Guāng, and Shēntú Dí were used,
how could a ruler ever make use of them?
Therefore, an enlightened ruler does not hold their stains against them
or listen to criticisms of them,
but investigates how they can be used for himself.
Therefore, if someone can preserve the state,
even if there is external slander, the ruler does not listen;
even if someone has a reputation that transcends the world,
if they lack even an inch of merit, they are not rewarded.
Thus, the ministers dare not approach the ruler with empty desires.”
The King of Qín said:
“True.”
He then continued to employ Yáo Jiǎ and executed Hán Fēi.
Chǔ Wēi Wáng won a battle at Xúzhōu
and wished to drive Yīngzǐ out of Qí.
Yīngzǐ was afraid.
Zhāng Chǒu said to the King of Chǔ:
“Your Majesty won the battle at Xúzhōu
because Pànzǐ was not employed.
Pànzǐ has merit with the state,
and the common people serve him.
Yīngzǐ is not capable
and he employed Shēn Zhuàn.
As for Shēn Zhuàn,
the ministers and common people will not serve him;
therefore, Your Majesty defeated them.
Now if Yīngzǐ is driven out,
Pànzǐ will certainly be employed.
He will reorganize the soldiers to face Your Majesty,
which will certainly not be to Your Majesty's advantage.”
The King of Chǔ therefore did not drive him out.
Qí was about to enfeoff Tián Yīng in Xuē.
The King of Chǔ heard this
and was very angry,
intending to attack Qí.
The King of Qí began to waver.
Gōngsūn Hàn said:
“Whether the enfeoffment happens or not
does not depend on Qí;
it will depend on Chǔ.
I, Hàn, will persuade the King of Chǔ
to make him want to enfeoff you
even more than Qí does.”
Yīngzǐ said:
“I entrust this to you.”
Gōngsūn Hàn said to the King of Chǔ:
“Lǔ and Sòng serve Chǔ, while Qí does not,
because Qí is large while Lǔ and Sòng are small.
Your Majesty only benefits from the smallness of Lǔ and Sòng;
why do you not dislike the largeness of Qí?
Now, if Qí carves out land to enfeoff Tián Yīng,
this is how it will be weakened.
I hope you do not stop it.”
The King of Chǔ said:
“Good.”
He therefore did not stop it.
Jìngguō Jūn was about to build a wall around Xuē.
Many guests came to remonstrate.
Jìngguō Jūn said to the usher:
“Do not allow any guests to pass through.”
A man from Qí made a request, saying:
“I request to speak only three words!
If I add even one more word,
I ask to be boiled alive.”
Jìngguō Jūn therefore granted him an audience.
A guest hurried forward and said:
"Giant sea fish."
Then he turned and ran away.
The Lord said:
"The guest has something to say here."
The guest said:
"Your humble servant does not dare to make a joke of death."
The Lord said:
"Forget it,
speak of it again."
He replied:
"Has my Lord not heard of the giant fish?
Nets cannot stop it,
hooks cannot pull it;
but if it is tossed out and loses the water,
then mole crickets and ants can have their way with it.
Now, Qí
is also my Lord's water.
If my Lord long possesses the protection of Qí,
what need has he for Xuē?
As for Qí, even if the walls of Xuē were built up to the heavens,
it would still be of no benefit."
The Lord said:
"Good."
Thereupon he ceased the fortification of Xuē.
Jìng Guō Jūn said to the King of Qí:
"The accounts of the five bureaus
must be heard daily
and frequently reviewed."
The King said:
"Speaking of these five things tires me."
Now he entrusted them to Jìng Guō Jūn.
Jìng Guō Jūn was on good terms with Qí Mào Biàn.
Qí Mào Biàn was a man of many flaws,
and the retainers were not pleased with him.
Shì Wèi tried to remonstrate with Jìng Guō Jūn,
but Jìng Guō Jūn did not listen,
so Shì Wèi took his leave and departed.
Mèng Chǎng Jūn also secretly offered a remonstrance,
Jìng Guō Jūn was greatly enraged and said:
"Even if I were to exterminate your kind
and destroy my house,
if it could satisfy Qí Mào Biàn,
I would do it without hesitation."
Thereupon he lodged him in the finest guest house,
ordered his eldest son to drive the carriage for him,
and provided meals morning and evening.
After several years,
Wēi Wáng passed away,
and Xuān Wáng was enthroned.
The relationship of Jìng Guō Jūn
was very poor with Xuān Wáng,
so he took his leave and went to Xuē,
and stayed there together with Qí Mào Biàn.
Not long after,
Qí Mào Biàn took his leave to depart,
requesting to see Xuān Wáng.
Jìng Guō Jūn said:
"The King's dislike of Yīng is extreme;
if you go, you will surely meet your death."
Qí Mào Biàn said:
"I certainly do not seek to live;
I request that I must go."
Jìng Guō Jūn could not stop him.
Qí Mào Biàn traveled and arrived in Qí,
and when Xuān Wáng heard of it,
he harbored his anger while waiting for him.
Qí Mào Biàn saw Xuān Wáng,
and the King said:
"You,
are the one whom Jìng Guō Jūn listens to and favors!"
Qí Mào Biàn said:
"As for favor, there is indeed some;
but as for listening, there was none.
When Your Majesty was still the Crown Prince,
Biàn said to Jìng Guō Jūn:
『The Crown Prince's appearance is not benevolent;
he has a heavy jaw and pig-like eyes.
One such as this will surely be treacherous.
It would be better to depose the Crown Prince
and instead install the son of Consort Wèi, Jiāo Shī.』
Jìng Guō Jūn wept and said:
『It cannot be;
I cannot bear it.』
If he had listened to Biàn and done it,
there would certainly not be today's trouble.
This is the first instance.
When he was at Xuē,
Zhāo Yáng requested
to exchange several times the land for Xuē.
Biàn said again:
『You must listen to him.』
Jìng Guō Jūn said:
『I received Xuē from the late King;
although I am disliked by the current King,
what would I say to the late King
anyway?
Furthermore, the late King's ancestral temple is in Xuē;
how could I take the late King's ancestral temple
and give it to Chǔ?』
Again he was unwilling to listen to Biàn.
This is the second instance."
Xuān Wáng sighed deeply,
his expression moved,
and said:
"Has Jìng Guō Jūn's devotion to me reached such a point!
I was young
and truly did not know this.
Would you be willing, for my sake,
to bring Jìng Guō Jūn back?"
Qí Mào Biàn replied:
"I respectfully agree."
Jìng Guō Jūn wore the clothes of Wēi Wáng,
donned the cap and brandished his sword.
Xuān Wáng personally welcomed Jìng Guō Jūn in the outskirts,
weeping upon seeing him from afar.
When Jìng Guō Jūn arrived,
the King then requested him to be Chancellor.
Jìng Guō Jūn declined,
but accepted when he could not avoid it.
After seven days,
he pleaded illness and firmly resigned.
Jìng Guō Jūn's resignation was not accepted,
but after three days the King granted it.
At that time,
Jìng Guō Jūn could be said to truly know people!
Because he could know people,
even though others criticized him
he was not discouraged.
This was why Qí Mào Biàn disregarded his life,
delighted in danger,
and hurried toward difficulty.
During the crisis of Hándān,
Zhào sought help from Qí.
Tián Hóu summoned his high ministers
and deliberated, saying:
"Between saving Zhào
and not saving it, which is better?"
Zōu Zǐ said:
"It is better not to save them."
Duàn Gān Lún said:
"If we do not save them,
then it will be to our disadvantage."
Tián Hóu said:
"Why is that?"
"If the Wèi clan annexes Hándān,
how could that be of any benefit to Qí!"
Tián Hóu said:
"Good."
Thereupon he raised an army,
and said:
"Encamp in the outskirts of Hándān."
Duàn Gān Lún said:
"What I meant by seeking advantage or disadvantage
is not this.
If we save Hándān
by encamping in its outskirts,
this will mean Zhào is not captured but Wèi remains intact.
Therefore, it is better to attack Xiāng Líng to the south to exhaust Wèi;
when Hándān is captured, we can then take advantage of Wèi's exhaustion.
This will mean Zhào is broken and Wèi is weakened."
Tián Hóu said:
"Good."
Thereupon he raised an army and attacked Xiāng Líng in the south.
In the seventh month,
Hándān was captured.
Qí then took advantage of Wèi's exhaustion
and soundly defeated them at Guì Líng.
During the crisis of Nán Liáng,
the Hán clan requested help from Qí.
Tián Hóu summoned his high ministers
and deliberated, saying:
"Between saving them early
and saving them late, which is more convenient?"
Zhāng Gài replied:
"If we save them late,
Hán will be broken and absorbed into Wèi;
it is better to save them early."
Tián Chén Sī said:
"This will not do.
The armies of Hán and Wèi are not yet exhausted,
and if we save them now,
we will receive the brunt of Wèi's army on behalf of Hán,
and instead we will end up taking orders from Hán.
Furthermore, Wèi has the ambition to destroy Hán;
when Hán sees it is about to perish,
it will surely appeal to the east to Qí."
"I will secretly establish an alliance with Hán,
and later take advantage of Wèi's exhaustion.
Then the state can be held in high regard,
profit can be gained,
and our reputation can be honored."
Tián Hóu said,
"Excellent."
He then secretly informed the envoy of Hán and sent him back.
Hán, believing it had the sole support of Qí,
fought five battles without a single victory.
It appealed for help to the east in Qí.
Qí then raised troops to attack Wèi
and soundly defeated them at Mǎlíng.
Wèi was broken and Hán was weakened;
the rulers of Hán and Wèi, through Tián Yīng,
faced north and paid homage to Tián Hóu.
Chénghóu Zōu Jì served as the Chancellor of Qí,
and Tián Jì served as the General.
They did not like each other.
Gōngsūn Hàn said to Zōu Jì,
"Why do you not advise the King to attack Wèi?
If victorious,
it will be due to your strategy,
and you can take the credit.
If the battle is not won
and Tián Jì does not advance,
or if he fights and survives,
he can be executed for his failure and retreat."
Zōu Jì thought this was correct,
so he persuaded the King to send Tián Jì to attack Wèi.
Tián Jì won three victories in three battles.
Zōu Jì reported this to Gōngsūn Hàn.
Gōngsūn Hàn then sent someone with ten pieces of gold
to go to the market for a divination
and say,
"I am one of Tián Jì's men.
We have won three victories in three battles;
our fame awes the world.
We wish to undertake a great enterprise;
will it be auspicious?"
When the diviner came out,
Gōngsūn Hàn then had the man who performed the divination arrested
and verified his testimony before the King.
Tián Jì then fled.
While Tián Jì was a general for Qí,
he captured Tàizǐ Shēn of Liáng
and took Páng Juān prisoner.
Sūn Zǐ said to Tián Jì,
saying,
"Can the General now undertake a great enterprise?"
Tián Jì said,
"How so?"
Sūn Zǐ said,
"The General should not disband the troops to enter Qí.
Have the exhausted and weak guard
the Sovereign.
The 'Sovereign's position'
is a well-traveled road,
where axle-caps strike and chariots rub as they pass each other.
If you have those exhausted and weak guard the sovereign's position,
one will surely be a match for ten,
ten for a hundred,
and a hundred for a thousand.
Then, with your back to Tàishān,
the Jì River on your left,
and Tiāntáng on your right,
station your main army at Gāoyuǎn
and send light chariots and elite cavalry to charge Yōngmén. If so,
the ruler of Qí can be set right,
and Chénghóu can be driven away.
Otherwise,
the General will not be able to enter Qí."
Tián Jì did not listen,
and indeed he could not enter Qí.
Tián Jì fled Qí and went to Chǔ,
and Zōu Jì replaced him as Chancellor.
Qí feared that Tián Jì would use the power of Chǔ to return to Qí.
Dù Hè said,
"I beg to keep him in Chǔ on your behalf."
He said to the King of Chǔ,
"The reason Zōu Jì is not on good terms with Chǔ
is that he fears Tián Jì will use Chǔ's power to return to Qí.
Your Majesty would do better to enfeoff Tián Jì in Jiāngnán
to show that Tián Jì will not return to Qí.
Then Zōu Jì will serve Chǔ generously with the resources of Qí.
Tián Jì is a fugitive;
if he receives a fief,
he will surely be grateful to Your Majesty.
If he does return to Qí,
he will surely serve Chǔ with the resources of Qí.
This is the way to make use of both 'Jì's."
Chǔ indeed enfeoffed him in Jiāngnán.
Zōu Jì served Xuān Wáng;
he brought many people into service,
but Xuān Wáng was not pleased.
Yàn Shǒu was honored, but the number of people he brought into service was small,
and the King was pleased with him.
Zōu Jì said to Xuān Wáng,
"I have heard that the filial piety of one son
is not as good as the filial piety of five sons.
Now, among those whom Shǒu has brought into service,
how many are there?"
Xuān Wáng therefore realized that Yàn Shǒu was an obstruction.
Zōu Jì was over eight feet tall
and had a handsome and elegant physique.
One morning, dressed in his court robes and cap, he looked in the mirror
and said to his wife,
"Between me and Xú Gōng of the north of the city, who is more beautiful?"
His wife said,
"You are extremely beautiful;
how could Xú Gōng compare to you!"
Xú Gōng of the north of the city
was a famous beauty in the state of Qí.
Zōu Jì did not believe himself,
and asked his concubine again,
"Between me and Xú Gōng, who is more beautiful?"
His concubine said,
"How could Xú Gōng compare to you!"
The next day, a guest came from outside,
and while sitting and talking with him,
Zōu Jì asked the guest,
"Between me and Xú Gōng, who is more beautiful?"
The guest said,
"Xú Gōng is not as beautiful as you!"
The following day,
Xú Gōng came to visit.
After looking at him carefully,
Zōu Jì considered himself inferior;
looking in the mirror to see himself,
he felt he was far inferior.
At evening,
as he lay in bed thinking about it, he said,
"The reason my wife calls me beautiful
is that she is biased toward me;
the reason my concubine calls me beautiful
is that she fears me;
the reason my guest calls me beautiful
is that he wants something from me."
Thereupon he went to court to see Wēiwáng and said,
"I truly know that I am not as beautiful as Xú Gōng.
My wife is biased toward me,
my concubine fears me,
and my guest wants something from me;
so they all say I am more beautiful than Xú Gōng.
Now Qí has a territory of a thousand lǐ
and a hundred and twenty cities.
Among the palace ladies and attendants,
none is not biased toward Your Majesty;
among the ministers at court,
none does not fear Your Majesty;
within the four borders,
none does not want something from Your Majesty.
From this perspective,
Your Majesty is greatly deluded!"
The King said,
"Excellent."
He then issued an order:
"Any official or commoner
who can criticize my faults to my face
shall receive the highest reward;
those who submit written remonstrances to me
shall receive the middle reward;
those who can spread criticisms in public
so they reach my ears
shall receive the lowest reward."
When the order was first issued,
the ministers came forward to remonstrate,
and the gate and courtyard were as crowded as a marketplace.
After several months,
they would only come occasionally.
After a full year,
even if someone wanted to speak,
there was nothing left to submit.
When Yàn, Zhào, Hán, and Wèi heard of this,
they all paid homage to Qí.
This is what is called winning a victory within the court.
Qín borrowed a route through Hán and Wèi to attack Qí,
and Wēiwáng of Qí sent Zhāng Zǐ as general to meet them.
They engaged with Qín
and set up camp.
Envoys traveled back and forth several times,
and Zhāng Zǐ changed their insignias
to intermingle them with the Qín army.
Scouts reported
that Zhāng Zǐ was leading Qí to surrender to Qín,
but Wēiwáng did not respond.
Within a short time,
scouts again reported
that Zhāng Zǐ had surrendered to Qín with the Qí army.
King Wēi did not respond.
This happened three times.
The officials petitioned, saying:
“Those who say Zhāng Zǐ has been defeated
are different people but tell the same story.
Why does Your Majesty not dispatch a general to attack him?”
The King said:
“It is clear that he would not betray me;
why should I attack him!”
Shortly thereafter,
news came that the Qí army had won a great victory
and the Qín army was soundly defeated.
Thereupon, the King of Qín bowed as a subject of the western border
and apologized to Qí.
Those close to the king asked:
“How did you know it would be so?”
He replied:
“Zhāng Zǐ’s mother, Qǐ, had offended his father;
his father killed her
and buried her beneath the horse stables.
When I sent Zhāng Zǐ as a general,
I encouraged him, saying:
‘With your excellence,
when you return with the army intact,
you must certainly rebury the general’s mother.’
He replied:
‘It is not that I am unable to rebury my late mother.
My mother, Qǐ, offended my father.
My father died before he could instruct me otherwise.
If I were to rebury my mother without receiving my father’s instruction,
this would be to deceive my dead father.
Therefore, I do not dare.’
Now, if a man as a son will not deceive a dead father,
would he, as a subject, deceive a living ruler?”
Chǔ was about to attack Qí,
and Lǔ was friendly toward them;
the King of Qí was worried about this.
Zhāng Gài said:
“I request permission to make Lǔ neutral.”
He then went to see the Ruler of Lǔ on behalf of Qí.
The Ruler of Lǔ said:
“Is the King of Qí afraid?”
He said:
“That is not for me to know,
but I have come to offer my condolences to Your Excellency.”
The Ruler of Lǔ said:
“Why condolences?”
He said:
“Your Excellency’s plan is flawed.
Why do you not side with the victor but rather with the one who will not win?”
The Ruler of Lǔ said:
“Between Qí and Chǔ, which do you think will win?”
He replied:
“Even the ghosts do not know.”
“If that is so, then why do you offer me condolences?”
He said:
“Qí
is a rival of equal power to Chǔ;
it matters not whether they have Lǔ or not.
Why does Your Excellency not instead command your people
to join with the survivor of the two states?
If Chǔ wins a great victory over Qí,
its elite officers and chosen soldiers will certainly be slaughtered,
and its remaining troops will only be sufficient to defend against the world;
if Qí is the victor,
its elite officers and chosen soldiers will also be slaughtered.
Then, if you join the victor with the forces of Lǔ after the battle,
the virtue of this act will be great indeed,
and the gratitude you receive will also be great.”
The Ruler of Lǔ thought this was correct
and personally withdrew his troops.
Qín attacked Wèi.
Chén Zhěn united the Sān Jìn
and went east to speak to the King of Qí, saying:
“When the kings of old attacked,
they desired to rectify the world
and establish merit and fame
for future generations.
Now, the six states of Qí, Chǔ, Yān, Zhào, Hán, and Liáng
are increasingly aggressive toward one another;
this is not sufficient to establish merit and fame,
but is only enough to strengthen Qín and weaken yourselves.
This is not the best plan for the land east of the mountains.
The one capable of endangering the land east of the mountains
is powerful Qín.
Instead of worrying about powerful Qín,
you take turns exhausting and weakening each other,
and both end up surrendering your states to Qín;
this is why I am concerned for the land east of the mountains.
The world is carving itself up for Qín,
yet Qín has not exerted any effort;
the world is cooking itself for Qín,
yet Qín has not provided any firewood.
Why is Qín so wise and the land east of the mountains so foolish?
I hope Your Majesty will examine this.
“When the Five Emperors, Three Kings,
and Five Hegemons of old attacked,
they attacked those who were unprincipled.
Now Qín’s attacks on the world are not like that;
it must desire to overturn everything;
rulers will certainly die in disgrace,
and the people will certainly die as captives.
Now the eyes of Hán and Liáng have never been dry,
yet only the people of Qí are not so;
it is not that Qí is close
and Hán and Liáng are distant,
but that Qí is far from Qín
and Hán and Liáng are near.
Now Qí is about to be near!
Now Qín desires to attack Liáng's Jiàng and Ānyì;
if Qín gains Jiàng and Ānyì to descend east along the river,
it will certainly use the river as a shield and attack Qí to the east,
seize all of Qí up to the sea,
and facing south, it will isolate Chǔ, Hán, and Liáng,
and facing north, it will isolate Yān and Zhào;
then Qí will have no way to carry out its plans.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully!
“Now the Sān Jìn have already united;
they have again made a brotherly pact
and sent out sharp troops
to garrison Liáng's Jiàng and Ānyì;
this is a plan for ten thousand generations.
If Qí does not quickly use sharp troops
to join with the Sān Jìn,
there will certainly be future worries.
If the Sān Jìn unite,
Qín will certainly not dare to attack Liáng,
and will instead attack Chǔ to the south.
While Chǔ and Qín are in conflict,
the Sān Jìn will be angry that Qí did not join them,
and will certainly attack Qí to the east.
This is why I say Qí will certainly have great worries;
it would be better to quickly use troops to join with the Sān Jìn.”
The King of Qí respectfully agreed,
and indeed used troops to join with the Sān Jìn.
Sū Qín formed the Vertical Alliance for Zhào
and persuaded King Xuān of Qí, saying:
“To the south of Qí is Tài Shān,
to the east is Lángyé,
to the west is the Qīng Hé,
and to the north is the Bó Hǎi;
this is what is called a state protected by four barriers.
Qí’s territory is two thousand li square,
its armored soldiers number hundreds of thousands,
and its grain is like hills and mountains.
The excellence of Qí's chariots,
and the soldiers from its households,
are as swift as arrows,
fight like thunder and lightning,
and disperse like wind and rain;
even when there are military campaigns,
they have never had to cross behind Tài Shān,
cross over the Qīng Hé,
or wade through the Bó Hǎi.
Within Línzī there are seventy thousand households;
I humbly estimate that
with at least three adult males per household,
three times seven makes two hundred and ten thousand;
without waiting to mobilize from distant counties,
the soldiers of Línzī
already number two hundred and ten thousand.
Línzī is extremely wealthy and prosperous;
among its people, there are none who do not play the reed pipes,
strum the zither,
strike the lute, play the harp,
cockfight, race dogs,
play board games, or play kickball;
on the roads of Línzī,
wheel hubs strike each other,
shoulders rub against shoulders,
the connected lapels of robes form a curtain,
raised sleeves form a canopy,
and the wiping of sweat forms rain;
families are substantial and wealthy,
and their spirits are high and soaring.
With Your Majesty’s worthiness and Qí’s strength,
the world cannot withstand you.
Now, to face west and serve Qín,
I humbly feel ashamed for Your Majesty.
“Furthermore, the reason Hán and Wèi fear Qín
is that they share borders with Qín.
When troops are sent out and face each other,
in less than ten days,
the crucial moment of victory or defeat, survival or ruin, is decided.
If Hán or Wèi fight and defeat Qín,
then half their troops will be lost,
and their four borders will be undefended;
if they fight and do not win,
then destruction follows behind them.
This is why Hán and Wèi consider fighting Qín a serious matter and find it easy to be its subjects.”
"Now, if Qín attacks Qí, it is not so;
it would have to turn its back on the lands of Hán and Wèi,
reach the road of Wéi Yáng Jìn,
and pass through the dangerous passes of Kàng Fù.
Chariots could not travel abreast,
and horses could not walk side-by-side.
If a hundred men guard the pass,
a thousand cannot pass through.
Even if Qín desired to penetrate deeply,
it would have to look back like a wolf,
fearing that Hán and Wèi would plot against its rear.
Therefore, they merely make threats and empty boasts,
prancing high but not daring to advance.
Thus, it is clear that Qín cannot harm Qí.
To not deeply consider that Qín can do nothing to us
and yet wish to face west to serve Qín
is a mistake in the planning of your ministers.
Now, without the reputation of serving Qín as a subject,
but having the reality of a powerful state,
I certainly wish the Dàwáng would give this a little more thought."
The Qí Wáng said:
"I am not clever.
Now that you, the Zhǔjūn,
instruct me with the teachings of the Zhào Wáng,
I respectfully offer my state to follow them."
Zhāng Yí formed the Liànhéng for Qín.
He said to the Qí Wáng:
"Among the powerful states of the world, none surpasses Qí;
among the ministers, fathers, and brothers who are numerous, wealthy, and happy,
none surpasses Qí.
However, those who plan for Your Majesty
all make arguments for the moment
without considering the interests of ten thousand generations.
Those who speak to the Dàwáng about the Zòng alliance
will surely say that to the west Qí has the powerful Zhào,
to the south it has Hán and Wèi,
and it is a land bordering the sea,
its territory is vast and its people numerous,
its army is strong and its soldiers brave;
even if there were a hundred Qín,
they could do nothing to us!
Your Majesty looks at their words
but does not examine the ultimate reality."
"Those of the Zòng alliance form cliques and cabals,
and none do not think the Zòng alliance is right.
I have heard
that Qí and Lǔ fought three battles
and Lǔ won three times,
yet the state was endangered,
and destruction followed;
although it had the name of victory,
it had the reality of ruin.
What was the reason for this?
Qí was large and Lǔ was small.
Now the relation between Zhào and Qín
is like that between Qí and Lǔ.
Qín and Zhào fought at the Hé Zhāng;
twice they fought and twice they defeated Qín.
They fought below Fān Wú;
twice they fought and twice they defeated Qín.
After four battles,
Zhào had lost hundreds of thousands of soldiers,
and Hán Dān barely survived.
Although it had the name of defeating Qín,
the state was broken!
What was the reason for this?
Qín is strong and Zhào is weak.
Now Qín and Chǔ have married off their children to one another
and become brotherly states;
Hán has offered Yí Yáng,
Wèi has surrendered Hé Wài,
and Zhào has paid court at Mǐn Chí,
ceding Hé Jiān to serve Qín.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qín,
Qín will drive Hán and Wèi to attack the southern lands of Qí,
and will summon all of Zhào to cross the Hé Guān
and point toward Tuán Guān;
Lín Zī and Jí Mò will then no longer be the Wáng's possession.
Once the state is attacked,
even if you wish to serve Qín,
it will be impossible.
Therefore, I wish
Your Majesty to consider this carefully."
The Qí Wáng said:
"Qí is remote, rustic, and secluded,
resting upon the Eastern Sea;
I have never heard of the long-term interests of the state.
Now that a Dàkè has fortunately come to instruct me,
I ask to offer my state to serve Qín."
He presented three hundred li of fish and salt producing land to Qín.
Hán and Qí were allied states.
Zhāng Yí used Qín and Wèi to attack Hán.
The Qí Wáng said:
"Hán
is my allied state.
Since Qín is attacking it,
I shall go to its rescue."
Tián Chén Sī said:
"Your Majesty's plan is a mistake;
it is better to listen to this.
When Zǐ Kuài gave the state to Zǐ Zhī,
the common people did not support him,
and the feudal lords did not side with him.
If Qín attacks Hán,
Chǔ and Zhào will surely rescue it;
this is the world bestowing Yàn upon me."
The Wáng said:
"Good."
He then gave a promise to the envoy of Hán and sent him away.
Hán, believing itself to have secured an alliance with Qí,
consequently went to war with Qín.
Chǔ and Zhào indeed quickly raised troops
to rescue Hán,
and Qí took the opportunity to raise troops to attack Yàn;
in thirty days, it took the whole state of Yàn.
Zhāng Yí served Qín Huì Wáng.
Huì Wáng died,
and Wǔ Wáng was established.
Those around the Wáng disliked Zhāng Yí,
saying:
"Zhāng Yí was not loyal in serving the late Wáng."
Before they had finished speaking,
a reprimand from Qí arrived again.
Zhāng Yí heard of this and
said to the Wǔ Wáng:
"I have a humble plan
and wish to offer it to Your Majesty."
The Wáng said:
"What is it?"
He replied:
"To plan for the state,
only after there is a great upheaval in the east
can Your Majesty carve out more territory.
Now the Qí Wáng greatly hates me;
wherever I am,
he will surely raise an army to attack.
Therefore, Yí wishes to beg for my unworthy self to go to Liáng;
Qí will surely raise an army to attack it.
When the armies of Qí and Liáng are locked in battle below the city walls
and cannot pull away,
Your Majesty can use that interval to attack Hán,
enter Sān Chuān,
send troops out of Hán Gǔ
without being attacked,
and so approach Zhōu.
The sacrificial vessels will surely be surrendered;
you will hold the Tiānzǐ in your power
and take control of the maps and registers;
this is the work of a Wáng."
The Wáng said:
"Good."
He then prepared thirty leather chariots
and sent Yí to Liáng.
Qí indeed raised an army to attack it.
The Liáng Wáng was greatly afraid.
Zhāng Yí said:
"Your Majesty, do not worry;
please allow me to make the Qí army withdraw."
He then sent his Shèrén Féng Xǐ to Chǔ
to use that mission to go to Qí.
After the business in Qí and Chǔ was finished,
he said to the Qí Wáng:
"Your Majesty greatly hates Zhāng Yí;
nevertheless,
Your Majesty's entrustment of Zhāng Yí
to the Qín Wáng has been generous."
The Qí Wáng said:
"I greatly hate Zhāng Yí;
wherever he is,
I will surely raise an army to attack him.
How have I entrusted him?"
He replied:
"That is exactly Your Majesty's entrustment of him.
When Zhāng Yí left Qín,
he made an agreement with the Qín Wáng, saying:
'To plan for Your Majesty,
only after there is a great upheaval in the east
can Your Majesty carve out more territory.
The Qí Wáng greatly hates me;
wherever I am,
he will surely raise an army to attack.
Therefore, Yí wishes to beg for my unworthy self to go to Liáng;
Qí will surely raise an army to attack Liáng.
When the armies of Liáng and Qí are locked in battle below the city walls and cannot pull away,
Your Majesty can use that interval to attack Hán,
enter Sān Chuān,
send troops out of Hán Gǔ without being attacked,
and so approach Zhōu.
The sacrificial vessels will surely be surrendered;
you will hold the Tiānzǐ in your power
and take control of the maps and registers;
this is the work of a Wáng.' "
The King of Qín thought this was correct,
and gave him thirty leather chariots to send Zhāng Yí to Liáng.
And he indeed attacked it,
which meant the King exhausted himself internally while attacking an allied state,
expanding the neighboring enemies that faced him,
and making the King of Qín trust Zhāng Yí.
“This is what I meant by ‘relying on Zhāng Yí’.”
The King said:
“Good.”
So he stopped.
Xīshǒu, leading Liáng on behalf of Qí, fought at Chéngkuāng
and did not win.
Zhāng Yí told the King of Liáng that by not following his advice, the King had endangered the state.
The King of Liáng then made Zhāng Yí Chancellor,
and Zhāng Yí used the strength of Qín and Liáng to form a horizontal alliance with Qí.
Xīshǒu wanted to ruin this
and said to the Lord of Wèi:
“I, Yǎn, have no grudge against Zhāng Yí;
it is only that our ways of serving the state are different.
You must reconcile Yǎn with him.”
The Lord of Wèi told Zhāng Yí this,
and Zhāng Yí agreed,
so he sat together with him in a group of three before the Lord of Wèi.
Xīshǒu moved forward on his knees
and offered a toast of longevity to Zhāng Yí.
The next day, Zhāngzǐ departed,
and Xīshǒu escorted him to the border of Qí.
When the King of Qí heard of this,
he was angry with Zhāng Yí
and said:
“Yǎn is my enemy,
yet Zhāng Yí is together with him;
this means he must be selling out my state along with Yǎn.”
Consequently, he did not listen to him.
Zhāoyáng attacked Wèi on behalf of Chǔ,
crushing their army, killing their general, and capturing eight cities,
then he moved his troops to attack Qí.
Chén Zhěn acted as an envoy for the King of Qí;
he met Zhāoyáng,
bowed twice,
and congratulated him on his victory.
Then he stood up and asked:
“According to the laws of Chǔ,
for crushing an army and killing a general,
what is the official rank and title?”
Zhāoyáng said:
“The office is Shàngzhùguó,
and the title is Shàngzhíguī.”
Chén Zhěn said:
“Is there anything more noble than this?”
He replied:
“Only that of Lìngyǐn.”
Chén Zhěn said:
“The Lìngyǐn is indeed noble!
But the King will not appoint two Lìngyǐns.
I beg to offer an analogy for you.
There was a man in Chǔ who offered a sacrifice
and gave his attendants a flagon of wine.
The attendants said to one another:
‘If several people drink this, it is not enough;
if one person drinks it, there is more than enough.
Let us draw snakes on the ground,
and the one who finishes first shall drink the wine.’
One man finished his snake first;
he took the wine and was about to drink it,
but then, holding the flagon in his left hand and drawing the snake with his right,
he said:
‘I can even make feet for it.’
Before he finished,
another man's snake was done;
he snatched the flagon and said:
‘A snake originally has no feet;
how can you make feet for it?’
Then he drank the wine.
The one who made feet for the snake
ended up losing his wine.
Now you are Chancellor of Chǔ and have attacked Wèi,
broken their army, killed their general, and captured eight cities without weakening your own troops;
now you wish to attack Qí.
Qí fears you greatly.
It is enough for you to rest upon the fame you have already gained;
for there are no higher offices that can be added.
To be victorious in every battle and yet not know when to stop
will lead to your own death,
and your titles will eventually return to the state;
this is just like ‘making feet for a snake’.”
Zhāoyáng thought this was correct,
and so he withdrew his army and left.
Qín attacked Zhào.
Zhào ordered Lóu Huǎn to offer five cities to seek peace with Qín,
and then join them in attacking Qí.
The King of Qí was afraid,
so he sent someone to offer ten cities to seek peace with Qín.
Master Lóu was afraid,
so he promised twenty-four counties of Shàngdǎng to the King of Qín.
Zhào Zú went to Qí
and said to the King of Qí:
“Does the King wish for Qín and Zhào to break their alliance?
It is better to follow and ally with Zhào,
for then Zhào will surely turn its back on Qín.
If they turn their back on Qín, then Qí will have no more worries.”
During the crisis of the balance of power,
Qí and Yàn were at war.
Qín sent Wèi Rǎn to Zhào
to send troops to help Yàn attack Qí.
The Lord of Xuē sent Wèi Chǔ to Zhào
to say to Lǐ Xiàng:
“If you help Yàn attack Qí,
Qí will surely be in desperate straits.
In desperation, they will surely cede land to make peace with Yàn,
and then they will turn to fight against Zhào themselves.
Thus, you would be using your eastern troops for the sake of Yàn,
and capturing land for Yàn.
Therefore, in planning for you,
it is better to hold back your troops and not send them out.
Qí will surely feel relieved,
and being relieved, they will surely fight with Yàn again.
If they fight and win,
their troops will be exhausted,
and Zhào can then take Táng and Qūní;
if they fight and do not win,
their fate will hang on Zhào.
In that case, we can remain neutral and carve up a destitute Qí and an exhausted Yàn;
the power over both states
will then return to you.”
Qín attacked Zhào at Chángpíng;
Qí and Chǔ went to save them.
Qín calculated, saying:
“If Qí and Chǔ save Zhào
and are in close accord,
then we shall withdraw our troops;
if they are not in close accord,
then we shall proceed to attack them.”
Zhào had no food,
so they requested grain from Qí,
but Qí would not grant it.
Sū Qín said to the King of Qí:
“It is better to grant it to drive back the Qín troops;
if you do not grant it, then the Qín troops will not be driven back.
This means Qín's plan will succeed,
and the plans of Qí and Yàn will have failed.
Moreover, Zhào is to Yàn and Qí
a protective screen,
just as teeth have lips;
if the lips are gone, the teeth will be cold.
If Zhào is destroyed today,
then tomorrow it will be the turn of Qí and Chǔ.
Furthermore, the task of saving Zhào
should be like holding a leaking container
or pouring water into a scorched cauldron.
Saving Zhào
is a matter of high righteousness;
driving back the Qín troops
is a matter of gaining a distinguished name.
To righteously save a dying Zhào
and majestically drive back the strong Qín troops—
if you do not strive for this,
but instead strive only to save your grain,
then you have failed in planning for the state.”
Someone said to the King of Qí:
“Zhōu and Hán have a strong Qín to their west
and Zhào and Wèi to their east.
When Qín attacks Zhōu and Hán from the west,
if Zhào and Wèi do not attack,
Zhōu and Hán will be partitioned,
and Hán will ward off the harm to Zhōu.
When Hán wards off the harm and Zhōu is partitioned,
Zhào and Wèi will also not escape having Qín as a threat.
Now if Qí and Qín attack Zhào and Wèi,
then it will also not result in Zhào and Wèi
responding to Qín by attacking Zhōu and Hán.
If Qí joins with Qín to attack Zhào and Wèi,
after Zhào and Wèi are destroyed,
Qín will face east and attack Qí;
how then could Qí save the world?”
The King of Chǔ died,
and the Crown Prince was a hostage in Qí.
Sū Qín said to the Lord of Xuē:
“Why do you not detain the Chǔ Crown Prince
to trade for their lower eastern territories?”
The Lord of Xuē said:
“That will not do.
If I detain the Crown Prince,
they will set up another king in Yǐng;
then I would be holding a useless hostage
and acting unrighteously before the world.”
Sū Qín said:
"Not so.
In Yǐng, they will set up a king.
You should then say to the new king:
'Give me Xià Dōng Guó,
and I will kill the Crown Prince for Your Majesty.
Otherwise,
I will join with the three states to establish him as king.'
Thus, Xià Dōng Guó can certainly be obtained."
The matters of Sū Qín
could be used to request a mission;
could be used to make the King of Chǔ quickly cede Xià Dōng Guó;
could be used to obtain more land from Chǔ;
could be used to show loyalty to the Crown Prince and make Chǔ cede more land;
could be used to drive away the Crown Prince for the King of Chǔ;
could be used to show loyalty to the Crown Prince by making him leave quickly;
could be used to slander Sū Qín to Xuē Gōng;
could be used to request a fief for Sū Qín in Chǔ;
could be used to have someone persuade Xuē Gōng to be kind to Sū Qín;
could be used to allow Sū Qín to explain himself to Xuē Gōng.
Sū Qín said to Xuē Gōng:
"I have heard that if a plot is leaked, it will fail;
if a plan is not decided upon, fame will not be achieved.
Now you are detaining the Crown Prince
in order to trade for Xià Dōng Guó.
If you do not obtain Xià Dōng Guó quickly,
then Chǔ's plans will change.
If they change, you will be left holding a useless hostage
and will bear a bad reputation throughout the world."
Xuē Gōng said:
"Excellent.
What should be done?"
The reply was:
"I request to go to Chǔ on your behalf
to make them quickly hand over the land of Xià Dōng Guó.
Once Chǔ fulfills the agreement,
then you will not fail."
Xuē Gōng said:
"Good."
He then sent him.
He said to the King of Chǔ:
"Qí wishes to support the Crown Prince and establish him as king.
I observe that the reason Xuē Gōng detains the Crown Prince
is to trade for Xià Dōng Guó.
Now if Your Majesty does not quickly hand over Xià Dōng Guó,
then the Crown Prince will double the land Your Majesty cedes
to have Qí support him."
The King of Chǔ said:
"I respectfully receive your instruction."
He then offered Xià Dōng Guó.
Therefore it is said
he could make Chǔ quickly hand over land.
He said to Xuē Gōng:
"Under the current situation of Chǔ, more land can be obtained."
Xuē Gōng said:
"How so?"
"Please tell the Crown Prince the situation,
and have the Crown Prince pay respects to you
to show loyalty to the Crown Prince.
When the King of Chǔ hears of this,
more land can be obtained."
Therefore it is said he could obtain more land from Chǔ.
He said to the Crown Prince:
"Qí wants to support you and establish you as king,
but the King of Chǔ has requested to cede land to have you detained.
Qí considers that land insufficient.
Why do you not double the land Chǔ cedes to provide for Qí?
Qí will then certainly support you."
The Crown Prince said:
"Good."
He doubled the land Chǔ was ceding to entice Qí.
The King of Chǔ was terrified when he heard this;
he ceded even more land and offered it,
still fearing his plan might fail.
Therefore it is said he could make Chǔ cede more land.
He said to the King of Chǔ:
"The reason Qí dares to demand so much land
is that they hold the Crown Prince.
Now they have obtained land yet their demands do not stop
because they are using the Crown Prince to pressure Your Majesty.
Therefore, I can make the Crown Prince leave.
Once the Crown Prince leaves,
Qí will have no excuse
and will certainly not turn against Your Majesty.
Your Majesty can then hasten to form an alliance with the powerful Qí.
If Qí is offered terms,
they will certainly listen to Your Majesty.
Thus Your Majesty removes an enemy and gains an alliance with Qí."
The King of Chǔ was greatly pleased,
and said:
"I request to entrust the state to you."
Therefore it is said
he could make the Crown Prince leave quickly for the King of Chǔ.
He said to the Crown Prince:
"The one who controls Chǔ is the King;
the one trading with an empty name is you, the Crown Prince.
Qí might not necessarily believe your words,
yet Chǔ's success is already visible.
Once the alliance with Chǔ is formed,
you will certainly be in danger.
You should consider this."
The Crown Prince said:
"I respectfully receive your instruction."
He then prepared his carriage and left at dusk.
Therefore it is said he could make the Crown Prince leave in haste.
Sū Qín sent someone to address Xuē Gōng, saying:
"The one who advised detaining the Crown Prince was Sū Qín.
Sū Qín did not do this truly for your sake,
but rather for the convenience of Chǔ.
Sū Qín feared you would realize this,
so he took much land from Chǔ to cover his tracks.
Now, the one who advised the Crown Prince to leave was also Sū Qín,
and you are unaware of it.
I privately have doubts about him on your behalf."
Xuē Gōng was greatly enraged at Sū Qín.
Therefore it is said
he could have someone slander Sū Qín to Xuē Gōng.
He also sent someone to say to the King of Chǔ:
"The one who made Xuē Gōng detain the Crown Prince
was Sū Qín.
The one who supported Your Majesty to replace the Crown Prince of Chǔ
was also Sū Qín.
The one who secured the ceded land and the treaty was also Sū Qín.
The one who was loyal to Your Majesty and drove away the Crown Prince was also Sū Qín.
Now people slander Sū Qín to Xuē Gōng
because he was stingy toward Qí and generous toward Chǔ.
I hope Your Majesty knows this."
The King of Chǔ said:
"I respectfully receive this."
He then enfeoffed Sū Qín as Wǔzhēn Jūn.
Therefore it is said he could request a fief for Sū Qín in Chǔ.
He also sent Jǐng Lǐ
to address Xuē Gōng, saying:
"The reason you are respected throughout the world
is that you can attract the world's scholars and hold power in Qí.
Now Sū Qín is a great debater of the world,
a rare talent in this age.
If you are not kind to Sū Qín,
then you will be blocking the world's scholars and discouraging the path of persuasion.
Those who do not like you will support Sū Qín,
and your affairs will be in danger.
Now Sū Qín is favored by the King of Chǔ;
if you do not become close to him early on,
then you will find yourself an enemy of Chǔ.
Therefore, it is better for you to be close to him,
honor him and respect him;
thus you will possess Chǔ."
Xuē Gōng then treated Sū Qín well.
Therefore it is said he could
persuade Xuē Gōng to be kind to Sū Qín.
The King of Qí's wife died,
and there were seven concubines who were all close to him.
Xuē Gōng wanted to know whom the King wished to appoint,
so he presented seven earrings,
one of which was especially beautiful.
The next day, he looked to see who wore the beautiful earring
and then advised the King to appoint her as the new queen.
Mèngcháng Jūn was about to enter Qín;
those who tried to stop him numbered in the thousands, but he would not listen.
Sū Qín wanted to stop him.
Mèngcháng said:
"As for human affairs,
I know them all;
the only things I have not heard about
are only the affairs
of ghosts."
Sū Qín said:
"I have come here
certainly not daring to speak of human affairs,
but indeed to see you regarding the affairs of ghosts."
Mèngcháng Jūn granted him an audience.
He said to Mèngcháng Jūn:
"Just now when I came,
I passed the banks of the Zī River.
There was a clay figurine
and a peachwood slip talking to each other.
The peachwood slip said to the clay figurine:
'You
are but soil from the west bank,
molded into a person.
When the eighth month comes
and the heavy rains fall,
and the waters of the Zī River arrive,
then you will be ruined.'"
The clay figure said:
"Not so.
I am the soil of the western bank;
being soil, I simply return to the western bank.
Now you are a peach-wood figurine from the eastern land,
carved and planed to be a person.
When the rains descend
and the Zī River arrives,
carrying you away in the current,
then what will become of you as you are tossed about?"
Now Qín is a state of four barriers,
which may be compared to a tiger's mouth.
If your Lordship enters it,
then I do not know how your Lordship will ever emerge."
Mèng Cháng Jūn then stopped.
When Mèng Cháng Jūn was in Xué,
the people of Jīng attacked him.
Chúnyú Kūn was serving as an envoy from Qí to Jīng
and passed through Xué on his return journey.
Mèng Cháng Jūn treated him with great courtesy
and personally went to the outskirts to welcome him.
He said to Chúnyú Kūn:
"The people of Jīng are attacking Xué;
if you, Master, do not show concern,
I, Wén, will no longer be able to serve you."
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"I respectfully hear your command."
When he reached Qí, he completed his report.
The King said:
"What did you see in Jīng?"
He replied:
"Jīng is very stubborn,
and Xué also does not measure its own strength."
The King said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"Xué does not measure its strength,
and yet it has established the Qīng Miào for the former kings.
Jīng is stubborn and attacks it;
the Qīng Miào will surely be in danger.
Therefore, I say Xué does not measure its strength,
and Jīng is also very stubborn."
The King of Qí softened his expression and said:
"Alas!
The temple of the former kings is there!"
He quickly raised troops to save it.
Pleas made while falling in desperation
and visits made with hopeful bowing,
even if granted, are meager.
Those who are good at persuasion
lay out the circumstances
and speak of the methods;
when people are in an emergency,
as if they were in the midst of a narrow and distressing situation,
how could they need to use forceful strength!
Mèng Cháng Jūn provided Xiàhóu Zhāng
with a carriage and four horses and food for a hundred men,
and he treated him with great joy.
Every time Xiàhóu Zhāng spoke,
he never failed to disparage Mèng Cháng Jūn.
Someone reported this to Mèng Cháng Jūn,
and Mèng Cháng Jūn said:
"I, Wén, have my reasons for serving Lord Xiàhóu;
do not speak of it,
but just oversee it."
Fán Jīng asked Lord Xiàhóu about this,
and Lord Xiàhóu said:
"Mèng Cháng Jūn’s importance is not that of a feudal lord,
yet he provides me with a carriage and four horses and food for a hundred men.
I have not even a tiny bit of merit, yet I receive this.
However, I disparage him in order to help him.
The reason the Lord can be considered a man of virtue
is because I disparage him.
Since I have committed my person to Mèng Cháng Jūn,
how could I just hold my words?"
While Mèng Cháng Jūn was sitting at a banquet,
he said to three gentlemen:
"I wish to hear if the gentlemen have any way to supplement my deficiencies."
One man said:
"Among the rulers of the world,
if there are those who encroach upon my Lord,
I beg
to wash their robes with my own blood."
Tián Mào said:
"As far as the wheels of a carriage can reach,
I beg to cover your Excellency's shortcomings
and recite your Excellency's virtues;
so that rulers of a thousand chariots and ministers of ten thousand chariots
will desire to have my Lord
as if they could never reach him."
Shèng said:
"I wish to use your Excellency’s treasury and goods
to gather the scholars of the world,
to be able to resolve
doubts and respond to crises for my Lord, just as Wèi Wén Hóu
had Tián Zǐfāng
and Duàngān Mù.
This is what I would obtain for my Lord."
Among Mèng Cháng Jūn’s retainers,
there was one who was
in love with the Lord’s wife.
Someone told Mèng Cháng Jūn:
"To be your Lordship's retainer
and yet have a secret love for your wife within the household
is also very unrighteous;
your Lordship should kill him."
The Lord said:
"To see a face and be pleased by it
is human nature;
set it aside and do not speak of it."
After a year had passed,
the Lord called the one who loved his wife
and said to him:
"You have traveled with me, Wén, for a long time;
a high office cannot yet be obtained,
and a minor office you also would not want.
The Ruler of Wèi and I are friends from our days as commoners;
please prepare a carriage, horses, and fine furs;
I wish for you to travel and follow the Ruler of Wèi with these."
He was held in great esteem in Wèi.
When relations between Qí and Wèi turned sour,
the Ruler of Wèi greatly desired
to ally with the world's armies to attack Qí.
This man said to the Ruler of Wèi:
"Mèng Cháng Jūn did not know I was unworthy
and sent me to serve your Lordship.
Furthermore, I have heard that the former rulers of Qí and Wèi
sacrificed a horse and a sheep
and made a covenant, saying:
'May the future generations of Qí and Wèi not attack each other;
if there are those who attack each other,
may their lives be like these.'
Now your Lordship is allying with the world's armies to attack Qí;
this is your Excellency betraying the former rulers' covenant and deceiving Mèng Cháng Jūn.
I wish your Lordship would not turn your heart against Qí.
If your Lordship listens to me, it will be well;
if you do not listen to me,
since I am unworthy,
I shall immediately wash your Excellency's lapel with the blood from my neck."
The Ruler of Wèi then stopped.
When the people of Qí heard of this, they said:
"Mèng Cháng Jūn can be said to be good at managing affairs,
turning a disaster into a success."
Mèng Cháng Jūn had a retainer with whom he was not pleased
and wished to expel him.
Lǔ Lián said to Mèng Cháng Jūn:
"When monkeys and macaques leave the trees and rely on the water,
they are not as good as fish and turtles;
in crossing dangers and riding through hazards,
then the fine steed Qíjì is not as good as a fox or a raccoon.
When Cáo Mò brandished his three-foot sword,
a whole army could not withstand him;
but if Cáo Mò were made to put down his three-foot sword
and handle a hoe and live among the farmers in the fields,
then he would not be as good as a farmer.
Therefore, if a thing abandons its strengths
and resorts to its weaknesses,
even Yáo would have shortcomings.
Now if you employ a person but they are not capable,
then you call them unworthy;
if you teach a person but they are not capable,
then you call them clumsy.
If they are clumsy, you dismiss them;
if they are unworthy, you discard them.
If you cause people to be discarded and expelled,
having no one to stay with,
and then they come to bring harm and seek revenge
—would that not be the very start of establishing such a lesson for the world!"
Mèng Cháng Jūn said:
"Good."
Thus he did not expel him.
Mèng Cháng Jūn went out
to travel through the states,
and reached Chǔ;
he presented an ivory bed.
Dēngtú of Yǐng
was simply ordered to deliver it,
but he did not wish to go.
Someone went to see Mèngcháng Jūn’s retainer Gōngsūn Shù
and said:
“I am
the Dēngtú of Yǐng,
and I have been ordered to deliver an ivory bed.
The ivory bed is worth a thousand pieces of gold;
if it is damaged even as slightly as a floating hair,
selling my wife and children would not be enough to compensate for it.
If you, sir, can make it so that I do not have to make the journey,
my ancestors have a precious sword
which I would like to offer to you.”
Gōngsūn said:
“Very well.”
He went in to see Mèngcháng Jūn and asked:
“Are you, my lord, going to accept
the ivory bed from Chǔ?”
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
“Yes.”
Gōngsūn Shù said:
“I wish that you would not accept it.”
Mèngcháng Jūn asked:
“Why is that?”
Gōngsūn Shù said:
“The reason all the small states present their prime ministerial seals to you
is that they have heard that in Qí you can aid the poor and destitute
and that you possess the righteousness to preserve those facing ruin and to continue the lineages of those facing extinction.
The heroic and eminent men of the small states
all entrust the affairs of their nations to you
because they are truly delighted by your righteousness
and admire your incorruptibility.
Now, if you go to Chǔ and accept an ivory bed,
how will the states you have not yet visited
treat you?
I, Shù, wish that you would not accept it.”
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
“Very well.”
Gōngsūn Shù hurried away.
Before he had gone out
and reached the inner gate,
the Lord called him and had him return,
saying:
“You taught Wén not to accept the ivory bed,
which was very good.
Now why do you lift your feet so high
and look so elated in spirit?”
Gōngsūn Shù said:
“I have three great joys
plus one precious sword.”
Mèngcháng Jūn asked:
“What do you mean by that?”
Gōngsūn Shù said:
“You have hundreds of retainers,
yet none dared to come in and remonstrate.
I alone came in to remonstrate;
that is my first joy.
My remonstrance was heard and followed;
that is my second joy.
My remonstrance stopped the Lord’s mistake;
that is my third joy.
As for delivering the ivory bed,
the Dēngtú of Yǐng did not wish to make the journey
and promised Shù his ancestors' precious sword.”
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
“Good.
Have you accepted it?”
Gōngsūn Shù said:
“I have not yet dared.”
