The Lord said:
“Accept it quickly.”
He then wrote on the gate board, saying:
“Anyone who can spread Wén’s fame,
stop Wén’s mistakes,
and privately obtain treasures from abroad,
come quickly and remonstrate.”
Chúnyú Kūn in a single day presented seven men to Xuān Wáng.
The King said:
“Come here.
I have heard
that a scholar found once in a thousand lǐ
is like standing shoulder to shoulder,
and a sage found once in a hundred generations
is as if they were arriving heel to heel.
Now you have presented seven scholars in a single morning;
are scholars then not too numerous?”
Chúnyú Kūn said:
“Not so.
Birds with the same wings dwell together;
beasts with the same feet travel together.
Now if one seeks cháihú or jiégěng in a marsh,
one will not find a single specimen in several generations.
But if one goes to the shady sides of Gāoshǔ or Liángfù,
then one could fill a cart with them.
All things belong to their own kind.
Now I, Kūn, belong to the kind of the worthy.
For the King to seek scholars from Kūn is like drawing water from the River
or taking fire from a flint.
I am going to present more;
how could it be only seven scholars?”
Qí wanted to attack Wèi. Chúnyú Kūn said to the King of Qí:
“Hánzǐlú
was the swiftest dog in the world.
Dōngguōqūn
was the craftiest rabbit within the seas.
Hánzǐlú chased Dōngguōqūn;
they ran around the mountain three times
and over the mountain five times.
The rabbit was exhausted in front,
and the dog collapsed behind.
Both dog and rabbit were worn out
and died in their places.
A farmer saw them
and, without the hardship of labor or fatigue,
took the prize for himself.
Now Qí and Wèi have long been in a standoff,
which has exhausted their soldiers
and weakened their people.
I fear that the powerful Qín or the great Chǔ will follow behind them
and gain the farmer’s profit.”
The King of Qí was afraid
and dismissed his generals to rest his troops.
Guózǐ said:
“Qín defeated the army of Mǎfú Jūn
and besieged Hándān.
Qí and Wèi also assisted Qín in attacking Hándān;
Qí took Zīshǔ
and Wèi took Yīshì.
Gōngzǐ Wùjì,
acting for the benefit of the world,
killed Jìn Bǐ
and led the Wèi army to rescue Hándān from its siege,
causing Qín not to possess it and to lose its hold on the world.
This was the merit of Qí entering Wèi
and saving Hándān.
Ānyì
is the pillar of the state of Wèi;
Jìnyáng
is the pillar of the state of Zhào;
Yānyǐng
is the pillar of the state of Chǔ.
Therefore, these three states wished to border Qín.
Qín attacked Wèi and took Ānyì,
attacked Zhào and took Jìnyáng,
and attacked Chǔ and took Yānyǐng.
It subjugated the rulers of the three states,
annexed the lands of the two Zhōu,
overthrew the Hán clan and took their territory,
which was nearly half the world.
Now it is again coercing Zhào and Wèi,
isolating the central states,
enfeoffing the Dōngyě of Wèi,
annexing the Hénán region of Wèi,
and cutting off the Dōngyáng of Zhào;
thus Zhào and Wèi are in danger.
If Zhào and Wèi are in danger,
then it is not to the advantage of Qí.
The intent of Hán, Wèi, Zhào, and Chǔ
is the fear that Qín will annex the world
and make their rulers into subjects;
therefore they have united their armies and their purpose to oppose Qín.
For the three states that border Qín, the danger is urgent;
for Qí, which does not border Qín, the danger is slow.
Therefore, given the situation of the world,
they cannot but serve Qí.
If Qín wins over Qí,
then its power will be greater than that of the central states;
if Zhào, Wèi, and Chǔ win over Qí,
then they will be sufficient to oppose Qín.
Thus, for Qín, Zhào, and Wèi, gaining Qí makes them powerful,
and losing Qí makes them weak.
Qí has this advantageous position,
yet why is it not dominant in the world?
Because those who use its power are in error.”
There was a man from Qí named Féng Xuān
who was so poor that he could not support himself.
He had someone recommend him to Mèngcháng Jūn,
wishing to be a guest in his household.
Mèngcháng Jūn asked:
“What does the guest like?”
He replied:
“The guest likes nothing.”
The Lord asked:
“What can the guest do?”
He replied:
“The guest has no special abilities.”
Mèngcháng Jūn laughed and accepted him, saying:
“Very well.”
His attendants, thinking the Lord looked down on him,
fed him with coarse food.
After living there for a while,
he leaned against a pillar and tapped his sword,
singing:
"Long sword, let us return!
There is no fish to eat."
The attendants reported this.
Mèng Cháng Jūn said:
"Feed him,
equal to the other guests of my gate."
After another while,
he again tapped his sword
and sang:
"Long sword, let us return!
There is no carriage when going out."
The attendants all laughed at him
and reported it.
Mèng Cháng Jūn said:
"Prepare a carriage for him,
equal to the guests who have carriages."
Thereupon he rode his carriage,
raised his sword,
and visited his friend, saying:
"Mèng Cháng Jūn treats me as a guest."
Later, after a while,
he again tapped his sword
and sang:
"Long sword, let us return!
I have no means to support a family."
The attendants all disliked him,
thinking he was greedy and did not know satisfaction.
Mèng Cháng Jūn asked:
"Does Master Féng have relatives?"
The reply was:
"He has an old mother."
Mèng Cháng Jūn sent people to provide her with food and necessities
so as not to let her lack anything.
Thereupon Féng Xuān did not sing again.
Later, Mèng Cháng Jūn issued a notice,
asking the various guests:
"Who is skilled in accounting
and can collect debts for Wén in Xuē?"
Féng Xuān signed his name, saying:
"I can."
Mèng Cháng Jūn found this strange
and asked:
"Who is this?"
The attendants said:
"It is the one who sang 'Long sword, let us return'."
Mèng Cháng Jūn laughed and said:
"The guest truly has ability;
I have failed him,
for I have never met him."
He requested to see him
and apologized, saying:
"I, Wén, am exhausted by affairs
and muddled by worries,
and my nature is weak and foolish;
I have been submerged in the affairs of the state,
thus I have offended you, Sir.
If you, Sir, are not ashamed,
do you truly intend to collect debts for me in Xuē?"
Féng Xuān said:
"I am willing."
Thereupon he prepared the carriage and luggage, loaded the contracts and bonds, and set off,
bidding farewell by asking:
"When the debts are all collected,
what shall I buy to return with?"
Mèng Cháng Jūn said:
"Look for what my house lacks."
He drove to Xuē
and ordered the officials to summon all the people who owed debts
to all come and verify their contracts.
When the contracts were all verified,
he stood up and forged an order to grant the debts to the people
and then burned their contracts;
the people shouted, "Ten thousand years!"
He drove straight back to Qí
and sought an audience in the morning.
Mèng Cháng Jūn was surprised by his speed
and put on his robes and cap to see him,
saying:
"Are the debts all collected?
How is it you returned so quickly!"
He said:
"They are all collected."
"What did you buy to return with?"
Féng Xuān said:
"You, My Lord, said,
'Look for what my house lacks.'
I humbly calculated that
Your Lordship's palace is filled with rare treasures,
dogs and horses fill the outer stables,
and beautiful women fill the lower ranks.
What Your Lordship's house lacks is only righteousness!
Therefore, I humbly bought righteousness for Your Lordship."
Mèng Cháng Jūn asked:
"How did you buy righteousness?"
He said:
"Now Your Lordship has the small land of Xuē,
but you do not cherish and treat its people as your children;
instead, you seek profit from them.
I humbly forged Your Lordship's order
to grant the debts to the people
and then burned their contracts;
the people shouted, 'Ten thousand years!'
This is how I bought righteousness for Your Lordship."
Mèng Cháng Jūn was displeased
and said:
"Very well,
you may rest now, Sir!"
One full year later,
the King of Qí said to Mèng Cháng Jūn:
"I do not dare to use the ministers of the former king as my own ministers."
Mèng Cháng Jūn went to his fief in Xuē.
Before he was within a hundred lǐ,
the people, supporting the old and carrying the young,
welcomed him on the road.
Mèng Cháng Jūn turned and said to Féng Xuān:
"That 'righteousness' you bought for me, Sir,
I finally see it today."
Féng Xuān said:
"A cunning rabbit has three burrows,
and only thus can it escape death.
Now Your Lordship has only one burrow;
you cannot yet sleep with a high pillow.
Please allow me to dig two more burrows for Your Lordship."
Mèng Cháng Jūn gave him fifty carriages
and five hundred catties of gold.
He traveled west to Liáng
and said to King Huì:
"Qí has dismissed its great minister Mèng Cháng Jūn to the various lords;
the lord who welcomes him first
will be wealthy and have a strong army."
Thereupon, the King of Liáng vacated the highest position
and made his former chancellor the Senior General,
sending messengers
with a thousand catties of gold
and a hundred carriages
to invite Mèng Cháng Jūn.
Féng Xuān rode ahead and warned Mèng Cháng Jūn, saying:
"A thousand catties of gold is a heavy gift;
a hundred carriages is a distinguished mission.
Qí will surely hear of it."
The messengers from Liáng returned three times,
but Mèng Cháng Jūn firmly declined and did not go.
The King of Qí heard of this,
and the king and his ministers were terrified.
He sent the Grand Preceptor with a thousand catties of gold,
two ornate carriages with four horses each,
a ceremonial sword,
and a sealed letter apologizing to Mèng Cháng Jūn, saying:
"I have been unfortunate
and suffered the misfortune of the ancestral temple;
I was submerged by flattering and fawning ministers
and offended Your Lordship.
I am not worth serving,
but I hope Your Lordship will look upon the ancestral temple of the former kings
and return to the state to govern the people."
Féng Xuān warned Mèng Cháng Jūn, saying:
"I request that you ask for the sacrificial vessels of the former kings
and establish an ancestral temple in Xuē."
When the temple was completed,
he returned and reported to Mèng Cháng Jūn:
"The three burrows are now complete;
Your Lordship may now sleep peacefully with a high pillow."
Mèng Cháng Jūn served as Chancellor for several decades
without the slightest disaster,
all due to the plans of Féng Xuān.
Mèng Cháng Jūn was forming an alliance.
Gōngsūn Hóng said to Mèng Cháng Jūn:
"Should you not send someone ahead to observe the King of Qín?
If the King of Qín is a ruler of emperors and kings,
Your Lordship may fear not being able to be his minister;
how would you have time to oppose him with an alliance?
If the King of Qín is an unworthy ruler,
it will not be too late
for Your Lordship to oppose him with an alliance."
Mèng Cháng Jūn said:
"Good.
I wish to request that you, Sir, go."
Gōngsūn Hóng respectfully assented,
and with ten chariots he went to Qín.
King Zhāo heard of this
and wished to embarrass him with words.
When Gōngsūn Hóng had an audience,
King Zhāo said:
"As for the land of the Lord of Xuè,
how large or small is it?"
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"One hundred lǐ."
King Zhāo laughed and said:
"My land is several thousand lǐ,
yet I still do not dare to create difficulties for others.
Now the Lord of Mèngcháng’s land is only one hundred lǐ square,
yet he wishes to create difficulties for me—
is that acceptable?"
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"The Lord of Mèngcháng loves men of talent;
Your Majesty does not love men of talent."
King Zhāo asked:
"The Lord of Mèngcháng’s love for men of talent—
what is it like?"
Gōngsūn Hóng said:
"Those who in righteousness would not be subjects to the Son of Heaven
nor be friends to the feudal lords,
who if they achieved their ambitions would not be ashamed to be rulers of men,
and if they did not would refuse to be subjects of men—
there are three such men.
Those whose governance could make them masters to Guǎn
or Shāng,
whose words on righteousness are listened to and acted upon,
and who can achieve such results—there are five such men.
Even against a formidable ruler of ten thousand chariots,
if his envoy were insulted,
they would withdraw and slit their own throats,
certain to stain his robes with their blood—
there are ten such men like me."
King Zhāo laughed and apologized to him,
saying:
"Why should the guest be like this?
I was simply discussing things with the guest!
I am fond of the Lord of Mèngcháng,
and I wish for the guest to surely convey my sentiments!"
Gōngsūn Hóng said:
"I respectfully obey."
Gōngsūn Hóng can be said to have remained unyielding.
King Zhāo
ruled a great state.
Mèngcháng
held a thousand chariots.
By establishing the righteousness of a thousand-chariot lord so that he could not be bullied,
he can be said to be a worthy envoy.
Lǔ Zhònglián said to Mèngcháng:
"You love scholars!
Yōngmén Yǎng and Jiāo Yì,
and Yáng Dézǐ,
ate and drank
and shared robes with their followers,
and all of them were willing to die for them.
Now your household is wealthier than those of these two gentlemen,
yet no scholar has yet been willing to go to the limit for the Lord."
The Lord said:
"It is because Wén has not obtained men like those two.
If Wén obtained such men,
how could they not go to the limit?"
The reply was:
"Your stables have a hundred chariots of horses,
all of which are covered in embroidered cloth and eat beans and grain;
are there any Qílín or Lù’ěr among them?
In your inner palace there are ten concubines,
all dressed in fine silk
and eating fine grain and meat;
are there any like Máo Qiáng
or Xī Shī among them?
Beauty and horses are taken from the present world;
why must scholars wait for those of antiquity?
Therefore I say your love for scholars is not yet complete."
The Lord of Mèngcháng was expelled from Qí and later returned.
Tán Shízǐ met him at the border
and said to the Lord of Mèngcháng:
"Does the Lord perhaps have some resentment toward the scholars and officials of Qí?"
The Lord of Mèngcháng said:
"I do."
"Does the Lord intend to kill them all?"
The Lord of Mèngcháng said:
"Yes."
Tán Shízǐ said:
"There are things that must come to pass,
and principles that are naturally so;
does the Lord know this?"
The Lord of Mèngcháng said:
"I do not."
Tán Shízǐ said:
"That which must come to pass
is death;
the principle that is naturally so
is that when one is rich and noble, people approach him,
and when one is poor and lowly, they leave him.
These are the things that must come to pass
and the principles that are naturally so.
Allow me to use the market as an illustration.
The market is full in the morning
and empty in the evening;
it is not that people love the market in the morning and hate it in the evening,
but they go because what they seek is there,
and they leave because it is gone.
I hope the Lord will not feel resentment."
The Lord of Mèngcháng then took the five hundred tallies of those he resented and scraped them away,
never daring to speak of it again.
King Xuān of Qí saw Yán Chù and said:
"Chù, come forward!"
Chù also said: "King, come forward!"
King Xuān was displeased.
His attendants said:
"The King
is a ruler of men.
Chù
is a subject of men.
When the King says 'Chù, come forward,'
and you also say
'King, come forward,'
is that acceptable?"
Chù replied: "If Chù goes forward,
it is for the sake of admiring power;
if the King comes forward, it is for the sake of seeking scholars.
Rather than having Chù appear to be a seeker of power,
it is better to have the King appear to be a seeker of scholars."
The King became angry, changed his expression, and said:
"Is a king noble? Or is a scholar noble?"
He replied: "The scholar is noble;
the king is not noble."
The King said:
"Is there an explanation for this?"
Chù said:
"There is.
Formerly, when Qín attacked Qí,
they issued an order:
'If anyone dares to go within fifty paces of Liǔxià Jì's grave
to gather firewood,
they shall be put to death without pardon.'
They also issued an order:
'To whoever can obtain the head of the King of Qí,
we will grant a marquisate of ten thousand households
and a gift of one thousand gold yì.'
Judging from this,
the head of a living king
is not even equal to the grave of a dead scholar."
King Xuān was silent and displeased.
His attendants all said: "Chù, come here! Chù, come here!
Great King possesses a land of a thousand chariots,
and has cast bells of a thousand shí
and ten thousand shí.
The scholars of the world,
both the humane and the righteous, all come to serve and dwell here;
the eloquent and the wise come forward together,
and none fail to come and speak;
from east, west, south, and north,
none dare not submit.
He seeks all things and none are missing,
and of the hundred officials, none are not close and attached to him.
Now, those among scholars who are considered high
are called commoners,
living on foot in the farm fields,
or at the lowest, in rustic villages as gatekeepers and alley-dwellers;
the lowliness of the scholar
is also extreme!"
Chù replied:
"It is not so.
Chù has heard that in the time of the ancient Great Yǔ,
there were ten thousand states of feudal lords.
Why was this?
It was because the way of profound virtue
relies on the strength of respecting scholars.
Thus Shùn arose from the farm fields,
coming out of the rustic wilderness,
and became the Son of Heaven.
By the time of Tāng,
there were three thousand feudal lords.
In the present generation,
those who face south and call themselves 'the solitary one'
are only twenty-four.
Judging from this,
is it not a matter of the policy of gaining or losing scholars?
Gradually they are executed and eliminated,
and when the time of the total destruction of the
clan comes,
even if one wished to be a gatekeeper or an alley-dweller,
how could that be possible?"
Therefore, does the *Yì Zhuàn*
not say:
“To dwell in a high position
without obtaining its reality,
yet delighting in its name,
one will surely use arrogance and extravagance
as one’s conduct.
If there is arrogance and extravagance,
misfortune will follow.
Thus, those without reality who delight in the name are diminished;
those without virtue who hope for blessings are constrained;
those without merit who receive emoluments are disgraced;
and calamity will surely take hold.”
Therefore it is said:
“Merit that is boasted of will not be established;
empty desires will not be attained.”
These all refer to those who find joy in their reputation,
being flowery but lacking actual virtue.
Thus Yáo had nine assistants,
Shùn had seven friends,
Yǔ had five ministers,
and Tāng had three aides;
from ancient times until now, one who could achieve a hollow name throughout the world
has never existed.
For this reason, kings were not ashamed to ask questions frequently
and were not embarrassed to learn from those below them;
thus, those who perfected their Way and virtue and spread their merit and fame to later generations
were Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, and Zhōu Wén Wáng.
Therefore it is said:
“That which is formless
is the ruler of form.
That which is without a beginning
is the root of all affairs.”
If those above perceive the source
and those below understand the flow,
reaching the enlightened learning of the sages,
what could there be that is not auspicious!
Lǎo Zǐ said:
“Though noble,
one must take the lowly as the root;
though high,
one must take the low as the foundation.
Is this not why marquises and kings call themselves ‘the lonely,’ ‘the solitary,’ and ‘the unworthy’?
Is this not taking the lowly as the root?”
Are “the lonely” and “the solitary” not
the distressed and lowly positions of men?
Yet marquises and kings use these to refer to themselves;
is this not humbling themselves before others to honor noble scholars?
Yáo passed the throne to Shùn,
Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
and Zhōu Chéng Wáng entrusted Zhōu Gōng Dàn;
for generations they have been called enlightened rulers,
because they were clear about the nobility of scholars.”
Xuān Wáng said:
“Alas!
How could a gentleman be insulted?
I have brought this distress upon myself!
Having now heard the words of a gentleman,
I now understand the conduct of a petty man.
I wish to be accepted as your disciple.
Moreover, if Master Yán will associate with me,
his meals will surely consist of the great sacrifice,
his travels will surely be by carriage,
and the clothing of his wife and children will be beautiful and elegant.”
Yán Chù declined and left, saying:
“Jade is born in the mountains;
if it is carved, it is broken.
It is not that it is no longer precious,
but the raw stone is no longer whole.
A scholar is born in the rustic countryside;
if recommended and selected, he receives an emolument.
It is not that he does not attain honor and success,
but his form and spirit are no longer complete.
I, Chù, wish to return home,
to eat late so that hunger serves as meat,
to walk calmly so that it serves as a carriage,
to be without guilt so that it serves as nobility,
and to find joy in being pure, quiet, and upright.
The one who issues commands is the King;
the one who exhausts loyalty with blunt speech is Chù.
The essential points of my words are complete.
I ask for permission to return
and walk peacefully back to my
humble dwelling.”
He then bowed twice and departed.
Chù knew contentment;
returning to his original simplicity,
he was never disgraced for the rest of his life.
Master Wáng Dòu arrived at the gate and wished to see Qí Xuān Wáng.
Xuān Wáng sent an usher to invite him in.
Wáng Dòu said:
“For Dòu to hasten to see the King would be to love power;
for the King to hasten to see Dòu would be to love scholars.
Which would the King prefer?”
The messenger returned and reported this.
The King said:
“Let the Master wait;
I shall comply.”
Xuān Wáng then hastened to welcome him at the gate,
entered with him,
and said:
“I serve the ancestral temple of my late lords
and protect the altars of earth and grain.
I have heard that the Master speaks directly and offers upright admonitions without evasion.”
Wáng Dòu replied:
“The King has heard wrongly.
I, Dòu, was born in a chaotic age
and serve a chaotic ruler;
how could I dare speak directly and offer upright admonitions?”
Xuān Wáng’s face flushed with anger,
and he was displeased.
After a while,
Wáng Dòu said:
“In the past, what the late lord Huán Gōng loved
allowed him to assemble the feudal lords nine times
and unite the world as one;
the Son of Heaven recognized him
and established him as the Great Hegemon.
Now the King possesses four of his qualities.”
Xuān Wáng was pleased
and said:
“I am ignorant and simple,
guarding the state of Qí
only fearing that I might lose it.
How could I have four of them?”
Wáng Dòu said:
“No.
The late lord loved horses;
the King also loves horses.
The late lord loved dogs;
the King also loves dogs.
The late lord loved wine;
the King also loves wine.
The late lord loved women;
the King also loves women.
The late lord loved scholars;
but in this, the King does not love scholars.”
Xuān Wáng said:
“In the present world there are no scholars;
what should I love?”
Wáng Dòu said:
“The world lacks the steeds Qí Lín and Lù Ěr,
yet the King’s teams of four are complete.
The world lacks dogs like Dōng Guō Jùn or the hounds of Lú,
yet the King’s hunting dogs are already provided.
The world lacks beauties like Máo Qiáng or Xī Shī,
yet the King’s palace is already filled.
The King simply does not love scholars;
why worry about there being no scholars?”
The King said:
“I worry for the state and love the people;
I truly wish to obtain scholars to govern it.”
Wáng Dòu said:
“The King’s worry for the state and love for the people
is not equal to the King’s love for a foot of fine silk.”
The King said:
“What do you mean?”
Wáng Dòu said:
“When the King has someone make a cap,
he does not use his close attendants
but uses a craftsman. Why?
Because of his ability.
Now, when the King governs Qí,
he employs none but his close attendants;
therefore I say it is not equal to your love for a foot of fine silk.”
Xuān Wáng apologized, saying:
“I have committed a crime against the state.”
Thereupon, he promoted five scholars to official positions,
and the state of Qí was greatly well-governed.
The King of Qí sent an envoy to inquire after Zhào Wēi Hòu.
Before the letter was opened,
Wēi Hòu asked the envoy:
“Is the harvest without harm?
Are the people without harm?
Is the King without harm?”
The envoy was displeased
and said:
“I have been sent on a mission to Wēi Hòu;
now you do not ask after the King,
but first ask after the harvest and the people.
Is this not putting the lowly first and the honorable and noble last?”
Wēi Hòu said: “Not so.
If there were no harvest,
how could there be a people?
If there were no people,
how could there be a ruler?
Therefore, should one ask by setting aside the root and inquiring after the branch?”
Then she stepped forward and asked him, saying:
"In Qí, there is a recluse named Zhōnglí Zǐ;
is he well?
Such is his character:
those with food he feeds,
and those without food he also feeds;
those with clothes he clothes,
and those without clothes he also clothes.
This is helping the King
nourish his people;
why is it that until now he has not been given an official post?
Is Yèyáng Zǐ well?
Such is his character:
he pities the widowers and widows,
cares for the orphans and the childless,
relieves the distressed and poor,
and supplements the needy.
This is helping the King sustain his people;
why is it that until now he has not been given an official post?
Is the daughter of Běigōng, Yīng'ér Zǐ, well?
She removed her
earrings and pendants,
remained unmarried until old age
in order to care for her parents.
These all lead the people to act out of filial devotion;
why is it that until now she has not been summoned to court?
If these two gentlemen are not given posts
and this one woman is not summoned to court,
how can one be King of Qí
and be a father to the myriad people?
Is Yúlíng Zǐzhòng still alive?
Such is his character:
above, he does not serve as a minister to the King;
below, he does not manage his family;
in between, he does not seek to associate with the feudal lords.
This leads the people to become
useless;
why is it that until now he has not been executed?"
A man of Qí saw Tián Pián
and said: "I have heard of your high-minded discussions, Master,
where you pretend not to desire officialdom,
yet wish to serve."
Tián Pián said: "How did you hear of this?"
He replied:
"I heard it from my neighbor's daughter."
Tián Pián said:
"What does that mean?"
He replied:
"My neighbor's daughter
pretended not to wish to marry,
yet at age thirty she has seven children;
though she says she is not married,
she has in fact done more than if she were married.
Now you, Master, pretend not to desire officialdom,
yet your wealth and maintenance are a thousand zhōng,
and your followers number a hundred;
though you say you are not an official,
you are in fact wealthier than those who are."
Tián Zǐ declined to answer.
Guǎn Yàn offended the King of Qí
and said to his attendants:
"Who among you will follow me to the feudal lords?"
The attendants remained silent and did not respond.
Guǎn Yàn's tears fell in succession as he said:
"How sad! Why are men of talent so easy to obtain but so difficult to employ?"
Tián Xū replied:
"A man of talent may not have enough to eat even after three meals,
while your geese and ducks have surplus food;
in your inner chambers, there is a mix of silks and fine gauze,
and you trail patterned satins,
while a man of talent cannot even afford them for a border on his clothes. Moreover, wealth is what you, my lord, value lightly,
while death is what the man of talent values heavily.
If you are unwilling to give what you value lightly to the man of talent,
yet demand that the man of talent serve you with what he values heavily,
it is not that men of talent are easy to obtain but difficult to employ."
Sū Qín went from Yān to Qí
and was received at the South Gate of Huázhāng.
The King of Qí said:
"Aha! You have come.
Qín has sent Wèi Rǎn to offer me the title of Emperor;
what do you think of this?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty’s question to me is abrupt,
but the root from which trouble arises is subtle.
If you do not listen now,
it will offend Qín;
if you do listen,
it will offend the world.
It would be better to listen to the proposal to satisfy Qín,
but do not actually assume the title for the sake of the world.
If Qín assumes the title
and the world accepts it,
then Your Majesty should also assume it;
whether done sooner or later,
the name of Emperor will not be harmed.
If Qín assumes the title
but the world does not accept it,
Your Majesty should then not assume it;
in this way you can win over the world,
which is a great asset."
Sū Qín said to the King of Qí:
"If Qí and Qín stand together as the two Emperors,
do you think the world will honor Qín
or honor Qí?"
The King said:
"They would honor Qín."
"If you renounce the title of Emperor, will the world love Qí
or love Qín?"
The King said:
"They would love Qí and hate Qín."
"If the two Emperors are established
and agree to attack Zhào,
how would that compare to the benefit of attacking Sòng?"
He replied:
"If you agree to become Emperor along with Qín,
the world will solely honor Qín and despise Qí; but if Qí renounces the title,
then the world will love Qí and hate Qín.
Attacking Zhào is not as beneficial as attacking Sòng.
Therefore, I wish Your Majesty would clearly renounce the title
to win over the world;
break the agreement and distance yourself from Qín,
so as not to contend for prestige;
and meanwhile, Your Majesty can take Sòng.
If you hold Sòng, then Yángchéng of Wèi will be in danger;
if you hold Huáiběi, then the eastern lands of Chǔ will be in danger;
if you hold Jìxī, then Hédōng of Zhào will be in danger;
if you hold Yīn and Pínglù, then the gates of Liáng will not open.
Therefore, by renouncing the title of Emperor and instead turning to the matter of attacking Sòng,
the state will be important and your name honored;
Yān and Chǔ will submit out of necessity,
and the world will not dare but obey.
This is the achievement of Tāng and Wǔ.
Show respect to Qín as a matter of pretense
and then cause the world to hate them;
this is what is called exchanging a lower position for a superior one!
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully!"
Sū Qín spoke to King Mǐn of Qí, saying:
"I have heard that those who use troops and take pleasure in being ahead of the world will have worries;
those who form alliances and take pleasure in leading resentment will be isolated.
To rise later is to use leverage;
to keep distance from resentment is to wait for the right time.
Therefore, when a sage handles affairs,
he must rely on leverage and strive to rise with the times.
Leverage
is the guide of all things,
and the momentum of the times
is the leader of all affairs.
Thus, without leverage
and going against the momentum of the times,
few can achieve success.
Now even with swords like Gānjiàng and Mòyé,
without human strength,
they cannot cut or wound.
Even with sturdy arrows and sharp metal,
without the advantage of the bowstring and trigger,
they cannot kill from afar.
It is not that the arrow is not sharp
or the sword is not keen;
why is this?
Because the leverage is not there.
How do we know this is so?
Formerly, when the Zhào clan attacked Wèi,
their chariots and men did not rest from their armor,
the walls of the state of Wèi were leveled,
and of its eight gates, the earth was piled against some and two were destroyed.
This was the shape of a falling state.
The Lord of Wèi walked barefoot
and appealed to Wèi.
The King of Wèi personally donned armor and gripped his sword
to challenge Zhào to battle.
Within Hándān, people fled in panic,
and the region between the River
and the mountains was in chaos.
Having gained this leverage,
Wèi also collected its remaining soldiers and faced north,
destroying Gāngpíng
and toppling the outer walls of Zhōngmóu.
It was not that Wèi was stronger than Zhào;
it is like Wèi being the arrow and Wèi being the bowstring and trigger.
By relying on the strength of Wèi, they gained the land of Hédōng.
The Zhào clan was afraid,
and the people of Chǔ saved Zhào by attacking Wèi.
They fought west of Zhōu,
came out of the Liáng Gate,
camped their army in the forest,
and watered their horses at the River.
Having gained this leverage,
Zhào also attacked Wèi north of the River, burned Jígōu,
and destroyed Huángchéng.
Therefore, the ruin of Gāngpíng,
the fall of Zhōngmóu,
the collapse of Huángchéng,
and the burning of Jígōu—
none of these were the original desires of Zhào and Wèi.
Yet, as for the reason these two states were encouraged to carry them out,
why was it?
It was because Wèi was clear about the leverage of the times.
Those who govern states in the present age are not like this.
Their armies are weak, yet they love to provoke the strong;
their states are exhausted, yet they love to incite mass resentment;
their affairs fail, yet they love to hold investigations;
their armies are weak, yet they despise their subordinates;
their lands are narrow, yet they love to provoke the great;
their affairs fail, yet they love to prolong deceptions.
To seek hegemony while practicing these six things
is indeed far-fetched.
"I have heard that those who are good at governing a state
follow the will of the people
and assess the capability of their troops,
and only then do they follow the affairs of the world.
Thus, in their alliances, they do not attract resentment for the sake of others,
and in their attacks, they do not exhaust the strong for the sake of others.
In this way,
their troops are not wasted,
their authority is not lightened,
their territory can be expanded,
and their desires can be fulfilled.
In the past,
when Qí joined with Hán and Wèi to attack Qín and Chǔ,
the fighting was not particularly intense,
and the land they divided was not more than that of Hán and Wèi.
Yet, why was it that only Qí was blamed by the world?
Why was that?
Because it attracted resentment for the sake of Hán and Wèi.
Furthermore, the whole world was using its armies;
Qí and Yàn were at war,
while the Zhào clan annexed Zhōngshān;
Qín and Chǔ fought Hán and Wèi without rest,
while Sòng and Yuè exclusively employed their troops.
Among these ten states,
all were intent on opposing one another,
yet why did they all direct their focus toward Qí?
Why was that?
Because in its alliances, Qí loved to attract resentment for others,
and in its attacks, it loved to exhaust the strong for others.
"Moreover, the calamity of the great and powerful
often comes from being intent on ruling others;
the misfortune of the weak and small
often comes from seeking profit through plotting against others.
Thus it is that great states are endangered
and small states are destroyed.
For the plan of a great state,
nothing is better than rising later and heavily punishing the unrighteous.
When one has the advantage of rising later, allies are many and troops are strong;
then one's affairs use the many and strong to face the exhausted and few,
and military success will surely be established.
If one's actions do not block the heart of the world,
then profit will surely follow.
If a great state practices this,
then fame and titles will arrive without being seized,
and kingship and hegemony will be established without effort.
For the situation of a small state,
nothing is better than remaining quiet and placing little trust in the feudal lords.
By remaining quiet,
the four neighbors will not turn against it;
by placing little trust in the feudal lords,
the world will not sell it out.
If it is not sold out externally
and there is no rebellion internally,
then the weapons of war will rot from disuse,
and the silks and fabrics will be worn by insects rather than used for tribute.
If a small state follows this path,
then it will find fortune without offering sacrifices
and will see itself sufficient without borrowing.
Therefore it is said:
Those who take benevolence as their ancestor rule as kings;
those who establish righteousness rule as hegemons;
those who exhaust their troops until they are spent will perish.
How do we know this is so?
In the past, King Fūchāi of Wú used his power and greatness to lead the world,
forcibly raided Yǐng and trapped Yuè,
made the rulers of the feudal lords follow him,
yet in the end, he died and his state was destroyed,
becoming a laughingstock to the world.
Why was that?
It was because Fūchāi plotted for kingship while living in peace,
and because being powerful, he loved to be the first to meet the world's calamities.
In the past, Lái and Jǔ loved to plot;
Chén and Cài loved to deceive.
Jǔ relied on Yuè and was destroyed;
Cài relied on Jìn and perished.
These are all cases of cultivating deception internally
and the misfortune of trusting the feudal lords externally.
Viewing it from this,
the calamities of the strong, weak, great, and small
can be seen in past events.
"The saying goes:
'When the Qíjì steed is failing,
a common horse will lead it;
when Mèng Bèn is exhausted,
a woman can defeat him.'
Now, the common horse and the woman,
in terms of the strength of their sinews and bones,
are not superior to the Qíjì or Mèng Bèn.
Why then?
It is the advantage of rising later.
Today, the states of the world do not perish all at once.
If one possesses strength, stays the troops, and rises later,
attributing resentment to others while punishing the unrighteous,
using the military sparingly and basing it on righteousness,
then the conquest of the world can be awaited while standing still.
One who is clear about the circumstances of the feudal lords
and perceptive about the principles of the terrain
does not need formal alliances to be close,
does not need to exchange hostages to be firm,
is not hurried yet is swift,
handles many affairs without reversals,
divides territory without mutual hatred,
and remains both strong and friendly.
Why then?
Because their situations share the same worries and their troops pursue the same profits.
How do we know this is so?
In the past, Yàn and Qí fought at Huánzhīqū;
Yàn was not victorious,
and its army of one hundred thousand was completely lost.
The Hú people raided several counties of Yàn in Lóufán,
taking their cattle and horses.
Now, the Hú and the Qí were not traditionally close,
and their use of troops was not based on any alliance or hostage to plot against Yàn;
yet they moved faster than those who had joined together.
Why was that?
It was because their situations shared the same worries and their troops pursued the same profits.
From this perspective,
an alliance in a shared situation makes the profit last;
by rising later, the feudal lords can be made to follow.
Therefore, if a wise ruler or a discerning minister
truly wishes to make kingship and hegemony their goal,
then war and attack should not be their priority.
War
is the ruin of a state
and the exhaustion of its capitals and counties.
When ruin and exhaustion have come first,
those who can make the feudal lords follow are few.
As for the ruin caused by those wars:
when soldiers hear of war, they hand over their private wealth to enrich the military markets,
they provide food and drink to prepare the death-defying soldiers;
they are ordered to break their wagon axles for fuel
and kill their oxen to feast the soldiers;
this is the way to bankrupt the ruler.
Common people offer prayers;
the ruler hides and drinks;
major capitals and small counties set up shrines;
every town with a market stops its business to serve the king.
This is a plan for an empty center.
On the day after the battle,
there are corpses to bury and wounded to tend.
Even if there seems to be merit,
the army's expenses go out
and weeping is heard within;
thus the heart of the ruler is wounded.
The families of the dead are broken by funeral costs,
the wounded empty their wealth to pay for medicine,
and those who return whole celebrate with drink and music;
thus their expenses are equal to those of the dead and wounded.
Therefore, what the people spend
cannot be repaid even by ten years of harvests.
Of what the army puts forth:
spears and halberds are broken,
bowstrings are snapped,
crossbows are damaged,
chariots are smashed,
horses are exhausted,
and more than half of the arrows are lost.
The equipment of armor and weapons,
whether provided by the officials,
hidden by the officers,
or stolen by the servants,
cannot be repaid even by ten years of harvests.
When the world has these double expenses,
those who can make the feudal lords follow are few.
As for the cost of attacking a city:
the common people prepare work-clothing,
they lift the battering rams,
families are thrown into disorder,
they live in holes and pits,
and they are exhausted by metal tools.
The soldiers are weary from earthworks,
and the generals do not take off their armor.
Only after a long period of time can they take a city quickly.
The superiors are tired of giving instructions,
and the soldiers are cut down by weapons;
thus, those who can take three cities and still defeat the enemy are few.
Therefore it is said:
those who engage in warfare and offense
do not prioritize correctly.
How is it known to be so?
Formerly, Zhì Bó Yáo attacked the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
killed their lords,
and extinguished their states.
He then moved west to besiege Jìnyáng;
having annexed two states,
he caused worry to another ruler.
This was the peak of his military power.
Yet Zhì Bó ultimately died and his state perished,
becoming a laughingstock to all under heaven.
What was the reason?
He prioritized warfare and offense,
and thus suffered the calamity of the two he extinguished.
In former times,
Zhōngshān raised its entire force to face Yān and Zhào.
They fought to the south at Zhǎngzǐ
and defeated the Zhào clan; they fought to the north in Zhōngshān,
overcame the Yān army,
and killed their general.
Now, Zhōngshān was a state of a thousand chariots,
yet it faced two states of ten thousand chariots.
Fighting twice and winning twice,
this was the highest achievement in the use of soldiers.
Nevertheless, the state ultimately perished,
and its ruler became a subject to Qí.
Why was this?
He was not sparing regarding the calamities of warfare and offense.
Viewing it from this perspective,
then the failure of warfare and offense
can be seen in past events.
“Those in the present age who are called experts in the use of soldiers
fight to the end and achieve victory after victory,
and their defenses cannot be breached.
All under heaven call them skilled,
and their state is preserved through this.
However, this is not a benefit to the state.
I have heard that when a battle is a great victory,
many of its soldiers die and the army becomes even weaker;
when a defense cannot be breached,
its people are exhausted and the city walls are left exposed.
When soldiers die abroad,
the people are harmed within,
and the city walls are exposed on the borders,
then this is not a joy for a king.
Now, a target has no grievance or fault against anyone, yet men prepare their bows and draw their crossbows to shoot at it.
Those who hit it are considered skilled,
while those who miss feel ashamed.
Young and old, noble and low,
all share the same mind in wanting to pierce it.
Why is this?
They dislike that it presents a challenge to people.
Now, to exhaust oneself in war and win every battle,
and to ensure defenses are never breached,
then this is not only presenting a challenge to people,
but also harming them.
If so, then all under heaven will surely treat them as enemies.
To exhaust soldiers and expose the state,
while making many enemies under heaven,
is something an enlightened ruler does not abide.
To habitually use strong troops and thus weaken them
is something a discerning minister does not practice.
Those enlightened rulers and discerning ministers
cause the feudal lords to follow them without moving the five types of weapons;
through courteous yielding, heavy bribes arrive.
Therefore, in the warfare of an enlightened ruler,
victory is won over enemy states without the armor and weapons leaving the camp;
border cities surrender without the deployment of battering rams or siege towers;
and the kingly achievement is attained without the soldiers or people even knowing of it.
In the undertakings of an enlightened ruler,
wealth used is minimal,
and though the time span is long, the benefits are lasting.
Therefore it is said:
if military force is used only as a last resort, the feudal lords can be made to serve.
“What I have heard is that
the way of offense and warfare does not rely on a large host;
though there be an army of a million,
it is as if compared in the hall;
though there be generals like Hélǘ or Wú Qǐ,
they are captured within the gates.
A city wall of a thousand zhàng
can be uprooted between the wine vessel and the meat stand;
a hundred-foot battering ram
can be broken upon the sleeping mat.
Thus, while the sounds of bells, drums, pipes, and zithers do not cease,
territory can be expanded and desires fulfilled.
While the laughter of harmonious music, entertainers, and jesters does not end,
the feudal lords can be summoned on the same day.
Therefore, having a name that rivals heaven and earth is not considered the height of honor,
and having profits that control all within the seas is not considered the height of abundance.
Thus, for one who is skilled in kingly achievement,
it lies in exhausting all under heaven while remaining at ease oneself,
bringing chaos to all under heaven while remaining secure oneself.
If the feudal lords have no successful plans,
then the state will have no long-standing worries.
How is this known to be so?
Ease and order reside with me,
while exhaustion and chaos reside in all under heaven;
such is the way of a king.
If sharp troops come, then repel them;
if calamity arrives, then hasten to meet it.
Ensure that the feudal lords have no successful plans,
and then the state will have no long-standing worries.
How is this known to be so?
Formerly, the Wèi Wáng held a thousand lǐ of land
and commanded three hundred and sixty thousand armored troops.
With his strength, he seized Hándān,
besieged Dìngyáng in the west,
and further led twelve feudal lords to pay court to the Son of Heaven,
planning to attack Qín in the west.
The Qín Wáng was terrified of him;
he could not sleep peacefully on his mat,
and his food had no flavor.
He issued orders within his borders,
turning everything within the battlements into war implements,
and completing defensive preparations.
He appointed generals for the suicide squads
to await the Wèi clan.
Wèi Yāng counseled the Qín Wáng, saying:
‘The achievements of the Wèi clan are great,
and their orders are carried out throughout all under heaven.
They have twelve feudal lords to pay court to the Son of Heaven,
so their allies must be many.
Therefore, for a single Qín to face the great Wèi,
I fear it is not equal to the task.
Why does Your Majesty not send me to see the Wèi Wáng?
Then I beg to surely cause the defeat of Wèi.’
The Qín Wáng agreed.
Wèi Yāng met with the Wèi Wáng and said:
‘Your Majesty’s achievements are great indeed,
and your orders are carried out throughout all under heaven.
Now, the twelve feudal lords that follow Your Majesty
are not Sòng or Wèi;
they are Zōu, Lǔ, Chén, and Cài.
These are merely those whom Your Majesty can drive with a whip;
they are not sufficient to rule all under heaven as a king.
Your Majesty would be better off taking Yān in the north
and attacking Qí in the east,
then Zhào will surely follow.
Take Qín in the west
and attack Chǔ in the south,
then Hán will surely follow.
If Your Majesty has the heart to attack Qí
and Chǔ, and the will to make all under heaven follow,
then the kingly achievement will be manifest.
Your Majesty should first adopt the royal garments of a king,
and only then plot against Qí and Chǔ.’
The Wèi Wáng was pleased with Wèi Yāng’s words.
Therefore, he expanded his palace,
made red-clothed pillars,
set up the nine-streamered banner, and followed the seven-starred flag.
These belong to the position of the Son of Heaven, yet the Wèi Wáng occupied it.
At this, Qí and Chǔ were enraged.
The feudal lords fled to Qí,
and the people of Qí attacked Wèi,
killing its crown prince
and overturning its army of a hundred thousand.
The Wèi Wáng was greatly terrified.
He walked barefoot, withdrew his troops to the capital,
and then traveled east to wait upon Qí.
Only then did all under heaven leave him alone.
At that time,
the Qín Wáng sat with folded arms and received the lands beyond the Xīhé,
without feeling any gratitude toward the Wèi Wáng.
Thus it is said that when Wèi Yāng first planned with the Qín Wáng,
the plan was made without leaving the mat;
the words were spoken between the wine vessel and the meat stand;
the strategy was completed in the hall;
and yet the Wèi general was captured by Qí.
Without the deployment of battering rams or siege towers,
the lands beyond the Xīhé were incorporated into Qín.
This is what I meant by “compared in the hall,
capturing the general within the gates,
uprooting cities between the wine vessel and the meat stand,
and breaking the assault upon the mat.”
Among the people of Qí living near the city walls, there was a man named Gūhú Xuǎn who criticized Mǐn Wáng with upright words;
the King had him executed at Tánqú,
and the common people no longer adhered to him.
Chén Jǔ, a member of the Qí royal clan, spoke directly;
the King killed him at Dōnglǘ,
and the royal clan became estranged in heart.
Sīmǎ Rángjū was one who conducted the administration;
the King killed him,
and the high ministers no longer felt close to him.
For this reason, Yān raised troops
and sent Chāngguó Jūn to lead them in an attack.
Qí sent Xiàngzǐ to lead the response.
The Qí army was broken,
and Xiàngzǐ fled with a single chariot.
Dázǐ gathered the remaining soldiers,
rallied them again, and fought with Yān.
He requested rewards to compensate them,
but Mǐn Wáng refused to give them,
so the army was broken and fled.
The Wáng fled to Jǔ,
and Nào Chǐ rebuked him, saying:
“Between Qiānshèng and Bóchāng,
across an area of several hundred lǐ,
it rained blood that soaked people’s clothes;
did the Wáng know of this?”
The Wáng said:
“I did not.”
“Between Yíng and Bó,
the earth split open down to the springs;
did the Wáng know of this?”
The Wáng said:
“I did not.”
“There was a person who stood before the palace gates and wailed;
when sought, he could not be found,
but when one left, his voice could be heard;
did the Wáng know of this?”
The Wáng said:
“I did not.”
Nào Chǐ said:
“The heaven raining blood that soaks clothes
was Heaven giving a warning;
the earth splitting down to the springs
was Earth giving a warning;
the person wailing before the palace gates
was Man giving a warning.
Heaven, Earth, and Man have all given warnings,
yet the Wáng did not know to take heed;
how can you escape being executed?”
Thereupon, he killed Mǐn Wáng at Gǔlǐ.
The Tàizǐ then removed his garments and discarded his official robes,
escaping to the house of the Tàishǐ clan to serve as a gardener.
Jūnwáng Hòu,
the daughter of the Tàishǐ clan,
recognized that he was a person of noble rank
and served him well.
Tián Dān used the city of Jímò
and the remaining defeated soldiers
to crush the Yān army,
deceiving Qí Jié.
He then restored Qí
and immediately welcomed the Tàizǐ at Jǔ,
establishing him as the Wáng.
When Xiāng Wáng ascended the throne,
Jūnwáng Hòu became his Hòu
and gave birth to Qí Wáng Jiàn.
Concerning the service to Mǐn Wáng:
Wángsūn Jiǎ was fifteen years old
and served Mǐn Wáng. When the Wáng fled,
he lost track of the Wáng’s location.
His mother said:
“If you go out in the morning and return late,
then I lean against the door and watch for you;
if you go out at dusk and do not return,
then I lean against the lane gate and watch for you.
You now serve the Wáng;
the Wáng has fled,
and you do not know his location.
How can you still return home?”
Wángsūn Jiǎ then entered the marketplace
and said:
“Nào Chǐ has brought chaos to the state of Qí
and killed Mǐn Wáng.
Those who wish to execute him with me,
bare your right shoulders!”
Four hundred people from the marketplace followed him,
and with them he executed Nào Chǐ,
stabbing and killing him.
Yān attacked Qí
and took more than seventy cities;
only Jǔ and Jímò did not fall.
Tián Dān of Qí used Jímò to defeat Yān
and killed Qí Jié.
Initially,
a general of Yān had attacked and captured Liáochéng,
but someone slandered him.
The Yān general feared execution
and thus held Liáochéng defensively,
not daring to return.
Tián Dān attacked it for over a year;
many soldiers died,
and yet Liáochéng did not fall.
Lǔ Lián then wrote a letter,
tied it to an arrow to shoot into the city,
and sent it to the Yān general, saying:
“I have heard that
a wise person does not turn against the times and abandon profit,
a brave warrior does not fear death and destroy his name,
and a loyal minister does not put his own person before his Jūn.
Now you, Gōng, are acting on a momentary anger,
disregarding that the Yān Wáng lacks ministers;
this is not loyalty.
To lose your life and lose Liáochéng,
while your prestige is not established in Qí;
this is not bravery.
With your achievements discarded and your name extinguished,
and no praise from future generations;
this is not wisdom.
Therefore, a wise person does not deliberate twice,
and a brave warrior does not fear death.
Now, life or death, glory or disgrace,
honor or lowliness, nobility or meanness—
this is the moment.
I hope you, Gōng, will plan carefully and not be like the common crowd.
Furthermore, Chǔ is attacking Nányáng,
Wèi is attacking Pínglù,
and Qí has no intention of facing south,
considering that the harm of losing Nányáng
is not as great as the profit of gaining Jǐběi.
Therefore, they have settled their plan and are holding it firmly.
Now that the Qín people have sent down their troops,
Wèi does not dare to face east.
When the Héng alliance with Qín is joined,
then the situation of the state of Chǔ will be perilous.
Moreover, to abandon Nányáng,
sever the right territory,
and preserve Jǐběi—
the plan will certainly be to do this.
Now that Chǔ and Wèi have both retreated,
and relief from Yān does not arrive,
Qí has no other global concerns.
To endure the weariness of holding Liáochéng for a full year—
I see that you, Gōng, will not be able to succeed.
Qí will certainly settle the matter at Liáochéng;
you, Gōng, should not deliberate twice.
That state of Yān is in great chaos;
the Jūn and ministers have miscalculated,
and those above and below are bewildered.
Lì Fù, with a million troops,
was defeated five times abroad.
A state of ten thousand chariots
was besieged in Zhào,
its territory was carved away and its Jūn was distressed,
becoming a laughingstock for the world.
Have you, Gōng, heard of this?
Now the Yān Wáng is shivering with fear and standing alone,
his ministers are not worth relying on,
the state is exhausted and full of disasters,
and the people’s hearts have nowhere to turn.
Now you, Gōng, again take the exhausted people of Liáochéng
to resist the army of the whole of Qí.
For a full year the siege has not been lifted;
this is the defense of Mò Dí.
Eating people and burning bones for fuel,
the soldiers have no intention of fleeing.
This is the kind of army led by Sūn Bìn or Wú Qǐ.
You have shown your ability to the world!
Therefore, in planning for you, Gōng,
it would be better to withdraw the troops and rest the soldiers,
keep the chariots and armor intact,
and return to report to the Yān Wáng.
The Yān Wáng will surely be pleased.
When the soldiers and people see you, Gōng,
it will be like seeing their parents.
Your associates will roll up their sleeves and speak of you to the world;
your achievements will be made clear.
Above, you can assist your isolated Jūn
to control the ministers;
below, you can nourish the common people
to provide for the traveling scholars.
Correcting the state and reforming customs before the world,
your merit and fame can be established.
Or perhaps,
will you also abandon Yān and renounce the world
to travel east to Qí?
Let them divide the land and grant you a fief,
with wealth comparable to Táo or Wèi,
where your descendants for generations will call themselves Gūguǎ,
enduring along with Qí.
This is also a plan.
Both options offer illustrious fame and substantial benefits.
I hope you, Gōng, will deliberate deeply and carefully choose one of them.
Furthermore, I have heard
that those who emulate small points of etiquette cannot exercise great authority,
and those who detest small shames cannot establish an honorable name.
In the past, Guǎn Zhòng shot Huán Gōng and hit his belt buckle;
that was an act of usurpation.
He abandoned Gōngzǐ Jiū and could not die for him;
that was cowardice.
He was bound in shackles and fetters;
that was a disgrace to his person.
These three behaviors
would not be accepted in one's home village,
and a Wáng of the age would not employ such a person as a minister.”
If Guǎn Zhòng had remained in poverty and suppression,
imprisoned and not released,
shamed and not seen,
until the end of his years and the end of his life,
he could not have avoided being a disgraced man of lowly conduct.
However, Guǎn Zǐ combined the faults of his three courses of action,
took charge of the government of Qí Guó,
unified and corrected the world,
convened the feudal lords nine times,
became the head of the Wǔ Bó,
gained a name high throughout the world,
and his light shone upon neighboring states.
Cáo Mò served as a general for the Lǔ Jūn,
fought three battles and suffered three defeats,
losing a thousand lǐ of land.
Had Cáo Zǐ’s feet not left the ranks,
had his plans not looked to the future, and had he gone out determined to die without living,
then he could not have avoided being a general of a defeated army and a captured commander.
For Cáo Zǐ, to be a general of a defeated army and a captured commander would not be bravery;
for his achievements to be discarded and his name extinguished,
with nothing to be praised by later generations, would not be wisdom.
Therefore, he put aside the shame of three defeats
and retreated to deliberate with the Lǔ Jūn;
Cáo Zǐ considered this a meeting of opportunity.
Qí Huán Gōng possessed the world
and held court for the feudal lords.
Cáo Zǐ, with the responsibility of a single sword,
kidnapped Huán Gōng atop the altar,
his expression unchanging
and his words and tone not defiant.
That which was lost in three battles,
he returned in a single morning.
The world was shaken and terrified;
his majesty and prestige reached Wú and Chǔ,
and his name was passed down to later generations.
As for these two gentlemen,
it was not that they could not practice small integrity
or die for a small shame,
but they believed that to kill oneself and end one's lineage
without establishing merit or a name
would not be wisdom.
Therefore, they set aside a heart of resentment
to achieve a name that would be repeatedly proclaimed;
they removed the shame of felt resentment
to establish merit for successive generations.
Thus their legacy competes in flow with the Three Kings,
and their names will only perish along with heaven and earth.
May you, General, consider this!
The Yàn general said:
“I respectfully hear your command!”
Thereupon he withdrew the troops and returned to Dù, then left.
Thus, the lifting of the siege of Qí Guó
and the saving of the common people from death
were the results of the persuasion of Zhòng Lián.
Yàn attacked Qí,
and Qí was broken.
Mǐn Wáng fled to Jǔ,
and Nào Chǐ killed Mǐn Wáng.
Tián Dān held the city of Jímò,
broke the Yàn army,
and restored the ruins of Qí.
Xiāng Wáng was summoned as the Crown Prince.
Because Qí had been broken by Yàn,
Tián Dān’s position was suspect;
the multitudes of Qí Guó
all thought that Tián Dān would establish himself.
When Xiāng Wáng was established,
Tián Dān served as his Prime Minister.
While crossing the Zī Shuǐ,
there was an old man wading through the Zī who was cold;
upon coming out he could not walk
and sat in the sand.
Tián Dān saw that he was cold
and wanted to have the following carriage share clothing with him,
but there was none to be shared.
Dān untied his own fur robe and clothed him.
Xiāng Wáng disliked this,
saying:
“Is Tián Dān’s charity
intended to take my state?
If I do not plan early,
I fear I will be surpassed by him.”
He looked around and saw no one,
but beneath the crags there was one who was stringing pearls;
Xiāng Wáng called and asked him, saying:
“Did you hear my words?”
He replied:
“I heard them.”
The King said:
“What do you think of them?”
He replied:
“It would be better for the King to take this as your own goodness.
If the King commends Dān’s goodness
and issues an order saying: ‘The Solitary One worried about the hunger of the people,
and Dān collected and fed them;
The Solitary One worried about the cold of the people,
and Dān untied his fur robe and clothed them;
The Solitary One worries and labors for the common people,
and Dān also worries for them,
matching the Solitary One’s intent.’
Dān having this goodness and the King commending it,
and treating Dān’s goodness as good,
is also the King’s own goodness.”
The King said:
“Excellent!”
He then bestowed cattle and wine upon Dān
and commended his conduct.
Several days later,
the pearl-stringer again saw the King and said:
“When the King goes to court,
you should summon Tián Dān and bow to him in the courtyard,
comforting him with words.
Then publish an order to seek out those among the common people who are hungry or cold,
and collect grain to give to them.”
He then sent people to listen in the neighborhoods,
and they heard the men speaking with one another,
all saying:
“How Tián Dān loves the people!
Ah, this is the influence of the King’s teaching!”
Diāo Bó often disliked Tián Dān,
saying:
“Ānpíng Jūn
is a petty man.”
Ānpíng Jūn heard of this,
and so he prepared wine and summoned Diāo Bó,
saying:
“How have I offended you, Sir,
that I am often praised by you at court?”
Diāo Bó said:
“Zhí’s dog barked at Yáo,
not because it valued Zhí and despised Yáo,
but because a dog naturally barks at those who are not its master.
Moreover, if we now suppose Gōngsūn Zǐ is worthy
and Xú Zǐ is unworthy,
yet if Gōngsūn Zǐ and Xú Zǐ were made to fight,
Xú Zǐ’s dog
would still occasionally seize Gōngsūn Zǐ’s calf and bite it.
If it were to leave the unworthy one
and become the dog of the worthy one,
would it only seize his calf and bite it?”
Ānpíng Jūn said: “I respectfully hear your command.”
The next day, he recommended him to the King.
Among the King’s favorites were nine men of a certain sort
who wished to harm Ānpíng Jūn.
They spoke together to the King, saying:
“At the time when Yàn attacked Qí,
the King of Chǔ sent a general leading ten thousand men to assist Qí.
Now that the state is settled
and the altars of soil and grain are secure,
why not send an envoy to thank the King of Chǔ?”
The King said: “Who among those around me is suitable?”
The nine men of that sort said:
“Diāo Bó is suitable.”
Diāo Bó was sent as an envoy to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ received him and toasted him,
and he did not return for several days.
The nine men of that sort spoke together to the King, saying:
“For a single person
to be detained by a state of ten thousand chariots—
is it not because he relies on his influence?
Moreover, regarding the relationship between Ānpíng Jūn and the King,
between lord and minister there is no ritual propriety,
and between superior and inferior there is no distinction.
Furthermore, his intent is to do what is not good.
Internally he tends to the common people,
following and comforting their hearts,
relieving the destitute and supplementing those who have not enough,
and spreading virtue among the people;
externally he cherishes the Róng and Dí and the worthy scholars of the world,
and secretly forms ties with the heroes and outstanding men of the feudal lords.
His intent is to take action.
We hope the King will observe this.”
On another day, the King said:
“Summon Minister Dān to come.”
Tián Dān removed his cap, went barefoot, and bared his torso to advance;
he withdrew and requested punishment for a capital crime.
Five days later,
the King said:
“You have no guilt toward the Solitary One;
you perform your ritual propriety as a minister,
and I perform my ritual propriety as a King, and that is all.”
Diāo Bó came back from Chǔ,
and the King granted him a seat before him.
When the wine had flowed freely,
the King said:
“Summon Minister Tián Dān to come.”
Diāo Bó left his mat, kowtowed, and said:
“How can the King speak such words that lead to the ruin of a state?
How does the King compare to Zhōu Wén Wáng?”
The King said:
"I am not his equal."
Diāo Bó said:
"True,
I certainly knew that Your Majesty was not his equal.
How do you compare to Duke Huán of Qí?"
The King said:
"I am not his equal."
Diāo Bó said:
"True,
I certainly knew that Your Majesty was not his equal.
However, King Wén of Zhōu gained Lǚ Shàng and regarded him as Tài Gōng;
Duke Huán of Qí gained Guǎn Yíwú and regarded him as Zhòngfù;
now Your Majesty has gained Ānpíng Jūn, yet you refer to him only as 'Dān'.
Furthermore, since the opening of heaven and earth
and the governance of the people,
among those who have performed the merits of a subject,
who has been more generous than Ānpíng Jūn?
Yet Your Majesty says 'Dān, Dān'.
How can you use such language that leads to the ruin of a state?
Moreover, Your Majesty could not protect the altars of the former kings;
the men of Yàn raised an army and raided the ruins of Qí,
and Your Majesty fled to the mountains of Chéngyáng.
With the trembling city of Jímò,
a city of three lǐ,
an outer wall of five lǐ,
and seven thousand exhausted soldiers, Ānpíng Jūn
captured their Sīmǎ
and recovered the thousand-lǐ territory of Qí;
this was the merit of Ānpíng Jūn.
At that time,
he could have enclosed Chéngyáng and declared himself king;
neither Chéngyáng nor the world could have stopped him.
However, considering the Way
and returning to righteousness,
he deemed it unacceptable.
Therefore, he constructed plank roads and wooden galleries
to welcome Your Majesty and the Queen from the Chéngyáng mountains;
Your Majesty was then able to return
and preside over the hundred surnames as their sovereign.
Now the state is settled
and the people are at peace,
yet Your Majesty says 'Dān'.
Even an infant's plan would not be like this.
If Your Majesty does not quickly kill these nine sons to apologize to Ānpíng Jūn,
otherwise,
the state will be in danger!"
The King then killed the nine sons and banished their families,
and increased Ānpíng Jūn's fief with ten thousand households in Yè Yì.
Tián Dān was about to attack Dí
and went to see Lǔ Zhòngzǐ.
Lǔ Zhòngzǐ said: "If the General attacks Dí,
he will be unable to take it."
Tián Dān said: "With a city of five lǐ,
an outer wall of seven lǐ,
and the remnants of a defeated army,
I broke the Yàn of ten thousand chariots
and restored the ruins of Qí.
Why should I be unable to take Dí?"
He got into his chariot and left without a word of thanks.
He then attacked Dí,
but for three months he could not conquer it.
The infants of Qí sang a nursery rhyme:
"A large cap like a winnowing basket,
a long sword propping up the chin.
Unable to attack Dí,
he is held at the dry mound of the fortress."
Tián Dān then became afraid
and asked Lǔ Zhòngzǐ:
"You said that I, Dān, could not take Dí;
I beg to hear your explanation."
Lǔ Zhòngzǐ said:
"When the General was in Jímò,
he sat and wove straw mats;
when he stood, he leaned on a shovel.
He led the soldiers, saying:
'We must go forward!
The ancestral temples are lost!
It is said they are gone!
To what kin shall we return!'
At that time,
the General had the heart to die,
and the soldiers had no spirit for life.
Hearing such words,
none did not wipe their tears and raise their arms, wanting to fight;
this is why you broke Yàn.
Nowadays, the General has the support of Yè Yì in the east
and the pleasures of the Zī River in the west.
With a golden belt across your waist,
you gallop between the Zī and Miǎn rivers.
You have the joy of living
and no heart for dying;
this is why you do not win."
Tián Dān said: "I, Dān, have the heart.
You have noted it, sir."
The next day,
he bolstered his spirit and inspected the walls.
Standing where arrows and stones fell,
he seized the drumsticks and beat the drum.
The people of Dí then surrendered.
Regarding the matter at Pǔshàng,
Zhuìzǐ died,
and Zhāngzǐ fled.
Pànzǐ said to the King of Qí:
"It is better to exchange our surplus grain with Sòng.
The King of Sòng will surely be pleased,
and the Liáng clan will not dare to pass through Sòng to attack Qí.
Qí is indeed weak,
and thus we use surplus grain to win over Sòng.
When the state of Qí becomes strong again,
even if we demand it back from Sòng, it will be possible;
if they do not repay,
then we can use that as a pretext to attack them,
which would also be possible."
When King Mǐn of Qí was killed,
his son Fǎzhāng changed his name
and became a servant in the household of Tàishǐ Jiǎo in Jǔ.
The daughter of Tàishǐ Jiǎo
was struck by the appearance of Fǎzhāng
and considered him no ordinary man.
Pitying him, she often secretly gave him food and clothing
and had a private affair with him.
The people in Jǔ and the refugee officials of Qí gathered together,
seeking the son of King Mǐn
with the intent to install him as king.
Fǎzhāng then revealed himself in Jǔ.
Together, they installed Fǎzhāng as King Xiāng.
When King Xiāng was established,
he made the daughter of the Tàishǐ clan his Queen,
and she gave birth to his son Jiàn.
Tàishǐ Jiǎo said:
"A daughter who marries without a matchmaker
is not of my kind;
she has defiled my lineage."
To the end of his life, he would not see her.
Jūnwáng Hòu was virtuous;
because of the refusal to see her,
she did not fail in the rites of a child toward a parent.
When King Xiāng died,
his son Jiàn was installed as the King of Qí.
Jūnwáng Hòu served Qín with diligence
and kept faith with the feudal lords.
For this reason, for more than forty years after Jiàn was installed, Qí did not suffer from military attacks.
Qín Shǐ Huáng once sent an envoy to present Jūnwáng Hòu with jade interlocking rings,
and said:
"Qí has much wisdom;
can they untie these rings?"
Jūnwáng Hòu showed them to the ministers,
but none of the ministers knew how to untie them.
Jūnwáng Hòu took a mallet and smashed them to pieces.
She thanked the envoy of Qín, saying:
"They have been respectfully untied."
When Jūnwáng Hòu was ill and about to die,
she cautioned Jiàn, saying:
"Among the ministers, those who can be employed are so-and-so."
Jiàn said:
"I request to write them down."
Jūnwáng Hòu said:
"Very well."
He took a brush and tablet to receive her words.
Jūnwáng Hòu said:
"This old woman has already forgotten!"
After Jūnwáng Hòu died,
later, Hòu Shèng served as the Prime Minister of Qí.
He received much gold and jade from Qín spies,
and sent guests to enter Qín.
They all used deceitful words
to persuade the King to pay court to Qín
and did not maintain preparations for attack or battle.
When King Jiàn of Qí was entering Qín for an audience,
the Sīmǎ of Yōngmén came forward and said:
"As for the reason for establishing a king,
is it for the sake of the altars of the state?
Or is the king established for the sake of the king himself?"
The King said:
"It is for the sake of the state."
The Sīmǎ said:
"If a king is established for the sake of the state,
why would the king leave the state to enter Qín?"
The King of Qí turned his chariot and returned.
If the Grandee of Jímò and the Sīmǎ of Yōngmén had remonstrated and been listened to,
then it would have been possible to devise strategies;
they immediately went in to see the King of Qí and said:
"Qí's territory is several thousand lǐ square,
with millions of armored soldiers.
Now, the grandees of the Three Jìn
all find Qín disadvantageous;
there are hundreds of them between Ā and Juàn.
If Your Majesty recruits them and gives them a host of a million,
and has them reclaim the former lands of the Three Jìn,
then the Línjìn Pass can be entered;
The dàfū of Yān and Yǐng,
who do not want to serve Qín,
and who have gathered to the south of the city numbered in the hundreds.
If the King gathers them and gives them an army of a million
to reclaim the former lands of Chǔ,
then Wǔguān can be entered.
If this is done,
then the prestige of Qí can be established,
and the state of Qín can be destroyed.
To abandon the title of sovereign facing south
and instead face west to serve Qín
is something Your Majesty should not choose."
The King of Qí did not listen.
Qín sent Chén Chí to entice the King of Qí to enter its borders,
promising him five hundred lǐ of land.
The King of Qí did not listen to the Jìmò dàfū but listened to Chén Chí
and consequently entered Qín.
They placed him among the pines and cypresses of Gòng,
where he starved to death.
Prior to this, the people of Qí made a song for him saying:
"O pines!
O cypresses!
The one who dwells in Jiàn and Gòng,
is he a guest?"
Qí was in chaos due to Nào Jūn.
Afterwards, Qín wanted to take Qí,
so it sent Sū Juān to Chǔ
and ordered Rèn Gù to Qí.
Qí Míng said to the King of Chǔ:
"The King of Qín's desire for Chǔ
is not as great as his desire for Qí.
He sent Juān here
to show Qí that he has Chǔ
and to assist Gù's standing in Qí.
When Qí sees Chǔ is aligned with Qín,
it will surely accept Gù.
Thus the King's listening to Juān
just serves to drive Gù to unite Qí and Qín.
If Qí and Qín unite,
it is not to Chǔ's advantage.
Moreover, the words of Juān's arrival
are surely not the words Gù used to go to Qí.
The King would do better to send someone to use Juān's words to deceive Gù in Qí;
then Qí and Qín will surely not unite.
If Qí and Qín do not unite,
then the King's influence will be great.
If the King wants to win over Qí to attack Qín,
Hànzhōng can be obtained.
If the King then wants to use Qín to attack Qí,
the area between the Huái and Sì rivers can also be obtained."
Qí and Chǔ were in conflict, and Sòng requested neutrality.
Qí pressured Sòng,
and Sòng agreed to it.
Zǐxiàng, on behalf of Chǔ, said to the King of Sòng:
"Chǔ lost Sòng through leniency
and will now follow Qí's example of pressure.
Qí gained Sòng through pressure
and will always use pressure hereafter.
Following Qí to attack Chǔ
is not necessarily advantageous.
If Qí wins against Chǔ,
it will surely endanger Sòng;
if it does not win,
then a weak Sòng will have offended a strong Chǔ.
To let two states of ten thousand chariots
always use pressure to seek what they want,
your state will surely be in danger."
Five states formed an alliance to attack Qí.
Zhāo Yáng said to the King of Chǔ:
"If the five states break Qí and Qín,
they will surely plot against Chǔ in the south."
The King said,
"If so, then what should be done?"
He replied:
"The Hán clan assists their state;
they love profit and hate trouble.
Since they love profit,
they can be enticed;
since they hate trouble,
they can be intimidated.
If I bribe them heavily with profit,
their hearts will surely be enticed.
If I mobilize all my troops to face them,
their hearts will surely fear me.
When they fear my troops and are enticed by my profit,
the alliance of the five states can surely be undermined.
After the alliance is broken,
even if we do not give them land, it will be fine."
The King of Chǔ said,
"Excellent."
He then ordered Dàgōng to serve in Hán,
who saw Gōngzhòng and said:
"The affair of Niúlán
and the trouble of Mǎlíng are things Your Majesty has seen personally.
If the King does not use troops with the five states,
I request to offer five cities
and request to mobilize all the masses of Chǔ
to act as a wall against Qí."
After Qí turned against Zhào and Wèi,
Chǔ indeed did not give the land,
and so the alliance of the five states was frustrated.
Jīng Xuān Wáng asked his ministers:
"I hear the North fears Zhāo Xīxù;
what is it really like?"
The ministers did not reply.
Jiāng Yī replied:
"A tiger seeks out all beasts to eat them
and caught a fox.
The fox said,
'You dare not eat me.
The Emperor of Heaven has made me the leader of all beasts.
If you eat me now,
it is to disobey the command of the Emperor of Heaven.
If you think I am untrustworthy,
I shall walk ahead for you
and you follow behind me;
see if any of the beasts see me and dare not run away!'
The tiger thought this was so,
so he followed and walked with it.
The beasts saw them and all fled.
The tiger did not know the beasts fled because they feared him
but thought they feared the fox.
Now the King's territory is five thousand lǐ square
with a million armored soldiers,
and he entrusts them exclusively to Zhāo Xīxù.
Therefore, the North's fear of Xīxù
is actually fear of the King's armored soldiers,
just as the beasts fear the tiger."
Zhāo Xīxù and Péngchéng Jūn debated before the King,
and the King summoned Jiāng Yǐ to ask him about it.
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"The words of both men are good;
I dare not say who is inferior.
This is called weighing the worthy."
During the crisis of Hándān,
Zhāo Xīxù said to the King of Chǔ:
"The King would do better not to rescue Zhào
and thereby strengthen Wèi.
When Wèi is strong,
its cutting into Zhào will surely be deep.
If Zhào cannot accept this,
it will surely hold out firmly;
thus both will be exhausted."
Jǐng Shè said:
"Not so.
Zhāo Xīxù does not understand.
When Wèi attacks Zhào,
it fears Chǔ attacking its rear.
If we do not rescue Zhào now,
Zhào will appear to be on the verge of perishing,
and Wèi will have no worry about Chǔ;
this is Chǔ and Wèi joining against Zhào,
and the harm will surely be deep!
How can there be exhaustion of both?
Furthermore, if Wèi orders its troops to cut deeply into Zhào,
and Zhào sees its own perishing state
and sees that Chǔ will not rescue it,
it will surely unite with Wèi to plot against Chǔ.
Therefore, the King would do better to dispatch a few troops
to act as support for Zhào.
Zhào, relying on the strength of Chǔ,
will surely battle Wèi.
Wèi, angry at Zhào's strength
and seeing that Chǔ's rescue is not to be feared,
will surely not let go of Zhào.
When Zhào and Wèi are both exhausted
and Qí and Qín respond to Chǔ,
then Wèi can be broken."
Chǔ consequently sent Jǐng Shè to raise troops and rescue Zhào.
Hándān was captured,
and Chǔ took the territory between the Suī and Huì rivers.
Jiāng Yǐn wanted to slander Zhāo Xīxù before the King of Chǔ
but his power was insufficient,
so he requested a fief from Chǔ on behalf of Shānyáng Jūn of Liáng.
The King of Chǔ said,
"Very well."
Zhāo Xīxù said:
"Shānyáng Jūn has no merit for the state of Chǔ
and should not be enfeoffed."
Jiāng Yǐn thereby gained Shānyáng Jūn as an ally to slander Zhāo Xīxù together.
The Wèi clan slandered Zhāo Xīxù before the King of Chǔ;
the King of Chǔ told Zhāo Zǐ.
Zhāo Zǐ said:
"Your servant listens for commands day and night to serve,
yet Wèi comes between my lord and his servant;
your servant is greatly afraid."
I do not fear Wèi!
Indeed, if one leaks the interactions between my lord and his minister,
and the whole world believes it,
then this person’s character is nearly miserable.
If he finds it not difficult to act this way externally,
how could he forget to do so internally?
The day I face punishment is not far off."
The King said: "I know this;
what do you worry about, Dàfū?"
Jiāng Yǐ disliked Zhāo Xīxù
and said to the King of Chǔ:
"There was a man who loved his dog because he believed it was a good hunter.
The dog once fell into a well.
A neighbor saw the dog drowning in the well
and wanted to enter to tell the owner.
The dog hated him
and stood at the gate to bite him.
The neighbor feared it
and so was unable to enter to speak.
During the crisis of Hándān,
Chǔ advanced its troops to Dàliáng
and took it.
Zhāo Xīxù took the precious vessels of Wèi;
because he resided there, Wèi knows of this,
and therefore Zhāo Xīxù always dislikes me seeing the King."
Jiāng Yǐ wished to slander Zhāo Xīxù in Chǔ,
so he said to the King of Chǔ:
"When subordinates form cliques,
then the superior is in danger;
