when subordinates compete and dispute,
then the superior is secure.
Does the King also know this?
I hope the King will not forget it.
Furthermore, if there is a person who loves to proclaim the virtues of others,
what does the King think of him?"
The King said:
"This is a Jūnzǐ;
keep him close."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"If there is a person who loves to proclaim the faults of others,
what does the King think of him?"
The King said:
"This is a Xiǎorén;
keep him at a distance."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"In that case, if there were a son who killed his father
or a minister who assassinated his lord,
and the King ultimately remained unaware,
why would that be?
It is because the King loves to hear of people’s virtues and hates to hear of people’s faults."
The King said:
"Good.
I wish to hear both."
Jiāng Yǐ spoke persuasively to Ānlíng Jūn, saying:
"You do not possess a single foot of land
nor are you of the King’s own flesh and blood,
yet you occupy a high position
and receive a generous salary;
among the people of the whole state,
none fail to straighten their robes and bow when they see you,
bowing down and submitting;
why is this so?"
He replied:
"It is only because the King mistakenly promoted me.
Otherwise,
I could not have reached this position."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"Those who associate based on wealth
will find their association severed when the wealth is exhausted;
those who associate based on beauty
will find their love fading when the bloom withers.
Therefore, a favored woman’s bed-mat does not wear out,
and a favored minister does not use the same carriage for long.
Now you wield the power of the State of Chǔ,
yet you have no means to bind yourself deeply to the King;
privately, I consider this dangerous for you."
Ānlíng Jūn said:
"In that case, what should I do?"
"I wish that you would surely ask to follow him in death,
to sacrifice your own body as his funerary attendant;
in this way, you will surely remain highly valued in the State of Chǔ for a long time."
He said:
"I respectfully receive your instruction."
Three years passed and he did not speak of it.
Jiāng Yǐ saw him again and said:
"The course of action I proposed for you
has not yet been effective.
Since you do not use my plan,
I ask that I no longer dare to see you again."
Ānlíng Jūn said: "I do not dare to forget your words, sir,
but I have not yet found the opportunity."
Thereupon,
the King of Chǔ went hunting at Yúnmèng,
with a thousand chariots drawn by teams of four;
banners and flags blotted out the sun;
the fires rising from the fields were like clouds and rainbows,
and the roars of rhinoceroses and tigers were like thunder.
A wild beast came charging toward the wheels of the chariot;
the King personally drew his bow and shot,
killing it with a single arrow.
The King pulled out a banner and held down the beast's head,
then looked up to the heavens and laughed, saying:
"What joy!
Today’s hunt.
After I have passed away thousands of years from now,
with whom shall I share such joy?"
Ānlíng Jūn stepped forward with tears streaming down and said:
"When I am indoors, I arrange your mats;
when I go out, I accompany your carriage.
After Your Majesty has passed away thousands of years from now,
I wish to offer my body to the Huángquán
to serve as a mat for the mole crickets and ants;
what greater joy could there be than to have shared this pleasure and then join you?"
The King was greatly pleased
and thereafter enfeoffed him at Tán as Ānlíng Jūn.
A Jūnzǐ hearing this said:
"Jiāng Yǐ can be said to be good at planning,
and Ānlíng Jūn can be said to know the right time."
Jiāng Yǐ served as an envoy from Wèi to Chǔ
and said to the King of Chǔ:
"I have entered your borders
and heard that the customs of Chǔ
are to not conceal the virtues of others
and not to speak of the faults of others;
is this truly so?"
The King said: "It is truly so."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"In that case, regarding the rebellion of Bái Gōng,
would it not have succeeded?
If it were truly like this,
then the crimes of people like me would be excused."
The King of Chǔ said: "Why is that?"
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"Zhōuhóu serves as the Chancellor of Chǔ;
he is extremely noble and makes all decisions,
yet those on the left and right all say 'there is no such thing,'
as if speaking with one voice."
A man of Yǐng had a legal case that remained undecided for three years;
so he purposely ordered someone to request his house
to divine the outcome of his offense.
A guest, on his behalf, said to Zhāo Xīxù:
"The house of a certain man of Yǐng, I desire it."
Zhāo Xīxù said:
"That certain man of Yǐng
is not supposed to be convicted of a crime,
so his house cannot be obtained."
The guest took his leave and departed.
Afterward, Zhāo Xīxù regretted it
and so said to the guest:
"I have been able to serve you;
why did you treat me with such a pretext?"
The guest said:
"It was not a pretext."
Zhāo said:
"I told you it could not be obtained,
yet you had a joyful look;
if it was not a pretext, what was it?"
Chéng Hún left Zhōu;
three men traveled together,
journeying south to Chǔ
and arriving at Xīnchéng.
Chéng Hún spoke persuasively to its Magistrate, saying:
"Zhèng and Wèi
are weak states compared to Chǔ;
whereas Qín
is a powerful enemy of Chǔ.
Despite the weakness of Zhèng and Wèi,
Chǔ responds to them with Shàngliáng;
while Yíyáng is large,
Chǔ surrounds it with the weak Xīnchéng.
Púfǎn and Píngyáng are a hundred lǐ apart;
the people of Qín could raid them in a single night,
and Ānyì would not know;
Xīnchéng and Shàngliáng are five hundred lǐ apart;
if the people of Qín raid one in a night,
Shàngliáng would also not know.
Now, what the border towns rely on
is not the region south of the Jiāng or the area above the Sì River.
Therefore, why does the King of Chǔ not make Xīnchéng the primary commandery?
The border towns would benefit greatly from it."
The Lord of Xīnchéng was greatly pleased
and so prepared a carriage with a team of four horses and five hundred gold pieces to go to Chǔ.
Chéng Hún obtained these
and then traveled south to interact in Chǔ;
the King of Chǔ indeed made Xīnchéng the primary commandery.
Hán Gōngshū relied on Qí and Wèi,
while the Tàizǐ relied on Chǔ and Qín
to contest the state.
Zhèng Shēn served as an envoy for Chǔ to Hán,
and he falsely claimed to grant Xīnchéng and Yángrén to the Tàizǐ.
The Chǔ Wáng was angry
and was about to punish him.
He replied:
"I falsely granted them
for the sake of our state.
I obtained Xīnchéng and Yángrén for the Tàizǐ so that he could contest the state with Gōngshū and win it.
Qí and Wèi will surely attack Hán.
When the Hán clan is in dire straits,
they will surely entrust their lives to Chǔ,
so how would they then dare to ask for Xīnchéng and Yángrén back?
If the Tàizǐ does not win,
but yet does not die,
he will come to us with his cap inverted,
and then how would he dare speak of land?"
The Chǔ Wáng said:
"Excellent."
He then did not punish him.
Dù Hè of Chǔ persuaded the Chǔ Wáng to take Zhào.
The Wáng was about to grant him the rank of Wǔdàfū,
and ordered him to go privately.
Chén Zhěn said to the Chǔ Wáng:
"Hè cannot win over Zhào,
and the rank of Wǔdàfū cannot be taken back;
he would have received a reward without merit.
If he wins over Zhào and the Wáng gives him no further reward,
that would not be good.
The Wáng would be better off sending him with ten chariots;
if the mission is successful,
then grant him the rank of Wǔdàfū."
The Wáng said:
"Excellent."
He then sent him with ten chariots.
Dù Hè was angry and did not go.
Chén Zhěn said to the Wáng: "This shows he could not have won over Zhào."
The Chǔ Wáng asked Fàn Huán:
"I wish to place a Xiàng in Qín,
who would be suitable?"
He replied: "I am not sufficient to know this."
The Wáng said: "Would my Xiàng Gān Mào be acceptable?"
Fàn Huán replied: "No."
The Wáng said:
"Why?"
He said:
"Consider Shǐ Jǔ;
he was a gatekeeper in Shàngcài.
In great matters, he was not good at serving a lord,
and in small matters, he was not good at managing a household,
yet he was known to the world for his strict integrity.
Gān Mào served him obediently.
Therefore, with the brilliance of Huì Wáng,
the discernment of Wǔ Wáng,
and the slanderous nature of Zhāng Yí,
Gān Mào served them,
holding ten offices without being blamed.
Mào is truly a worthy man;
nevertheless, he cannot be the Xiàng of Qín.
For Qín to have a worthy Xiàng
is not to the advantage of the state of Chǔ.
Furthermore, Your Majesty once used Huá in Yuè and took Gùzhāng;
during the troubles of Mèi,
Yuè fell into chaos;
thus Chǔ explored Làihú in the south and treated Jiāngdōng as its outskirts.
The reason Your Majesty's achievements could be like this
was because Yuè was in chaos while Chǔ was well-governed.
Now Your Majesty has applied this to Yuè
but forgotten it regarding Qín;
I believe Your Majesty has forgotten it all too quickly.
If Your Majesty wishes to place a Xiàng in Qín,
someone like Gōngsūn Hǎo would be suitable.
Gōngsūn Hǎo's relationship with the Qín Wáng
is one of kinship.
As youths, they wore the same clothes;
as adults, they shared the same carriage;
he even wears the Wáng's clothes to attend to affairs;
he is truly Your Majesty's Xiàng.
If the Wáng makes him the Xiàng,
it will be of great benefit to the state of Chǔ."
Sū Qín, on behalf of Zhào, formed the Vertical Alliance
and persuaded Chǔ Wēiwáng, saying:
"Chǔ
is a powerful state in the world.
Your Majesty
is a worthy Wáng in the world.
The land of Chǔ has Qiánzhōng and Wūjùn to the west,
Xiàzhōu and Hǎiyáng to the east,
Dòngtíng and Cāngwú to the south,
and the fortress of Fénxíng and
Xúnyáng to the north.
The territory is five thousand li square,
with a million armored soldiers,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
and grain to last ten years;
these are the resources of a hegemon-king.
With the strength of Chǔ and the worthiness of Your Majesty,
none in the world can stand against you.
If you now wish to face west and serve Qín,
then the feudal lords will all face south and pay homage at the foot of Zhāngtái.
Among those who threaten the world, none is more harmful to Qín than Chǔ;
when Chǔ is strong, Qín is weak,
and when Chǔ is weak, Qín is strong.
Their positions are mutually exclusive.
Therefore, the best plan for Your Majesty is to join the Vertical Alliance to isolate Qín.
If Your Majesty does not join the Alliance,
Qín will surely raise two armies:
one army will exit Wǔguān;
one army will go down to Qiánzhōng.
In such a case,
Yān and Yǐng will be shaken.
I have heard that one should govern before there is chaos
and act before things exist;
to worry only after disaster has arrived
is already too late.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will plan for this early.
"If Your Majesty can truly listen to me,
I shall ask the states of Shāndōng
to offer their seasonal tributes
to receive Your Majesty's enlightened commands,
entrust their altars and ancestral temples to you,
and train their officers and sharpen their weapons
for Your Majesty's use.
If Your Majesty can truly listen to my humble plan,
then the exquisite music and beautiful women of Hán, Wèi, Qí, Yān, Zhào, and Wèi
will surely fill your back palace.
The fine horses and tuótuó of Zhào and Dài
will surely fill your outer stables.
Thus, if the Vertical Alliance is formed, Chǔ will be Wáng;
if the Horizontal Alliance succeeds, Qín will be Dì.
Now to abandon the career of a hegemon-king
for the reputation of serving others,
I humbly believe Your Majesty should not choose this.
"Now Qín
is a state of tigers and wolves
with the heart to swallow the world.
Qín
is the enemy of all the world.
Advocates of the Horizontal Alliance all wish to carve up the lands of the feudal lords to serve Qín;
this is what is called nurturing an enemy and serving a foe.
For a minister to carve up his lord's land
to strengthen the tiger-and-wolf Qín through diplomacy and invade the world—
when the Qín disaster eventually comes,
they disregard the calamity.
They rely on the prestige of powerful Qín from without
to coerce their lord within
in order to seek the ceding of land;
there is no greater treachery or disloyalty
than this.
Therefore, if you join the Vertical Alliance,
the feudal lords will carve up land to serve Chǔ;
if you join the Horizontal Alliance,
then Chǔ will carve up land to serve Qín.
These two strategies
are far apart
by a factor of hundreds of millions.
Between the two, where does Your Majesty stand?
Therefore, the Zhào Wáng of my humble state
has sent me to offer this humble plan
and present this enlightened covenant;
it awaits Your Majesty's command."
The Chǔ Wáng said: "My state
borders Qín to the west, and Qín
has the intention of taking Bā and Shǔ and annexing Hànzhōng.
Qín
is a state of tigers and wolves
and cannot be befriended.
Moreover, Hán and Wèi are hard-pressed by the threat of Qín
and cannot be plotted with deeply,
for fear they will turn against us and join Qín.
Thus, before the plot is even launched, the state is already in danger.
I have considered my own strength,
and if Chǔ opposes Qín,
I see no victory.
Consulting within with my ministers,
they are not to be relied upon.
I lie down but cannot find peace on my mat,
I eat but find no flavor in my food;
my heart wavers like a hanging banner,
with nowhere to finally rest.
Now you wish to unite the world,
bring peace to the feudal lords,
and save endangered states;
I respectfully offer my state to join you."
Zhāng Yí broke the Vertical Alliance on behalf of Qín and established the Horizontal Alliance;
he persuaded the King of Chǔ, saying:
“The land of Qín constitutes half of all under heaven,
its military strength can rival four great states,
it is shielded by mountains and girded by rivers,
and the four passes make it secure.
There are over a million brave warriors,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
and grain supplies as vast as hills.
The laws and decrees are clear,
and the soldiers are at ease with hardship and take joy in death.
The sovereign is stern and wise;
the generals are intelligent and martial.
Even without deploying armored troops,
they can sweep over the natural defenses of Chángshān
and break the spine of the world;
those who are last to submit among the states will be the first to perish.
Furthermore, those who advocate for the Vertical Alliance
are no different from those who drive a flock of sheep to attack a fierce tiger.
Between a tiger and sheep,
it is clear that they cannot contend.
Now, Your Majesty does not side with the fierce tiger but joins the flock of sheep;
I privately believe Your Majesty’s plan is mistaken.
Generally, among the powerful states under heaven,
if it is not Qín, it is Chǔ;
if it is not Chǔ, it is Qín.
When two such states are equal in power and contend with each other,
their positions are naturally incompatible.
If Your Majesty does not side with Qín,
Qín will deploy its armored troops
and occupy Yíyáng,
so that Hán’s upper lands will be cut off;
they will descend to Hédōng,
seize Chénggāo,
and Hán will surely submit as a servant to Qín.
Once Hán submits,
Wèi will move according to the wind.
If Qín attacks Chǔ from the west,
while Hán and Wèi attack from the north,
how can the state altars avoid being endangered?
Furthermore, those who contract the Vertical Alliance
gather a group of the weak to attack the supremely strong.
Attacking the strong with the weak,
engaging in battle lightly without gauging the enemy,
and repeatedly mobilizing troops while the state is poor—
this is the technique of peril and ruin.
I have heard that
if one’s military is not equal,
one should not offer a challenge;
if one’s grain supply is not equal,
one should not engage in a prolonged conflict.
Those who follow the Vertical Alliance
use flowery rhetoric and empty words,
extolling the ruler’s integrity and conduct,
speaking of the benefits and not the harms.
When disaster eventually strikes Chǔ,
it will be too late to do anything;
therefore, I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
To the west of Qín lie Bā and Shǔ,
where they lash ships together and stockpile grain,
starting from Wèn Shān
and following the Jiāng downstream;
it is over three thousand lǐ to Yǐng.
Large boats carry the soldiers,
with one boat holding fifty men
and three months' worth of rations.
Floating down the river,
they travel over three hundred lǐ in a single day.
Although the distance in lǐ is great,
it does not exhaust the horses with the toil of sweat.
In less than ten days, they reach Hànguān.
Once Hànguān is alarmed,
then from Jìnglíng eastward,
all will be cities on defensive guard,
and Qiánzhōng and Wǔjùn will no longer be possessed by Your Majesty.
If Qín raises its armor and exits Wǔguān
to attack facing south,
then the northern lands will be cut off.
When the Qín army attacks Chǔ,
the crisis will arrive within three months.
Yet Chǔ relies on the rescue of the feudal lords,
which would be more than half a year away;
thus, the timing of their positions will not coincide.
Relying on the rescue of weak states
while forgetting the disaster of powerful Qín—
this is what I consider a calamity for Your Majesty.
Furthermore, Your Majesty once fought five battles against the people of Wú, winning three and eventually destroying them,
but your soldiers were exhausted;
you have partial defenses at Xīnchéng, and the inhabitants are suffering.
I have heard that
those who attack the great are easily endangered,
and when the people are exhausted, they resent their superiors.
Maintaining achievements that are easily endangered
while defying the intentions of powerful Qín—
I privately find this perilous for Your Majesty.
Moreover, the reason Qín has not deployed its armor from Hángǔ Guān for fifteen years to attack the feudal lords
is that it has a secret plan with the intent of swallowing all under heaven.
Chǔ once had a conflict with Qín
and fought at Hànzhōng.
The people of Chǔ did not win;
over seventy men of the ranks of Tōnghóu and Zhíguī died,
and Hànzhōng was subsequently lost.
The King of Chǔ was greatly enraged
and raised an army to raid Qín;
they fought at Lántián
and were again repulsed.
This is what is called two tigers fighting each other.
Qín and Chǔ exhausted each other,
while Hán and Wèi, remaining intact, controlled them from behind.
No plan could be more mistaken than this;
therefore, I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
If Qín sends troops to attack Wèi and Yángjìn,
it will surely open the chest of the world.
If Your Majesty raises all your troops to attack Sòng,
Sòng can be taken within a few months.
Having taken Sòng and pointing eastward,
the twelve lords along the Sì River
will all become Your Majesty’s possessions.
The one in whom the world trusted to keep the Vertical Alliance and its kinship firm was Sū Qín;
he was enfeoffed as Wǔ'ān Jūn and served as Prime Minister of Yān,
yet he secretly plotted with the King of Yān to destroy Qí and divide its land.
He then feigned a crime,
fled, and entered Qí,
and the King of Qí consequently received him and made him Prime Minister.
After two years, he was discovered;
the King of Qí was greatly enraged
and had Sū Qín torn apart by chariots in the marketplace.
With a man as deceitful and fickle as Sū Qín
wanting to manage the world
and unite the feudal lords,
it is clear that it could not be accomplished.
“Now, regarding Qín and Chǔ,
their territories are adjacent and their borders touch;
they are naturally states that should be close.
If Your Majesty can truly listen to me,
I request that the Crown Prince of Qín enter Chǔ as a hostage,
and the Crown Prince of Chǔ enter Qín as a hostage.
I request that a daughter of Qín serve as Your Majesty's concubine to hold the broom,
and Qín will offer a city of ten thousand households
to serve as your town for bathing.
We shall forever be brotherly states,
never attacking each other for the rest of our lives.
I believe no plan is more convenient than this.
Therefore, the King of Qín of my humble state
has sent me as an envoy to offer this letter to Your Majesty's carriage attendants,
awaiting your decision on the matter.”
The King of Chǔ said:
“The state of Chǔ is remote and crude,
situated upon the Eastern Sea.
I am young
and not practiced in the long-term planning of the state.
Now that an honored guest has fortunately taught me with clear regulations,
having heard them,
I respectfully follow your advice with my state.”
He then dispatched an envoy with a hundred chariots
to present 'chicken-startle' rhinoceros horn and night-shining jade discs to the King of Qín.
When Zhāng Yí was Prime Minister of Qín,
he said to Zhāo Jū:
“Without Yān, Yǐng, and Hànzhōng,
has Chǔ gained anything else?”
Zhāo Jū said:
“Nothing.”
Zhāng Yí said:
“Without Zhāo Jū and Chén Zhěn,
has the King gained anything else?”
Zhāo Jū said:
“He has gained nothing else.”
Zhāng Yí said:
“On my behalf, tell the King of Chǔ to banish Zhāo Jū and Chén Zhěn,
and I shall request the return of Yān, Yǐng, and Hànzhōng.”
Zhāo Jū returned and reported this to the King of Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ was pleased.
Someone said to Zhāo Jū:
“How extreme!
The King of Chǔ does not perceive the nature of those who contend for fame.
When Hán requested to make Chén Jí Prime Minister, Zhōu did not listen;
when Wèi requested to make Qímǔ Huī Prime Minister, Zhōu did not listen.
Why was this?
It was because Zhōu treated us as if we were but its subordinate counties.
Now Chǔ
is a powerful state of ten thousand chariots,
and Your Majesty is a wise ruler of the world.
Now Zhāng Yí says to banish you and Chén Zhěn, and the King listens to him;
this means Chǔ’s own conduct is inferior to that of Zhōu,
and Zhāng Yí is held in higher regard than the Kings of Hán and Wèi.”
Moreover, what Yí practices,
that which achieves merit and fame belongs to Qín,
and that which desires nobility and wealth belongs to Wèi.
If he wishes to conduct an attack for the sake of Wèi,
he must strike south against Chǔ.
Therefore, his attack follows a method:
externally, to sever its alliances;
internally, to expel its strategists.
Chén Zhěn
is a man of Xià
and is well-versed in the affairs of the Sānjìn;
therefore, if he is expelled,
then Chǔ will have no strategists.
Now, you are able to employ the masses of Chǔ;
therefore, if you are also expelled,
then the masses of Chǔ will not be employed.
This is what is called attacking from within,
yet the King does not realize it.
Now, why do you not present me to the King
and request that I serve the King as an envoy to Qí so that the alliance is not severed?
If the alliance with Qí is not severed,
and Yí hears of this,
then his delivery of Yān, Yǐng, and Hànzhōng will surely be delayed.
This will mean that Zhāo Jū’s words are untrustworthy,
and the King will certainly hold him in low esteem."
King Wēi asked Mò’áo Zǐhuá, saying: "From the time of the former ruler King Wén down to my own person,
have there also been those who were not encouraged by rank,
and not motivated by salary,
but who worried for the sake of the state?"
Mò’áo Zǐhuá replied: "A man like Huá is not sufficient to know this."
The King said: "Other than from the grand masters,
from whom would I hear of it?"
Mò’áo Zǐhuá replied: "What kind of person would the Great King like to ask about?
There are those who were modest about their rank,
lived in poverty themselves,
and worried for the sake of the state;
there are those who exalted their rank,
increased their salary,
and worried for the sake of the state;
there are those who had their necks severed and bellies slit,
closing their eyes once and not seeing for ten thousand generations,
not knowing what they benefited,
yet worried for the sake of the state;
there are those who toiled with their bodies,
and grieved their minds,
yet worried for the sake of the state;
and there are also those who were not encouraged by rank and not motivated by salary,
yet worried for the sake of the state."
The King said: "What do these words
of the grand master mean?"
Mò’áo Zǐhuá replied: "In the past, Lìngyǐn Zǐwén
wore clothes of black silk to court
and deerskin robes at home;
he stood at court before it was light
and returned home to eat after the sun had set;
in the morning he did not plan for the evening,
and he did not have even a month's worth of provisions.
Therefore, he who was modest about his rank,
lived in poverty himself,
and worried for the sake of the state
was Lìngyǐn Zǐwén.
In the past, Shègōng Zǐgāo
attained his status from among the humble
and gained wealth as the Zhùguó;
he quelled the disaster caused by Báigōng
and settled the affairs of the state of Chǔ;
he expanded the legacy of the former kings to cover the lands beyond Fāngchéng,
so that the four borders were not invaded
and his reputation was not diminished among the feudal lords.
At that time,
no one in the world dared to face south with an army.
Shègōng Zǐgāo
was granted six hundred fields for his sustenance;
therefore, he who exalted his rank,
increased his salary,
and worried for the sake of the state
was Shègōng Zǐgāo.
In the past, Wú and Chǔ fought at Báijǔ,
and between the two lines of chariots the soldiers clashed.
Mò’áo Dàxīn placed his hand on the driver’s hand,
looked back and sighed deeply, saying:
'Alas, my friend!
The month of the destruction of the state of Chǔ has arrived!
I shall charge deep into the Wú army;
if I strike down one man
or seize one man
to join with Dàxīn,
then perhaps the state may be saved.'
Therefore, he who had his neck severed and belly slit,
closing his eyes once and not seeing for ten thousand generations,
not knowing what they benefited,
yet worried for the sake of the state
was Mò’áo Dàxīn.
In the past, Wú and Chǔ fought at Báijǔ,
and after three battles they entered Yǐng.
Our sovereign fled in person,
the grand masters all followed him,
and the common people were scattered.
Fénmào Bósū said:
'If I don armor and hold sharp weapons,
rushing at the powerful enemy to die,
that is but like a single soldier;
it is better to hasten to the feudal lords.'
Thereupon, carrying provisions and traveling secretly,
he climbed Shēngshān
and crossed deep valleys;
his soles were pierced and his knees exposed,
and in seven days he reached the court of the King of Qín.
He stood like a bird without moving,
chanting by day and wailing by night.
For seven days he could not deliver his message.
No water or soup passed his lips,
and he was so exhausted that he fainted,
dazed and not recognizing anyone.
The King of Qín heard of this and rushed to him,
his cap and belt not even properly fastened;
with his left hand he supported Bósū’s head,
and with his right he moistened his mouth, and Bósū then revived.
The King of Qín personally asked him:
'Who are you, sir?'
Fénmào Bósū replied:
'I am none other than
Chǔ’s envoy, the newly appointed Xīnlí
Fénmào Bósū.
Wú and the men of Chǔ fought at Báijǔ,

and after three battles they entered Yǐng; our sovereign fled in person, the grand masters all followed him, and the common people were scattered. He sent this humble servant to announce the destruction and to seek aid.'
The King of Qín looked around and ordered that he not rise:
'I have heard
that if the ruler of a state of ten thousand chariots offends a single scholar, his state will be in peril;
this is what is meant by that.'
He then sent out a thousand leather-covered chariots
and ten thousand soldiers,
placing them under the command of Zǐmǎn and Zǐhǔ.
They went through the passes toward the east,
fought the people of Wú at Zhuóshuǐ
and decisively defeated them,
as was also heard at Suìpǔ.
Therefore, he who toiled with his body
and grieved his thoughts
to worry for the sake of the state
was Fénmào Bósū.
"When Wú and Chǔ fought at Báijǔ,
after three battles they entered Yǐng.
The King fled in person,
the grand masters all followed him,
and the common people were scattered.
Méng Gǔ was engaged in combat at Gōngtáng,
but he abandoned the fight and rushed to Yǐng, saying:
'If the sovereign survives,
perhaps the state of Chǔ can be saved?'
He then entered the Great Palace,
carried the records of Jīcì on his back to float down the Jiāng,
and escaped into Yúnmèng.
When King Zhāo returned to Yǐng,
the five ministries had lost their laws
and the common people were in chaos;
Méng Gǔ presented the records,
the five ministries regained their laws,
and the common people were well-governed.
This achievement of Méng Gǔ
is largely equal to that of preserving the state.
He was enfeoffed as a Zhíguī
and given six hundred fields.
Méng Gǔ said angrily: 'Gǔ is not a servant of a man,
but a servant of the state.
If the state receives its sacrifices,
then how can I say I have no ruler?'
He then abandoned himself into the midst of Mòshān,
and until now no one has replaced him.
Therefore, he who was not encouraged by rank
and not motivated by salary, yet worried for the sake of the state,
was Méng Gǔ."
The King then sighed deeply and said: "These were the men of antiquity.
The people of today,
how could they have such qualities?"
Mò’áo Zǐhuá replied: "In the past, the late predecessor King Líng favored small waists,
so the scholars of Chǔ restricted their eating,
needing to lean on something to stand,
and needing to use a rail to rise.
Food was something to be desired,
yet they endured and did not let it enter;
death was something to be loathed,
yet they did not avoid it.
Huá has heard that
if a ruler favors archery,
his subjects will wear arm-guards.
It is simply that the King does not favor it;
if the King truly favors the worthy,
these five ministers
could all be obtained and brought to you."
Zhái Qiáng, the Prime Minister of Wèi, died.
On behalf of Gān Mào, someone spoke to the King of Chǔ, saying:
"Among the candidates for the premiership of Wèi
is Gōngzǐ Jìn.
If Jìn becomes the Prime Minister of Wèi,
the relations between Wèi and Qín will surely be good.
Once the relations between Qín and Wèi are secure,
then Chǔ will be treated lightly.
Therefore, it would be better for Your Majesty to make a pact with Qí
to support Gān Mào as Prime Minister in Wèi.
The King of Qí likes to elevate people for the sake of fame;
if his envoy now requests the premiership of Wèi for his own sake,
Qí will surely be pleased.
If the Wèi clan does not comply,
their relations with Qí will sour;
once the relations between Qí and Wèi sour,
they will surely compete to serve Chǔ.
If the Wèi clan complies,
Gān Mào and Chūlǐ Jí
are mortal enemies;
thus the relations between Wèi and Qín will surely sour,
and they will both value their relations with Chǔ."
Qí and Qín made a pact to attack Chǔ.
Chǔ ordered Jǐng Cuì to bribe Qí with six cities,
with the Crown Prince serving as a hostage.
Zhāo Jū said to Jǐng Cuì:
"Qín fears that it will soon have to cede land to Chǔ through Jǐng Lǐ and Sū Lì.
You are giving up land to win over Qí,
while Lǐ and Lì are about to win over Qín by recovering land;
your mission will surely fail.
You should instead have the King heavily bribe Jǐng Lǐ and Sū Lì
and send them to Qín.
Qín will be frightened
and will surely not seek land but will ally with Chǔ.
If Qí does not seek the land,
then you have succeeded in your pact."
Shù Shì attacked Chǔ.
Chǔ ordered Zhāo Shǔ to lead a hundred thousand troops to Hànzhōng.
Zhāo Jū defeated Qín at Zhòngqiū.
Sū Lì said to the Duke of Wǎn, Zhāo Shǔ:
"The King wants Zhāo Jū to take advantage of Qín's defeat;
he will surely divide your troops to reinforce him.
When Qín knows your troops are divided,
they will surely emerge from Hànzhōng.
Let me have Xīn Róng say to the King on your behalf:
'Qín's troops are about to emerge from Hànzhōng.'
Then your troops will remain whole."
Four states attacked Chǔ.
Chǔ ordered Zhāo Jū to lead the army to resist Qín.
The King of Chǔ wanted to attack Qín,
but Zhāo Hóu did not want to.
Huán Zāng, on behalf of Zhāo Jū, said to the King of Chǔ:
"If Zhāo Jū wins the battle,
the three states will detest Chǔ's strength;
fearing that Qín might change its stance and listen to Chǔ,
they will surely attack Chǔ deeply to strengthen Qín's position.
The King of Qín will be angry at his defeat
and will surely mobilize all his forces to attack Chǔ.
Thus Your Majesty and Qín will exhaust each other,
while the three states will benefit.
If you do not win the battle against Qín,
Qín will advance its troops to attack.
It is better to reinforce Zhāo Jū's troops
and order him to show Qín that he is determined to fight.
The King of Qín dislikes exhausting himself against Chǔ while the rest of the world looks on;
Qín can then cede a little to avoid further harm.
With Qín and Chǔ allied,
Yān, Zhào, and Wèi will not dare to disobey,
and the three states can be settled."
King Huái of Chǔ detained Zhāng Yí
and intended to kill him.
Jìn Shàng, on behalf of Zhāng Yí, said to the King of Chǔ:
"By detaining Zhāng Yí,
the King of Qín will surely be angry.
When the world sees Chǔ is without Qín's support,
Chǔ will surely be treated lightly."
He also said to the King's favored lady, Zhèng Xiù:
"Do you realize that you are about to be devalued by the King?"
Zhèng Xiù said: "Why is that?"
Jìn Shàng said: "Zhāng Yí
is a loyal, trustworthy, and meritorious minister to the King of Qín.
Now that Chǔ has detained him,
the King of Qín wants to get him out.
The King of Qín has a beloved and beautiful daughter,
and he has also selected from his palace the finest trinkets, beauties, and those skilled in music
to accompany her for pleasure;
he will provide her with gold, jade, and precious vessels,
and offer the six counties of Shàngyōng as her bath-and-comb estate,
intending to use Zhāng Yí to present her to the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ will surely love her.
The daughter of Qín will rely on the powerful Qín to be valued,
and use the precious land as her resource;
she will be in a position to become the King's wife and oversee Chǔ.
The King will be enchanted by her entertainments
and will surely show her great respect and love while forgetting you.
You will become more devalued and more estranged day by day."
Zhèng Xiù said: "I wish to entrust myself to you;
what should be done?"
He said: "Why do you not urgently speak to the King
to release Zhāng Zǐ?
If Zhāng Zǐ is released,
his gratitude toward you will never end;
the girl from Qín will surely not come,
and Qín will surely value you.
Internally, you will monopolize the nobility of Chǔ;
externally, you will forge a bond with Qín.
By keeping Zhāng Zǐ for your use,
your children and grandchildren will surely be the Crown Princes of Chǔ;
this is no small benefit for a commoner."
Zhèng Xiù immediately persuaded the King of Chǔ to release Zhāng Zǐ.
The King of Chǔ was about to release Zhāng Zǐ,
but feared that he might harm him.
Jìn Shàng said to the King of Chǔ:
"I request to follow him.
If Zhāng Yí does not serve Your Majesty well,
I request to kill him."
A minor official of Chǔ,
who was an enemy of Jìn Shàng,
said to Zhāng Máo:
"With Zhāng Yí's intelligence
and his employment by both Qín and Chǔ,
you will surely be in difficulty.
You should
have someone secretly intercept Jìn Shàng and assassinate him.
The King of Chǔ will surely be furious with Zhāng Yí.
When Zhāng Yí is in difficulty,
then you will be valued.
When Chǔ and Qín are at odds,
then Wèi will have no worries."
Zhāng Máo indeed sent someone to intercept and assassinate Jìn Shàng.
The King of Chǔ was furious,
and Qín mobilized troops for war.
Qín and Chǔ competed to serve Wèi,
and Zhāng Máo indeed became highly valued.
Qín defeated Chǔ at Hànzhōng.
The King of Chǔ entered Qín,
and the King of Qín detained him.
Yóu Téng, on behalf of Chǔ, said to the King of Qín:
"If Your Majesty holds the King of Chǔ
and attacks Chǔ with the rest of the world,
then your conduct will be harmed.
If you do not join the world in attacking him,
then you will lose profit.
It is better for Your Majesty to make a pact with him and send him back.
The King of Chǔ is afraid
and surely will not dare to break the pact.
Your Majesty can then join the three states in attacking him;
this would be righteous."
When Chǔ Xiāng Wáng was the Crown Prince,
he was a hostage in Qí.
When King Huái died,
the Crown Prince took leave of the King of Qí to return home.
The King of Qí constrained him, saying:
"Give me five hundred lǐ of your eastern lands,
and then I will let you return.
If you do not give them to me,
you shall not return."
The Crown Prince said: "I have a tutor;
please let me go and ask him."
The tutor Shèn Zǐ said:
"Offering the land
is for the sake of your person.
To cherish land and not send off a deceased father
is unrighteous.
Therefore, I say
it is advantageous to offer it."
The Crown Prince entered
and delivered his message to the King of Qí, saying: "I respectfully offer five hundred lǐ of land."
The King of Qí returned the Crown Prince of Chǔ.
When the Crown Prince returned,
he ascended the throne as King.
Qí sent an envoy with fifty chariots
to claim the eastern lands from Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ told Shèn Zǐ: "The envoy of Qí has come to seek the eastern lands;
what should be done?"
Shèn Zǐ said: "Tomorrow, Your Majesty should hold court for the ministers
and order them all to present their plans."
The Shàng Zhù Guó, Zǐ Liáng, entered for an audience.
The King said:
"I was able to return to the royal tombs,
restore my ministers, and return to the state altars
by promising five hundred lǐ of the eastern lands to Qí.
Qí has now sent an envoy to claim the land;
what should be done?"
Zǐ Liáng said: "Your Majesty cannot but give it.
Your Majesty's words are as precious as the sound of jade;
if you promise land to the powerful Qí of ten thousand chariots and then do not give it,
you will be untrustworthy,
and later you will not be able to form pacts with the feudal lords.
I request that you give it and then attack them again.
Giving it shows your trustworthiness;
attacking them shows your martial prowess. Therefore, I say give it."
Zǐliáng left,
and Zhāo Cháng entered for an audience.
The King said: "The envoy of Qí has come to demand five hundred lǐ of our eastern lands.
What should be done about this?"
Zhāo Cháng said: "They must not be given.
A state of ten thousand chariots
is considered such because its territory is large.
If you now give away five hundred lǐ of the eastern lands,
this is to give away half of a Warring State.
You would have the title of ten thousand chariots but without the utility of even a thousand chariots.
This is unacceptable.
Thus, I say do not give them.
I, Cháng, request to defend them."
Zhāo Cháng left,
and Jǐng Lǐ entered for an audience.
The King said:
"The envoy of Qí has come to demand five hundred lǐ of our eastern lands.
What should be done about this?"
Jǐng Lǐ said:
"They must not be given.
However,
Chǔ cannot defend them alone.
Your Majesty has personally uttered precious words,
promising them to the powerful Qí, a state of ten thousand chariots. If you then do not give them,
you will be seen as unrighteous by all under Heaven.
Chǔ also cannot defend them alone.
I request to go west to seek rescue from Qín."
Jǐng Lǐ left,
and Shèn Zǐ entered.
The King told Shèn Zǐ of the plans of the three high officials, saying:
"Zǐliáng saw me and said,
'They must be given,
and after giving them, attack them to take them back.'
Cháng saw me and said,
'They must not be given;
I, Cháng, request to defend them.'
Lǐ saw me and said,
'They must not be given,
although Chǔ cannot defend them alone,
I request to seek rescue from Qín.'
Whose plan among the three should I use?"
Shèn Zǐ replied: "Your Majesty should use them all."
The King flushed with anger and said:
"What do you mean?"
Shèn Zǐ said:
"I request to explain the reasoning,
and Your Majesty will see that it is truly so.
Your Majesty should dispatch fifty chariots for the Shàngzhùguó Zǐliáng
to go north and offer the five hundred lǐ of land to Qí.
The day after Zǐliáng's departure,
appoint Zhāo Cháng as Dàsīmǎ
and order him to go and defend the eastern lands.
The day after Zhāo Cháng's departure,
dispatch fifty chariots for Jǐng Lǐ
to go west and seek rescue from Qín."
The King said: "Excellent."
He then dispatched Zǐliáng north to offer the land to Qí.
The day after Zǐliáng's departure,
he appointed Zhāo Cháng as Dàsīmǎ
and sent him to defend the eastern lands.
He also dispatched Jǐng Lǐ west to seek rescue from Qín.
When Zǐliáng reached Qí,
the King of Qí sent men in armor to receive the eastern lands.
Zhāo Cháng responded to the Qí envoy, saying:
"I am in charge of the eastern lands,
and I shall live or die with them.
Everyone from the height of five feet to the age of sixty,
with more than three hundred thousand sets of worn armor and blunt weapons,
is willing to face your dust in battle."
The King of Qí said to Zǐliáng: "You came to offer the land,
but now Cháng is defending it. What is going on?"
Zǐliáng said: "I personally received the command from the King of my humble state.
This Cháng must be acting on his own authority.
Your Majesty should attack him."
The King of Qí raised a great army,
attacked the eastern lands,
and campaigned against Zhāo Cháng.
Before they had crossed the border,
Qín approached the western territories of Qí with five hundred thousand troops.
They said:
"To detain the Crown Prince of Chǔ and not let him leave
is unkind;
and then to want to seize five hundred lǐ of his eastern land
is unrighteous.
If you withdraw your troops, it will be fine;
otherwise,
we wish to await battle."
The King of Qí was afraid.
He then requested Zǐliáng to travel south through Chǔ
and go west as an envoy to Qín
to resolve the crisis for Qí.
The soldiers were not used,
and the eastern lands remained whole.
Nǚ Ā said to Sū Zǐ:
"The one who caused Qín to detain the King of Chǔ
and endangered the Crown Prince
was you.
Now that the King of Chǔ is returning
and the Crown Prince is heading south,
you will certainly be in danger.
You would do better to send someone to tell the Crown Prince:
'Sū Zǐ knows the Crown Prince resents him,
so he will surely strive to work against the Crown Prince's interests.
The Crown Prince would do better to be kind to Sū Zǐ;
then Sū Zǐ will surely act on the Crown Prince's behalf.'"
Sū Zǐ then sent someone to tell the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince in return requested to be on good terms with Sū Zǐ.
Sū Zǐ said to the King of Chǔ:
"A benevolent man's relation to the people
is to love them with his heart
and serve them with good words.
A filial son's relation to his parents
is to love them with his heart
and serve them with wealth.
A loyal minister's relation to his lord
must be to promote worthy men to assist him.
Now your high officials and kinsmen
like to harm the worthy to provide for themselves,
they levy heavy taxes on the other ministers and the common people,
making Your Majesty hated by the people;
they are not loyal ministers.
The high officials broadcast Your Majesty's faults to the common people
and give many bribes to the feudal lords using Your Majesty's land;
thus they distance those whom Your Majesty loves.
This is also not being a loyal minister,
and this is why the state is in danger.
I wish that you would not listen to the mutual slandering of the officials,
and be cautious of the high officials and kinsmen;
use what the people find good,
restrain your own desires
for the sake of the people.
For a minister, nothing is more difficult than to promote worthy men without jealousy.
To die for one's lord is easy;
in the affair at Chuíshā,
those who died were numbered in the thousands.
To bear humiliation for one's lord is easy;
from the Lìngyǐn on down,
those who serve the King are numbered in the thousands.
But as for promoting worthy men without jealousy,
I have not seen a single person.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler examines his ministers,
he must know if they promote worthy men without jealousy.
When a worthy man serves his lord,
he also must promote worthy men without jealousy.
The reason why promoting worthy men is difficult is that
if a worthy man is used, one might be discarded,
and if the other becomes noble, one might become lowly.
That is why people find it difficult."
Sū Qín went to Chǔ,
and it was three days before he could see the King.
When the conversation was finished,
he took his leave and prepared to depart.
The King of Chǔ said:
"I have heard of you, sir,
as if I were hearing of the ancients.
Now you have come from a thousand lǐ away to visit me,
yet you are not willing to stay;
I wish to hear your explanation."
He replied:
"In the state of Chǔ, food is more precious than jade,
firewood is more precious than cassia,
attendants are as difficult to see as ghosts,
and the King is as difficult to see as the Heavenly Emperor.
Now you order me to eat jade and cook with cassia,
and to see the Emperor through the help of ghosts."
The King said:
"Please return to your lodgings, sir;
I have received your instruction."
The King of Chǔ expelled Zhāng Yí to Wèi.
Chén Zhěn said: "Why does Your Majesty expel Zhāng Zǐ?"
He said:
"Because as a minister he is neither loyal nor trustworthy."
Chén Zhěn said:
"If he is not loyal, Your Majesty should not have him as a minister;
if he is not trustworthy, Your Majesty should not make agreements with him.
Moreover, if a minister of Wèi is not loyal or trustworthy,
how does that harm Your Majesty?
If he were loyal and trustworthy,
how would that benefit Your Majesty?
If you expel him and they listen to him, then it is fine;
but if they do not listen to him,
then Your Majesty is simply putting him in a difficult position.
Furthermore, to make a state of ten thousand chariots dismiss its chancellor
is something that happens in a forced treaty under the city walls."
Zhāng Yí went to Chǔ
and was poor.
His retainers were angry and wanted to return home.
Zhāng Yí said: "You must want to return
because your clothes and caps are worn out.
Wait for me to see the King of Chǔ on your behalf."
At that time,
Nán Hòu and Zhèng Yòu were honored in Chǔ.
Zhāng-zǐ met the King of Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ was not pleased.
Zhāng-zǐ said:
“If Your Majesty has no use for your servant,
I request to go north to see the Lord of Jìn.”
The King of Chǔ said:
“Very well.”
Zhāng-zǐ said:
“Does Your Majesty seek nothing from the state of Jìn?”
The King said:
“Gold, pearls, rhinoceros horns, and ivory are produced in Chǔ;
I have nothing to seek from the state of Jìn.”
Zhāng-zǐ said:
“Is it merely that Your Majesty does not favor beauty?”
The King said: “Why is that?”
Zhāng-zǐ said:
“Those women of Zhèng and Zhōu,
using white powder and black ink,
stand at the gates of the thoroughfares;
those who see them without knowing them
take them for goddesses.”
The King of Chǔ said: “Chǔ
is a remote and humble state;
I have never seen the women of the Central States be so beautiful as this.
How could I alone not favor beauty?”
Thereupon he provided him with pearls and jade.
Nán Hòu and Zhèng Bào heard of this and were greatly terrified.
They sent someone to say to Zhāng-zǐ:
“We have heard that the General is going to the state of Jìn;
we happen to have a thousand catties of gold,
to offer to your attendants
to provide for fodder.”
Zhèng Bào also provided five hundred catties of gold.
Zhāng-zǐ took leave of the King of Chǔ, saying:
“The world's passes are closed and travel is blocked;
I know not when I shall see the sun again.
I wish for Your Majesty to bestow a parting cup.”
The King said: “Very well.”
Then he toasted him.
While Zhāng-zǐ was in the middle of drinking,
he bowed twice and requested, saying:
“There are no others present here;
I wish Your Majesty would summon those you are familiar with to drink with us.”
The King said: “Very well.”
He then summoned Nán Hòu and Zhèng Bào and toasted them.
Zhāng-zǐ bowed twice and requested, saying:
“I, Yí, have committed a capital offense against Your Majesty.”
The King said:
“Why is that?”
He said:
“I have traveled everywhere in the world,
but I have never seen anyone as beautiful as these.
Yet I spoke of finding beauties;
this was deceiving Your Majesty.”
The King said:
“You are excused.
I certainly believed that in all the world, none could compare to these two.”
The King of Chǔ ordered Zhāo Jū to go to Qín to show respect to Zhāng Yí.
Before he arrived,
Huì Wáng died.
Wǔ Wáng banished Zhāng Yí.
The King of Chǔ then recalled Zhāo Jū in order to ally with Qí.
Huán Zāng spoke for Jū to the King of Chǔ, saying:
“The Horizontal Alliance has failed to come together because
Yí was honored by Huì Wáng and was on good terms with Jū.
Now Huì Wáng is dead
and Wǔ Wáng has been enthroned;
Yí has fled,
and Gōngsūn Hǎo and
Gān Mào are honored.
Gān Mào is friendly with Wèi,
and Gōngsūn Hǎo is friendly with Hán.
These two are certainly not on good terms with Jū,
and they will surely use Qín to ally with Hán and Wèi.
When Hán and Wèi respected Yí,
Yí had Qín and Jū had Chǔ to make him important.
Now Yí is troubled by Qín and Jū has been recalled by Chǔ;
if Hán and Wèi wish to gain favor with Qín,
they must be friendly with those two.
They will ally with Hán and Wèi, disregard Yí, and attack Chǔ;
Fāngchéng will surely be in danger.
It would be better for Your Majesty to restore Jū
and emphasize Yí's importance to Hán and Wèi.
Yí will lean on Chǔ's power,
hold Wèi's weight,
and compete with Qín.
If Wèi does not ally with Qín
and Hán does not follow,
then Fāngchéng will have no worries.”
Zhāng Yí banished Huì Shī from Wèi.
Huì-zǐ went to Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ received him.
Féng Hǎo said to the King of Chǔ:
“The one who banished Huì-zǐ
was Zhāng Yí.
Yet Your Majesty personally makes an agreement with him;
this is deceiving Zhāng Yí.
I do not think Your Majesty should do this.
Huì-zǐ came for Yí's sake,
but if he hates Your Majesty’s alliance with Zhāng Yí,
Huì-zǐ will certainly not proceed.
Moreover, the King of Sòng regards Huì-zǐ as worthy;
there is no one in the world who has not heard of this.
That he is currently not on good terms with Zhāng Yí,
there is no one in the world who does not know this.
Now, for the sake of affairs,
to abandon one who is valued to an enemy—
I believe Your Majesty is acting lightly.
Is it for the sake of affairs?
Your Majesty would do better to promote Huì-zǐ and send him to Sòng,
and say to Zhāng Yí:
‘I ask for your sake not to receive him.’
Yí will surely be grateful to Your Majesty.
As Huì-zǐ is a man in distress
and Your Majesty supports him,
he will also surely be grateful to Your Majesty.
This does not lose the substance of favoring Yí,
and yet can make Huì-zǐ grateful.”
The King of Chǔ said: “Excellent.”
Thereupon he supported Huì-zǐ and sent him to Sòng.
Five states attacked Qín.
Wèi wanted peace,
and sent Huì Shī to Chǔ.
Chǔ was about to introduce him to Qín to facilitate the peace.
Dù Hè said to Zhāo Yáng:
“Essentially, the one who led the attack on Qín was Chǔ.
Now Shī comes from Wèi,
and if you introduce him to Qín,
this clearly shows Chǔ’s aggression while validating Wèi’s desire for peace.
You would do better not to listen to Huì Shī,
but secretly send someone to request peace from Qín.”
Zhāo-zǐ said: “Excellent.”
He then said to Huì Shī:
“Essentially, the one who led the attack on Qín was Wèi.
Now you seek peace through Chǔ;
Chǔ would gain the benefit,
while Wèi would bear the resentment.
You should return; I will send someone to seek peace through Wèi.”
Huì-zǐ returned,
and the King of Wèi was not pleased.
Dù Hè said to Zhāo Yáng:
“Wèi fought first for you
and lost half its army.
They reported their exhaustion but were not heard;
they requested peace but did not get it.
If Wèi turns away and joins with Qí and Qín,
how will you save the situation?
To the east is the burden of Yuè,
to the north there is no Jìn,
and diplomatic relations are not yet settled with Qí
or Qín; this would leave Chǔ isolated.
It is better to make peace quickly.”
Zhāo-zǐ said:
“Excellent.”
He then sent someone to request peace through Wèi.
Chén Zhěn left Chǔ for Wèi.
Zhāng Yí spoke ill of him to the King of Wèi, saying:
“Zhěn is still friendly toward Chǔ
and is working very hard to seek land for them.”
Zuǒ Shuǎng said to Chén Zhěn:
“Yí is on good terms with the King of Wèi,
and the King of Wèi trusts him deeply.
Although you may explain yourself a hundred times,
he still will not listen.
You would do better to use Yí's words to your advantage
to be reinstated in Chǔ.”
Chén Zhěn said: “Excellent.”
He then sent someone to let Yí's words be heard in Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ was pleased
and wished to reinstate him.
Qín attacked Yíyáng.
The King of Chǔ said to Chén Zhěn:
“I have heard that Hán Chǐ is a clever man,
well-versed in the affairs of the feudal lords,
and can likely save himself.
Because he will surely save himself,
I wish to support him first to increase his gratitude toward me.”
Chén Zhěn replied: “Leave it be; Your Majesty should not support him.
With Hán Chǐ's wisdom,
he is trapped here.
Among the beasts of the mountains and marshes,
none are more cunning than the elk.
The elk knows that the hunter has spread nets
and is driving it from the front,
so it turns back and charges at the people,
doing so several times.
The hunter knows its trick,
so he pretends to lift the net and advances,
and thus the elk is caught.”
Now the feudal lords clearly know that this is full of deception,
so those who falsely present themselves to advance will surely be many.
Set it aside;
Great King, do not rely on it.
The wisdom of Hán Chǐ
is exhausted here."
The King of Chǔ listened to him,
and Yíyáng was indeed captured.
Chén Zhěn had known this beforehand.
Táng Qiě went to see Chūnshēn Jūn and said:
"The people of Qí adorn themselves and cultivate their conduct to gain benefit,
but I am ashamed of it and do not learn it.
Not avoiding the crossing of the Jiāng and Hé rivers,
I have traveled over a thousand lǐ to come here,
privately admiring your righteousness, Great Lord,
and wishing to improve your endeavors.
I have heard that
when Bēn and Zhū carried even a small blade,
the whole world considered them brave;
when Xī Shī wore coarse cloth, the whole world called her beautiful.
Now you are the Chancellor of the ten-thousand-chariot state of Chǔ,
warding off the troubles of the Central States;
yet what you desire is not achieved,
and what you seek is not obtained,
because I and my likes are few.
Now, the reason the leading chess piece can perform
is that the secondary pieces assist it.
That one leading piece is not as effective as five secondary pieces
is also clear.
Why do you not act as the leader of the world,
and let us be your assistants?"
Someone spoke to the King of Chǔ, saying:
"I have heard
that the proponents of the Vertical Alliance wish to unite the world to pay homage to you, Great King;
I hope you will listen to them.
To turn submission into extension,
to turn old troubles into success,
the brave consider this righteous.
To transform calamity into fortune,
to turn the few into the many,
the wise manage this.
Returning reward for reward,
and the transformation of the silent and obscure,
only a Great Lord can achieve this.
Calamity and fortune are interlinked;
life and death are neighbors.
One who does not lean toward death,
nor lean toward life,
is insufficient to carry a great name.
Without any hardship or suffering,
one is insufficient to dominate the world.
Qín has abandoned virtue and severed lives for a long time,
yet the world does not realize it.
Now the proponents of the Horizontal Alliance use sweet words and sharp schemes;
above, they disturb the ruler's mind;
below, they exploit the common people.
They claim to act for the public while seeking private gain.
Therefore, the state's power is lighter than a swan's feather,
and the accumulated calamities are heavier than a mountain."
The King of Wèi sent a beautiful woman to the King of Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ was pleased with her.
His consort Zhèng Bāu knew the King was pleased with the newcomer,
so she treated the newcomer with great affection.
Regarding clothes and playthings,
she chose what the newcomer liked for her;
regarding palace rooms and bedding,
she chose what the newcomer preferred for her.
She loved her even more than the King did.
The King said: "The means by which a woman serves her husband
is her beauty;
but jealousy
is her natural emotion.
Now Zhèng Bāu knows I am pleased with the newcomer,
yet she loves her even more than I do;
this is how a filial son serves his parents,
and how a loyal minister serves his lord."
Zhèng Bāu knew the King considered her not to be jealous,
so she said to the newcomer:
"The King loves your beauty.
Although this is so,
he dislikes your nose.
When you go to see the King,
you must cover your nose."
When the newcomer saw the King,
she accordingly covered her nose.
The King said to Zhèng Bāu:
"When the newcomer sees me,
she covers her nose;
why is that?"
Zhèng Bāu said:
"I know why."
The King said:
"Even if it is unpleasant, you must tell me."
Zhèng Bāu said:
"It seems she dislikes smelling the odor of the King."
The King said:
"How insolent!"
He ordered her nose to be cut off,
and let no one disobey the command.
After the Queen of the King of Chǔ died,
a new queen had not yet been established.
Someone said to Zhāo Yú:
"Why do you, sir, not request the establishment of a queen?"
Zhāo Yú said: "If the King does not listen,
it will show my wisdom is exhausted and my relationship with the future queen will be severed."
"In that case, why not buy five pairs of earrings,
make one pair exceptionally fine and present them to the King?
Tomorrow, observe where the fine earrings are,
and then request to establish that person as queen."
Zhuāng Xīn said to King Xiāng of Chǔ:
"Your Majesty has the Marquis of Zhōu on your left
and the Marquis of Xià on your right;
your carriage is followed by the Lord of Yānlíng and the Lord of Shòulíng.
You devote yourself solely to debauchery and extravagance,
ignoring state affairs.
The capital of Yǐng will surely be in danger."
King Xiāng said: "Is the gentleman old and confused?
Or do you intend to bring ill omens to the state of Chǔ?"
Zhuāng Xīn said: "I truly see that it is inevitable;
I do not dare to bring ill omens to the state.
If Your Majesty continues to favor these four men without end,
the state of Chǔ will surely perish.
I request to withdraw to Zhào
and stay there to observe what happens."
Zhuāng Xīn left and went to Zhào,
staying for five months.
Qín indeed captured the lands of Yān, Yǐng, Wū, Shàngcài, and Chén;
King Xiāng was forced to take refuge in Chéngyáng.
Thereupon, he sent a messenger to drive quickly
and summon Zhuāng Xīn from Zhào.
Zhuāng Xīn said:
"Yes."
When Zhuāng Xīn arrived,
King Xiāng said:
"I was unable to use your words,
and now matters have come to this;
what should be done about it?"
Zhuāng Xīn replied: "I have heard a common saying:
'To look for the dog only after seeing the rabbit
is not too late;
to mend the fold after the sheep are lost
is not too delayed.'
I have heard that in the past, Tāng and Wǔ flourished with only a hundred lǐ,
while Jié and Zhòu perished despite possessing the whole world.
Now, although the state of Chǔ is small,
if we cut off the long and patch the short,
it still covers several thousand lǐ;
how could it be only a hundred lǐ?
"Does Your Majesty not see the dragonfly?
With six legs and four wings,
it flies between heaven and earth,
bowing its head to peck at mosquitoes and gadflies for food,
and looking up to receive sweet dew for drink.
It considers itself without worry
and has no conflict with men.
It does not know that a five-foot-tall boy
is preparing lead glue and silk thread
to catch it from over four rèn high,
and then it falls to be eaten by mole crickets and ants.
The dragonfly is a small thing,
and so it is with the yellow bird.
It bows to peck at white grains,
and looks up to perch in lush trees,
flapping its wings and soaring with vigor,
considering itself without worry
and having no conflict with men.
It does not know that princes and noble grandsons,
with a catapult in the left hand
and pellets in the right,
are about to strike it from over ten rèn high,
using its own kind as a lure.
In the daytime, it roams in lush trees;
by evening, it is seasoned with sour and salty flavors,
and in a sudden moment,
it falls into the hands of the prince.
"The bird is a small thing,
and so it is with the yellow swan.
It roams over rivers and seas,
stays in great marshes,
bows to peck at eels and carp,
and looks up to nibble on water chestnuts and herbs.
It spreads its six powerful feathers
to ride the clear wind,
soaring high and floating in the air,
considering itself without worry
and having no conflict with men.
It does not know that the archer is just then preparing his bow and arranging his silk string,
about to strike it from over a hundred rèn high.
That sharp arrow, pulling the fine silk string,
cuts through the clear wind and brings it down.
Thus, in the daytime it roams in the rivers,
and by evening it is seasoned in the cooking pots.
“The yellow swan is but a small thing.
The affair of Cài Shèng Hóu is like this.
He traveled south to Gāobēi,
and ascended north to Wùshān.
He drank from the Rǔxī stream
and ate the fish of the Xiāng waves.
On his left he held a young concubine;
on his right he embraced a favored woman.
He galloped with them in the midst of Gāocài,
and did not take the affairs of the state as his concern.
He did not know that Zǐfā was then receiving orders from Xuānwáng
to bind him with red silk and present him.
“The affair of Cài Shèng Hóu was a small thing;
your Majesty’s affair is like this.
With Zhōuhóu on the left
and Xiàhóu on the right,
and the group including Yānlíng Jūn and Shòulíng Jūn following behind,
you eat the grain of your fiefs
and wear the gold of the square treasury.
You gallop with them in the midst of Yúnmèng,
and do not take the affairs of the world and the state as your concern.
You do not know that Rǎng Hóu is then receiving orders from the Qín Wáng
to occupy the inside of Mǐnsài,
and cast you outside of Mǐnsài.”
When Xiāngwáng heard this,
his countenance changed and grew stern,
and his body trembled.
Thereupon, he took a jade tablet and granted it to him, making him Yánglíng Jūn,
and gave him the lands of Huáiběi.
Qí Míng persuaded Zhuó Huá to attack Qín,
but Zhuó Huá would not listen.
Qí Míng said to Zhuó Huá,
“The reason for my coming
was to divine a friendship for Chú lǐ Jí.
I have persuaded the grand masters of Chǔ to attack Qín,
and they all accepted my counsel;
only you did not accept it.
I have words with which to report back to Chú lǐ Zǐ.”
Zhuó Huá therefore held him in high regard.
Someone said to Huáng Qí,
“Everyone says that you are not on good terms with Fù Zhì.
Have you not heard of Lǎo Láizǐ’s teaching to Kǒngzǐ about serving a ruler?
He showed him how his teeth were hard,
but by age sixty they had all worn each other down.
Now Fù Zhì is capable,
yet you repeatedly are not on good terms with him;
this is for both to be exhausted.
A proverb says:
‘When you see the ruler’s carriage,
descend from yours;
when you see his staff,
stand up.’
Now, the King loves Fù Zhì,
but you are not on good terms with him;
this is to fail as a subject.”
During the crisis in Chángshā,
the Chǔ Crown Prince Héng was a hostage in Qí.
The King of Chǔ died,
and Xuē Gōng returned Crown Prince Héng to Chǔ,
and then, with the troops of Hán and Wèi,
followed and attacked the Eastern State.
The Crown Prince was afraid.
Zhāo Gài said: “It is better to order Qū Shǔ to offer the new Eastern State as a peace settlement to Qí to provoke Qín.
Qín will fear that Qí will defeat the Eastern State
and that its orders will then prevail throughout the world,
so Qín will certainly come to our rescue.”
The Crown Prince said: “Excellent.”
He immediately ordered Qū Shǔ to offer the Eastern State as a peace settlement to Qí.
When the Qín Wáng heard this, he was afraid,
and ordered Xīn Róng to tell Chǔ:
“Do not give the Eastern State to Qí;
I will send out troops for you.”
Someone offered an elixir of immortality to the Jīng Wáng.
An usher held it and entered.
An officer of the Inner Guard asked:
“Can it be eaten?”
The usher said: “Yes.”
The officer then snatched it and ate it.
The King was angry
and sent men to kill the officer.
The officer sent someone to persuade the King, saying:
“I asked the usher,
and the usher said it could be eaten,
so I ate it.
Thus I am without guilt,
and the guilt lies with the usher.
Furthermore, the guest offered an elixir of immortality;
I ate it and yet the King kills me,
so it is an elixir of death.
If the King kills a guiltless subject,
it makes clear that someone has deceived the King.”
The King then did not kill him.
A guest said to Chūnshēn Jūn:
“Tāng used Bó,
and Wǔ Wáng used Hào;
neither exceeded a hundred lǐ, yet they possessed the world.
Now Sūnzǐ
is a worthy man of the world;
if you grant him the power of a hundred lǐ,
I privately think it will not be advantageous for you.
How does that sound?”
Chūnshēn Jūn said: “Excellent.”
Thereupon he sent someone to decline Sūnzǐ.
Sūnzǐ left for Zhào,
and Zhào made him a high minister.
Another guest said to Chūnshēn Jūn:
“In the past, Yī Yǐn left Xià and entered Yīn,
and the Yīn king reigned while Xià perished.
Guǎn Zhòng left Lǔ and entered Qí,
and Lǔ became weak while Qí became strong.
Wherever a worthy man is,
his ruler is never without honor,
and the state is never without glory.
Now Sūnzǐ
is a worthy man of the world.
Why did you dismiss him?”
Chūnshēn Jūn also said: “Excellent.”
Thereupon he sent someone to invite Sūnzǐ from Zhào.
Sūnzǐ wrote a letter in reply, saying:
“A leper pities the king—
these are disrespectful words.
Nevertheless,
one cannot but examine them.
This is spoken for rulers who are coerced, assassinated, or perish.
If a ruler is young and arrogant of his talent
and has no methods or techniques to recognize wickedness,
then the great ministers will monopolize the state’s decisions for their own gain to prevent punishment upon themselves.
Therefore, they assassinate the worthy and elder and set up the young and weak;
they depose the legitimate heir and set up the unrighteous.
The Chūnqiū warns of this, saying:
‘Prince Wéi of Chǔ went on a mission to Zhèng.
Before he had left the borders,
he heard the King was ill.
He returned to inquire after the illness,
and then used his cap strings to strangle the King,
killing him,
and then set himself up as King.
Cuì Zhù of Qí had a beautiful wife;
Zhuāng Gōng had an affair with her.
Cuì Zhù led his followers to attack.
Zhuāng Gōng asked to divide the state with him;
Cuì Zhù did not permit it.
He wished to take his own life in the temple;
Cuì Zhù did not permit it.
Zhuāng Gōng ran out
and climbed over the outer wall.
An arrow hit him in the thigh,
and then they killed him,
and set up his younger brother, Jǐng Gōng.’
In more recent times, we have seen:
Lǐ Duì took power in Zhào,
starved the Father of the Sovereign at Shāqiū,
and killed him after a hundred days.
Nào Chǐ took power in Qí,
pulled out the tendons of Mǐn Wáng,
and hung him from the beams of his temple,
and after a night he died.
Although a leper has ulcers, swellings, and pustules,
compared above to the former ages,
he has not come to being strangled by cap strings or shot in the thigh;
compared below to recent times,
he has not come to having his tendons pulled or starving to death.
As for rulers who are coerced, assassinated, or perish,
the anxiety and toil of their hearts
and the distress and suffering of their bodies
must be far worse than a leper’s.
Looking at it from this perspective,
it is acceptable for a leper to pity a king.”
He then composed an ode, saying:
“Treasures like the Suí Pearl,
they know not how to wear.
Between coarse cloth and silk,
they know not the difference.
The beauty of Lǘ and Zǐshē,
no one knows how to find a match.
If Mó mǔ is sought,
they are exceedingly pleased.
They take the blind for the sighted,
and take the deaf for the hearing.
They take right for wrong,
and take good fortune for calamity.
Alas, High Heaven!
How could they be the same?”
The Shī says:
“High Heaven is most divine;
do not bring distress upon yourself.”
The world joined in a Vertical Alliance.
Zhào sent Wèi Jiā to see Lord Chūn Shēn of Chǔ and said:
“Does your lordship have a general?”
He said: “I have;
I wish to make Lord Lín Wǔ the general.”
Wèi Jiā said: “When your servant was young, I loved archery.
Your servant wishes to use an analogy about archery;
is that acceptable?”
Lord Chūn Shēn said:
“It is.”
Jiā said:
“In days past,
Gèng Léi and the King of Wèi were at the foot of the Jīngtái Terrace,
looking up, they saw flying birds.
Gèng Léi said to the King of Wèi:
‘Your servant can draw the bow and fire without an arrow for your Majesty, yet bring down a bird.’
The King of Wèi said: ‘Then can archery really reach such a level?’
Gèng Léi said:
‘It can.’
After a short while,
a wild goose came from the east;
Gèng Léi fired without an arrow and brought it down.
The King of Wèi said: ‘Then can archery really reach such a level?’
Gèng Léi said:
‘This was a wounded bird.’
The King said:
‘How did the Master know this?’
He replied: ‘Its flight was slow and its cry was mournful.
Flying slowly
because its old wounds were painful;
crying mournfully
because it had long been separated from its flock.
Thus, its old wounds had not yet healed,
and its startled heart had not yet subsided.
Hearing the sound of the bowstring,
it strained to fly high,
and so its old wounds reopened and it fell.’
Now Lord Lín Wǔ
has previously been wounded by Qín;
he cannot be the general to resist Qín.”
Hàn Míng went to see Lord Chūn Shēn;
he waited for an audience for three months
before he was granted one.
When the talk ended,
Lord Chūn Shēn was greatly pleased with him.
Hàn Míng wished to speak again,
Lord Chūn Shēn said:
“I already know the Master;
the Master should rest now.”
Hàn Míng, looking troubled, said:
“I, Míng, wish to ask your lordship a question but fear being too forward.
I do not know how your lordship's sagacity
compares with that of Yáo?”
Lord Chūn Shēn said: “The Master is mistaken.
How could I, your servant, be worthy to be compared to Yáo?”
Hàn Míng said:
“Then how does your lordship reckon I compare with Shùn?”
Lord Chūn Shēn said: “The Master is indeed Shùn.”
Hàn Míng said: “Not so.
Please let your servant finish speaking for your lordship.
Your lordship's virtue is in truth not equal to Yáo's,
and my ability does not reach Shùn's.
Now, even with the virtuous Shùn serving the sagacious Yáo,
it was only after three years that they understood each other.
Now your lordship knows me in a single session;
this means your lordship is more sagacious than Yáo and your servant is more virtuous than Shùn.”
Lord Chūn Shēn said: “Good.”
He summoned the gate official to record Master Hàn in the guest register,
to be seen once every five days.
Hàn Míng said: “Has your lordship also heard of the Jì horse?
When the Jì horse was old,
it was harnessed to a salt cart to climb Mount Tàiháng.
Its hooves splayed and its knees buckled,
its tail was soaked and its skin was raw,
its sweat and fluids sprinkled the ground,
white sweat poured off it.
Midway up the slope it faltered,
straining against the shafts but unable to go up.
Bó Lè happened upon it;
he climbed down from his carriage, embraced it, and wept for it,
taking off his hempen robe to cover it.
The Jì horse then lowered its head and snorted,
then raised its head and neighed,
the sound reached the heavens,
like the sound of striking metal or stone.
Why was this?
Because it saw that Bó Lè understood it.
Now, I, your unworthy servant,
have been constrained in local districts,
living in holes and dead-end alleys,
submerged in filth and vulgar customs for a long time.
Does your lordship alone not intend to cleanse and rescue me,
so that I might neigh loudly for your lordship in Liáng?”
King Kǎo Liè of Chǔ had no son.
Lord Chūn Shēn was worried about this,
and sought women likely to bear children to present to him.
They were very many,
but in the end, there was no son.
Lǐ Yuán, a man of Zhào,
brought his younger sister,
wishing to present her to the King of Chǔ.
Hearing that the King was unlikely to have children,
he feared she would also fail to gain favor.
Lǐ Yuán sought to serve Lord Chūn Shēn as a retainer.
After a while, he asked for leave to go home
and deliberately missed his return date.
When he returned to report,
Lord Chūn Shēn asked for the circumstances.
He replied: “The King of Qí sent an envoy to ask for my sister.
I was drinking with that envoy,
therefore I missed the date.”
Lord Chūn Shēn said:
“Has the betrothal gift been received?”
He replied:
“Not yet.”
Lord Chūn Shēn said:
“Can I see her?”
He said: “You may.”
Thereupon Yuán presented his sister,
and she was favored by Lord Chūn Shēn.
Knowing she was pregnant,
Yuán then conspired with his sister.
Lǐ Yuán's sister took an opportunity to persuade Lord Chūn Shēn, saying:
“The King of Chǔ honors and favors you,
more so than even his own brothers.
Now you have been Chancellor to the King of Chǔ for over twenty years,
and the King has no son;
thus after a hundred years, he will surely establish one of his brothers.
If the King of Chǔ establishes someone else,
that person will surely honor those he was personally close to,
so how could you long maintain your favor?
Is that not so?
You have been in power for a long time,
and have often been discourteous to the King's brothers.
If a brother is truly established,
disaster will surely reach your person;
then how will you preserve the Chancellor's seal and your fief in Jiāngdōng?
Now I know myself to be pregnant,
but no one else knows.
My favor with you has not been for long;
if you use your influence to present me to the King of Chǔ,
the King will surely favor me.
If I rely on Heaven and have a boy,
then your son will be the King;
the fiefs of the State of Chǔ can all be obtained;
how does that compare with facing an unpredictable crime?”
Lord Chūn Shēn greatly agreed with this.
He moved Lǐ Yuán's sister out to a private residence,
and spoke of her to the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ summoned her to enter
and favored her.
Subsequently, she gave birth to a boy,
who was established as the Crown Prince,
and Lǐ Yuán's sister was established as the Queen.
The King of Chǔ honored Lǐ Yuán,
and Lǐ Yuán came into power.
Once Lǐ Yuán had his sister established as the Queen
and her son as the Crown Prince,
he feared Lord Chūn Shēn would leak the secret and become increasingly arrogant,
so he secretly raised assassins,
wishing to kill Lord Chūn Shēn to silence him,
and some people in the state knew of this.
Lord Chūn Shēn had been Chancellor of Chǔ for twenty-five years
when King Kǎo Liè fell ill.
Zhū Yīng said to Lord Chūn Shēn:
“The world has unexpected blessings,
and also unexpected disasters.
Now you live in an age of unexpectedness,
serving an unexpected lord,
how can there not be an unexpected person?”
Lord Chūn Shēn said: “What is meant by ‘unexpected blessings’?”
He said: “You have been Chancellor of Chǔ for over twenty years;
though you are called the Chancellor,
in reality, you are the King of Chǔ.
Your five sons are all chancellors to the feudal lords.
Now the King's illness is severe;
he will pass away at any moment.
The Crown Prince is young and weak,
and the King is sick and will not recover.
You will serve as Chancellor to a young ruler,
and thus stand in for him to govern the state,
like Yī Yǐn or the Duke of Zhōu.
When the King grows up, you return the government;
if not,
you may even face south and call yourself ‘The Lone One’,
and thus possess the State of Chǔ.
This is what is called ‘unexpected blessings’.”
Chūnshēn Jūn said: "What is meant by an unforeseen calamity?"
Zhū Yīng said: "Lǐ Yuán does not govern the state;
he is the King's brother-in-law.
He does not serve as a military general,
yet he has secretly maintained men of sacrifice for a long time.
When the King of Chǔ passes away,
Lǐ Yuán will certainly enter first.
Based on his original plans, he will seize control and issue edicts to preempt your commands,
grasping authority and killing you to silence you.
This is what is meant by an unforeseen calamity."
Chūnshēn Jūn said: "What is meant by an unforeseen person?"
Zhū Yīng said: "You first appoint me as a Palace Attendant.
When the King passes away,
and Lǐ Yuán enters first,
I request to stab him in the chest and kill him for you.
This is what is meant by an unforeseen person."
Chūnshēn Jūn said: "Master, set this aside
and speak no more of it.
Lǐ Yuán
is a weak person,
and I am also on good terms with him.
How could it come to this?"
Zhū Yīng was afraid,
and so he fled and left.
Seventeen days later,
King Kǎoliè of Chǔ passed away,
and Lǐ Yuán indeed entered first.
He stationed men of sacrifice, stopping them within the Jímén gate.
When Chūnshēn Jūn entered later,
he was stopped at Jímén.
Yuán's men of sacrifice attacked from both sides and stabbed Chūnshēn Jūn,
cut off his head,
and threw it outside the Jímén gate.
Thereupon, officials were sent to completely exterminate Chūnshēn Jūn's family.
As for Lǐ Yuán's younger sister,
who had originally been favored by Chūnshēn Jūn and become pregnant
before being presented to the King where she bore a son,
that son was subsequently established as King Yōu of Chǔ.
This year,
it was the ninth year of Qín Shǐhuáng's reign.
Lào Ǎi also incited a rebellion in Qín.
It was discovered, his three generations were exterminated,
and Lǚ Bùwéi was deposed.
Yú Qīng said to Chūnshēn Jūn:
"I have heard it from the Chūnqiū
that in times of safety one should think of danger,
and in times of danger one should contemplate safety.
Now the King of Chǔ is advanced in years,
and your fiefdom
must be settled early.
In considering a fief for the Lord,
nothing is better than being far from Chǔ.
Duke Xiào of Qín enfeoffed Shāng Jūn;
after Duke Xiào died,
he was eventually not spared from being killed.
King Huì of Qín enfeoffed Rǎn Zǐ;
after King Huì died,
the King then seized the fief back.
Gōngsūn Yāng
was a meritorious official;
Rǎn Zǐ
was a relative by marriage.
Yet they were not spared from being deprived or killed
because their fiefs were near the capital.
Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed in Qí,
and Shào Gōng Shì was enfeoffed in Yān,
because they were far from the royal house.
Now Yān's offense is great and Zhào's anger is deep;
therefore, it would be better for you to lead troops north to earn the gratitude of Zhào,
trample the disordered Yān,
and secure your own fief. This is a once-in-a-hundred-generations
opportunity."
The Lord said:
"The path spoken of to attack Yān
must pass through either Qí or Wèi.
Wèi and Qí have new resentments against Chǔ;
even if the King of Chǔ wishes to attack Yān,
what path would he take?"
Yú Qīng replied:
"Please allow me to make the King of Wèi agree."
The Lord said:
"How so?"
He replied:
"I request to go to Wèi
and use a way to make him believe it."
Then he said to the King of Wèi:
"Chǔ is indeed powerful,
with no match in the world,
and it is about to attack Yān."
The King of Wèi said:
"Just now,
you said it has no match in the world;
now,
you say it is about to attack Yān.
Why is that?"
Yú Qīng replied:
"Now, to say a horse has much strength is one thing,
but to say it can lift a thousand jūn is not so.
Why?
A thousand jūn is not a horse's burden.
Now, to say Chǔ is powerful is one thing,
but if it crosses over Zhào
and Wèi to engage in battle in Yān,
then how could that be Chǔ's burden?
If it is not Chǔ's burden yet Chǔ does it,
this will wear out Chǔ.
A worn-out Chǔ facing a strong Wèi,
which one is more convenient for the King?"
Zhì Bó led the troops of Hán
and Wèi to attack Zhào, surrounding Jìnyáng and flooding it,
until the water was only three boards below the top of the city walls.
Xī Cī said to Zhì Bó:
"The lords of Hán and Wèi will surely rebel."
Zhì Bó said:
"How do you know this?"
Xī Cī said:
"I know it by observing their human affairs.
If you lead the troops of Hán and Wèi to attack Zhào,
and Zhào is destroyed,
disaster will surely reach Hán and Wèi next.
