Now you have agreed to defeat Zhào and divide its land into three.
Now the city walls are only three boards from being submerged,
it is said frogs are born in the hearths and mortars,
and men and horses eat each other.
The day the city falls is near,
yet the lords of Hán and Wèi show no joy in their hearts but have looks of worry.
If this is not rebellion, then what is it?"
The next day,
Zhì Bó told this to the lords of Hán and Wèi, saying:
"Xī Cī says you are about to rebel."
The lords of Hán and Wèi said:
"By defeating Zhào and dividing its land into three,
the city is now about to be captured.
Even if the three houses are foolish,
they would not cast away such great benefit before them,
break the oath of the alliance,
and do something dangerous and difficult that cannot be achieved.
The situation is plain to see.
This Cī is planning for Zhào's sake,
making you doubt the hearts of us two rulers
so that you slacken in the attack on Zhào.
Now you listen to the words of a slandering official
and distance yourself from the friendship of two rulers;
we feel regret for your sake."
They hurried out.
Xī Cī said to Zhì Bó:
"Why did you tell my words to the lords of Hán and Wèi?"
Zhì Bó said:
"How did you know of it?"
Xī Cī replied:
"The lords of Hán and Wèi looked at me directly and then hurried away."
Xī Cī knew his words were not being heard,
so he requested to be an envoy to Qí,
and Zhì Bó sent him.
The lords of Hán and Wèi did indeed rebel.
Zhì Bó led Zhào, Hán, and Wèi to attack the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
and destroyed them.
After resting for several years,
he sent someone to request land from Hán.
Hán Kāngzǐ wanted not to give it,
but Duàn Guī remonstrated, saying:
"You cannot.
As for Zhì Bó's character,
he is greedy for gain and fierce in retribution.
If he comes to request land and you do not give it,
he will surely bring troops against Hán.
You should give it to him.
Having given it to him, he will become habituated,
and will then request land from other states.
If the other states do not comply,
he will surely turn his troops toward them.
In this way, Hán can avoid misfortune and trouble
and wait for things to change."
Kāngzǐ said: "Good."
He sent an envoy to deliver a city of ten thousand households to Zhì Bó.
Zhì Bó was pleased,
and again sent someone to request land from Wèi.
Wèi Xuānzǐ wanted not to give it.
Zhào Jiā remonstrated, saying:
"He requested land from Hán,
and Hán gave it to him.
Now he requests land from Wèi;
if Wèi does not give it,
then Wèi will be strengthening its internal resolve
while externally angering Zhì Bó.
Thus, he will surely direct his troops toward Wèi!
It is better to give it to him."
Xuān Zǐ said: "Agreed."
He then sent someone to deliver a fief of ten thousand households to Zhì Bó.
Zhì Bó was pleased,
and again sent someone to Zhào,
requesting the lands of Cài and Gāoláng.
Zhào Xiāng Zǐ did not give them.
Zhì Bó then secretly allied with Hán and Wèi,
intending to use them to attack Zhào.
Zhào Xiāng Zǐ summoned Zhāng Mèng Tán and told him:
"As for Zhì Bó's character,
he is outwardly friendly but inwardly distant.
He has sent messengers to Hán and Wèi three times,
but I have not been included.
It is certain he will move his troops against me.
Now where would be a safe place for me to stay?"
Zhāng Mèng Tán said: "Dǒng Ān Yú
was a talented minister of Jiǎn Zhǔ.
He governed Jìnyáng for generations,
and Yǐn Zé followed his methods.
The remnants of their governance and instruction still exist.
You should settle in Jìnyáng."
The Lord said: "Agreed."
He then sent Yánlíng Wáng to lead the chariots and cavalry ahead to Jìnyáng,
and the Lord followed him.
Upon arrival, he inspected the city walls,
checked the treasuries and armories,
and viewed the granaries.
He summoned Zhāng Mèng Tán and said:
"My city walls are intact,
the treasuries and armories are sufficient,
and the granaries are full,
but what can be done about the lack of arrows?"
Zhāng Mèng Tán said: "I have heard that when Dǒng Zǐ governed Jìnyáng,
the walls of the public palaces
were all fenced with reeds, artemisia, and vitex.
Their height reaches over a zhàng.
You should take them and use them."
Thereupon, they took them and tested them;
their hardness was such that even the strength of jùnlù bamboo could not surpass it.
The Lord said:
"That is enough.
What about our shortage of bronze?"
Zhāng Mèng Tán said:
"I have heard that when Dǒng Zǐ governed Jìnyáng,
the rooms of the public palaces all used refined bronze for the pillar bases.
Please take them and use them,
and there will be surplus bronze."
The Lord said: "Excellent."
Orders were issued and settled,
and defensive preparations were complete.
The armies of the three states pressed upon the city of Jìnyáng,
and battle ensued.
After three months, they could not take it.
So they spread out their troops to besiege it
and diverted the Jìn River to flood it.
They besieged Jìnyáng for three years.
In the city, people lived in nests,
and hung their cauldrons to cook.
Wealth and food were nearly exhausted,
and the soldiers were sick and weak.
Xiāng Zǐ said to Zhāng Mèng Tán: "Grain is depleted,
the city's strength is exhausted,
the officials are sick.
I can no longer defend it.
I wish to surrender the city, what do you think?"
Zhāng Mèng Tán said: "I have heard that
if one cannot preserve what is perishing
or stabilize what is in danger,
then there is no reason to value wise scholars.
You should abandon this plan
and speak no more of it.
I request to see the lords of Hán and Wèi."
Xiāng Zǐ said: "Agreed."
Zhāng Mèng Tán then secretly saw the lords of Hán and Wèi and said:
"I have heard that if the lips are gone, the teeth will be cold.
Now Zhì Bó is leading the lords of the two states to attack Zhào.
Zhào is about to perish.
If it perishes, the two lords will be next."
The two lords said: "We know it is so.
As for Zhì Bó's character,
he is coarse within and has little affection.
If our plot is discovered before it succeeds,
then disaster will surely come.
What should we do?"
Zhāng Mèng Tán said: "The plan comes from the mouths of you two lords
and enters my ears.
No one else knows of it."
The two lords then made a secret pact with Zhāng Mèng Tán regarding the three armies,
and set a date with him.
That night,
he was sent back into Jìnyáng.
Zhāng Mèng Tán reported this to Xiāng Zǐ,
and Xiāng Zǐ bowed to him twice.
Zhāng Mèng Tán then attended Zhì Bó's court and departed,
encountering Zhì Guò outside the camp gate.
Zhì Guò went in to see Zhì Bó and said:
"The two lords are likely to have a change of heart."
The Lord said:
"Why so?"
He replied:
"I met Zhāng Mèng Tán outside the camp gate.
His spirit was proud,
and his stride was high."
Zhì Bó said: "Not so.
My agreement with the two lords is very firm.
After destroying Zhào, we will divide its land into three parts; I have treated them with intimacy,
they surely will not deceive me.
You should let it go
and let no more words come from your mouth."
Zhì Guò went out and saw the two lords,
then returned to advise Zhì Bó, saying:
"The complexions of the two lords have shifted and their intentions have changed.
They will certainly betray you.
It is better to order them killed."
Zhì Bó said:
"Our troops have been at Jìnyáng for three years; we should take it and enjoy its benefits any day now.
How could they have other intentions?
It is impossible.
You must be careful not to speak of it again."
Zhì Guò said:
"If you do not kill them, then you must at least draw them closer."
Zhì Bó said:
"How should I draw them closer?"
Zhì Guò said: "Wèi Xuān Zǐ's advisor is named Zhào Jiā,
and Kāng Zǐ's advisor is named Duàn Guī.
These are both men who can change their lords' plans.
You should make an agreement with the two lords
that after destroying Zhào, you will enfeoff these two men each with a county of ten thousand households.
If you do this, the hearts of the two lords will not change,
and you will obtain what you desire."
Zhì Bó said:
"If I destroy Zhào and divide its land into three parts,
and also enfeoff those two men each with a county of ten thousand households,
then what I obtain will be too little.
It cannot be done."
Zhì Guò saw that the Lord would not use his advice
and did not listen to his words.
He went out,
changed his surname to Fǔ Shì,
and then left, not to be seen again.
Zhāng Mèng Tán heard of this,
went in to see Xiāng Zǐ and said:
"I met Zhì Guò outside the camp gate.
His look showed that he suspected me.
He went in to see Zhì Bó
and upon coming out, he changed his surname.
If we do not strike this evening,
we will surely be too late."
Xiāng Zǐ said: "Agreed."
He sent Zhāng Mèng Tán to see the lords of Hán and Wèi, saying:
"The night's appointed time is here.
Kill the officers guarding the dikes
and divert the water to flood Zhì Bó's army."
Zhì Bó's army fell into chaos as they tried to deal with the water.
Hán and Wèi attacked them from the flanks,
while Xiāng Zǐ led his soldiers to charge them from the front.
They decisively defeated Zhì Bó's army and captured Zhì Bó.
Zhì Bó himself died,
his state perished and his land was divided.
He became a laughingstock to the world.
This was because of his insatiable greed.
Not listening to Zhì Guò
was also the reason for his downfall.
The Zhì clan was entirely wiped out;
only the Fǔ Shì branch survived.
After Zhāng Mèng Tán had secured the Zhào ancestral line,
expanded its borders,
and dismissed five hundred men,
he then cited the path of Zhào Jiǎn Zhǔ to report to Xiāng Zǐ:
"In the past,
the rulers of the former states had a saying about governance:
'The reason for a state of five hundred li to bring the world to submission
is to ensure that the lord's power can control the ministers,
and not let the ministers be able to control the lord.
Therefore, those honored as ranked marquises
are not allowed to hold the position of prime minister;
from the rank of general and above,
they do not serve as close-attendant officials.'
Now my name is illustrious and my person is honored,
my power is great and the masses are submissive.
I wish to give up my merit and name, leave my power and status, and separate myself from the masses."
Xiāng Zǐ said with regret:
"Why is that?
I have heard that those who assist their lord have illustrious names,
those with great merit are honored in person,
and those who take charge of the state have great power;
if loyalty and trustworthiness reside in oneself, the masses will be submissive.
This is how the former sages unified states
and stabilized the altars of soil and grain!
Why are you like this?"
Zhāng Mèngtán replied:
“What Your Lordship says
is the beauty of successful achievement.
What I speak of
is the Way of maintaining the state.
I have observed accomplished matters
and heard of ancient times;
while the beauty of the world is shared,
that the power of minister and lord be equal and yet still be beautiful,
is something that has never existed.
Not forgetting past events
is a teacher for future matters.
If Your Lordship does not plan for this,
then my strength will be insufficient.”
He looked sorrowful and had a look of determination.
Xiāngzǐ left him.
He lay down for three days,
then sent someone to tell him:
“Regarding the administration of Jìnyáng,
what should be done with subordinates who do not follow orders?”
The reply was: “Execution.”
Zhāng Mèngtán said: “The Zuǒ Sīmǎ was employed by the state
to secure the Altars of Shèjì,
not evading his death
to fulfill his loyalty;
may Your Lordship carry this out.”
The Lord said:
“You attend to the matter.”
Thus he granted it.
Zhāng Mèngtán then utilized his wealth to facilitate his reputation,
returned his lands and relinquished his duties to distance himself from power and status,
and farmed at the hill of Fùqīn.
Therefore it is said,
the conduct of a worthy person
is the governance of an enlightened ruler.
After he had farmed for three years,
Hán, Wèi, Qí, and Yān used Fùqīn as a pretext to plot against Zhào.
Xiāngzǐ went to see Zhāng Mèngtán and told him:
“Formerly, when the lands of the Zhì clan
were divided and the Zhào clan gained ten more cities,
they have now come back,
and currently the feudal lords are plotting against me;
what should be done about it?”
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
“If Your Lordship would carry your sword and drive the chariot for me to return to the capital,
lodge me in the ancestral temple,
and grant me the rank of Lì Dàfū,
I will try to plan for it.”
The Lord said: “Agreed.”
Zhāng Mèngtán then set out;
his wife went to Chǔ,
his eldest son went to Hán,
his second son went to Wèi,
and his youngest son went to Qí.
The four states became suspicious and their plot failed.
Yù Ràng, the grandson of Bì Yáng of Jìn,
initially served the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans but was not pleased;
he left and went to Zhì Bó,
and Zhì Bó favored him.
When the Three Jìn divided the Zhì clan,
Zhào Xiāngzǐ resented Zhì Bó the most
and used his skull as a drinking vessel.
Yù Ràng escaped into the mountains
and said:
“Alas!
A scholar dies for one who knows him,
as a woman beautifies herself for one who delights in her.
I shall seek revenge for the Zhì clan’s grievance.”
He then changed his name
and became a convict,
entering the palace to plaster the latrines,
wishing to use this chance to assassinate Xiāngzǐ.
When Xiāngzǐ went to the latrine,
his heart was stirred; he seized and questioned the man plastering the wall,
and it was Yù Ràng.
He held a blade to the wall
and said:
“I wish to seek revenge for Zhì Bó!”
The attendants wanted to kill him.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ said: “He is a man of honor;
I will simply take care to avoid him.
Moreover, Zhì Bó is already dead
and has no heirs,
yet his minister goes so far as to seek revenge for him;
this is a worthy person of the world.”
In the end, he released him.
Yù Ràng then lacquered his body to cause sores,
removed his beard and eyebrows,
and mutilated himself to change his appearance,
acting as a beggar and going out to beg.
His wife did not recognize him
and said:
“Your appearance does not resemble my husband,
but why does your voice so greatly resemble my husband's?”
He then swallowed charcoal to become hoarse,
changing his voice.
His friend said to him:
“Your way is extremely difficult and brings no success;
if one says you have a strong will, then that is so,
but if one says you are wise, then no.
With your talent,
if you were to serve Xiāngzǐ well,
Xiāngzǐ would surely treat you as a close favorite;
once you are close, you could carry out your desire;
this would be very easy and success would be certain.”
Yù Ràng then laughed and replied to him, saying:
“This would be using the first benefactor who knew me to betray the later benefactor who knew me,
and for the sake of an old lord, murdering a new lord;
there is nothing that would more greatly disrupt the righteousness of lord and minister than this.
All that I have done by doing this
is to make clear the righteousness of lord and minister,
not because it is easy.
Furthermore, to pledge oneself and serve a man
and then seek to kill him,
is to serve a lord while harboring a double heart.
What I do is difficult,
but it will also shame those ministers of the world and future generations who harbor a double heart.”
After a short while,
when Xiāngzǐ was about to go out,
Yù Ràng lay in ambush under a bridge he was to cross.
When Xiāngzǐ reached the bridge, his horse was startled.
Xiāngzǐ said: “This must be Yù Ràng.”
He sent someone to ask,
and it was indeed Yù Ràng.
Thereupon Zhào Xiāngzǐ confronted and rebuked Yù Ràng, saying:
“Did you not formerly serve the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans?
Zhì Bó destroyed the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
yet you did not seek revenge for them,
but instead pledged yourself to serve Zhì Bó.
Now that Zhì Bó is dead,
why do you alone seek revenge so profoundly?”
Yù Ràng said: “When I served the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans treated me as an ordinary man,
so I repaid them as an ordinary man;
Zhì Bó treated me as a distinguished state scholar,
so I repay him as a distinguished state scholar.”
Xiāngzǐ then sighed deeply with tears and said:
“Alas, Yù Zǐ!
In what Yù Zǐ has done for Zhì Bó,
your name is already established;
for me to have released you
was also already enough.
You must plan for yourself;
I shall not release you again.”
He ordered soldiers to surround him.
Yù Ràng said:
“I have heard that an enlightened ruler does not obscure a person's righteousness,
and a loyal minister does not grudge his death to establish his name.
Previously, Your Lordship magnanimously released me,
and there is no one in the world who does not praise Your Lordship's worthiness.
Regarding today's matter,
I should naturally submit to execution,
but I wish to request Your Lordship's garment so that I may strike it,
and then I would die without regret.
This is more than I could hope for,
yet I dare to lay bare my innermost heart.”
Thereupon Xiāngzǐ considered him righteous,
so he sent an attendant to bring his garment to Yù Ràng.
Yù Ràng drew his sword, leaped three times,
and cried out to Heaven as he struck it, saying:
“With this, I can repay Zhì Bó!”
He then fell upon his sword and died.
On the day he died,
when the scholars of the state of Zhào heard of it,
they all wept for him.
Wèi Wén Hóu requested passage through Zhào to attack Zhōngshān.
The Lord of Zhào was not going to allow it.
Zhào Lì said:
“This is a mistake.
If Wèi attacks Zhōngshān and cannot take it,
then Wèi will surely be exhausted;
if they are exhausted, then Zhào will be more powerful.
If Wèi captures Zhōngshān,
they will certainly be unable to cross Zhào to hold Zhōngshān.
Thus, the one who employs the troops
is Wèi;
but the one who gains the land
is Zhào.
It would be better for Your Lordship to grant it;
if you grant it with great encouragement,
they will realize that it benefits us,
and will surely stop.
It is better for Your Lordship to grant them passage
while showing that you do so out of necessity.”
Qín and Hán besieged Liáng;
Yān and Zhào went to its rescue.
Someone said to Shānyáng Jūn:
“If Qín fights and defeats the three states,
Qín will certainly pass through Zhōu and Hán to possess Liáng.
If the three states defeat Qín,
the strength of the three states,
though insufficient to attack Qín,
will be sufficient to capture Zhèng.
The best plan is to come to terms with the three states and attack Qín.”
Fù Jī built a house and it was huge;
Jīng Gǎn spoke of it to the Lord.
He said to Fùzǐ:
"For what reason is the house so huge?"
Fù Jī said:
"I am but a sojourner;
my rank is high but my salary is meager,
and while my residence is small, my family is not numerous.
Although the Lord trusts me,
the common people all say:
'If the state has a major crisis,
Jī will certainly not be of use.'
Now that Jī builds a huge palace,
it is to gain the trust of the common people."
The Lord said:
"Good."
Sū Qín persuaded Lǐ Duì, saying:
"I am Sū Qín of Luòyáng who rides in a high carriage.
My family is poor and my parents are old.
Lacking even a worn-out carriage or a weary horse,
with wheels of mulberry, chests of mugwort, and a lean traveling bag,
I carry my books and shoulder my sack,
encountering dust
and braving frost and dew.
Crossing the Zhāng and Hé rivers,
my feet are heavily calloused.
Traveling a hundred li a day before lodging,
I have reached the Wàiquē
and wish to appear before you
to orally speak of the affairs of the world."
Lǐ Duì said:
"If the Master sees me with the words of ghosts, it will do;
but if with the affairs of men,
Duì already knows them all."
Sū Qín replied:
"I indeed intended to see the Lord with the words of ghosts,
not with the words of men."
Lǐ Duì received him.
Sū Qín said:
"Today my arrival was late,
after the Guòmén were closed.
I could find no mat to sleep on
and stayed in someone's field,
beside a large thicket.
At midnight,
an earth figurine and a wooden figurine were arguing. The earth figurine said:
'You are not as good as me.
I am made of earth.
If I encounter gale winds and pouring rain
and am destroyed,
I simply return to the earth.
But you, if not a root of wood,
are but a branch of wood.
If you encounter gale winds and pouring rain,
you will be washed into the Zhāng and Hé rivers,
flowing east into the sea,
drifting without end.'
I privately thought the earth figurine won.
Now that the Lord has killed the Zhǔfù and exterminated his clan,
the Lord's standing in the world
is more precarious than a stack of eggs.
If the Lord listens to my plan, you will live;
if you do not listen, you will die."
Lǐ Duì said:
"Master, go to your lodgings,
and come see Duì again tomorrow."
Sū Qín went out.
Lǐ Duì's retainer said to Lǐ Duì:
"I privately observed the Lord's conversation with Master Sū.
His eloquence exceeds the Lord's,
and his knowledge exceeds the Lord's.
Can the Lord listen to Master Sū's plan?"
Lǐ Duì said:
"I cannot."
The retainer said:
"If the Lord cannot,
I wish the Lord would firmly block both ears
and not listen to his talk."
The next day they met again,
and after talking all day, he left.
The retainer went out to see Master Sū off.
Sū Qín said to the retainer:
"Yesterday my talk was rough and your Lord was moved;
today it was refined and your Lord was not moved.
Why?"
The retainer said:
"The Master's plan is grand and his scope is high;
my Lord cannot use it.
Thus I asked the Lord to block both ears
and not listen to the speaker.
Nevertheless,
Master, come again tomorrow,
and I will ask him to provide the Master with generous funds."
The next day he came
and they clapped hands and talked.
Lǐ Duì gave Sū Qín pearls of the bright moon,
the jade bi of Hé Shì,
a robe of black sable,
and a hundred gold yì.
Sū Qín obtained these to use
and went west into Qín.
Zhào gathered the world
to attack Qí.
Sū Qín, on behalf of Qí, submitted a memorial to persuade the King of Zhào, saying:
"I have heard that the worthy kings of old,
their virtuous conduct was not necessarily spread throughout the world,
their teachings of obedience and compassion
were not necessarily distributed among all the people,
and their seasonal sacrificial offerings
were not necessarily exactly what the ghosts and spirits required.
Yet sweet dew fell,
wind and rain arrived in their seasons,
the farmers prospered,
the annual harvest was abundant,
and while the multitudes rejoiced,
the worthy ruler remained wary of it.
Now Your Excellency's achievements
have not repeatedly inflicted pain upon the state of Qín,
and the accumulated resentment and malice
have not yet deeply oppressed Hán.
I have privately heard the discussions of the high ministers and lower officials outside,
who all say that the Lord previously relied solely on his own position,
thinking that Qín loves Zhào and hates Hán.
I have privately observed the matter:
how could Qín possibly love Zhào and hate Hán?
It wishes to destroy Hán and swallow the lands of the Two Zhōu;
therefore it uses Hán as bait,
first sending word out to the world,
wanting the neighboring states to hear and watch.
Fearing its goal would not be achieved,
it sent out troops to feign a show to Zhào and Wèi.
Fearing the world would wake up in alarm,
it weakened Hán to create division.
Fearing the world would doubt it,
it sent out hostages to gain trust.
It claims virtue to its allies,
but actually attacks a weakened Hán.
I have privately observed its plans;
discussing Qín's strategies,
they must come from this.
"Moreover, the plans of the persuaders
all say that if Hán loses Sānchuān
and Wèi loses its Jìn lands,
as long as Hán is not exhausted,
calamity will reach Zhào.
Furthermore, things naturally have different situations but identical dangers,
and also identical situations but different dangers.
In the past,
the people of Chǔ attacked for a long time, and Zhōngshān was destroyed.
Now if Yān takes all of Hán's Hénán,
the distance from Shāqiū
to the border of Jùlù is three hundred li;
from Hànguān
to Yúzhōng is one thousand five hundred li.
If Qín takes all of Hán and Wèi's Shàngdǎng,
then the distance between its lands and the state capital and its dependencies is seven hundred li.
With three armies and strong crossbows, Qín sits atop Yángtáng,
which is only twenty li from Hándān.
Moreover, if Qín attacks Your Majesty's Shàngdǎng with three armies and endangers its north,
then the west of Gòuzhù
will no longer be Your Majesty's possession.
Now if Lǔ and Gòuzhù are blocked and Chángshān is defended,
reaching three hundred li to Yān's Táng and Qūwú,
then the horses of Dài and the colts of the Hú will not come east,
and the jade of Kūnshān will not come out.
These three treasures
will again not be Your Majesty's possession.
Now if you follow powerful Qín to attack Qí,
I fear that calamity will arise from this.
In the past,
the kings of the five states
once formed a horizontal alliance to plot an attack on Zhào,
dividing the territory of Zhào into three parts,
recording it on plates and bowls
and assigning it to Chóuzuò.
The date for the five states' troops was set,
but Hán then moved its army west to restrain the state of Qín,
causing Qín to issue orders wearing plain white clothes in submission,
returning Wēn, Zhǐ, and Gāopíng to Wèi,
and returning Sāngōng and Shíqīng to Zhào;
this is something Your Majesty clearly knows.
Hán's service to Zhào should rightly be a superior alliance;
yet now it is being attacked as if to pay for a crime.
I fear that those who serve Your Majesty in the future will not dare to trust in their own security.
Now if Your Majesty gathers the world,
they will certainly consider Your Majesty successful.
Since Hán endangers its own state to serve Your Majesty,
the world will certainly respect Your Majesty.
Thus, if Hán regards Your Majesty as righteous and the world follows you,
and Hán admires Your Majesty and the world is gathered to you,
this is the mandate of a generation
controlled by Your Majesty alone.
I wish Great King would deeply calculate and reconsider with your surrounding ministers,
thinking through the matter beforehand and planning maturely."
Qí was attacking Sòng,
and Fèngyáng Jūn did not desire this.
A guest petitioned Fèngyáng Jūn, saying:
"Your Lordship's years are advanced,
yet your fiefdom is not yet determined;
you must not fail to plan for this thoroughly.
Qín is greedy, and Hán and Wèi are in danger;
Wèi and Chǔ are stable;
the land of Zhōngshān is meager;
the crimes of Sòng are heavy;
and the anger of Qí is deep.
By destroying and attacking the chaotic Sòng,
you can secure your own fief
and earn the gratitude of the powerful Qí.
This is a once-in-a-hundred-generations opportunity."
The King of Qín said to Gōngzǐ Tā: "In years past, during the affair at Xiáo,
Hán served as the center army
to join the other feudal lords in attacking Qín.
Hán shares a border with Qín,
and its territory does not reach a thousand lǐ,
yet it wavers and cannot be bound by treaties.
Recently, when Qín and Chǔ fought at Lántián,
Hán sent elite troops to assist Qín;
but when the battle went poorly for Qín,
they turned to join Chǔ.
They do not firmly adhere to alliances,
following only what is advantageous.
Hán's presence near me
is a disease in the vitals.
I intend to attack them;
what do you think?"
Gōngzǐ Tā said: "If Your Majesty sends troops against Hán,
Hán will certainly be afraid;
being afraid, you can obtain a deep cession of land without fighting."
The King said: "Excellent."
He then raised an army;
one army approached Yíngyáng,
and another army approached Tàiháng.
Hán was terrified
and sent Yángchéng Jūn to apologize to Qín,
requesting to hand over the land of Shàngdǎng to make peace.
The King of Hán ordered Hán Yáng to inform the Governor of Shàngdǎng, Jìn Tǒu, saying:
"Qín has raised two armies to approach Hán,
and Hán cannot keep this land.
Now the King orders the mobilization of troops to hand over Shàngdǎng to Qín for peace;
he has sent me, Yáng, to tell the Governor
that the Governor should hand it over."
Jìn Tǒu said:
"People have a saying:
'The wisdom of one who carries a water jar
is not to lose the vessel they hold.'
The King may have his orders,
but I am the Governor;
even between a king and his subject, there is suspicion.
I ask to mobilize all defenders to resist Qín;
if I cannot succeed,
I shall die for it."
Hán Yáng hurried back to report to the King.
The King said: "I have already given my word to Yìng Hóu;
if I do not give it now,
I am deceiving him."
He then sent Féng Tíng to replace Jìn Tǒu.
Féng Tíng held the position for thirty days,
and secretly sent someone to petition the King of Zhào, saying:
"Hán cannot defend Shàngdǎng
and is about to give it to Qín.
Its people all do not wish to be subjects of Qín,
but wish to be subjects of Zhào.
Now there are seventy walled cities and towns;
we wish to bow and offer them to the King.
Only Your Majesty can decide what to do with them."
The King of Zhào was pleased;
he summoned Píngyuán Jūn and told him:
"Hán cannot defend Shàngdǎng
and is about to give it to Qín.
Its officials and people do not wish to be subjects of Qín
but all wish to be subjects of Zhào.
Now Féng Tíng has sent an envoy to give them to me;
what do you think?"
Zhào Bào replied: "I have heard that the sages were extremely wary of profit that comes without cause."
The King said:
"The people cherish my righteousness;
how can you say it is without cause?"
Zhào Bào replied:
"Qín has been nibbling away at Hán's territory like a silkworm,
cutting it off in the middle so they cannot communicate;
therefore they believe they will sit back and receive Shàngdǎng.
Furthermore, the reason Hán is offering it to Zhào
is that they wish to transfer the calamity to us.
Qín has endured the toil,
while Zhào receives the benefit.
Although a powerful state cannot take it from the small and weak,
can the small and weak instead take it from the powerful?
If Your Majesty takes it now,
can it be said there is a 'cause'?
Moreover, Qín uses oxen for farming
and water to transport grain;
their death-defying soldiers are all stationed in the upper lands.
Their orders are strict and their administration effective;
one cannot do battle with them.
Your Majesty should consider this yourself!"
The King was greatly enraged and said:
"If I deploy a million men
and fight for years on end,
I might not see a single city taken.
Now without using troops, I get seventy cities;
why should I not do it?"
Zhào Bào went out.
The King summoned Zhào Shèng
and Zhào Yǔ and told them:
"Hán cannot defend Shàngdǎng;
now its governor is giving it to me.
It has seventy walled cities and towns."
The two replied:
"To use troops for years
without seeing a single city taken,
yet now to receive cities while sitting still—
this is a great profit."
He then sent Zhào Shèng to go and receive the land.
Zhào Shèng arrived and said:
"The King of my humble state
has sent me, his servant Shèng, as an envoy.
For the Governor there is a decree;
the King has ordered me, Shèng, to say:
'I ask to enfeoff the Governor with a city of thirty thousand households,
enfeoff the County Magistrates with a thousand households each,
and all officials shall be promoted by three ranks.
For those among the people who can keep their communities together,
each family shall be granted six pieces of gold.'"
Féng Tíng shed tears and forced himself to say:
"This puts me in a position of three unrighteous acts:
to defend the land for my lord but be unable to die for it,
and to give it to others instead—
this is the first unrighteousness.
My lord intended to hand it to Qín,
but I did not obey his command—
this is the second unrighteousness.
To sell my lord's land and then live off the reward—
this is the third unrighteousness."
He declined the fief and entered Hán, saying to the King of Hán:
"Zhào heard that Hán could not defend Shàngdǎng
and has now sent troops and taken it."
Hán informed Qín, saying:
"Zhào has raised troops and taken Shàngdǎng."
The King of Qín was enraged
and ordered Gōngsūn Qǐ and Wáng Yǐ to meet Zhào in battle with troops at Chángpíng.
Sū Qín served as the King of Zhào's envoy to Qín;
he returned,
but for three days he could not get an audience.
He said to the King of Zhào:
"When the Qín people recently passed Zhùshān,
there were two trees there.
One seemed to be calling its companion,
and the other seemed to be weeping.
When asked why,
it replied:
'I am already large
and my years are many;
I suffer because of the craftsmen
who are about to use ink lines, compasses, and squares to carve me.'
The other said:
'This is not what I suffer from,
for this is my destiny.
What I suffer from is the iron drill
that enters here and comes out there.'
Now I have been an envoy to Qín
and for three days have not been seen.
Could it be that someone is calling me an 'iron drill'?"
Gān Mào made an agreement with Wèi on behalf of Qín to attack Yíyáng in Hán.
He then went north to Zhào.
Lěng Xiàng said to the powerful state [Zhào]:
"It would be better to have Zhào detain Gān Mào
and not let him out,
in order to bargain with Qí, Hán, and Qín.
The King of Qí wants to save Yíyáng,
so he will surely offer the county of Húshì.
Hán wants to keep Yíyáng,
so they will surely bribe Zhào with Lùshè and Duānshì.
The King of Qín wants to obtain Yíyáng
and will not begrudge famous treasures;
moreover, by detaining Gān Mào,
one can also use the opportunity to install Gōngsūn Hè and Chūlǐ Jí."
To Pí Xiàngguó it was said:
“With Zhào being weak and Jiànxìn Jūn in control of it,
why are they so hostile like the enmity of Shè Mèng?
It is because they believe joining the Vertical Alliance is meritorious.
If Qí does not join the alliance,
Jiànxìn Jūn will know that the alliance will have no merit.
How can Jiànxìn Jūn afford to offend Qín for no gain?
If he cannot afford to offend Qín for no gain,
then he will send troops to assist Qín in attacking Wèi,
and divide Qí with Chǔ and Zhào;
then his strength will be exhausted.
If Jiànxìn Jūn and Chūnshēn Jūn join the alliance,
they will offend Qín without gain.
If Qín divides Qí,
and Qí destroys Wèi,
then they will have merit and be on good terms with Qín.
Therefore, between these two lords,
which choice between having merit and having no merit would be considered wise?”
Someone said to Pí Xiàngguó:
“Wèi killed Lǚ Liáo and guarded with troops;
by losing its Běiyáng, Liáng is in danger.
The fief of Héjiān is not settled, so Qí is in danger.
Wénxìn Hóu did not get his way,
which is a worry for the Sānjìn who turned their backs on him.
Now that Wèi’s humiliation is not yet erased
and Zhào’s troubles have arisen again,
Wénxìn Hóu’s worries are great.
If Qí does not join the alliance,
the hearts of the Sānjìn will be full of doubt.
Those with great worries make peace without calculation;
those with doubting hearts serve Qín with urgency.
A settlement between Qín and Wèi
will be achieved without waiting for the ceding of land.
If Qín follows Chǔ
and Wèi to attack Qí and swallows Zhào alone,
then Qí and Zhào will surely both perish.”
Zhào Wáng enfeoffed Mèngshǎng Jūn with Wǔchéng.
Mèngshǎng Jūn chose retainers to serve as officials of Wǔchéng,
and sent them off, saying:
“Does the common proverb not say,
‘He who borrows a carriage gallops it,
and he who borrows clothes wears them’? ”
They all replied:
“Yes, it does.”
Mèngshǎng Jūn said: “I, Wén, very much disapprove of this.
Those from whom one borrows clothes and carriages
are either close friends
or brothers.
Galloping a friend’s carriage
or wearing out a brother’s clothes,
I, Wén, believe this is unacceptable.
Now Zhào Wáng, despite my lack of talent,
has enfeoffed me with Wǔchéng.
I wish for you Dàfū to go there,
but do not cut down the trees,
do not demolish the houses,
and act in such a way as to make Zhào Wáng realize and know Wén’s character.
Carefully ensure it is kept whole and return it to him.”
Someone said to Zhào Wáng:
“When the Sānjìn unite, Qín is weak;
when the Sānjìn separate, Qín is strong.
This is clear to everyone under heaven.
Qín uses Yān to attack Zhào,
and uses Zhào to attack Yān;
it uses Liáng to attack Zhào,
and uses Zhào to attack Liáng;
it uses Chǔ to attack Hán,
and uses Hán to attack Chǔ.
This is clearly seen by everyone under heaven.
Yet the states of Shāndōng cannot change their path
because their armies are weak.
Being weak and yet unable to unite,
this shows how wise Chǔ is
and how foolish the states of Shāndōng are.
This is what I worry about for Shāndōng.
When a tiger is about to seize its prey,
the prey does not know the tiger is coming for them,
and they fight each other until both are exhausted,
and then they give their lives to the tiger.
If the prey knew the tiger was coming for them,
they would certainly not fight each other.
Now the rulers of Shāndōng do not know that Qín is coming for them,
and yet they still fight each other until both are ruined,
and then they surrender their states to Qín.
Their wisdom is far inferior to that of the prey.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this deeply.”
“Now there are matters of urgency.
Qín’s desire to attack Hán and Liáng and to eye the Zhōu royal house in the east is very great;
it never ceases even in sleep.
Now it attacks Chǔ in the south
because it fears the great union of the Sānjìn.
It has attacked Chǔ, rested, and then attacked again
for five years now,
seizing over a thousand lǐ of land.
Now it says to Chǔ Wáng:
‘If you will simply lift your jade feet and come see me,
I will certainly make Chǔ a brother state,
I will certainly attack Hán and Liáng for Chǔ,
and return Chǔ’s former lands.’
Chǔ Wáng finds Qín’s words pleasant,
and is angry at Hán and Liáng for not rescuing him,
so he will surely go to Qín.
Qín has a plan, so it will kill the envoy sent to Zhào,
use Yān to bait Zhào,
and separate the Sānjìn.
Now Your Majesty finds Qín’s words pleasant and wishes to attack Yān.
If you attack Yān,
before you have had your fill, disaster will already have arrived.
When Chǔ Wáng enters Qín,
Qín and Chǔ will become one,
and they will face east to attack Hán.
To the south of Hán, there will be no Chǔ;
to the north, no Zhào.
Hán will not even wait to be attacked;
it will cede its territory and flee swiftly like a horse or rabbit.
Once Qín and Hán are in close alliance,
Qín’s disaster will then move to Liáng.
With Qín’s strength,
and having the use of Chǔ and Hán,
Liáng will not even wait to be attacked.
It will cede its territory and flee swiftly like a horse or rabbit.
Once Qín and Liáng are in close alliance,
Qín’s disaster will then move to Zhào.
With strong Qín possessing Hán, Liáng, and Chǔ,
and with Yān’s anger,
the loss of land will surely be deep.
This is how the state will be captured;
this is why I have come.
Therefore I say:
There are matters that should be done urgently.”
“Before Chǔ Wáng enters Qín,
if the Sānjìn become close and firm with each other,
and send elite troops to guard the western borders of Hán and Liáng,
when Chǔ Wáng hears of this,
he will surely not enter Qín.
Qín will surely be angry and continue to attack Chǔ,
so Qín’s disaster will not leave Chǔ,
which is beneficial for the Sānjìn.
Even if Chǔ Wáng enters Qín,
if Qín sees that the Sānjìn are firmly united,
it will surely not let Chǔ Wáng out
unless he cedes much land.
This way, Qín’s disaster will not leave Chǔ,
which is also beneficial for the Sānjìn.
I hope Your Majesty will urgently consider this deeply!”
Zhào Wáng therefore raised troops to guard the western borders of Hán and Liáng in the south.
When Qín saw the firmness of the Sānjìn,
it indeed did not release Chǔ Wáng Áng,
and demanded much land.
Sū Qín went from Yān to Zhào.
To begin forming the Vertical Alliance,
he spoke to Zhào Wáng:
“Among the high ministers and officials of the world,
and even among the common scholars,
there is no one who does not admire Your Majesty’s noble and righteous conduct.
They have all long wished to receive your instructions and offer their loyalty before you.
Although this is so,
Fèngyáng Jūn was jealous,
and Your Majesty was not in control of affairs.
Therefore, guest advisors and traveling orators
did not dare to offer their full loyalty before you.
Now that Fèngyáng Jūn has passed away,
Your Majesty is finally able to be close with the scholars and people.
Therefore, I dare to offer my humble thoughts
and show my humble loyalty.
In planning for Your Majesty,
nothing is better than making the people peaceful and free from trouble.
I ask that you do not engage in unnecessary actions.
The foundation of making the people peaceful
lies in choosing allies.
If the choice of allies is correct, the people will be at peace;
if the choice of allies is incorrect, the people will never find peace.
Let me speak of external threats:
Qí and Qín are two enemies,
and the people cannot find peace.
If you rely on Qín to attack Qí,
the people cannot find peace.
If you rely on Qí to attack Qín,
the people cannot find peace.
Therefore, those who plot for rulers
and attack other countries
often suffer from using harsh words to sever relations with others.
I hope Your Majesty will be careful not to let such words leave your mouth.”
“Please dismiss your attendants.
My words about why things differ
are just a matter of Yīn and Yáng.
If Your Majesty can truly listen to me,
Yān will certainly offer territory rich in felt, furs, dogs, and horses;
Qí will certainly offer territory rich in fish and salt from the sea’s edge;
Chǔ will certainly offer territory rich in oranges, pummelos, and the Yúnmèng marshes.
Hán and Wèi can both be made to offer fiefs and bath-towns,
and your noble relatives and elder brothers can all receive titles of lords.”
Indeed, ceding land and offering wealth
are what the Wǔ Bà sought by overthrowing armies and capturing generals;
enfeoffing nobles and honoring relatives were why Tāng and Wǔ resorted to exile, execution, and conflict.
Now Your Great King has obtained both while sitting with folded robes;
this is what I wish for Your Great King.
If Your Great King sides with Qín,
then Qín will surely weaken Hán and Wèi;
if you side with Qí, then Qí will surely weaken Chǔ and Wèi.
When Wèi is weakened, it will cede Héwài;
when Hán is weakened, it will offer Yíyáng.
When Yíyáng is offered, Shàngjùn will be cut off;
when Héwài is ceded, the roads will be impassable.
When Chǔ is weakened, there will be no aid.
These three strategies
must be carefully considered.
If Qín descends upon Zhǐdào, then Nányáng will be shaken;
if it coerces Hán and surrounds Zhōu, then Zhào will wither away on its own;
if it occupies Wèi and takes the Qí River, then Qí will surely pay court.
Once Qín's desires are fulfilled in Shāndōng,
it will surely raise its armor and turn toward Zhào.
When Qín’s armor crosses the Hé and leaps over the Zhāng,
occupying Pánwú,
then its troops will surely battle beneath the walls of Hándān.
This is why I am concerned for Your Great King.
“In the present time,
among the established states of Shāndōng,
none are as strong as Zhào.
The territory of Zhào is two thousand lǐ square,
with hundreds of thousands of armored soldiers,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
and grain to last ten years;
to its west is Chángshān,
to its south are the Hé and Zhāng rivers,
to its east is the Qīnghé,
and to its north is the state of Yàn.
Yàn is inherently a weak state
and is not to be feared.
Furthermore, of all those in the world that Qín fears and considers harmful,
none is like Zhào.
Yet the reason Qín does not dare raise its troops and armor to attack Zhào, why is that?
It fears Hán and Wèi plotting against its rear.
Thus Hán and Wèi
are the southern shields of Zhào.
Qín’s attack on Hán and Wèi,
however, is different.
They lack the defenses of famous mountains and great rivers;
Qín gradually encroaches on them like a silkworm,
stopping only when it reaches their capitals.
Hán and Wèi cannot withstand Qín
and will surely submit as subjects.
Once Hán and Wèi are subjects to Qín,
Qín will no longer be separated by Hán and Wèi,
and disaster will strike the heart of Zhào.
This is why I am concerned for Your Great King.
“I have heard
that Yáo did not have the portion of three men,
and Shùn did not have a foot of land,
yet they possessed the world.
Yǔ did not have a gathering of a hundred people,
yet he ruled over the feudal lords.
The soldiers of Tāng and Wǔ did not exceed three thousand,
their chariots did not exceed three hundred,
yet they were established as the Sons of Heaven.
Truly, they attained the Way.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler externally assesses the strength and weakness of enemy states,
and internally gauges the number of his own soldiers, their worthiness and unworthiness.
Without waiting for two armies to face each other,
the critical points of victory or defeat, survival or ruin,
are already seen within his heart;
how could he be obscured by the words of the crowd
and decide matters in the dark?
“I have privately examined the maps of the world.
The land of the feudal lords is five times that of Qín;
assessing the soldiers of the feudal lords,
they are ten times those of Qín.
If the six states combined their power as one
to face west and attack Qín,
Qín’s defeat would be certain.
Now, being defeated by Qín,
they face west to serve it
and appear as subjects to Qín.
Indeed, defeating others versus being defeated by others,
making others subjects versus being made a subject by others,
how can these be spoken of in the same breath!
The advocates of the Horizontal Alliance
all wish to cede the land of the feudal lords to make peace with Qín.
Once peace is made with Qín,
they enjoy high towers and beautiful palaces,
listen to the sounds of pipes and zithers,
savor the harmony of the five flavors,
with Xuānyuán chariots in front
and long courtyards in the rear,
and the clever smiles of beauties.
When disaster from Qín eventually arrives,
they do not share in the worry.
Therefore, the advocates of the Horizontal Alliance day and night strive to use Qín's power to terrify and coerce the feudal lords
in order to seek the ceding of land.
I wish for Your Great King to carefully consider this.
“I have heard
that an enlightened king cuts off suspicion and discards slander,
removes the traces of rumors,
and blocks the gates of factions;
thus, regarding strategies to honor the ruler, expand territory, and strengthen the army,
I am able to present my loyalty before you.
Therefore, I privately plan for Your Great King:
nothing is better than unifying Hán, Wèi, Qí, Chǔ, Yàn, and Zhào
in a Zòng Qīn alliance
to reject and oppose Qín.
Let the generals and ministers of the world
meet together on the banks of the Huán Shuǐ,
exchange hostages, and sacrifice a white horse to swear an oath.
The covenant shall say:
If Qín attacks Chǔ,
Qí and Wèi shall each send elite troops to assist it,
Hán shall cut off the grain routes,
Zhào shall cross the Hé and Zhāng,
and Yàn shall guard the north of Chángshān.
If Qín attacks Hán or Wèi,
then Chǔ shall cut off its rear,
Qí shall send elite troops to assist them,
Zhào shall cross the Hé and Zhāng,
and Yàn shall guard Yúnzhōng.
If Qín attacks Qí,
then Chǔ shall cut off its rear,
Hán shall guard Chénggāo,
Wèi shall block Wǔdào,
Zhào shall cross the Hé, Zhāng, and Bóguān,
and Yàn shall send elite troops to assist it.
If Qín attacks Yàn,
then Zhào shall guard Chángshān,
Chǔ shall station troops at Wǔguān,
Qí shall cross the Bóhǎi,
and Hán and Wèi shall send elite troops to assist it.
If Qín attacks Zhào,
then Hán shall station troops at Yíyáng,
Chǔ shall station troops at Wǔguān,
Wèi shall station troops at Héwài,
Qí shall cross the Bóhǎi,
and Yàn shall send elite troops to assist it.
Should any of the feudal lords be the first to break the covenant,
the other five states shall jointly attack them.
When the six states form a Zòng Qīn alliance to reject Qín,
Qín will surely not dare send troops out of Hángǔ Guān to harm Shāndōng!
In this way, the work of a hegemon will be accomplished!”
The King of Zhào said:
“I am young
and have presided over the state for but a short time,
having never had the chance to hear of the long-term plans for the altars of soil and grain.
Now that our honored guest has the intention to preserve the world
and bring peace to the feudal lords,
I respectfully follow with my whole state.”
Thereupon, he enfeoffed Sū Qín as Wǔ'ān Jūn,
provided him with a hundred decorated chariots,
a thousand yì of gold,
a hundred pairs of white jade discs,
and a thousand rolls of embroidered silk
to form alliances with the feudal lords.
When Qín attacked Zhào,
Sū Zǐ spoke on its behalf to the King of Qín, saying:
“I have heard that concerning an enlightened king and his people,
he broadly deliberates and tests their skills;
thus, the offices lack no business and the people's strength is not exhausted.
Concerning their words,
he listens to many and employs them at the right time;
thus, affairs do not end in failed undertakings and evil does not flourish.
I wish for the King to examine what I present
and test its usefulness for the present time.
I have heard that those who carry precious treasures
do not travel at night;
those who are tasked with great achievements
do not underestimate the enemy.
Therefore, the worthy take on heavy responsibilities and act with reverence;
the wise achieve greatness and speak with deference.
Thus, the people do not resent their high status,
and the world does not envy their accomplishments.
I have heard:
In a state that is a hundred times stronger,
the people do not delight in lagging behind;
when achievements and deeds surpass the age,
the ruler does not repeat the same course;
people whose strength is exhausted
are not used by the benevolent;
to seek, to obtain, and then return to tranquility
is the regulation of a sagely ruler;
to achieve greatness and then allow the people to rest
is the way of employing the military.
Now, if one employs troops throughout their life without rest,
and though their strength is exhausted, they do not stop,
Zhào's anger will surely fall upon its own cities,
and Zhào will barely survive!
Yet it is a state surrounded on four sides.
Now, even if Hándān is captured,
it is not the long-term interest of the state.
It is thought that,
if the land is vast but not cultivated,
and the people are weak but given no rest,
and if they are further treated harshly with punishments,
then even if they follow the ruler, they will not stay.
As the saying goes:
"Those whose state is in danger despite being victorious in battle
are those whose resources do not last.
Those whose merit is great but whose authority is light
are those whose territory does not increase."
Therefore, regarding tasks that exceed one's duty,
a father cannot obtain them from a son;
regarding demands that have no end,
a lord cannot obtain them from a minister.
Thus, those who can make the subtle manifest become strong;
those who perceive the utility of letting the people rest become Hegemons;
those who are clear that treating the light as heavy become Kings."
The King of Qín said:
"If I halt the troops and let the people rest,
then the world will surely form a vertical alliance
in order to oppose Qín."
Sū Zǐ said: "I have means to know that the world cannot form a vertical alliance to oppose Qín.
I consider Tián Dān and Rú Ěr to be in great error.
Is it only Tián Dān and Rú Ěr who are in great error?
The lords of the world are all in error!
Contemplating the gathering of ruined Qí, exhausted Chǔ, worn-out Wèi, and the unpredictable Zhào,
wishing to corner Qín and break Hán,
I consider this the ultimate stupidity.
Now, Wēi and Xuān of Qí
were the worthy lords of their age;
their virtue was broad and their land was vast,
the state was rich and the people were employed,
the generals were brave and the troops were strong.
King Xuān used them,
and subsequently made Hán wealthy and Wèi powerful,
attacking Chǔ to the south
and attacking Qín to the west,
yet the Qí troops were trapped at the passes of Xiáo.
For ten years they strove for land,
but the people of Qín kept their distance and did not submit,
while Qí became hollow and ruined.
Why were the Qí troops broken
and Hán and Wèi barely able to survive?
Why was this?
It was because they attacked Chǔ and Qín
and subsequently suffered the calamity.
Now your wealth does not have the surplus of Qí's Wēi and Xuān,
your elite troops do not have the armories of wealthy Hán and strong Wèi,
and your generals do not have the strategies of Tián Dān and Sīmǎ.
To gather ruined Qí, exhausted Chǔ, worn-out Wèi, and the unpredictable Zhào,
wishing to corner Qín and break Hán,
I consider this a great mistake.
I believe a vertical alliance cannot be achieved.
A guest may raise objections;
now I have concerns about the world.
The School of Forms and Names
all say
thus.
If 'a white horse is not a horse' were already as if 'a white horse is indeed a horse,'
then it would cause there to be the reality of a white horse.
This is what I worry about.
"In the past,
the people of Qín sent troops down to attack Huái
and subjugated its people,
and the three states followed them in alliance.
Zhào Shē and Bào Nìng were the generals,
and four people from Chǔ rose to follow them.
They approached Huái but did not rescue it,
and when the people of Qín left, they did not pursue.
I do not know if it was because the three states hated Qín and loved Huái?
Or did they forget their hatred for Huái and love Qín?
Now, to attack without rescuing
and to leave without pursuing,
this is why the troops of the three states were trapped,
and this was the capability of Zhào Shē and Bào Nìng.
Thus they ceded land and were defeated by Qí.
Tián Dān led the elite of Qí
and marched across the central regions for fourteen years,
yet all his life he did not dare to station troops to attack Qín or break Hán,
but instead galloped within his own borders.
I do not know how a successful vertical alliance could exist."
Thereupon the King of Qín demobilized the troops and did not send them beyond the borders; the feudal lords rested,
the world was at peace,
and for twenty-nine years they did not attack one another.
Zhāng Yí formed a horizontal alliance for Qín
and persuaded the King of Zhào, saying:
"The King of my humble state, Qín, has sent me to dare offer this letter to Your Majesty's attendants.
Your Majesty led the world to reject Qín,
so that Qín's troops have not dared to exit Hángǔ Pass for fifteen years.
Your Majesty's prestige
has spread throughout the world east of the mountains.
My humble state, in fear and submission,
has repaired armor and sharpened weapons,
adorned chariots and cavalry,
practiced riding and archery,
worked the fields and stored grain,
and guarded within our four borders,
living in sorrow and dwelling in fear,
not daring to stir,
fearing only that Your Majesty might intend to punish our faults.
Now Qín, by Your Majesty's leave,
has taken Bā and Shǔ in the west,
annexed Hànzhōng,
captured the Two Zhōu in the east and moved the Nine Tripods to the west,
and guarded the ford of Báimǎ.
Although Qín is remote,
it has felt indignation and harbored anger for a long time.
Now Xuān Jūn has some armor and dull weapons
and is stationed at Miǎnchí,
wishing to cross the River and leap over the Zhāng,
occupy Pānwú,
and meet in battle below Hándān.
He wishes to engage in battle on the day of Jiǎzǐ
to settle matters as was done with Yīn and Zhòu.
I respectfully serve as an envoy to first inform your attendants.
"As for all that Your Majesty trusts in for the vertical alliance,
it relies on the plans of Sū Qín.
He deluded the feudal lords,
making right into wrong
and wrong into right;
he wished to subvert the state of Qí but failed,
and ended up being torn apart by chariots in the market of Qí.
It is clear that the world cannot be unified.
Now Chǔ and Qín are brotherly states,
while Hán and Wèi call themselves ministers of the eastern borders,
and Qí has offered its lands of fish and salt;
this is like cutting off Zhào's right arm.
To cut off one's right arm and seek to fight others,
to lose one's allies and live in isolation,
and seek to be without danger—how could that be possible?
Now Qín has dispatched three generals:
one army to block Wǔdào,
telling Qí to raise troops and cross the Qīnghé
to station an army to the east of Hándān;
one army to station at Chénggāo,
driving Hán and Wèi to station troops beyond the River;
and one army to station at Miǎnchí.
The agreement says
that the four states as one
will attack Zhào,
and after crushing Zhào, divide its land into four parts.
Therefore, I do not dare hide my intentions or conceal the truth,
and first inform your attendants.
I humbly plan for Your Majesty:
nothing is better than meeting Qín at Miǎnchí,
meeting face to face and bonding in person.
I request to halt the troops and not attack,
and wish Your Majesty would settle the plan."
The King of Zhào said:
"In the time of the late King,
Fèngyáng Jūn was the Prime Minister;
he monopolized power and usurped authority,
deceiving the late King
and alone controlled government affairs.
I lived in the palace,
under the care of my tutors,
and could not participate in state deliberations.
Since the late King passed away,
I have been young,
and the days I have performed sacrifices are few;
in my private heart, I have indeed harbored doubts.
I truly thought that unifying the vertical alliance and not serving Qín
was not the long-term interest of the state.
Now I am willing to change my mind and alter my thoughts,
to divide land to apologize for past errors and serve Qín.
I was just about to prepare my carriage and set out
when I heard the envoy's clear instructions."
Thereupon, with three hundred chariots, he went to court at Miǎnchí
and ceded Héjiān to serve Qín.
Wǔlíng Wáng was sitting at leisure in the middle of the day,
and Féiyì was attending him;
the King said:
"Do I consider the changes in worldly affairs,
weigh the use of armor and weapons,
think of the traces of Jiǎn and Xiāng,
and calculate the benefits concerning the Hú and the Dí?"
The King said:
"To succeed to the throne and not forget the virtues of one’s predecessors
is the way of a ruler;
to offer one’s services and strive to illuminate the strengths of an enlightened lord
is the principle of a minister.
Therefore, a worthy ruler, in stillness, possesses the teachings of the Way that benefit the people in their affairs,
and in action, achieves the clear merits of the ancient forefathers.
As for those who serve as ministers,
in obscurity, they have the integrity of fraternal respect and yielding; in prominence, they have the achievements of aiding the people and benefiting the lord.
These two things
are the respective duties of ruler and minister.
Now, I wish to continue the legacy of Xiāng Zhǔ,
opening up the regions of the Hú and the Zhái,
but even to the end of my life, I might not see it realized.
When the enemy is weak,
one exerts little effort but achieves great merit,
and can avoid exhausting the labor of the common people,
while enjoying the honors of the ancients.
Now, he who achieves merit that transcends the age
must inevitably bear the burden of defying custom;
he who possesses insights known only to himself
must inevitably suffer the apprehensions of the masses.
Now, I intend to teach the common people the Hú attire and mounted archery,
and the world will surely criticize me."
Féi Yì said:
"I have heard that
hesitant actions lead to no achievement,
and hesitant conduct brings no fame.
Now, if the King has already set his mind upon defying custom,
then there is no need to heed the criticisms of the world.
Indeed, he who discusses supreme virtue
does not harmonize with custom;
he who accomplishes great merit
does not consult with the masses.
In the past, Shùn danced with the Yǒu Miáo,
and Yǔ bared his body to enter the Land of the Naked,
not to indulge their desires or please their whims,
but because they wished to establish virtue and seek merit.
The foolish are blind to things already accomplished,
while the wise see things before they have even sprouted.
May the King proceed with it."
The King said:
"I do not doubt the Hú attire,
but I fear the world will mock it.
The joy of a madman
is a source of sorrow for the wise;
the laughter of the foolish
is a source of distress for the worthy.
If there are those in the world who follow me,
then the merit of the Hú attire remains to be seen.
Even if the whole world is driven to laugh at me,
the lands of the Hú and Zhōngshān I shall certainly possess."
The King then adopted the Hú attire.
He sent Wángsūn Xiè to inform Gōngzǐ Chéng, saying:
"I have adopted the Hú attire,
and I am about to wear it to court;
I also wish for you, Uncle, to wear it.
In the family, one listens to one’s kin;
in the state, one listens to the ruler;
this is the common practice from ancient times to the present.
A son does not turn against his parents,
and a minister does not oppose his lord;
this is the universal righteousness of the former kings.
Now, I have issued an order to change our attire,
but if you, Uncle, do not wear it,
I fear the world will criticize this.
In governing a state, there are constants,
and benefiting the people is the foundation.
In conducting administration, there are principles,
and the execution of orders is paramount.
Thus, manifesting virtue lies in deliberating with the lowly,
and executing administration lies in securing the trust of the noble.
Now, the intention of the Hú attire
is not to indulge desires or please the whims.
Affairs have their origin,
and merit has its objective.
Only after the affair is successful and merit established will virtue be seen.
Now, I fear that you, Uncle, will oppose the principles of administration
and thus support the criticisms against me.
Moreover, I have heard that
he whose actions benefit the state acts without deviance,
and he who relies on noble kin is not burdened by reputation.
Therefore, I wish to rely on your righteousness, Uncle,
to achieve the merit of the Hú attire.
I have sent Xiè to visit you, Uncle,
and request that you wear it."
Gōngzǐ Chéng bowed twice and said:
"I have indeed heard of the King’s adoption of the Hú attire.
I am unworthy and have been confined to bed with illness,
unable to move about,
which is why I did not come forward earlier.
Now that the King has commanded it,
I shall certainly dare to exhaust my humble loyalty.
I have heard that
Zhōngguó
is where the intelligent and wise reside,
where all things and resources gather,
where the worthy and sagely teach,
where benevolence and righteousness are practiced,
where the Shī, Shū, Lǐ, and Yuè are used,
where extraordinary talents and skills are tested,
where those from distant places look towards and flock to,
and where the Mányí people follow the example of righteousness.
Now, the King is abandoning this
and adopting the attire of distant lands,
changing the ancient teachings,
altering the ancient Way,
defying the hearts of the people,
turning against the scholars,
and distancing himself from Zhōngguó.
I hope the Great King will reconsider this."
The messenger reported back to the King.
The King said:
"I had indeed heard of my uncle’s illness."
He then went to the home of Gōngshū Chéng,
and personally requested of him, saying:
"Now, attire
is what provides convenience in use;
ritual
is what provides convenience in affairs.
Therefore, the sage observes the local customs and follows what is appropriate,
and institutes rituals based on the circumstances,
so as to benefit the people and strengthen the state.
Cutting the hair and tattooing the body,
with bared arms and left-fastening robes,
are the people of Ōuyuè.
Blackened teeth and tattooed foreheads,
with fish-skin caps and coarse-stitched clothes,
are the state of Dà Wú.
Their rituals and attire differ,
but their convenience is the same.
Therefore, when regions differ, their uses change;
when circumstances differ, their rituals are altered.
Thus, if the sage can benefit the people,
he does not keep their usage uniform;
and if he can provide convenience in affairs,
he does not keep their rituals identical.
Among scholars of the same master, rituals may differ;
within Zhōngguó, customs may be the same but teachings diverge,
how much more so then for the convenience of mountain and valley?
Therefore, the changes in what to adopt and what to discard
cannot be unified even by the wise;
the attire of those far and near
cannot be made identical even by the worthy and sagely.
Remote regions have many differences,
and narrow learning leads to many arguments.
Not to know yet not to doubt,
and for things to differ from oneself yet not to condemn them,
is to be impartial in seeking what is good.
Now, what you speak of
is custom.
What I speak of
is the means to regulate custom.
Now, our state has to the east the waters of the Hé and the Bóluò,
shared with Qí and Zhōngshān,
yet we lack the use of boats and oars.
From Chángshān to Dài and Shàngdǎng,
to the east we have the borders of Yān and the Dōnghú,
to the west we have the borders of Lóufán, Qín, and Hán,
yet we lack the preparation of mounted archery.
Therefore, I shall gather the use of boats and oars, seek out people who live on the water, to defend the waters of the Hé and the Bóluò;
and change our attire to mounted archery,
to guard our borders against the Cānhú, the Lóufán, Qín, and Hán.
Moreover, in the past, Jiǎn Zhǔ did not fortify Jìnyáng
and reach Shàngdǎng,
and Xiāng Wáng annexed the Róng and took Dài
to drive out the various Hú tribes;
this is clear to both the foolish and the wise.
Previously, Zhōngshān, relying on the strong armies of Qí,
invaded and plundered our lands,
bound and took our people captive,
and diverted water to besiege Hào.
Were it not for the spiritual protection of the state altars,
Hào would have almost been lost.
The former King was indignant at this,
but his grievance has not yet been avenged.
Now, the attire of mounted archery,
locally, can prepare us for the terrain of Shàngdǎng,
and from afar, can avenge the grievances against Zhōngshān.
Yet you, Uncle, follow the customs of Zhōngguó to oppose the intentions of Jiǎn and Xiāng;
you loathe the reputation of changing attire,
but forget the shame of our state’s affairs.
This is not what I expected from you!"
Gōngzǐ Chéng bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and said:
"I am foolish and did not understand the King’s considerations,
and dared to speak within the limits of common custom.
Now that you wish to continue the intentions of Jiǎn and Xiāng,
and follow the will of the former kings,
how could I dare not obey your command?"
He bowed twice again.
The King then bestowed upon him the Hú attire.
Zhào Wén entered to remonstrate, saying:
"That the farmers labor and the gentlemen are nourished by them is
the constant principle of governance.
That the ignorant express their views and the wise deliberate upon them is
the way of instruction.
If a minister has no hidden loyalty
and a ruler has no blocked words,
this is the prosperity of the state.
Although I am ignorant,
I wish to exhaust my loyalty."
The King said:
"Deliberation is not harmed by disturbance,
and loyalty is not penalized for being excessive;
you should speak."
Zhào Wén said:
"To assist the customs of the current age is
the way of antiquity.
That clothing has its constants is
the regulation of ritual.
To cultivate the law without error is
the duty of the people.
These three are
what the former sages taught.
Now Your Majesty abandons these
and adopts the clothing of distant regions,
changing the teachings of old
and altering the way of antiquity;
therefore, I wish Your Majesty would reconsider it."
The King said:
"You speak of the realm of common customs.
Ordinary people are drowned in habits and customs,
and scholars are submerged in what they have heard.
These two groups
are why one fills offices and follows administration,
but they are not those with whom one observes the far-reaching or discusses beginnings.
Furthermore, the Sān Dài did not have the same attire yet they ruled as kings,
and the Wǔ Bà did not have the same teachings yet they governed.
The wise create teachings,
while the ignorant are restrained by them.
The worthy discuss customs,
while the unworthy are bound by them.
People who are restrained by attire
are not worth discussing the heart with;
the masses who are bound by custom
are not worth conveying ideas to.
Thus, to transform power along with customs
and for ritual to change along with transformations is
the way of the sages.
To act upon receiving instruction
and follow the law without selfishness is
the duty of the people.
A man of learning
can move along with what he hears;
one who understands the variations of ritual
can transform with the times.
Therefore, one who acts for himself does not wait for others,
and one who regulates the present does not model himself on antiquity;
you should let this go."
Zhào Zào remonstrated, saying:
"To hide loyalty and not exhaust it
belongs to the category of treachery.
To deceive the state for private reasons
belongs to the category of the base.
Those who commit treachery suffer death;
those who debase the state have their clans exterminated.
To reverse these two things is
the clear punishment of the former sages and
the great crime of a minister.
Although I am ignorant,
I wish to fully express my loyalty
and not evade death."
The King said:
"To exhaust one's thoughts without concealment is
loyalty.
For a superior to have no blocked words is
brilliance.
Loyalty does not avoid danger,
and brilliance does not reject people.
You should speak."
Zhào Zào said:
"I have heard that
the sage does not change the people to teach them,
and the wise person does not change customs to act.
Those who teach by following the people
achieve success without toil; those who act by relying on customs
have plans that are direct and easily seen.
Now Your Majesty changes the beginnings and does not follow custom,
adopting Hú attire without considering the world;
this is not how one teaches the people or completes ritual.
Furthermore, those who wear strange clothes have excessive ambitions,
and those with perverse customs disorder the people.
For this reason, those who preside over a state do not adopt strange or perverse attire,
and Zhōng Guó does not draw near to the conduct of the Mán or Yí;
these are not ways to teach the people or complete ritual.
Moreover, to follow the law leads to no error,
and to cultivate ritual leads to no deviance;
I wish Your Majesty would reconsider it."
The King said:
"Ancient and modern times do not have the same customs;
which antiquity should one follow?
Emperors and kings did not inherit from each other;
which ritual should one follow?
Mì Xī and Shén Nóng taught but did not execute;
Huáng Dì, Yáo, and Shùn executed but did not show anger.
Coming to the Sān Wáng,
they observed the times to establish laws
and relied on circumstances to establish rituals;
legal measures and institutional orders
each followed what was appropriate;
clothing and equipment
each facilitated their use.
Therefore, in ritualizing the world, one need not unify the path;
in benefiting the state, one need not model himself on antiquity.
When sages arose,
they did not inherit from each other yet they ruled as kings.
When Xià and Yīn declined,
they did not change their rituals yet they were destroyed.
If that is so, then to go against antiquity is not necessarily to be criticized,
and to follow ritual is not necessarily to be praised.
Furthermore, as for 'wearing strange attire and having excessive ambitions,'
that would mean Zōu and Lǔ had no strange behavior;
as for 'perverse customs and the people changing,'
that would mean Wú and Yuè had no talented people.
For this reason, the sage calls what benefits the body 'attire'
and calls what facilitates affairs 'teaching.'
Advancement and retreat are called 'moderation.'
Regulations of clothing
are for standardizing ordinary people,
not for discussing the worthy.
Thus the sage flows with the customs,
and the worthy change with the transformations.
A proverb says:
'One who uses books to drive a chariot
does not fully grasp the nature of the horse.
One who uses antiquity to regulate the present
does not understand the changes of affairs.'
Therefore, the merit of following the law
is not enough to rise above the age;
the learning of modeling oneself on antiquity
is not enough to regulate the present.
You should not oppose this anymore."
The King appointed Zhōu Shào as a tutor
and said:
"When I first toured the counties
and passed Fān Wú,
back when you were a youth,
everyone capable of stepping over a stone spoke of your filial piety.
Therefore, I requested you with jade discs,
sent you wine and food,
and sought to see you.
You pleaded illness and declined.
People have said of you:
'A filial son to his father
is a loyal minister to his lord.'
Therefore, I consider your wisdom and deliberation
to have eloquence enough to guide people,
gravity enough to hold firm in difficulties,
loyalty that can express my intentions,
and trustworthiness that can be relied upon for the long term.
The Shī says:
'Subdue difficulties with courage,
and govern disorder with wisdom—
this is the planning of affairs.
Appointing a tutor to implement actions,
and teaching the young through learning—
this is the constant principle of righteousness.
Affairs that follow a plan
bring trouble if they fail;
actions that seek out deliberation
leave no worry even if exhausted.'
Therefore, I wish for you to adopt Hú attire to serve as the King's tutor."
Zhōu Shào said:
"Your Majesty’s judgment is mistaken;
this is not a responsibility your humble servant dares to assume."
The King said:
"No one knows a son better than his father,
and no one judges a minister better than his lord.
The lord is I."
Zhōu Shào said:
"There are six ways of establishing a tutor."
The King said:
"What are these six?"
Zhōu Shào said:
"Wisdom and deliberation that are not impulsive and understand change;
personal conduct that is broad and benevolent and understands ritual;
dignity that is not easily moved from its position;
heavy profit that is not enough to change the heart;
reverence for teaching without being complacent;
and harmony with subordinates without being in danger.
These six are
the talents of a tutor,
and I possess not one of them.
To hide loyalty and not exhaust it
is my crime.
To have a tutor command the palace officials
and trouble the authorities
is a shame for the officers.
I ask Your Majesty to reconsider your judgment."
The King said: “Knowing these six things
is the reason I employ you.”
Zhōu Shào said: “The state has not yet understood Your Majesty’s Hú-style attire.
Even so, I am Your Majesty’s servant,
and since Your Majesty has repeatedly commanded it,
how could I dare not obey the order?”
He bowed twice
and was granted the Hú-style attire.
The King said:
“I have entrusted the Prince to you as your responsibility,
desiring that you love him deeply
and ensure he is never humiliated.
Guide him with the path of righteous conduct,
and do not let him be overwhelmed by the hardships of study.
One who serves a ruler
follows his intentions
and does not oppose his will.
One who serves a predecessor
illuminates his lofty virtues
and does not turn his back on his heirs.
Therefore, to have a minister who can be commanded
is a blessing for the state.
If you can do this,
your service to me will be complete.
The *Shū* says:
‘Remove the wicked without hesitation;
employ the worthy without doubt.’
Between me and you,
there is no need for others.”
Then he granted Zhōu Shào the Hú-style clothing and cap,
along with a belt and a golden *shībǐ* buckle,
so that he might serve as tutor to the Prince.
Zhào Yàn was late in adopting the Hú-style attire,
so the King sent a messenger to reprimand him, saying:
“The conduct of serving a lord
involves exhausting one’s mind and strength,
offering subtle remonstrance without clamor,
responding without resentment,
not defying superiors to boast of oneself,
and not establishing private views to gain fame.
The way of a son is to be compliant and not obstructive;
the conduct of a minister is to be yielding and not contentious.
A son who follows a private path will surely bring chaos to his family;
a minister who follows a private sense of righteousness will surely endanger the state.
To act in opposition to one’s kinsmen
means a compassionate father will not treat one as a son;
to defy a lord to fulfill oneself
means a benevolent lord will not treat one as a minister.
I have donned the Hú-style attire,
yet you alone do not.
In defying your lord,
no crime is greater.
To treat governance as a burden
and consider defiance of the lord as lofty conduct—
no private action is greater than this.
Therefore, I fear my relative has committed a crime deserving of execution,
which would demonstrate the laws of the officials.”
Zhào Yàn bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and said:
“When the officials previously ordered the adoption of Hú-style attire
and it reached your humble servant,
I failed the command and exceeded the time limit.
That I have not yet been punished or disgraced
is Your Majesty’s mercy.
I respectfully follow the change in clothing
and await this day.”
The King conquered Yuányáng
and made it a cavalry base.
Niú Zàn came forward to remonstrate, saying:
“A state has its fixed records;
an army has its constant principles.
To change the records is to cause chaos;
to lose the principles is to become weak.
Now Your Majesty has conquered Yuányáng
and made it a cavalry base;
this is changing the records and abandoning the principles.
Furthermore, those practiced in their weapons make light of their enemies;
those accustomed to their use find the difficult easy.
Now the people are accustomed to their use, yet Your Majesty changes it;
this harms the ruler and weakens the state.
Therefore, unless the benefit is a hundredfold, one does not change customs;
unless the achievement is tenfold, one does not change implements.
Now Your Majesty breaks up the ranks and scatters the soldiers
to serve cavalry archery;
I fear the gains from conquest
will not equal the costs of what is lost.”
The King said:
“Ancient and modern times have different benefits;
far and near have different uses.
Yin and Yang follow different paths;
the four seasons are not suitable for the same things.
Therefore, a worthy man observes the times
but is not constrained by them;
he controls the military
but is not controlled by it.
You know the records of the government offices,
but you do not know the advantages of weapons;
you know the use of soldiers and armor,
but you do not know the suitability of Yin and Yang.
Therefore, if weapons are not suited for use,
why should they not be changed?
If teachings are not convenient for affairs,
why should the customs not be altered?
Long ago, our predecessor Xiāng Zhǔ exchanged land with Dài;
he built cities and borders to mark it,
calling it the Wúqióng zhī Mén,
in order to enlighten his successors and look toward the distant future.
Now heavy armor and slow soldiers
cannot cross dangerous terrain;
benevolence, righteousness, and virtue
cannot bring them to pay court.
I have heard that the trustworthy do not discard achievements,
and the wise do not miss the time.
Now you use the records of the government offices
to interfere with my affairs;
this is not something you understand.”
Niú Zàn bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and said:
“How could I dare not obey your command?”
In the end, he donned the Hú-style attire,
led the cavalry into the Hú lands,
went out through the Yíyí zhī Mén,
crossed the strongholds of Jiǔ Xiàn,
traversed the dangers of Wǔ Jìng,
reached Yúzhōng,
and opened up a thousand *lǐ* of land.
In the thirtieth year of Zhào Huìwén Wáng,
the Chancellor and Dūpíng Jūn,
Tián Dān, asked Zhào Shē, saying:
“It is not that I do not admire
the General’s military strategies;
the reason I am not convinced
is solely the General’s use of massive numbers of troops.
Using massive numbers
prevents the people from farming
