and establish your name."
Xīmén Bào said:
"I venture to ask if there is a method
for accomplishing work and establishing a name?"
Wén Hóu said:
"There is.
Regarding the elders of the villages and those scholars who are given seats of honor,
when you enter, inquire after the worthy and good among them and serve them as teachers.
Seek out those who like to conceal the beauty of others while spreading their ugliness,
and examine them through multiple sources.
For many things appear similar but are not:
the young of dark weeds look like grain;
the yellow of a black ox looks like a tiger;
white bones can be mistaken for ivory;
the wǔfū stone looks like jade.
These are all things that seem like something else but are not."
Wén Hóu had an appointment with a gamekeeper for a hunt.
On that day,
while he was enjoying drinking, it rained.
Wén Hóu was about to set out.
His attendants said:
"Today we are enjoying drinking,
and it is raining;
where does Your Grace intend to go?"
Wén Hóu said:
"I have an appointment with the gamekeeper for a hunt.
Although I am enjoying myself,
how can I not keep the appointment!"
So he went
and personally called it off.
It was from this that Wèi began to become strong.
Wèi Wén Hóu was drinking wine with Tián Zǐfāng and praising the music.
Wén Hóu said:
"The sound of the bells is not in harmony;
the left side is too high."
Tián Zǐfāng laughed.
Wén Hóu said:
"Why do you laugh?"
Zǐfāng said:
"I have heard that
if a ruler is enlightened, he takes pleasure in his officials; if he is not enlightened, he takes pleasure in musical tones.
Now that Your Lordship is so discerning of sounds,
I fear Your Lordship might be deaf to your officials."
Wén Hóu said:
"Good.
I respectfully receive your instruction."
Wèi Wǔ Hóu was floating on the Xī Hé with his grand officers.
He remarked:
"The strategic difficulty of these rivers and mountains,
are they not truly solid and secure?"
Wáng Zhōng, who was attending the King, said:
"This is why the state of Jìn was strong.
If they are well maintained,
then the enterprise of a hegemon or king is complete."
Wú Qǐ replied: "My Lord's words
are the way to endanger a state;
and since you, sir, also second them,
this is truly dangerous."
Wǔ Hóu said indignantly: "Do your words have an explanation?"
Wú Qǐ replied:
"The strategic difficulty of rivers and mountains
is truly insufficient to rely upon;
for the enterprise of a hegemon or king
does not follow from this.
In the past,
the territory of the Sānmiáo
had the waves of Pénglǐ on its left,
the waters of Dòngtíng on its right,
Wénshān to its south,
and Héngshān to its north.
Relying on these natural defenses,
their governance was not good,
and Yǔ banished them.
The state of Xià Jié
had the shade of Tiānmén on its left
and the sun of Tiānxī on its right,
Lú and Yì to its north,
and the Yī and Luò rivers flowing to its south.
Having these natural defenses,
yet because his governance was not good,
Tāng attacked him.
The state of Yīn Zhòu
had Mèngmén on its left and the Zhāng and Fǔ rivers on its right,
belted by the Yellow River in front
and backed by mountains.
Having these natural defenses,
yet because his governance was not good,
Wǔ Wáng attacked him.
Furthermore, you personally lead your subjects and conquer surrendered cities;
it is not that the walls are not high,
nor that the people are not numerous,
yet they can be annexed
because their governance is evil.
From this perspective,
how can the strategic difficulty of terrain
be sufficient to make one a hegemon or king?"
Wǔ Hóu said: "Good.
Today I have heard the words of a sage!
The governance of Xī Hé
I shall entrust entirely to you."
Gōngshū Cuò of Wèi served as a general for Wèi
and fought with Hàn and Zhào to the north of the Huì River,
capturing Lè Zuò.
The King of Wèi was pleased and welcomed him in the suburbs,
rewarding him with land worth a million units of revenue.
Gōngshū Cuò stepped back, bowed twice, and declined, saying:
"That the soldiers did not break,
stood straight and did not lean,
and despite exhaustion did not flee,
this was the residual teaching of Wú Qǐ;
I could not have achieved this.
Previously surveying the terrain's strategic difficulty,
deciding on the preparations for benefit and harm,
and ensuring the soldiers of the three armies were not confused,
this was the power of Bā Níng and Cuàn Xiāng.
Hanging rewards and punishments before them
so the people clearly believed in them afterward,
this was Your Majesty's enlightened law.
Seeing the enemy was vulnerable and drumming the advance,
not daring to be idle or weary,
that was me.
Since Your Majesty has rewarded me specifically for being your tireless right hand,
why is this so?
If it is because I have merit, what power did I truly have?"
The King said: "Excellent."
Thereupon he sought out the descendants of Wú Qǐ
and granted them land of two hundred thousand.
Bā Níng and Cuàn Xiāng were each granted land of one hundred thousand.
The King said: "Is Gōngshū not indeed a superior man!
Not only has he defeated a strong enemy for me,
but he also does not neglect the descendants of the worthy
nor cover the tracks of capable men.
How can Gōngshū not be further rewarded?"
Therefore, he gave him another four hundred thousand in land,
adding it on top of the million,
making it one million four hundred thousand.
Therefore, the *Lǎozǐ* says:
"The Sage does not accumulate.
The more he does for others,
the more he has for himself;
the more he gives to others,
the more he possesses."
*Gōngshū Cuò* lived up to this.
When *Gōngshū Cuò* of *Wèi* was ill,
*Huì Wáng* went to visit him and said:
"If your illness, *Gōngshū*,
should lead to the unavoidable,
what shall be done for the sake of the state and its altars?"
*Gōngshū Cuò* replied: "I have a subordinate, *Gōngsūn Yāng*;
I hope the King will listen to him regarding the affairs of state.
If you cannot listen to him,
do not let him leave the borders."
The King did not respond.
When he came out, he said to his attendants:
"How tragic!
With the virtue of *Gōngshū*,
yet he tells me I must listen to *Yāng* regarding state affairs;
is this not perverse?"
When *Gōngshū Cuò* died,
and *Gōngsūn Yāng* heard of it,
after the burial was completed,
he went west to *Qín*.
*Xiào Gōng* received and employed him.
Consequently, *Qín* indeed became stronger by the day,
and *Wèi* was weakened by the day.
This was not the perversity of *Gōngshū Cuò*,
but the perversity of *Huì Wáng*.
The trouble with those who are perverse
is that they invariably regard those who are not perverse as being perverse themselves.
When *Sū Zǐ* was forming the Vertical Alliance for *Zhào*,
he persuaded *Huì Wáng* of *Wèi*, saying:
"Your Majesty’s land,
to the south has the *Hónggōu* canal, *Chén*, and *Rǔnán*;
it has *Xǔ*, *Yān*, *Kūnyáng*, *Shàolíng*, *Wǔyáng*, and *Xīnqī*.
To the east it has the *Huái*, *Yǐng*, *Yí*, and *Huáng* rivers, *Zhǔzǎo*, *Wúhǎi* salt, and
*Shū*; to the west it has the boundary of the Long Wall.
To the north it has *Héwài*, *Juǎn*, *Yǎn*, *Yàn*, and *Suānzǎo*.
The territory is a thousand *lǐ* square.
Although the names of the places are small,
the fields, cottages, and dwellings are so dense
that there is no space for grazing cattle or horses.
The population is so numerous,
and the carriages and horses so many,
that they travel day and night without ceasing,
no different from the multitude of the three armies.
I have ventured to estimate
that Your Majesty’s state
is not inferior to *Chǔ*.
Yet the proponents of the Horizontal Alliance scheme for the King
to seek diplomacy abroad with the strong, tiger-like and wolf-like *Qín*,
in order to invade the world.
Should a national disaster eventually occur,
they would not suffer its misfortune.
Relying on the power of strong *Qín*
to coerce their own ruler from within,
there is no crime greater than this.
Furthermore, *Wèi*
is a strong state in the world,
and Your Majesty is a virtuous ruler of the world.
Yet now you intend to face west and serve *Qín*,
calling yourself an Eastern Vassal,
building a palace for an Emperor,
receiving hats and belts of office,
and offering sacrifices in spring and autumn.
I venture to feel ashamed of this on Your Majesty’s behalf.
"I have heard that King *Gōujiàn* of *Yuè*, with three thousand scattered soldiers,
captured *Fūchāi* at *Gānsùi*.
*Wǔ Wáng* had three thousand soldiers
and three hundred leather-clad chariots
when he decapitated *Zhòu* in the wilds of *Mù*.
Was it because their soldiers were numerous?
It was because they could truly exert their awe.
Now I have heard that Your Majesty’s soldiers
include over twenty thousand elite warriors,
twenty million common infantry,
two hundred thousand valiant strikers,
one hundred thousand auxiliary laborers,
six hundred chariots,
and five thousand horses.
This far exceeds King *Gōujiàn* of *Yuè* and *Wǔ Wáng*!
Yet now you are coerced by the words of sycophants
and wish to serve *Qín* as a subject.
Serving *Qín* requires ceding land and offering hostages;
thus, before the troops are even used, the state is already diminished.
All those among the ministers who speak of serving *Qín*
are treacherous officials,
not loyal ones.
As a minister,
to cede his ruler's land to seek foreign diplomacy,
snatching a momentary achievement without regard for the consequences,
ruining the public house to establish a private one,
and relying on the power of strong *Qín* from without to coerce his ruler from within to seek the ceding of land—
I hope Your Majesty will examine this maturely.
"The *Zhōu Shū* says:
'That which continues incessantly,
what can be done if it becomes unmanageable?
If a single hair is not plucked,
it will grow to become an axe handle.'
If the initial planning is not settled,
there will be great trouble later;
what will you do then?
If Your Majesty can truly listen to me,
and the Six States join in the Vertical Alliance,
focusing their minds and combining their strength,
then there will surely be no trouble from strong *Qín*.
Therefore, the King of my humble state, *Zhào*, has sent me to offer this humble plan,
to present a clear covenant,
and it rests with Your Majesty’s decree."
The King of *Wèi* said: "I am unworthy
and have never had the chance to hear such brilliant instruction.
Now that the Master has delivered the decree of the King of *Zhào*,
I respectfully follow with my state."
When *Zhāng Yí* was forming the Horizontal Alliance for *Qín*,
he persuaded the King of *Wèi*, saying:
"The territory of *Wèi* is not even a thousand *lǐ* square,
and its soldiers do not exceed three hundred thousand men.
The land is flat on all four sides,
accessible to the feudal lords from all directions,
with roads converging like the spokes of a wheel,
and without the barriers of famous mountains or great rivers.
From *Zhèng* to *Liáng* is not more than a hundred *lǐ*;
from *Chén* to *Liáng* is over two hundred *lǐ*.
With horses galloping and men rushing, they arrive at *Liáng* before becoming weary.
To the south you border *Chǔ*,
to the west you border *Hán*,
to the north you border *Zhào*,
and to the east you border *Qí*.
Your troops must guard the four quarters,
and those defending the watchposts are lined up in succession.
The grain and provisions transported
are no less than one hundred thousand units.
The geographical situation of *Wèi*
is essentially a battlefield.
If *Wèi* joins with *Chǔ* in the south but not with *Qí*,
then *Qí* will attack its east.
If it joins with *Qí* in the east but not with *Zhào*,
then *Zhào* will attack its north.
If it does not harmonize with *Hán*,
then *Hán* will attack its west.
If it is not friendly with *Chǔ*,
then *Chǔ* will attack its south.
This is what is called the path of being torn into four or split into five.
"Moreover, those among the feudal lords who form the Vertical Alliance
do so to secure their states, honor their rulers, strengthen their armies, and make their names famous.
Those in the Vertical Alliance seek to unite the world as one,
binding themselves as brothers, and sacrificing a white horse to swear an oath at the *Huán Shuǐ* River to strengthen one another.
Even blood brothers
from the same parents
still fight over money and property.
To want to rely on the deceitful and fickle remnant schemes of *Sū Qín*—
it is clear that they cannot succeed.
"If Your Majesty does not serve *Qín*,
*Qín* will send down troops to attack *Héwài*,
seize *Juǎn*, *Yǎn*, *Yàn*, and *Suānzǎo*,
coerce *Wèi* and take *Jìnyáng*;
then *Zhào* will not come south.
If *Zhào* does not come south,
then *Wèi* cannot go north.
If *Wèi* cannot go north,
then the path of the Vertical Alliance is severed.
If the path of the Vertical Alliance is severed,
then it is impossible for Your Majesty’s state to avoid danger.
If *Qín* enlists *Hán* to attack *Wèi*,
*Hán* being coerced by *Qín*,
will not dare not to obey.
When *Qín* and *Hán* become as one country,
the destruction of *Wèi* can be expected in an instant.
This is why I am concerned for Your Majesty.
In planning for Your Majesty,
nothing is better than serving *Qín*.
If you serve *Qín*, then *Chǔ* and *Hán* will surely not dare to move.
Without the threat of *Chǔ* and *Hán*,
Your Majesty can sleep on a high pillow,
and the state will certainly have no worries.
"Moreover, among those *Qín* wishes to weaken, none is like *Chǔ*,
and the one most capable of weakening *Chǔ* is *Wèi*.
Although *Chǔ* has the reputation of being wealthy and large,
in reality it is hollow and empty.
Although its soldiers are numerous,
they are talkative and flee easily;
they are easily defeated
and do not dare to fight a hard battle.
If the troops of *Wèi* face south and attack,
victory over *Chǔ* is certain.
To diminish Chǔ and benefit Wèi,
to attack Chǔ and accommodate Qín,
and to internally divert calamities to ensure the security of the state—
these are good deeds.
If your Dàwáng does not listen to me,
once the Qín troops march out and move east,
even if you wish to serve Qín, it will be impossible to do so.
"Furthermore, proponents of the zòng alliance mostly use impassioned rhetoric but are seldom trustworthy.
They persuade the king of a vassal state,
and come out riding in his carriage;
they negotiate a treaty for a country and return,
establishing the foundation for being enfeoffed as a marquis.
Therefore, among the traveling scholars of the world,
there is none who does not day and night wring their wrists, glare their eyes, and gnash their teeth to speak of the advantages of the zòng alliance
in order to persuade the masters of men.
When a master of men reads their words
and is led by their theories,
how can he not be dazzled?
I have heard that accumulated feathers can sink a boat,
a crowd of light objects can break an axle,
and many mouths can melt gold.
Therefore, I hope your Dàwáng will consider this matter thoroughly."
The Wèi Wáng said:
"I have been dull and foolish,
and my previous plans were failures.
I request to call myself a vassal of the eastern border,
build a palace for the Emperor,
receive the official cap and sash,
offer sacrifices in spring and autumn,
and cede the lands of Héwài."
Qí and Wèi formed an alliance to attack Chǔ,
and Wèi sent Dǒng Qìng as a hostage to Qí.
Chǔ attacked Qí
and defeated it soundly,
but Wèi did not come to the rescue.
Tián Yīng was furious
and was about to kill Dǒng Qìng.
Gàn Yí spoke on behalf of Dǒng Qìng to Tián Yīng, saying:
"When Chǔ attacked Qí
and defeated it soundly,
the reason they did not dare to penetrate deeper
was that they thought Wèi would be brought into Qí
to strike their rear.
Now, if you kill Dǒng Qìng,
this will show Chǔ that Wèi is not with Qí.
If Wèi in anger joins with Chǔ,
Qí will surely be in danger.
It would be better to treat Dǒng Qìng with honor to maintain good relations with Wèi,
and thus make Chǔ suspicious of Wèi's intentions."
Sū Qín was detained in Wèi
and wanted to flee to Hán,
but the house of Wèi closed the passes and would not let him through.
Qí sent Sū Lì to speak on his behalf to the Wèi Wáng, saying:
"Qí requested to enfeoff Jīngyáng Jūn with the lands of Sòng,
but Qín would not accept it.
It is not that it would be disadvantageous for Qín to ally with Qí and gain the Sòng lands;
rather, the reason they did not accept
was that they did not trust the King of Qí and Sū Qín.
Now, when Qín sees that the discord between Qí and Wèi is so severe,
then Qí will surely not deceive Qín,
and Qín will trust Qí.
If Qí and Qín unite and Jīngyáng Jūn possesses the Sòng lands,
then this will not be to Wèi's advantage.
Therefore, it would be better for your King to return Sū Qín to the east;
Qín will then surely suspect Qí and not listen to them.
If Qí and Qín do not unite,
the world will have no worries.
If the attack on Qí is successful,
then your territory will be expanded."
Chén Zhěn was sent by Qín as an envoy to Qí
and passed through Wèi,
where he sought to see Xīshǒu.
Xīshǒu declined to see Chén Zhěn.
Chén Zhěn said:
"The reason I have come
is for business.
If you do not see me,
I will be on my way
and cannot wait for another day."
Xīshǒu then saw him.
Chén Zhěn said: "Do you dislike business?
Why do you eat and drink without any business to attend to?
If you have no business, I will surely come."
Xīshǒu said: "I, Yǎn, am unworthy
and cannot obtain any business,
so how could I dare to dislike it?"
Chén Zhěn said:
"I request to transfer the affairs of the world to you."
Xīshǒu said:
"How?"
Chén Zhěn said:
"The Wèi Wáng has sent Lǐ Cóng with a hundred carriages as an envoy to Chǔ.
You can place yourself in the midst of this and make them suspicious.
You should say to the Wèi Wáng:
'I have old ties with Yān and Zhào,
and they have several times sent people to summon me,
saying if I have no business, I must come.
Now that I have no business,
I request to pay my respects and go.
It will not be for long—
a period of ten or fifteen days.'
The King will surely have no reason to stop you.
Once you are permitted to go,
you should then personally say at court:
'I am urgently being sent to Yān and Zhào,
and I am urgently preparing the carriages and travel equipment.'"
Xīshǒu said: "Agreed."
He requested an audience with the Wèi Wáng,
and the King granted it,
whereupon he immediately stated publicly that he was being sent to Yān and Zhào.
When the guests of the various feudal lords heard this,
they all sent people to tell their kings:
"Lǐ Cóng is being sent to Chǔ with a hundred carriages,
and Xīshǒu is also being sent to Yān and Zhào with thirty carriages."
When the King of Qí heard this,
he feared that he would be the last in the world to win over Wèi,
so he entrusted his affairs to Xīshǒu.
Xīshǒu accepted the affairs of Qí.
The Wèi Wáng stopped his mission.
When Yān and Zhào heard of this,
they also entrusted their affairs to Xīshǒu.
When the King of Chǔ heard of this,
he said:
"Lǐ Cóng made a treaty with me,
but now Yān, Qí, and Zhào have all relied on Xīshǒu for their affairs.
Xīshǒu will surely want me to do the same,
and I wish to do so."
He then went back on his word to Lǐ Cóng
and relied on Xīshǒu for his affairs.
The Wèi Wáng said:
"The reason I did not use Xīshǒu
was because I thought he was not capable.
Now that the four states have entrusted their affairs to him,
I shall also rely on him for my affairs."
Xīshǒu thus took charge of the affairs of the world
and again became the Chancellor of Wèi.
Zhāng Yí spoke ill of Chén Zhěn to the Wèi Wáng, saying:
"Chén Zhěn is good at serving Chǔ,
and in seeking territory for them, he exerts great effort."
Zuǒ Huá said to Chén Zhěn:
"Zhāng Yí is on good terms with the Wèi Wáng,
and the Wèi Wáng is very fond of him.
Although you may try a hundred times to persuade him otherwise,
he still will not listen.
It would be better for you to use Zhāng Yí's words as your capital and return to the King of Chǔ."
Chén Zhěn said: "Excellent."
He then sent someone ahead to speak to the King of Chǔ.
Zhāng Yí wanted to drive Chén Zhěn into a corner,
so he had the Wèi Wáng summon him to make him Chancellor,
intending to confront him when he arrived.
When he was about to depart,
his son Chén Yìng stopped his father from going,
saying: "In matters that are obscure,
one must not fail to investigate.
When Zhèng Qiáng left Qín, he said
that I, Yìng, should know.
Wèi wants to sever ties with Chǔ and Qí,
so they will surely offer you a grand welcome.
Those in Yǐng who are not well-disposed toward you
want you to leave,
and will surely urge the King to provide many carriages for you.
When you reach Sòng,
claim illness on the road and do not proceed,
and send someone to tell the King of Qí:
'The reason Wèi is welcoming me
is that they wish to sever the ties between Qí
and Chǔ.'"
The King of Qí said:
"If you indeed do not go to Wèi but come to see me instead,
I request to enfeoff you."
Consequently, he sent the carriage of the Lǔ Hóu to welcome him.
Zhāng Yí fled to Wèi,
and Wèi was about to welcome him.
Zhāng Chǒu remonstrated with the King,
wishing for him not to let him in,
but his advice was not accepted by the King.
Zhāng Chǒu withdrew
and again remonstrated with the King, saying:
"Has your King also heard of the old concubine who serves the mistress of the house?
When the children are grown and her beauty has faded,
she only values the family.
Now, my service to your King
is like that of the old concubine serving her mistress."
The Wèi Wáng therefore did not admit Zhāng Yí.
Zhāng Yí wanted to align Wèi with Qín and Hán to attack Qí and Chǔ.
Huì Shī wanted to align Wèi with Qí and Chǔ to keep the troops at rest.
Many people spoke in favor of Zhāng Zǐ at the King's court.
Huì Zǐ said to the King:
"In minor matters,
those who say it is possible and those who say it is impossible are exactly half and half;
how much more so in major matters?
Aligning Wèi with Qín and Hán to attack Qí and Chǔ
is a major matter,
yet Your Majesty’s ministers all think it is possible.
I do not know if its possibility
is so clear,
or if the ministers’ knowledge and methods
are so identical?
If its possibility
is not so clear,
and the ministers’ knowledge and methods
are also not all identical,
then this is because half of them are being suppressed.
What is called 'coercing the sovereign'
is losing that other half."
Zhāng Zǐyí served as Prime Minister of Wèi on behalf of Qín;
Qí and Chǔ were angry and wanted to attack Wèi.
Yōng Jǔ said to Zhāng Zǐ:
"The reason Wèi made you its Prime Minister
was that with you as Prime Minister, the state would be secure
and the common people would have no troubles.
Now that you are Prime Minister and Wèi is under attack,
this means Wèi’s plan was a mistake.
If Qí and Chǔ attack Wèi,
you will certainly be in danger."
Zhāng Zǐ said:
"In that case, what should be done?"
Yōng Jǔ said: "Please let me make Qí and Chǔ call off the attack."
Yōng Jǔ said to the Kings of Qí and Chǔ:
"Have your Majesties heard of Zhāng Yí’s agreement with the King of Qín?
He said:
'If Your Majesty makes me Prime Minister in Wèi,
Qí and Chǔ will hate me
and will certainly attack Wèi.
If Wèi fights and wins,
then the armies of Qí and Chǔ will be broken,
and I will firmly hold Wèi;
if Wèi does not win,
Wèi will certainly serve Qín to preserve its state,
and will certainly cede land to bribe Your Majesty.
Even if they wish to attack again,
their exhaustion will make them unable to respond to Qín.'
This is how Yí secretly allied with the King of Qín.
Now if Yí is Prime Minister of Wèi and you attack it,
you are making Yí’s plan succeed for Qín;
this is not the way to exhaust Yí’s options."
The Kings of Qí and Chǔ said: "Good."
They then immediately called off the attack on Wèi.
Zhāng Yí wanted to be Prime Minister of both Qín and Wèi simultaneously,
so he said to the King of Wèi:
"I ask that Qín attack Sānchuān,
while Your Majesty uses the opportunity to seize Nányáng;
then the House of Hán will perish."
Shǐ Yàn said to Zhào Xiàn:
"Why do you not use Chǔ to assist Yí in seeking the premiership in Wèi?
Hán will fear destruction
and will certainly flee south to Chǔ.
If Yí is concurrently Prime Minister of Qín and Wèi,
then you will certainly also be concurrently Prime Minister of Chǔ and Hán."
The King of Wèi was going to appoint Zhāng Yí as Prime Minister.
Xīshǒu found this disadvantageous,
so he sent someone to say to Gōngshū of Hán:
"Zhāng Yí has united Qín and Wèi.
His words are:
'Wèi will attack Nányáng,
and Qín will attack Sānchuān;
the House of Hán must perish.'
Moreover, the reason the King of Wèi values Zhāng Zǐ
is because he wants to gain land;
then Hán’s Nányáng will be taken.
Why do you not yield a little of it to
make it Yǎn’s achievement?
Then the alliance between Qín and Wèi can be discarded.
In this way,
Wèi will certainly plot against Qín and abandon Yí,
and will win over Hán and make Yǎn Prime Minister."
Gōngshū believed this,
and consequently yielded the land.
Xīshǒu took the credit for it
and indeed became Prime Minister of Wèi.
Chǔ promised Wèi six cities to join it in attacking Qí and saving Yàn.
Zhāng Yí wanted to ruin this,
so he said to the King of Wèi:
"Qí fears the alliance of the three states,
so it will certainly return the land of Yàn to submit to Chǔ.
Chǔ and Zhào will certainly listen to it
and will not give Wèi the six cities.
Thus Your Majesty will have lost your strategy with Chǔ and Zhào,
while establishing enmity with Qí and Qín.
Qí will then attack Zhào,
take Chéngqiū,
and reclaim the invaded lands;
Xū and Dùnqiū will be in danger.
Chǔ will break Nányáng and the Jiǔyí,
enter Pèi,
and Xǔ and Yānlíng will be in danger.
What Your Majesty will gain
is only Xīnguān.
But the roads through Sòng and Wèi will be controlled by others;
if the matter fails, you will be driven by Zhào;
if the matter succeeds, you will be subservient to Sòng and Wèi."
The King of Wèi did not listen.
Zhāng Yí told Gōngzhòng
to use the famine
as a reason to reward the King of Hán with lands near Héwài.
The King of Wèi was afraid
and asked Zhāng Zǐ.
Zhāng Zǐ said:
"Qín wants to save Qí,
and Hán wants to attack Nányáng.
Qín and Hán aligning to attack Nányáng
is no different.
Furthermore, I have divined for Your Majesty;
if Your Majesty does not meet with Qín,
Hán’s divination for success is certain."
The King of Wèi then went to meet with Qín,
trusting Hán, expanding Wèi, and saving Zhào,
while distancing the men of Chǔ,
acting with haste at Bìxià.
The campaign to attack Qí thus failed.
During the campaign of Xúzhōu,
Xīshǒu said to the King of Liáng:
"Why not openly side with Qí while secretly aligning with Chǔ?
Both states will rely on Your Majesty,
and Qí and Chǔ will surely fight.
If Qí wins over Chǔ,
you can join in taking advantage of it,
and will surely take the lands outside Fāngchéng;
if Chǔ wins and Qí is defeated,
and you join in taking advantage of it,
then the Crown Prince’s grievance will be avenged."
Qín defeated Dōngzhōu
and fought with Wèi at Yīquē,
killing Xīwǔ.
Wèi ordered Gōngsūn Yǎn to take advantage of the victory
by staying at the border
and asking to use humble words and cede land to make peace with Qín.
For the sake of Dòu Lǚ, someone said to the King of Wèi:
"I do not know how much land Yǎn will follow Qín's demands to cede,
however, I can halve the land Yǎn would cede
and still have Qín make peace with Your Majesty."
The King said:
"How?"
The reply was:
"Your Majesty should grant Dòu Lǚ the title of Guānnèi Hóu
and send him to Zhào.
Your Majesty should emphasize his mission and provide him with generous support.
Then spread a rumor saying:
'I hear Zhōu and Wèi have ordered Dòu Lǚ to cede Wèi’s land to Fèngyáng Jūn
and follow Qín.'
Now, the Lord of Zhōu,
Dòu Lǚ,
and Fèngyáng Jūn
are mortal enemies of Ràng Hóu.
Now the one mediating peace
is Dòu Lǚ,
and the one controlling the land cession
is Fèngyáng Jūn.
The Queen Mother will fear they are not working through Ràng Hóu
and will want to ruin their plan;
she will surely ask for less land to align with Your Majesty
and make peace with Dōngzhōu and Wèi."
The King of Qí was going to meet with the Prime Ministers of Yàn,
Zhào, and Chǔ in Wèi,
agreeing to exclude Wèi.
The King of Wèi was afraid,
fearing they were plotting to attack Wèi.
He told Gōngsūn Yǎn.
Gōngsūn Yǎn said:
"If Your Majesty gives me a hundred catties of gold,
I can ruin their plan."
The King prepared a carriage
and loaded it with the hundred catties of gold.
Xīshǒu timed it for the day the King of Qí was to arrive;
he first took fifty carriages to Wèi
to observe Qí.
Using the hundred catties of gold,
he requested to see the King of Qí first,
and was granted an audience.
He then sat for a long time at ease,
leisurely talking about the mutual grievances of the three states' Prime Ministers.
A messenger spoke to the King of Qí:
"Your Majesty has an agreement with three other states to exclude Wèi.
Wèi sent Gōngsūn Yǎn here,
and now you have been talking with him for a long time.
This implies that Your Majesty is plotting against the three states."
The King of Qí said:
"When the King of Wèi heard I was coming,
he sent Gōngsūn-zǐ to greet me.
I have nothing to say to him."
The three states did not believe the King of Qí's explanation regarding the meeting,
and the affairs of the meeting were subsequently ruined.
Wèi ordered Gōngsūn Yǎn to request peace from Qín.
Qímǔ Huī instructed him on what to say:
"Do not cede many territories.
Say,
'If peace is achieved,
it is certainly because Qín values peace
and thus meets with the King.
If peace is not achieved,
then in the future, no one will be able
to bring Wèi and Qín together again.'"
Gōngsūn Yǎn served as a general for Wèi,
but he was not on good terms with the Prime Minister Tián Xū.
Jì-zǐ spoke on behalf of Yǎn to the King of Liáng, saying:
"Does Your Majesty not see a carriage with an ox and a thoroughbred horse harnessed together?
It cannot travel even a hundred paces.
Now Your Majesty believes Yǎn is capable of being a general,
and so you employ him;
yet you also listen to the Prime Minister’s plans.
This is like harnessing an ox and a thoroughbred horse together.
Both the ox and the horse will die,
and the objective will not be achieved.
Your Majesty's state will surely suffer!
I hope Your Majesty will examine this."
Xīshǒu and Tián Pàn wanted to use the troops of Qí and Wèi to attack Zhào,
but the Lord of Liáng and the Lord of Tián did not wish to.
Xīshǒu said:
"I request that each state provides fifty thousand men,
and Zhào will be crushed in no more than five months."
Tián Pàn said:
"One who uses troops lightly
endangers his state;
one who uses plans lightly
exhausts himself.
You now say crushing Zhào is very easy,
but I fear there will be future consequences."
Xīshǒu said:
"You are not wise.
The two lords
already did not want to do it.
Now you speak of difficulties to frighten them;
thus Zhào will not be attacked,
and the plans of us two gentlemen will be frustrated.
Furthermore, if you simply say it is easy
and the matter is already decided,
then when difficulties arise and the troops are engaged,
the Lord of Tián and the Lord of Liáng will see the danger.
How would they then dare to withhold the troops and not give them to us?"
Tián Pàn said:
"Good."
He then encouraged the two lords to listen to Xīshǒu.
Xīshǒu and
Tián Pàn thus obtained the troops of Qí and Wèi.
Before the troops even left the borders,
the Lord of Liáng and the Lord of Tián feared their arrival would lead to defeat in battle,
so they mobilized all their forces to follow them
and soundly defeated the Zhào clan.
Xīshǒu saw the Lord of Liáng and said:
"I have exhausted my strength and wisdom
wishing to expand Your Majesty's territory and gain a great name.
But Tián Xū thwarts me from within.
If Your Majesty continues to listen to him,
I will ultimately never succeed.
If Xū leaves,
I will stay;
if Xū stays,
I request to leave."
The King said:
"Xū
is a minister close to my heart.
Because he is inconvenient for you,
to kill or exile him
would leave me with no explanation to the world,
nor to my other ministers!
Now I will exclude him from external affairs for you
and order him not to dare interfere in your matters.
If he interferes in your matters,
I will kill or exile him for you.
How does that sound?"
Xīshǒu agreed.
Then he went east to see Tián Yīng
and formed an alliance with him.
He summoned Wén-zǐ to be Prime Minister of Wèi
and himself became Prime Minister of Hán.
Sū Dài spoke for Tián Xū to the King of Wèi, saying:
"I would like to ask, regarding Wén’s service to Wèi,
how does it compare to his service to Qí?"
The King said:
"It is not as good as his service to Qí."
"And Yǎn’s service to Wèi,
how does it compare to his service to Hán?"
The King said:
"It is not as good as his service to Hán."
Sū Dài then said:
"Yǎn will favor Hán and neglect Wèi;
Wén will favor Qí and neglect Wèi.
These two men
will use Your Majesty's state
to manage affairs in the world.
If they fail halfway,
Your Majesty will hear nothing of it.
Even if Your Majesty's state follows them and finds some joy, that is fine.
But it would be better for Your Majesty to keep Xū by your side
to monitor what these two men are doing.
These two men will say,
'Xū is not one of us.
If we manage affairs and it is not beneficial to Wèi,
Xū will certainly discredit us before the King.'
These two will then surely not have divided loyalties.
Whether what they do
is beneficial or not beneficial to Wèi,
if Your Majesty places Xū by your side to monitor them,
I believe it will be personally beneficial
and convenient for state affairs."
The King said:
"Good."
He indeed kept Xū by his side.
Shǐ Jǔ criticized Xīshǒu to the King.
Xīshǒu wanted to corner him
and said to Zhāng Yí:
"I request that you have the King offer the state to you;
the King will then be like Yáo or Shùn,
and if you do not accept,
you will be like Xǔ Yóu.
I also ask to have the King
grant a fief of ten thousand households to you."
Zhāng Yí was pleased
and consequently had Shǐ Jǔ meet with Xīshǒu several times.
The King heard of this and no longer employed him;
Shǐ Jǔ left without taking his leave.
The King of Chǔ attacked the south of Liáng, and the Hán clan consequently besieged Qiáng.
Chéng Huī spoke for Xīshǒu to the King of Hán:
"If you attack Qiáng swiftly,
the Chǔ army will surely advance.
Wèi will be unable to withstand it
and will submit to Chǔ.
The Hán clan will surely be in danger.
Therefore, it is better for Your Majesty to release Qiáng.
If Wèi has no worry from Hán,
it will surely fight with Chǔ.
If they fight and do not win,
Dàliáng cannot be held, so how much less could Qiáng be preserved?
If they fight and win,
their troops will be exhausted,
and it will be easy for Your Majesty to attack Qiáng."
King Huì of Wèi died,
and the day for the burial was set.
There was a heavy snowstorm
reaching as high as the eyes of an ox,
destroying the city walls,
and they were going to build a wooden road for the burial.
Many ministers advised the Crown Prince,
saying:
"The snow is so heavy, yet the funeral proceeds;
the people will surely suffer greatly.
I also fear the official expenses will be insufficient.
Please relax the deadline and change the day."
The Crown Prince said:
"As a son,
for the reason of the people's labor and official expenses,
not to carry out the late King's funeral
would be unrighteous.
Do not speak of this again."
The ministers all dared not speak further,
but told Xīshǒu. Xīshǒu said:
"I have no way to say anything to him;
only Huì Gōng can do it!
I will tell Huì Gōng."
Huì Gōng said:
"Agreed."
He prepared his carriage and went to see the Crown Prince, saying:
"The day for the funeral has been set."
The Crown Prince said:
"Indeed."
Huì Gōng said:
"In the past, when King Jì Lì was buried at the base of Mount Chǔ Shān,
the Luán Shuǐ River eroded his tomb,
exposing the front panel of the coffin.
Wén Wáng said:
'Alas!
Our late lord must surely wish to see his ministers and people once more,
which is why he has caused the Luán Shuǐ to reveal him.'
Thereupon, he brought the coffin out and displayed it in the court for the people to see,
and all the commoners saw it.
After three days, he reburied him.
This was Wén Wáng’s sense of righteousness.
Now the day for the funeral has been set,
but the snow is so heavy
that it reaches the eyes of the oxen,
making it difficult to travel.
Because the Crown Prince wishes to keep to the scheduled day,
might he be suspected of wishing to bury the late king too hastily?
I hope the Crown Prince will change the day.
The former king surely wishes to stay a little longer to support the state and bring peace to the common people,
which is why he has caused such heavy snow.
By relaxing the deadline and choosing another day,
you would be following Wén Wáng’s sense of righteousness.
If you do not do this,
does it mean you are ashamed to follow the example of Wén Wáng?"
The Crown Prince said:
"Very well.
I respectfully postpone the date
and will choose another day."
Huì Zǐ not only succeeded in carrying out his proposal,
but he also caused the Crown Prince of Wèi, before burying his predecessor,
to follow the righteousness of Wén Wáng.
To promote the righteousness of Wén Wáng to the whole world,
was this not a great achievement?
Five states attacked Qín and returned without success.
Later,
Qí wanted to attack Sòng,
but Qín forbade it.
Qí ordered Sòng Guō to go to Qín
to request an alliance to attack Sòng.
The King of Qín agreed.
The King of Wèi, fearing the alliance between Qí and Qín,
wished to make peace with Qín.
[The speaker] said to the King of Wèi:
"The King of Qín said to Sòng Guō:
'Those who would divide the cities of Sòng
and subdue its strength
are the six states.
Those who would take advantage of Sòng’s exhaustion
to compete with me for gains
are Chǔ and Wèi.
I ask the King not to forbid Chǔ from attacking Wèi,
so that the King alone can take over Sòng.
When the King attacks Sòng,
please use both firm and soft tactics.
As for a state like Sòng,
to deceive it is not seen as betrayal,
and to kill its people is not seen as making enemies.
Do not negotiate with them to take territory;
once you have obtained the land,
attack them again with force.
The goal is simply to devour Sòng.'
I have heard these words
and secretly grieve for Your Majesty;
Qín will surely apply this to Your Majesty as well.
They will certainly ask Your Majesty for land, and after they have it, they will attack you with force.
They will also surely tell Your Majesty to treat Qí lightly;
once the relations between Qí and Wèi have soured,
they will win over Qí to make further demands from Your Majesty.
Qín once used this tactic on Chǔ,
and also on Hán.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this deeply.
Whether Qín's friendship toward Wèi is sincere cannot be known.
Therefore, in planning for Your Majesty,
the best course is to attack Qín;
the next best is to make Qín a subordinate;
the next is to hold firmly to alliances
while feigning peace negotiations,
so that the allied states do not drift apart.
If Qín and Qí unite,
nothing can be done for the state.
If Your Majesty listens to me,
you must not make peace with them.
Qín's power is greater than Wèi's.
Wèi has repeatedly made its stance clear,
and therefore, those who would harm Qín for Your Excellency's sake
dare not do so openly.
If the world can be moved to attack Qín,
they secretly encourage it but do not dare to plan it openly.
Seeing the world harming Qín,
they would first sell out their allies to exonerate themselves.
If the world can be moved to make Qín a subordinate,
they would act as if they were coerced by their allies
and had no other choice.
If the world cannot,
they would be the first to leave
and treat Qín as their primary ally to increase their own importance.
Such people
use the King as a resource to sell out;
how can they save the state from trouble?
To save the state from trouble,
one must exhaust the three strategies
and implement the highest one.
If the highest is not possible,
then implement the middle;
if the middle is not possible,
then implement the lowest.
If the lowest is not possible,
then clearly show that you are not with Qín,
and live to weaken Qín,
so that Qín finds neither massive resentment nor massive profit,
and only your own peace is secured.
To let Your Excellency sell them out to align with Qín,
is this a plan to save the state from trouble?
How could I be worthy of such a task?
Nevertheless,
I hope Your Excellency will evaluate my plan.
Yān and Qí are enemy states;
Qín and [Your Majesty] are allies by marriage.
To unite with an enemy state to attack a marriage relation
is something I find painful.
When Huáng Dì fought in the fields of Zhuō Lù,
the troops of the Xī Róng did not arrive;
when Yǔ attacked the Sān Miáo,
the people of the Dōng Yí
did not rise up.
To use Yān to attack Qín
was difficult even for Huáng Dì,
yet I have brought forth the armor of Yān and raised the troops of Qí.
I have also served the officials of the Sān Jìn,
such as Fèng Yáng Jūn, Mèng Cháng Jūn, Hán Mǐn,
Zhōu Zuì, Zhōu, and Hán Yú Wéi,
following them as a subordinate
for fear they might doubt the attack on Qín.
I have also personally made myself an enemy of Qín.
The one who requested that the world burn Qín's tallies
was me;
the one who next transmitted the agreement to burn the tallies
was me;
the one who wished to make the five states agree to close the passes of Qín
was me.
After Fèng Yáng Jūn and Hán Yú Wéi had reached an agreement,
and Sū Xiū and Zhū Yīng were both secretly in Hán Dān,
I then persuaded the King of Qí
and went to ruin it.
When the world negotiated peace together,
taking advantage of Sū Xiū’s traveling rhetoric,
they treated Qí as their primary ally;
when the troops requested to attack Wèi,
I fought against it to the death.
In the end, because of Sū Xiū, heavy reports came from the west.
It is not that I do not know the importance of Qín's encouragement,
but the reason I did all this
was for Your Excellency."
Wèi Wén Zǐ, Tián Xū, and Zhōu Xiāo were on good terms
and wished to frame Xī Shǒu for a crime.
Xī Shǒu was worried about this
and said to the King of Wèi:
"The current concern
is Qí.
Yīng Zǐ's words are influential with the King of Qí.
If Your Majesty wishes to win over Qí,
then why not summon Wén Zǐ and make him Prime Minister?
He will surely devote himself to serving Your Majesty through Qí."
The King said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon he summoned Wén Zǐ and made him Prime Minister.
Xī Shǒu thus distanced himself from Tián Xū and Zhōu Xiāo.
The King of Wèi ordered Huì Shī to go to Chǔ
and ordered Xī Shǒu to go to Qí.
Both men were equal
and had equal numbers of carriages,
so as to test their diplomatic relations.
When the King of Chǔ heard of it,
Shī took the opportunity to send someone ahead to Chǔ
to say:
"The King of Wèi has ordered Xī Shǒu to go to Qí
and Huì Shī to go to Chǔ.
Both men are equal
and will test their diplomatic relations."
When the King of Chǔ heard this,
he went out to the outskirts to welcome Huì Shī.
King Huì of Wèi raised the masses within his borders,
and was about to have Crown Prince Shēn attack Qí.
A guest said to the tutor of Prince Lǐ:
“Why not have the Prince weep to the King’s Grand Queen Mother
to stop the Crown Prince’s departure?
If the matter is successful, you will establish merit;
if it is not successful, he will eventually become the King.
The Crown Prince is young
and unpracticed in military affairs.
Tián Bān is a veteran general,
and Sūnzǐ is skilled in the use of troops.
Battle will surely not result in victory,
and without victory, he will surely be captured.
If the Prince contests this with the King,
and the King listens to the Prince,
the Prince will not be enfeoffed;
if he does not listen to the Prince,
the Crown Prince will surely be defeated;
once defeated,
the Prince will surely be established as heir;
once established,
he will surely become the King.”
Qí and Wèi fought at Mǎlíng;
Qí greatly defeated Wèi,
killed Crown Prince Shēn,
and destroyed an army of one hundred thousand.
The King of Wèi summoned Huì Shī and told him:
“As for Qí,
they are my enemy;
my resentment toward them is such that I will not forget it until death.
Though the state is small,
I constantly wish to raise all my troops to attack them;
what do you think?”
He replied:
“It cannot be done.
I have heard
that a true King attains measure,
and a hegemon knows strategy.
Now, what the King tells me
is sparse in measure and far from strategy.
Your Majesty previously attached resentment to Zhào,
and then fought with Qí.
Now, having fought without victory,
the state has no defenses for protection or war;
if Your Majesty again wishes to raise everyone to attack Qí,
this is not what I call strategy.
If Your Majesty wishes to take revenge on Qí,
it would be better to change your clothes, humble yourself, and pay court to Qí;
the King of Chǔ will surely be angry.
If Your Majesty sends envoys to incite them to fight,
then Chǔ will surely attack Qí.
Using a rested Chǔ to attack an exhausted Qí,
Qí will surely be captured by Chǔ.
Thus Your Majesty uses Chǔ to destroy Qí.”
The King of Wèi said:
“Good.”
He then sent someone to report to Qí,
wishing to serve as a subject and pay court.
Tián Yīng agreed.
Zhāng Chǒu said:
“It cannot be done.
If one did not defeat Wèi in battle,
yet received the rites of their court,
making peace with Wèi while humbling Chǔ,
this would be a great victory.
Now, having defeated Wèi in battle,
destroyed an army of one hundred thousand,
and captured Crown Prince Shēn;
to make a state of ten thousand chariots like Wèi a servant
while belittling Qín and Chǔ,
this will certainly reveal your arrogance.
Moreover, the King of Chǔ is a man
who loves using troops and is very concerned with reputation;
the one who will ultimately become a problem for Qí
will surely be Chǔ.”
Tián Yīng did not listen
and finally brought in the King of Wèi,
and repeatedly attended court with the Marquis of Qí.
The house of Zhào was disgusted by it.
The King of Chǔ was angry
and personally led troops to attack Qí;
Zhào responded to it,
and they greatly defeated Qí at Xúzhōu.
Huì Shī acted as an intermediary between Hán and Wèi
and had Crown Prince Míng become a hostage in Qí.
The King wished to see him.
Zhū Cāng said to the King:
“Why not claim to be ill?
I request to speak to Yīngzǐ, saying:
‘The King of Wèi is advanced in years
and is now ill;
it would be better for you to return the Crown Prince to gain the King’s gratitude.
Otherwise,
Prince Gāo is in Chǔ,
and Chǔ will bring him in and establish him;
in that case, Qí will be holding a hollow hostage while performing an unrighteous act.’”
Tián Xū was favored by the King of Wèi.
Huìzǐ said:
“You must be kind to those around you.
Now, take the willow tree:
plant it horizontally and it grows;
plant it upside down and it grows;
break it and plant it, and it still grows.
Yet if ten people plant willow trees
and one person pulls them up,
then no willow trees will survive.
Therefore, with a crowd of ten people
planting something that grows easily,
yet being unable to overcome one person,
why is this?
Because planting is difficult and removing is easy.
Now, although you plant yourself firmly with the King,
those who wish to remove you are many,
so you will surely be in danger.”
Tián Xū died.
Zhāo Yú said to Sū Dài:
“Tián Xū has died.
I fear that one among Zhāng Yí,
Xuē Gōng,
or Xīshǒu will become the Chancellor of Wèi.”
Dài said:
“Then, among those who could be Chancellor, who
would be convenient for you?”
Zhāo Yú said:
“I wish for the Crown Prince to serve as his own Chancellor.”
Dài said:
“Please let me go north for you to see the King of Liáng;
I will surely make him the Chancellor.”
Zhāo Yú said:
“How?”
Dài said:
“Assume the role of the King of Liáng,
and let me speak to you.”
Zhāo Yú said:
“How?”
He replied:
“I have come from Chǔ,
and Zhāo Yú is very worried.
I asked:
‘Why is my lord worried?’
He said:
‘Tián Xū has died,
and I fear that one among Zhāng Yí,
Xuē Gōng,
or Xīshǒu will become the Chancellor of Wèi.’
I said:
‘Do not worry.
The King of Liáng
is a wise and experienced ruler,
and will surely not appoint Zhāng Yí as Chancellor.
If Zhāng Yí is Chancellor of Wèi,
he will surely favor Qín and disadvantage Wèi.
If Xuē Gōng is Chancellor of Wèi,
he will surely favor Qí and disadvantage Wèi.
If Xīshǒu is Chancellor of Wèi,
he will surely favor Hán and disadvantage Wèi.
The King of Liáng
is a wise ruler
and will surely not employ them as Chancellor.’
I said:
‘Nothing is better than the Crown Prince serving as his own Chancellor.
These three men will all consider the Crown Prince's position as Chancellor as not being permanent,
and they will all strive to serve Wèi with their respective states’ affairs,
desiring the seal of the Prime Minister.
With the strength of Wèi,
and three states of ten thousand chariots supporting it,
Wèi will surely be secure.
Therefore I say,
nothing is better than the Crown Prince serving as his own Chancellor.’”
He then went north to see the King of Liáng
and told him these words;
the Crown Prince indeed served as his own Chancellor.
Qín summoned the Chancellor of Wèi, Lord Xìn’ān.
Lord Xìn’ān did not wish to go.
Sū Dài spoke to the King of Qín for him, saying:
“I have heard
that what is loyal is not necessarily appropriate,
and what is appropriate is not necessarily loyal.
Now, I wish to state my foolish opinion to Your Majesty;
I fear being disloyal to your subordinates
and bringing upon myself a capital offense.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this.
Now, Your Majesty has sent someone to manage affairs in Wèi
to perfect your relations with them,
but I fear that Wèi’s diplomatic relations will become increasingly suspicious.”
If this is used to block Zhào,
I also fear that Zhào will become even stronger.
Indeed, the King of Wèi's affection for and familiarity with Wèi Xìn
is extreme;
his appreciation of his wisdom and ability and his employment of him
is profound;
and his fear and loathing, yet strict respect, for Qín
is clear.
Now if Your Majesty sends someone into Wèi and they are not employed,
then Your Majesty sending someone into Wèi is of no benefit.
If they are employed,
Wèi must certainly abandon those he loves and is familiar with to employ those he fears and loathes;
this is the reason why the King of Wèi would be uneasy.
To abandon the affairs of a state of ten thousand chariots and retire,
this is something difficult for Wèi Xìn to carry out.
To cause another's ruler to dwell in unease
and to cause another's minister to perform what he cannot,
and to use this to establish a close relationship,
then it will be difficult for it to last long.
I therefore fear that the alliance with Wèi will become increasingly suspicious.
Furthermore, if Wèi Xìn abandons his duties,
then the strategists of Zhào will certainly say:
"If he is set aside for the sake of Qín,
Qín will certainly order those it loves and trusts to be employed in Zhào."
This means Zhào survives while we perish;
Zhào is secure while we are in danger.
Thus, above there will be the spirit of open battle,
and below there will be the determination for steadfast defense;
I therefore fear that Zhào will become even stronger.
"If Your Majesty wishes to perfect the alliance with Wèi
and cause Zhào to be cautious,
it would be better to employ Wèi Xìn and honor him with prestige.
If Wèi Xìn serves Your Majesty,
the state will be secure and his reputation honored;
if he leaves Your Majesty,
the state will be in danger and his power diminished.
In that case, regarding Wèi Xìn's service to his lord,
above, that which he does for his lord is loyal,
and below, that which he does for himself is substantial;
his service to Your Majesty will certainly be complete.
Those in power in Zhào will certainly say:
'The prestige of the Wèi clan is no higher than ours,
and the substance of their land is no richer than ours.
Wèi Xìn used Hán and Wèi to serve Qín,
and Qín treated him very well;
his state obtained security thereby,
and he himself attained honor thereby.
Now we are engaged in hostilities with Qín's troops and serve as targets,
the state is in a position of being carved up and endangered;
this is not a successful strategy.
Forming resentments abroad,
causing the lord anxiety within,
and placing oneself in a place of death—this is not a complete way of doing things.'
They will be pained by their former actions
and regret their past conduct;
hoping for such benefits,
they will certainly cede much land to humble themselves deeply before Your Majesty.
Then this is Your Majesty, with hands folded,
receiving ceded land as a major profit—
something that Yáo and Shùn sought but could not obtain.
I hope Your Majesty will examine this."
The Siege of Pí Shì.
Qín and
Chǔ attacked Wèi,
and besieged Pí Shì.
On behalf of Wèi, someone said to the King of Chǔ:
"If Qín and Chǔ defeat Wèi,
the King of Wèi's fear will be of imminent destruction;
he will certainly submit to Qín.
Why does Your Majesty not turn your back on Qín and ally with the King of Wèi?
The King of Wèi will be delighted
and will certainly send the Crown Prince as a hostage.
Qín will fear losing Chǔ
and will certainly offer cities and land to Your Majesty;
then Your Majesty may even join them again to attack Wèi."
The King of Chǔ said,
"Excellent."
He then turned his back on Qín and allied with Wèi.
Wèi sent the Crown Prince to Chǔ.
Qín was afraid and
promised Chǔ cities and land, wishing to join them in attacking Wèi again.
Chū Lǐ Jí was angry
and wished to join Wèi to attack Chǔ,
but he feared Wèi would be unwilling because the Crown Prince was in Chǔ.
On behalf of Jí, someone said to the King of Chǔ:
"Your humble servant Jí has sent me to report to you,
saying:
'The King of my humble state wishes to offer cities and land,
but because the Crown Prince of Wèi is still in Chǔ,
he has not yet dared to do so.
If Your Majesty releases the hostage of Wèi,
I request to offer them,
and then once again solidify the alliance between Qín and Chǔ
to swiftly attack Wèi.'"
The King of Chǔ said,
"Agreed."
He then released the Crown Prince of Wèi.
Qín thereupon joined with Wèi to attack Chǔ.
When Páng Cōng was to accompany the Crown Prince as a hostage to Hándān,
he said to the King of Wèi:
"If now one person says there is a tiger in the market,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The King said,
"No."
"If two people say there is a tiger in the market,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The King said,
"I would have my doubts."
"If three people say there is a tiger in the market,
would Your Majesty believe it?"
The King said,
"I would believe it."
Páng Cōng said:
"Indeed, it is clear there is no tiger in the market,
yet when three people say it, a tiger is created.
Now Hándān is further from Dàliáng than the market is,
and those who will criticize me are more than three people.
I hope Your Majesty will examine this."
The King said,
"I shall know for myself."
Thereupon Páng Cōng took his leave and departed,
but slanders arrived before him.
Later, when the Crown Prince finished his time as a hostage and returned,
Páng Cōng was indeed not granted an audience.
The King of Liáng, Wèi Yīng, hosted a banquet for the feudal lords at Fàn Tái.
When they were merry with wine,
he requested the Lord of Lǔ to raise his cup.
The Lord of Lǔ rose,
stepped away from his mat, and chose his words carefully, saying:
"In the past,
the Emperor's daughter ordered Yí Dí to make wine, and it was excellent;
she presented it to Yǔ.
Yǔ drank it and found it sweet,
but then he distanced himself from Yí Dí
and gave up fine wine,
saying:
'In later generations, there will surely be those who lose their states because of wine.'
Duke Huán of Qí was not satisfied in the middle of the night;
Yì Yá then fried, boiled, roasted, and grilled,
harmonizing the five flavors and presenting them.
Duke Huán ate them until he was full
and did not wake until dawn,
saying:
'In later generations, there will surely be those who lose their states because of flavors.'
Duke Wén of Jìn obtained Nán Zhī Wēi
and for three days did not attend court;
he then pushed Nán Zhī Wēi away and distanced himself from her,
saying:
'In later generations, there will surely be those who lose their states because of beauty.'
The King of Chǔ climbed Qiáng Tái and gazed upon Bēng Shān,
with the Jiāng to the left and the lake to the right;
looking down and wandering about,
his pleasure made him forget death.
He then made a vow at Qiáng Tái never to climb it again,
saying:
'In later generations, there will surely be those who, through high terraces and deep pools,
lose their states.'
Now my Lord's cup
is like the wine of Yí Dí;
my Lord's delicacies
are like the seasonings of Yì Yá;
having Bái Tái on your left and Lǘ Xū on your right
is like the beauty of Nán Wēi;
having Jiā Lín in front and Lán Tái behind
is like the pleasure of Qiáng Tái.
To have even one of these
is enough to lose a state.
Now my Lord combines all four;
can you not be cautious!"
The King of Liáng continuously praised the excellence of his words.
Qín and Zhào made a pact to attack Wèi;
the King of Wèi was troubled by this.
Máng Mǎo said:
"Your Majesty, do not worry.
I request to dispatch Zhāng Yǐ as an envoy to say to the King of Zhào:
'Regarding Yè,
I truly do not intend to possess it.
Now Your Majesty has joined with Qín to attack Wèi;
I request to offer Yè to serve Your Majesty.'"
The King of Zhào was delighted;
he summoned his Chancellor and ordered him, saying:
"The King of Wèi requests to offer Yè to serve me
so that I will break off with Qín."
The Chancellor said:
"If we join with Qín to attack Wèi,
the profit would not exceed Yè.
Now we can obtain Yè without using troops;
I request that you agree to Wèi's offer."
Zhāng Yǐ then spoke to the King of Zhào, saying:
"The officials of my humble state who are tasked with surrendering the cities
are already in Yè.
How will your Majesty repay Wèi?"
The King of Zhào then ordered the passes closed to sever relations with Qín.
Qín and Zhào became great enemies.
Máng Mǎo replied to the Zhào envoy, saying:
"The reason my humble state serves your Majesty
is to keep Yè intact.
Now, as for the surrender of Yè,
it is the envoy's fault;
I, Mǎo, knew nothing of it."
The King of Zhào feared that Wèi would yield to Qín’s anger,
so he hastily ceded five cities to align with Wèi and resist Qín.
Máng Mǎo said to the King of Qín:
"Your Majesty’s retainers
have not yet acted as mediators for you.
I have heard that an enlightened king does not wait for a mediator before acting.
What your Majesty desires from Wèi
are the lands of Chángyáng, Wángwū, and Luòlín
If your Majesty can make me the Sītú of Wèi,
then I can make Wèi present them."
The King of Qín said:
"Excellent."
He then appointed him to be the Sītú of Wèi.
Máng Mǎo said to the King of Wèi:
"What your Majesty worries about is Shàngdì.
What Qín desires from Wèi
are the lands of Chángyáng, Wángwū, and Luòlín.
If your Majesty presents them to Qín,
then Shàngdì will have no worries or troubles.
You can then request to send troops down to attack Qí in the east,
and the territory seized will surely be vast."
The King of Wèi said:
"Excellent."
He then presented them to Qín.
Several months after the land was handed over,
the Qín troops had not come down.
The King of Wèi said to Máng Mǎo:
"The land has already been handed over for several months,
and yet the Qín troops have not come down.
Why?"
Máng Mǎo said:
"I have committed a capital offense.
Even so,
if I die,
then the agreement with Qín will be broken,
and your Majesty will have no way to hold Qín accountable.
If your Majesty pardons my crime,
I will hold Qín to the agreement for your Majesty."
He then went to Qín
and said to the King of Qín:
"The reason Wèi presented the lands of Chángyáng, Wángwū,
and Luòlín
was with the intention of wanting your Majesty to send down your troops
to attack Qí in the east.
Now that the land has been handed over,
but the Qín troops cannot be sent down,
I am as good as a dead man.
Even so,
hereafter the men of Shāndōng
will have no incentive to serve your Majesty."
The King of Qín, startled, said:
"The state had matters to attend to
and had not yet had the leisure to send down the troops.
I will send the troops now."
Ten days later,
the Qín troops came down.
Máng Mǎo commanded the combined troops of Qín and Wèi
to attack Qí in the east,
opening up twenty-two counties of territory.
Qín defeated Wèi at Huà,
putting Máng Mǎo to flight and besieging Dàliáng.
Xū Jiǎ spoke for Wèi to the Ráng Hóu, saying:
"I have heard that the high officials and elders of the Wèi clan all say to the King of Wèi:
'In earlier times, when Huì Wáng attacked Zhào,
he was victorious at Sānliáng,
and an army of one hundred thousand captured Hándān;
the Zhào clan did not cede land,
and Hándān was eventually returned.
When the people of Qí attacked Yān,
they killed Zǐzhī
and crushed the old state;
Yān did not cede land,
and the state of Yān was eventually returned.
The reason Yān and Zhào remained whole and their armies strong,
and their lands were not annexed by the feudal lords,
was that they could endure hardships
and were reluctant to give up land.
Sòng and Zhōngshān were attacked several times and ceded land several times,
and subsequently perished.
I believe Yān and Zhào can be taken as models,
while Sòng and Zhōngshān should not be imitated.
Qín is a greedy and perverse state without kin;
it is encroaching upon Wèi like a silkworm,
exhausting the land of Jìn.
They were victorious over Gǎozǐ
and took eight counties;
before the land was fully handed over, the troops set out again.
What could ever satisfy Qín!
Now they have again put Máng Mǎo to flight
and entered the northern lands;
this is not only to attack Liáng,
but also to coerce the King into ceding more land;
your Majesty must not listen to them.
If your Majesty now follows Chǔ and Zhào to negotiate,
Chǔ and Zhào will be angry and compete with your Majesty to serve Qín;
Qín will surely accept them.
If Qín uses the troops of Chǔ and Zhào to attack again,
then saving the state from destruction will be impossible.
I wish your Majesty would surely not negotiate.
If your Majesty wishes to negotiate,
you must cede little and have a hostage;
otherwise, you will certainly be deceived.'
This is what I have heard from Wèi,
and I wish your Lordship would consider matters in this light.
The *Zhōushū* says:
'The Mandate is not constant.'
This means that good fortune cannot be counted upon repeatedly.
Being victorious over Gǎozǐ
and taking eight counties
was not due to the excellence of military strength
nor the skill of planning,
but was mostly heavenly luck.
Now you have again put Máng Mǎo to flight
and entered the northern lands
to attack Dàliáng;
this is taking heavenly luck as a constant.
The wise do not act so.
I have heard that the Wèi clan has mobilized the best troops of its hundred counties
to defend Dàliáng;
I believe they are no fewer than three hundred thousand.
With a multitude of three hundred thousand
to guard a wall ten *rèn* high,
I believe even if Tāng and Wǔ were born again,
it would not be easy to attack.
To lightly trust the troops of Chǔ and Zhào,
to scale a wall ten *rèn* high,
to face a multitude of three hundred thousand,
and be determined to capture it—
I believe since the world was first divided until now,
such a thing has never happened.
If you attack and cannot capture it,
the Qín troops will surely be exhausted,
Yīn will surely be lost,
and previous achievements will surely be abandoned.
Now Wèi is currently in doubt
and can be settled by ceding a small amount.
I hope that before the troops of Chǔ and Zhào are deployed at Dàliáng,
you will quickly take a small amount of ceded land and settle.
Wèi is currently in doubt,
and if they can make peace by ceding a small amount,
they will surely desire it.
Then your Lordship will obtain what you desire.
Chǔ and Zhào will be angry that Wèi preceded them in negotiating,
and they will surely compete to serve Qín.
The alliance will thus be scattered,
and your Lordship can choose among them afterward.
Furthermore, when your Lordship once carved up Jìn to take land,
why did it have to be with troops?
Without using troops,
Wèi handed over Jiàng and Ānyì,
and you also opened up two secret paths for Yīn,
exhausted the former Sòng,
and made Wèi follow the example in fear.
Once the Qín troops are under orders
and your Lordship controls them,
what request will not be granted?
What action will not succeed?
I wish your Lordship would plan maturely and not take risks."
Ráng Hóu said:
"Excellent."
He then lifted the siege of Liáng.
Qín defeated Wèi at Huà,
and the King of Wèi was about to enter the Qín court.
Zhōu Xìn said to the King:
"There was a scholar in Sòng
who returned after three years and called his mother by her name.
His mother said:
'You have studied for three years,
and yet you return and call me by my name;
why?'
The son said:
'Those whom I consider worthy
do not surpass Yáo and Shùn,
and Yáo and Shùn are called by their names."
Of the things I regard as great,
none are greater than Tiāndì,
yet Tiāndì has a name.
Now, a mother’s virtue is no greater than that of Yáo or Shùn,
and a mother’s greatness is no greater than Tiāndì;
therefore, I address my mother by name."
His mother said:
"Regarding your studies,
do you intend to practice everything you learn?
I wish for you to have a reason to change how you address your mother by name.
Regarding your studies,
will there be things you do not practice?
I wish for you to at least put addressing your mother by name last."
Now, regarding Wèi Wáng’s service to Qín,
is there still a way to change the matter of entering the court?
I wish for Wèi Wáng to have a way to change it
and put entering the court last."
Wèi Wáng said:
"Are you worried that I will enter and not come out?
Xǔ Wǎn has prayed for me, saying:
'If he enters and does not come out,
I request to sacrifice my head for the Guǎrén.'"
Zhōu Xìn replied:
"As for my humble self,
if someone said to me today,
'Enter a bottomless abyss and you will surely come out;
if you do not come out,
I ask to sacrifice a rat’s head for you,'
I would certainly not do it.
Now, Qín is an unpredictable state,
like a bottomless abyss;
and Xǔ Wǎn’s head
is like a rat’s head.
To deliver the Wáng into the unpredictable Qín,
and offer a sacrifice for the Wáng with a rat’s head,
I personally think the Wáng should not accept this."
"Furthermore, which is more urgent: losing Liáng or losing Hénèi?"
The Wáng said:
"Liáng is more urgent."
"Which is more urgent: losing Liáng or losing one’s person?"
The Wáng said:
"One’s person is more urgent."
He said:
"Among these three,
your person
is the highest;
Hénèi
is the lowest.
Qín has not yet demanded the lowest,
yet the Wáng offers the highest.
Is this acceptable?"
The Wáng still did not listen.
Zhī Qī said:
"Wáng, look at Chǔ Wáng.
When Chǔ Wáng entered Qín,
the Wáng preceded him with three chariots;
if Chǔ Wáng does not enter,
Chǔ and Wèi will become one,
which is enough to defend against Qín."
The Wáng then stopped.
The Wáng said to Zhī Qī:
"I have already given my promise to Yìng Hóu;
if I do not go now, I will be deceiving him."
Zhī Qī said:
"Wáng, do not worry.
I will have Chángxìn Hóu
request not to let the Wáng enter.
Wáng, wait for me."
Zhī Qī persuaded Chángxìn Hóu, saying:
"The Wáng has ordered to summon the Xiàngguó."
Chángxìn Hóu said:
"What does the Wáng want with me?"
Zhī Qī said:
"I do not know,
but the Wáng urgently summons you."
Chángxìn Hóu said:
"As for my bringing the Wáng into Qín,
do you think it is for the sake of Qín?
I did it for the sake of Wèi."
Zhī Qī said:
"Do not plan for the sake of Wèi;
you should plan for your own sake.
Where is death?
Where is life?
Where is poverty?
Where is nobility?
You should first plan for yourself,
and later plan for Wèi."
Chángxìn Hóu said:
"Lóu Gōng is about to enter;
I will follow now."
Zhī Qī said:
"The Wáng urgently summons you;
if you do not go,
blood will splatter your robe!"
Chángxìn Hóu went,
and Zhī Qī followed behind him.
Just before seeing the Wáng,
Zhī Qī went in first and said to the Wáng:
"Feign illness when you see him;
I have already frightened him."
Chángxìn Hóu entered to see the Wáng.
The Wáng said:
"I am very ill, what can be done?
I have already given my promise to Yìng Hóu;
even if I were to die on the way, should I go?"
Chángxìn Hóu said:
"Wáng, do not go!
I can deal with this with Yìng Hóu.
I hope the Wáng will not worry."
In the Battle of Huá Jūn,
Wèi was not victorious against Qín.
The next year,
Duàngān Chóng was going to be sent to cede land and negotiate.
Sūn Chén said to Wèi Wáng:
"Wèi did not cede land immediately after the defeat;
this can be called being good at using a loss.
But Qín did not demand land immediately after the victory;
this can be called being unable to use a victory.
Now, a year later, you wish to cede land;
this is the private interest of the ministers, and the Wáng does not realize it.
Moreover, the one who wants the seal
is Duàngān Zǐ,
and the Wáng therefore sends him to cede land;
the one who wants the land
is Qín,
and the Wáng therefore sends them to receive the seal.
The one who wants the seal controls the land,
and the one who wants the land controls the seal;
this situation will surely lead to the end of Wèi.
Furthermore, treacherous ministers all desire to serve Qín with land.
Serving Qín with land
is like carrying firewood to put out a fire.
As long as the firewood is not exhausted,
the fire will not stop.
Now the Wáng’s land has a limit,
but Qín’s demands are infinite.
This is the explanation of the firewood and the fire."
Wèi Wáng said:
"Excellent.
However,
I have already promised Qín,
and it cannot be changed."
He replied:
"Has the Wáng alone not seen how a gambler uses the owl piece?
If they want to take a piece, they take it;
if they want to hold, they hold.
Now the Wáng is coerced by the ministers into promising Qín,
and then says it cannot be changed;
why is your use of wisdom not as good as that of the owl piece?"
Wèi Wáng said:
"Excellent."
He then halted his departure.
Qí wanted to attack Wèi.
Wèi sent a messenger to speak to Chúnyú Kūn,
saying: "Qí wants to attack Wèi.
The only one who can resolve Wèi's trouble
is you, sir.
Our humble state has two pairs of precious jade discs
and four teams of patterned horses;
we wish to present these to you, sir."
Chúnyú Kūn
said: "Agreed."
He went in to persuade Qí Wáng, saying:
"Chǔ
is the mortal enemy of Qí;
Wèi
is the allied state of Qí.
To attack an allied state
and allow the enemy to take advantage of the remaining exhaustion
is to have an ugly reputation and be in actual danger;
it is something the Wáng should not do."
Qí Wáng said:
"Excellent."
He then did not attack Wèi.
A guest said to Qí Wáng:
"The reason Chúnyú Kūn said not to attack Wèi
was that he received jade discs and horses from Wèi."
The Wáng spoke to Chúnyú Kūn,
saying:
"I heard that you, sir, received jade discs and horses from Wèi.
Is this true?"
He said:
"It is so."
"If that is the case, how would the Master plan for me?"
Chúnyú Kūn
said: "The matter of attacking Wèi is not advantageous.
Even if Wèi were to disparage Kūn,
what benefit would that be to the King?
If it is truly disadvantageous,
even if Wèi were to enfeoff Kūn, what loss would that be to the King?
Furthermore, the King would not have the ill repute of attacking an allied state,
Wèi would not have the danger of facing destruction,
the common people would not have the suffering of war,
and Kūn would have the treasures of jade and horses.
How would this harm the King?"
Qín was about to attack Wèi.
The King of Wèi heard of this
and visited Mèngcháng Jūn at night,
telling him:
"Qín is about to attack Wèi.
Will you please devise a plan for me?
What should be done?"
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"If there is rescue from the feudal lords,
then the state can be preserved."
The King said:
"I wish for you to go."
He generously prepared a hundred chariots for him.
Mèngcháng Jūn went to Zhào
and said to the King of Zhào:
"Wén wishes to borrow troops to rescue Wèi."
The King of Zhào said:
"I cannot."
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"The reason I dare to borrow troops
is out of loyalty to the King."
The King said:
"May I hear the reason?"
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"The troops of Zhào
are not necessarily stronger than those of Wèi;
and the troops of Wèi
are not necessarily weaker than those of Zhào.
However, the land of Zhào is not endangered every year,
and its people do not die every year;
whereas the land of Wèi is endangered every year,
and its people die every year.
Why is this?
It is because Wèi serves as a shield for Zhào to the west.
Now, if Zhào does not rescue Wèi,
and Wèi swears a covenant with Qín,
then Zhào will share a border with the powerful Qín.
Your land will then be endangered every year,
and your people will die every year.
This is why Wén is being loyal to the Great King."
The King of Zhào agreed
and raised a hundred thousand troops
and three hundred chariots.
He then went north to see the King of Yān and said:
"Previously, Gōngzǐ Cháng arranged the alliance between the two kings.
Now Qín is about to attack Wèi,
and I wish for the Great King to rescue them."
The King of Yān said:
"I have had two years of poor harvests.
Now to travel several thousand lǐ to assist Wèi,
how can that be done?"
Tián Wén said:
"To travel several thousand lǐ to rescue others
is to the benefit of this state.
Now if the King of Wèi were to step out of his city gate and see the enemy army,
even if he then wished to travel several thousand lǐ to assist others,
could he do so?"
The King of Yān had not yet agreed.
Tián Wén said:
"I have presented an advantageous plan to the King,
but the King does not use my loyal plan.
I, Wén, request to depart.
I fear that a great change will occur in the world."
The King said:
"May I hear about this great change?"
He said:
"Qín has attacked Wèi but has not yet been able to conquer it;
however, the towers are already burned
and the pleasure grounds already seized.
If Yān does not rescue Wèi,
the King of Wèi will humble himself and cede land,
giving half of his state to Qín.
Qín will then surely depart.
Once Qín has left Wèi,
the King of Wèi will mobilize all the troops of Hán and Wèi,
borrow troops from Qín to the west,
and combine them with the masses of Zhào
to attack Yān with the forces of four states.
What benefit will the King have then?
Is it better to travel several thousand lǐ to assist others?
Or is it better to step out of the southern gate of Yān and see the enemy army?
In that case, the distance is short and transport is easy;
what benefit would the King have?"
The King of Yān said:
"You may go,
I shall listen to you."
He then raised eighty thousand troops
and two hundred chariots
to follow Tián Wén.
The King of Wèi was greatly pleased
and said:
"You have obtained troops from Yān and Zhào
in great numbers and with great speed."
The King of Qín was greatly terrified
and ceded land to request a settlement with Wèi.
Consequently, the troops of Yān and Zhào were sent back,
and Tián Wén was enfeoffed.
Wèi was about to join Qín in attacking Hán.
Zhū Jǐ said to the King of Wèi:
"Qín shares the same customs as the Róng and Dí.
It has the heart of a tiger or wolf,
is greedy, perverse, fond of profit, and untrustworthy,
and has no knowledge of ritual, righteousness, or virtuous conduct.
If there is profit to be gained,
it ignores relatives and brothers,
acting like a mere beast.
This is known by everyone in the world;
it is not a state upon which one can bestow generosity or accumulate merit.
Thus, even though the Queen Dowager was his mother,
she died in distress;
although Ráng Hóu was his uncle
and no one's achievements were greater than his,
he was eventually banished;
his two brothers were guiltless,
yet he twice stripped them of their domains.
If he treats his own relatives and brothers like this,
how much more so will he treat rival enemy states?
Now the Great King attacks Hán with Qín and moves closer to Qín;
I am very troubled by this,
yet the King does not realize it,
which shows a lack of clarity.
The ministers know this but none use it to remonstrate,
which shows a lack of loyalty.
Now the Hán clan has a single woman supporting a weak ruler;
internally there is great chaos,
so how can they outwardly withstand the powerful troops of Qín and Wèi?
Does the King believe they will not be broken?
Once Hán is destroyed,
Qín will possess all the lands of Zhèng
and be a neighbor to Dàliáng.
Does the King believe this will be safe?
The King wishes to regain his old lands,
yet now you invite the calamity of a powerful Qín;
does the King believe this is profitable?
Qín is not a state that remains idle;
after Hán is destroyed,
it will surely find a new matter to pursue.
In pursuing a new matter,
it will surely seek what is easy and profitable.
In seeking what is easy and profitable,
it will surely not attack Chǔ or Zhào.
Why is this?
To cross mountains and pass over rivers,
to cut through Hán’s Shàngdǎng to attack the powerful Zhào,
would be a repeat of the affair at Èyǔ,
which Qín surely will not do.
If it takes the route through Hénèi,
putting Yè and Cháogē at its back,
crossing the Zhāng and Fǔ rivers
to decide the battle against the Zhào army in the outskirts of Hándān,
it would suffer the calamity of Zhì Bó,
which Qín also dares not do.
To attack Chǔ,
it must travel through fords and valleys for thirty lǐ
to attack a dangerous and narrow pass.
The distance traveled would be very far,
and the target of the attack would be very difficult,
so Qín will not do that either.
If it takes the route outside the River,
putting Dàliáng at its back,
and going up through Shàngcài and Zhàolíng
to decide the battle with the Chǔ army in the outskirts of Chén,
Qín again would not dare.
Therefore I say,
Qín will surely not attack Chǔ or Zhào,
nor will it attack Wèi or Qí.
After Hán is destroyed,
on the day the troops set out,
there will be no one but Wèi to attack.
Qín originally possessed the lands of Huái and Xíngqiū,
the city of Zhī, and Guǐjīn.
By using these to overlook Hénèi,
Gòng and Jí in Hénèi will all be in danger.
If Qín possesses the territory of Zhèng,
gains Yuányōng,
breaches the dykes of Yíngzé,
and floods Dàliáng,
Dàliáng will surely perish.
Your Majesty's envoy has erred greatly;
he slandered the Ānlíng clan to Qín.
Qín has long desired to grant this request.
However, Qín’s Yèyáng
and Kūnyáng are adjacent to Wǔyáng and Gāolíng.
By listening to the envoy's slander,
they followed the Ānlíng clan’s lead and desired to destroy them.
If Qín circles north of Wǔyáng
and faces Xǔ to the east,
then the southern states will surely be in danger.
Even if the southern states are not in danger,
how could the state of Wèi find peace?
Furthermore, it is acceptable to hate Hán for not accepting the Ānlíng clan,
but it is wrong not to worry that Qín has no love for the southern states.
In former days,
Qín was situated west of the Hé river.
The distance from the state of Jìn to Liáng was
more than a thousand lǐ,
with the Hé river and mountains to block them,
and Zhōu and Hán situated in between.
From the time of the Línjūn campaign until now,
Qín has attacked Wèi ten times,
five times entering the heart of the state,
and all the border cities have been seized.
The Wéntái tower was demolished,
the capital at Chuí was burned,
the forests were cut down,
the deer were exhausted,
and the state was subsequently besieged.
Furthermore, they drove deep into the north of Liáng,
reaching east to the outskirts of Táo and Wèi,
and north as far as Kàn.
What has been lost to Qín
are Shānběi, Héwài, and Hénèi,
hundreds of large counties,
and dozens of famous cities.
When Qín was still west of the Hé river,
the distance from Jìn to Dàliáng was still a thousand lǐ,
yet the calamity was like this.
How much more so if Qín is allowed to eliminate Hán and possess the territory of Zhèng,
with no Hé river or mountains to block them,
and no Zhōu or Hán in between,
being only a hundred lǐ from Dàliáng;
