in order to restore Jǐ Sè.
In this way, the Crown Prince will instead be abandoned.”
Hán Jiù was established as the ruler, but his position was not yet secure.
His younger brother was in Zhōu,
and Zhōu wanted to send him back with a grand escort of a hundred chariots,
fearing that Hán Jiù would not be firmly established after entering Hán.
Qímǔ Huī said:
“It would be better to have him carry a hundred pieces of gold.
If Hán Jiù is established,
use it as a gift of congratulations.
If he is not established,
then say he has come to surrender a criminal.”
Shǐ Jí went to Chǔ as an envoy for Hán.
The Chǔ Wáng asked, "What method do you follow?"
He said:
"I cultivate the words of Lièzǐ Yǔkòu."
The Wáng asked:
"What is valued in them?"
He said:
"They value correctness."
The Wáng said, "Can correctness also be used to govern a state?"
He said:
"It can."
The Wáng said, "The state of Chǔ has many thieves.
Can correctness be used to ward off thieves?"
He said:
"It can."
The Wáng asked:
"How can correctness be used to ward off thieves?"
A moment later, a magpie landed on the roof.
Shǐ Jí said:
"May I ask what the people of Chǔ call this bird?"
The Wáng said, "They call it a magpie."
Shǐ Jí said:
"If I call it a crow, would that be acceptable?"
The Wáng said:
"It would not."
Shǐ Jí said:
"Now your Majesty's state has the Zhùguó, Lìngyǐn, Sīmǎ, and Diǎnling.
When you appoint officials and establish officers,
you must say they are incorruptible, pure, and capable.
Now thieves and robbers operate openly,
and you cannot stop them.
This means the crow is not acting as a crow,
and the magpie is not acting as a magpie."
Hán Kuí served as the Xiàng of Hán.
Yán Suì was highly regarded by the ruler,
and the two men were at odds with each other.
Yán Suì's political advice was direct,
pointing out Hán Kuí's faults.
Hán Kuí used this to berate him in the court.
Yán Suì drew his sword and rushed toward him,
but was stopped by others.
Thereupon Yán Suì feared execution,
fled,
and traveled seeking someone who could take revenge on Hán Kuí.
He arrived in Qí.
Someone in Qí said:
"Niè Zhèng of Shēnjǐng Village in Zhǐ
is a brave man.
He is avoiding a feud and hiding among the butchers."
Yán Suì secretly associated with Niè Zhèng,
treating him with great generosity to show his intent.
Niè Zhèng asked:
"Where do you wish to use me?"
Yán Suì said, "The time I have been served by you is short,
and my service to you is currently meager.
How would I dare to ask anything of you?"
Thereupon Yán Suì prepared wine
and offered a toast before Niè Zhèng’s mother.
Yán Zhòngzǐ presented one hundred yì of gold,
stepping forward to offer it for the longevity of Niè Zhèng’s mother.
Niè Zhèng was startled
and found this generosity even more extraordinary.
He firmly declined Yán Zhòngzǐ.
Yán Zhòngzǐ insisted,
but Niè Zhèng declined, saying:
"I have an elderly mother,
and my family is poor.
I am a traveler living as a dog butcher
so that I may obtain sweet and delicate food morning and evening to nourish my parent.
Since my parent's provisions are sufficient,
in righteousness, I do not dare to accept Zhòngzǐ's gift."
Yán Zhòngzǐ cleared the room
and then spoke to Niè Zhèng, saying:
"I have an enemy
and have traveled among many feudal lords.
However, when I arrived in Qí,
I heard your righteousness is very high.
Therefore I directly offered a hundred pieces of gold
only to serve as the cost of coarse food for the lady
and to secure your friendship;
how could I dare have any request of you?"
Niè Zhèng said:
"The reason I have lowered my ambitions and debased my person
to live in the marketplace
is solely for the hope of nourishing my elderly mother.
While my mother lives,
I do not dare to pledge my life to anyone."
Yán Zhòngzǐ insisted,
but Niè Zhèng ultimately would not accept.
Nevertheless, Zhòngzǐ completed the etiquette of guest and host and departed.
After a long time,
Niè Zhèng's mother died.
Once she was buried
and the mourning period was over,
Niè Zhèng said:
"Alas!
I am but a man of the marketplace,
brandishing a knife to butcher,
yet Yán Zhòngzǐ is a Qīngxiàng of the feudal lords.
He did not consider a thousand lǐ too far
and turned his carriage and horses to associate with me.
My treatment of him was extremely meager,
and I have no great merit worth mentioning,
yet Yán Zhòngzǐ offered a hundred pieces of gold for my mother's longevity.
Even though I did not accept it,
it showed he deeply understood me.
A worthy man, out of a sense of resentment over a slight,
places his trust in an impoverished and obscure person.
How could I alone remain silent and do nothing?
Moreover, when he asked me before,
I only refused because of my elderly mother.
Now that my mother has finished her natural years,
I shall be used by the one who knows me."
He then went west to Púyáng,
saw Yán Zhòngzǐ, and said:
"The reason I did not grant your request before
was solely because my parent was alive.
Now that my parent has unfortunately passed away,
who is the enemy whom Yán Zhòngzǐ wishes to take revenge upon?"
Yán Zhòngzǐ told him everything, saying:
"My enemy is the Hán Xiàng, Hán Kuí.
Kuí is also the uncle of the Hán Jūn.
His clan is powerful
and his armed guards are numerous.
I sent people to assassinate him,
but in the end, none could succeed.
Now that you fortunately do not reject me,
I ask to provide more carriages, horses, and brave warriors
to serve as your support."
Niè Zhèng said, "Hán and Wèi
are not far from each other.
To kill a state's Xiàng now,
especially since the Xiàng is a relative of the ruler,
is a situation that does not allow for many people.
If there are many people, there will surely be mistakes.
If there are mistakes, words will leak.
If words leak,
then the entire state of Hán will become Zhòngzǐ's enemy.
Would that not be perilous?"
He then declined the carriages, horses, and followers,
took his leave,
and traveled alone with his sword to Hán.
Hán happened to be holding the assembly of Dōngmèng.
The Hán Wáng and the Xiàng were both there.
Those guarding with spears and halberds were very numerous.
Niè Zhèng went straight in,
went up the steps and stabbed Hán Kuí. Hán Kuí ran and embraced Āihóu.
Niè Zhèng stabbed him,
also hitting Āihóu.
The attendants fell into great chaos.
Niè Zhèng gave a great shout,
and those he killed numbered in the dozens.
Then he flayed his own face and gouged out his eyes,
disemboweled himself and let his intestines fall out,
and thus died.
The Hán authorities took Niè Zhèng's corpse to the market
and offered a reward of a thousand pieces of gold for identification.
For a long time, no one knew whose son he was.
Niè Zhèng's sister heard of this
and said:
"My brother was extremely worthy; I cannot cherish my own person
and thus cause my brother's name to be extinguished.
This was not my brother's intent."
She then went to Hán.
She looked at him and said:
"How brave!
How great was his spirit and pride.
In this, he surpassed Bèn and Yù and was superior to Chéng Jīng.
Now he has died without a name.
Our parents have already passed away
and he has no brothers;
this was done for my sake.
To cherish my own life and not spread my brother's fame—
I cannot bear it."
She then embraced the corpse and wailed for him, saying:
"This was my brother,
Niè Zhèng of Shēnjǐng Village in Zhǐ!"
She then also killed herself beside the corpse.
When Jìn, Chǔ, Qí, and Wèi heard of this, they said:
"It was not only Niè Zhèng who was capable;
even his sister
was a heroic woman."
The reason Niè Zhèng's name was passed down to later generations
was that his sister did not avoid the punishment of being minced into meat
in order to spread his name.
Someone said to Hán Gōngzhòng:
"As for twin children who look alike,
only their mother can recognize them;
as for interests and harms that look alike,
only the wise can recognize them.
Now you govern the state;
the similarity of its interests and harms
is just like the similarity of twin children.
If you are able to handle it through the correct way,
then the ruler will be honored and your person will be safe;
if you do not follow the correct way,
then the ruler will be debased and your person will be in danger.
Now if peace between Qín and Wèi is achieved,
and if you do not personally manage it,
then Hán will certainly be plotted against.
If Hán follows Wèi to befriend Qín,
this is acting as a follower of Wèi;
then Hán will be lightly regarded and the ruler
will be debased.
Once Qín is on good terms with Hán,
it will certainly want to install those whom it loves and trusts,
ordering them to manage affairs in Hán to control it;
this means you will be in danger.
Now you and Ānchéng Jūn are making peace for Qín and Wèi;
success will certainly be a blessing,
and failure will also be a blessing.
If the peace between Qín and Wèi is achieved,
and you personally manage it,
then Hán will be the gateway for Qín and Wèi;
this means Hán will be important and the ruler will be honored.
Ānchéng Jūn will be important to the east in Wèi,
and noble to the west in Qín,
holding the right half of the tally to demand gratitude for you from the rulers of Qín and Wèi;
carving out land to become a feudal lord is within your reach.
As for stabilizing Hán and Wèi and serving as Chancellor for life,
these are but the least of your accomplishments;
this means the ruler is honored and your person is safe.
Qín and Wèi are not those who will always listen to each other.
Qí will be angry at not obtaining Wèi,
and will certainly want to befriend Hán to block Wèi;
Wèi will not listen to Qín,
and will certainly strive to befriend Hán to prepare against Qín—this is for you to choose the cloth and cut it as you please.
If Qín and Wèi are at peace,
then both countries will be grateful to you;
if they are not at peace,
then both countries will compete to serve you.
This is what is meant by success being a blessing,
and failure also being a blessing.
I hope you have no doubts."
Someone said to Gōngzhòng:
"Now there is a move that can be loyal to the ruler,
convenient for the state,
and beneficial for your person;
I hope you will carry it out.
Today, if the world is scattered and serves Qín,
then Hán will be the most lightly regarded;
if the world is united and remains apart from Qín,
then Hán will be the weakest;
if uniting and parting alternate,
then Hán will be the first to be in danger.
This is the great concern for one who governs a state and leads the people.
Now if you lead Hán to be the first to unite with Qín,
and the world follows,
then Hán is using the world to serve Qín,
and Qín's gratitude toward Hán will be profound.
If Hán and the world pay court to Qín,
and you alone receive profound gratitude,
this plan of yours
is truly loyal to the ruler.
If the world does not unite with Qín,
and they do not listen to Qín's orders,
Qín will certainly raise troops to punish those who do not submit.
If Qín for a long time harbors resentment and creates difficulties with the world,
and the war remains undecided,
Hán can rest its soldiers and people to wait for an opportunity;
this plan of yours
is for the state
greatly convenient.
Formerly,
Zhōu Jiǎo used Xī Zhōu to befriend Qín,
and was enfeoffed in Gěngyáng;
Zhōu Qǐ used Dōng Zhōu to befriend Qín,
and was enfeoffed in Píngyuán.
Now you use Hán to befriend Qín;
Hán's importance compared to the two Zhōu states is beyond measure,
and Qín's competitive opportunity
is ten thousand times that of the Zhōu period.
Now if you lead Hán to be the first in the world to unite with Qín,
Qín will certainly make you a feudal lord,
to clearly show it to the world;
this plan of yours
is of great benefit to your person.
I hope you will apply yourself to this."
The people of Hán attacked Sòng;
the King of Qín was greatly enraged and said:
"I love Sòng
as much as Xīnchéng and Yángjìn.
Hán Mín has relations with me,
yet he attacks what I love so much;
why is this?"
Sū Qín spoke to the King of Qín on behalf of Hán:
"Hán Mín's attack on Sòng
is for your sake.
With the strength of Hán,
supplemented by Sòng,
Chǔ and Wèi will certainly be afraid.
When they are afraid,
they will certainly face west to serve Qín.
You will not break a single weapon,
nor kill a single person,
and without effort will receive Ānyì;
this is why Hán Mín prays for Qín."
The King of Qín said:
"I have always been troubled that Hán is difficult to understand;
one moment for the Vertical Alliance, the next for the Horizontal Alliance;
what is the explanation for this?"
The reply was: "The world has made Hán naturally understandable.
Hán has already attacked Sòng;
if it faces west to serve Qín,
it will use the power of ten thousand chariots to support itself;
if it does not face west to serve Qín,
then its lands in Sòng will not be secure.
The white-haired traveling scholars within the central states
all pool their wisdom wanting to break the friendship between Qín and Hán.
Of those who lean on their carriage railings and tie their reins to gallop west,
there is not one person who speaks well of Hán;
of those who lean on their carriage railings and tie their reins to gallop east,
there is not one person who speaks well of Qín.
Why do they all not want Hán
and Qín to unite?
It is because Jìn
and Chǔ are wise while Hán and Qín are foolish.
If Jìn and Chǔ unite,
they will certainly watch Hán and Qín;
if Hán and Qín unite,
they will certainly plot against Jìn and Chǔ.
I ask you to decide the matter based on this."
The King of Qín said: "Good."
Someone said to the King of Hán:
"The King of Qín wants to go out and take action against Liáng,
and wants to attack Jiàng and Ānyì;
what plan will Hán come up with?
Qín's desire to attack Hán
in order to look east at the Zhōu royal house,
is so intense that he forgets it only in sleep.
Now if Hán does not perceive this,
and consequently wants to join with Qín,
it will certainly lead to great disaster for the regions east of the mountains.
Qín's desire to attack Liáng
is because it wants to obtain Liáng to overlook Hán;
fearing that Liáng will not listen,
it therefore wants to weaken it to solidify their relations.
If the King does not perceive this,
and consequently wants to remain neutral,
Liáng will certainly be angry at Hán for not siding with it,
and will certainly turn to be used by Qín,
then Hán will certainly be taken.
I hope the King considers this maturely.
It would be better to urgently send high-ranking envoys to Zhào and Liáng,
to agree to be brothers again,
and make all those east of the mountains use their elite troops to guard the western borders of Hán and Liáng;
if not for this,
those east of the mountains will have no way to save themselves from destruction;
this is a plan for ten thousand generations.
Qín's desire to annex the world and rule as king
is not the same as in ancient times.
Even if you serve them like a son serving a father,
they will still destroy you.
Even if your conduct is like that of Bó Yí,
they will still destroy you.
Even if your conduct is like that of Jié or Zhòu,
they will still destroy you.
Even if you serve them well, it is of no benefit.
It cannot be used for survival;
it is only enough to make your own destruction come quickly.
Therefore, unless those east of the mountains can follow the Vertical Alliance,
uniting and remaining firm as one,
they will all certainly perish."
Someone said to Zhèng Wáng:
"Zhāolí Hóu
was a brilliant ruler of his generation;
Shēn Bùhài
was a worthy scholar of his generation.
Hán and Wèi were states of equal power,
yet Shēn Bùhài and Zhāolí Hóu held jade tablets and had an audience with the ruler of Liáng;
this was not because they loved being humble and hated being honored,
nor because their considerations were wrong and their deliberations were flawed.
As for Shēn Bùhài's planning of affairs..."
It said:
"If I hold the jade tablet in Wèi,
the Ruler of Wèi will certainly achieve his ambition regarding Hán,
and will surely expend his strength externally against the world.
This will cause Wèi to be exhausted.
When the feudal lords detest Wèi, they will certainly serve Hán.
In this way, I will avoid being beneath one man
and establish my trustworthiness above ten thousand people.
To weaken the armies of Wèi
and increase the power of Hán,
there is nothing better than paying court to Wèi."
Zhāolí Hóu listened to and followed this;
he was an enlightened ruler.
Shēn Bùhài deliberated on the matter and spoke of it;
he was a loyal minister.
Now Hán is weaker than the Hán of the beginning,
and now Qín is stronger than the Qín of the beginning.
Now Qín has the heart of the Ruler of Liáng,
yet Your Majesty and your ministers do not act to honor Qín in order to stabilize Hán.
I privately consider Your Majesty’s enlightenment to be inferior to that of Zhāolí Hóu,
and among Your Majesty’s ministers, none is as loyal as Shēn Bùhài.
"In the past,
Mù Gōng achieved a single victory at Hányuán and became the hegemon of Xīzhōu.
Jìn Wén Gōng achieved a single victory at Chéngpú and stabilized the world.
This is using a single victory to establish an honored command
and achieve success and fame throughout the world.
Now Qín has been strong for several generations;
its great victories are numbered in the thousands,
and its small victories are numbered in the hundreds.
In great matters, it has not become King;
in small matters, it has not become Hegemon.
Its name and honor have nowhere to be established,
and its laws and orders have nowhere to be implemented.
However, those who used troops during the Chūnqiū period
did not do so only to seek the honor of their ruler and achieve fame in the world.
In the past, the attacks of the former kings
had those aimed at fame
and those aimed at reality.
Those aimed at fame attacked the heart;
those aimed at reality attacked the form.
Formerly,
when Wú fought with Yuè,
the people of Yuè suffered a great defeat
and took refuge atop Kuàijī.
The people of Wú entered Yuè and pacified the households.
The King of Yuè sent Dàfū Zhòng to negotiate peace with Wú,
requesting that the men serve as subjects,
the women as concubines,
and the King himself carry birds and follow the attendants.
The people of Wú indeed listened to his words
and made peace without a covenant.
This is what is meant by attacking the heart.
Later, when Yuè fought with Wú,
the people of Wú suffered a great defeat.
They also requested that the men serve as subjects
and the women as concubines,
returning to serve Yuè with the same rituals Yuè had used to serve Wú.
The people of Yuè did not listen
and subsequently destroyed the state of Wú and captured Fūchā.
This is what is meant by attacking the form.
Now, if one intends to attack the heart,
one should act like Wú;
if one intends to attack the form,
one should act like Yuè.
Now, attacking the form is not as effective as Yuè,
and attacking the heart is not as effective as Wú,
yet the ruler and ministers,
superiors and inferiors,
young and old, noble and low
all call themselves Hegemons and Kings.
I privately consider this to be like being in a well and saying:
'I shall seek fire for you.'
"At the meeting of Dōngmèng,
Niè Zhèng and Yáng Jiān assassinated the Chancellor and the Ruler together.
Xǔ Yì kicked Āi Hóu and killed him,
and set him up as the ruler of Zhèng.
Among the masses of the Hán clan, none did not follow his orders,
because Xǔ Yì took the lead.
Therefore, Āi Hóu became the ruler,
and Xǔ Yì served as his Chancellor for the rest of his life.
The Hán clan's honoring of Xǔ Yì
was like their honoring of Āi Hóu.
Today, the position of the ruler of Zhèng cannot be attained;
even if one were to serve as Chancellor for life,
to say 'I will not do it'
would surely be a faulty plan!
Formerly, Qí Huán Gōng assembled the feudal lords nine times,
and he never failed to do so under the command of Zhōu Xiāng Wáng.
Thus, although he honored Xiāng Wáng,
Huán Gōng also established his hegemony.
The honoring of Huán Gōng during the nine assemblies
was like the honoring of Xiāng Wáng.
Today, the position of the Son of Heaven cannot be attained;
to say 'even to be like Huán Gōng, I will not do it'
would surely be a faulty plan and a failure to understand honor!
The warriors of the Hán clan number in the hundreds of thousands;
they all support Āi Hóu as their ruler,
yet Xǔ Yì alone took the position of Chancellor.
There was no other reason.
Among the rulers of the feudal lords,
none did not serve in the Zhōu house,
yet Huán Gōng alone took the title of Hegemon.
There was also no other reason.
Now a strong state is about to have the opportunity for imperial kingship,
and the one who takes the lead with their state
is of the same kind as Huán Gōng and Xǔ Yì.
How could this not be called a good plan?
If one is the first to offer benefits to a strong state,
and the strong state is able to become the King,
then I will certainly become its Hegemon.
If the strong state cannot become the King,
then I can avoid its military
and ensure they do not attack me.
Thus, if the strong state's cause succeeds,
I establish an Emperor and become a Hegemon;
if the strong state's cause does not succeed,
they will still be deeply grateful to me.
Now, by aligning with a strong state,
if the strong state's cause succeeds, there is fortune;
if it does not succeed, there is no trouble.
Therefore, being the first to align with a strong state
is the strategy of a sage."
Hán Yáng was serving in Sānchuān and wished to return home.
Zú Qiáng spoke on his behalf to the King of Hán, saying:
"Sānchuān has submitted;
does Your Majesty know this?
The service there should be shared with the noble young lords."
The King then summoned the various young lords serving in Sānchuān and allowed them to return.
Qín
is a large state.
Hán
is a small state.
Hán is very distant from Qín.
Yet to be seen as close to Qín,
in planning for this,
there is nothing better than gold;
therefore, a beauty was sold.
The price of the beauty was high,
and the feudal lords could not buy her;
therefore, Qín bought her for three thousand pieces of gold.
Hán then used that gold to serve Qín,
so Qín in turn received its gold back and Hán's beauty.
Hán’s beauty then said to Qín: "Hán is very distant from Qín."
Viewing it from this,
Hán lost both the beauty and the gold,
and its distance from Qín became even more apparent.
Therefore, a guest persuaded Hán, saying:
"It would be better to stop excessive spending
and use that as gold to serve Qín.
This gold will certainly be effective,
and Hán’s distance from Qín will not be made apparent.
Beauties are those who know of internal conduct;
therefore, those who are good at planning
do not reveal internal conduct."
When Zhāng Chǒu arranged for Qí
and Chǔ to negotiate peace with Wèi,
he said to Gōngzhòng of Hán:
"Now, if you vigorously attack the transport routes of Wèi,
and Wèi is pressed,
it will certainly offer land to make peace with Qí
and Chǔ; therefore, it would be better for you not to attack.
If Wèi is given respite, it will certainly fight.
If they win the battle,
it will be easy to attack and take the transport routes.
If they do not win the battle,
then Wèi will offer submission to you."
Gōngzhòng said:
"Agreed."
Zhāng Chǒu then said to Qí
and Chǔ:
"Hán has already aligned with Wèi.
If you think this is not so,
then just observe Gōngzhòng’s attack."
Gōngzhòng did not attack,
so Qí and Chǔ were afraid
and subsequently negotiated peace with Wèi
without informing Hán.
Someone said to the Chancellor of Hán:
"The reason people treat Biǎn Què well
is because they have swellings and tumors;
if they treated Biǎn Què well and had no swellings or tumors,
then no one would do it.
Now, the reason Your Excellency uses your service to befriend Píngyuán Jūn
is because of the ill will from Qín;
but befriending Píngyuán Jūn is precisely what causes the ill will from Qín.
I wish Your Excellency would consider this carefully."
Gōngzhòng sent Hán Mín to Qín to seek Wǔsuì,
yet he feared the anger of Chǔ.
Táng Kè said to Gōngzhòng:
“As for Hán’s service to Qín
and its pursuit of Wǔsuì,
it is not something my humble state hates.
Once Hán has obtained Wǔsuì,
its situation can then be used to be on good terms with Chǔ.
I wish to have a word,
yet I do not dare to make plans for Chǔ.
Currently, among the fathers and brothers of Hán, those who have the support of the masses are not ministers;
Hán cannot stand independent,
and its momentum will inevitably lead it to not be on good terms with Chǔ.
The King says:
‘I wish to use the state to support Hán Mín and make him a minister, is that possible?
The fathers and brothers hate Mín,
so Mín will certainly protect Chǔ with his state.’”
Gōngzhòng was pleased
and recommended Táng Kè to the various lords,
and made him the primary person in charge of Hán and Chǔ affairs.
The Hán chancellors Gōngzhòng and Mín sent Hán Chǐ to Qín
to request an attack on Wèi,
and the King of Qín was pleased.
While Hán Chǐ was in Táng,
Gōngzhòng and Mín died.
Hán Chǐ said to the King of Qín:
“The envoy of Wèi said to the succeeding chancellor Hán Chén:
‘You must certainly punish Hán Chǐ on behalf of Wèi.’
Hán Chén said:
‘It cannot be done.
The King of Qín gave him an office,
and further made agreements with him.’
The envoy said:
‘As for Qín giving Hán Chǐ an office,
it was because they valued Gōngzhòng.
Now that Gōngzhòng is dead,
if Hán Chǐ goes to Qín,
Qín will certainly not admit him.
Even if he enters,
why would they support him to harbor a grudge against the King of Wèi?’
Hán Chén is worried about this
and is about to listen to him. Now, if Your Majesty does not summon Hán Chǐ,
Hán Chǐ will have to go into hiding in the mountains.”
The King of Qín said: “How could I have imagined my authority to be like this!
Where should he hide?”
He summoned Hán Chǐ and gave him an office.
A guest official, on behalf of Hán, said to the King of Qín:
“The proposals of Hán Mín
know their own ruler but not other rulers,
and know their own state but not other states.
That Gōngzhòng,
Qín’s power was able to make him submit.
As for Qín’s strength,
the one who spearheaded it,
Mín considered an affliction.
Bringing the troops of Qí and Sòng to Shǒutǎn,
and from afar pressing against the outer walls of Liáng,
the reason they did not reach Wèi
was that they thought peace was made and they passed through the road of Nányáng,
wishing to use the four states to head west.
The reason this was not so
was that everyone said it was because Yān was destroyed by Qí,
Wèi was destroyed by Qín,
and Chén and Cài were destroyed by Chǔ;
these were all cases of being cut off by the terrain,
and the various ministers colluded to obscure their superiors,
with great ministers acting for the feudal lords and taking their own state lightly.
Now Your Majesty’s position is correct;
Zhāng Yí’s nobility
cannot deliberate about Gōngsūn Hǎo,
which means the subordinate officials do not serve the great ministers;
Gōngsūn Hǎo’s nobility
cannot deliberate about Gān Wù,
then the great ministers cannot serve the close officials.
When high and low do not serve each other,
each holds their proper place,
converging like spokes to serve their superior,
then whether the various ministers are worthy or unworthy
can be known.
This is the first aspect of Your Majesty’s brilliance.
Gōngsūn Hǎo once detested Qí and Hán but was not given further nobility,
then the great ministers do not dare to take the state lightly for the feudal lords.
Qí and Hán once tried to use Gōngsūn Hǎo but were not accepted,
then the feudal lords do not dare to rely on the various ministers to show their influence.
When external and internal do not act for each other,
then the sincerity or falseness of the feudal lords can be known.
This is the second aspect of Your Majesty’s brilliance.
Gōngsūn Hǎo and Chūlǐ Jí requested not to attack Hán,
and Chén Sì went away,
yet Your Majesty still attacked it.
Gān Mào made agreements with Chǔ and Zhào but returned to show respect to Wèi;
this was their negotiation with us,
and while Mào was about to attack Yíyáng,
Your Majesty still contended with it.
The wisdom of the various ministers
is not much compared to Your Majesty’s brilliance.
I therefore wish for Gōngzhòng’s state to wait upon Your Majesty,
and not act of its own accord through those around you.”
Hán Mín was chancellor in Qí
and ordered an official to expel Gōngchóu Shù,
and was greatly angered at Zhōu for retaining Chéngyáng Jūn.
Someone said to Hán Mín:
“If you consider these two men to be worthy men,
and the states they enter
then employ them,
then it would be better for them to stay in small states.
Why is that?
Chéngyáng Jūn left Hán for Qín,
and as for Gōngchóu Shù,
the King of Chǔ was friendly with him.
Now if you expel them,
these two will certainly enter Qín and Chǔ,
and will certainly become a disaster for you.
Moreover, it will make it clear to the world that you are not good.
Those in the world who are not on good terms with you,
and those who wish to seek something from Qí,
will take them in
to use them against Qí and to bargain with you.”
Someone said to Shānyáng Jūn:
“Qín enfeoffed you with Shānyáng,
and Qí enfeoffed you with Jǔ.
Either Qí and Qín value Hán, or they value your conduct.
Now Chǔ has attacked Qí and taken Jǔ,
at best it does not associate with Qí,
and at second best it does not admit you;
this is to provoke the might of Qí and Qín and to slight Hán.”
Shānyáng Jūn then sent him to Chǔ.
Zhào and Wèi attacked Huáyáng,
and Hán requested emergency aid from Qín.
Envoys followed one after another,
but Qín did not provide rescue.
The Chancellor of Hán said to Tián Líng:
“The matter is urgent.
I wish that even though you are ill,
you would make a journey of one night.”
Tián Líng saw Ràng Hóu,
and Ràng Hóu said:
“Is Hán in an emergency?
Why did they send you?”
Tián Líng replied: “It is not yet an emergency.”
Ràng Hóu said angrily: “How can you be the envoy of your king?
Envoys followed one after another,
telling my humble state it was very urgent,
yet you say it is not yet an emergency.
Why?”
Tián Líng said:
“If Hán were in an emergency, then it would change its alliances.”
Ràng Hóu said:
“You need not see the King.
I shall request the dispatch of troops to rescue Hán.”
Within eight days,
they greatly defeated Zhào and Wèi below Huáyáng.
Qín recruited Chǔ to attack Qí.
Xiè Xiàng said to Chén Zhěn:
“The King of Qín will certainly look outward.
Those from Chǔ who are in Qí know that in the west they do not align with Qín,
and will surely strive to align Chǔ with Qí.
If Qí and Chǔ align,
Yān and Zhào will not dare not to follow.
If Qí uses four states to oppose Qín,
then Qí will not be in dire straits.”
Xiè Xiàng said:
“Does the King of Qín truly wish to attack Qí?
It would be better first to win over those from Chǔ who are in Qí;
if those from Chǔ who are in Qí first strive to align Chǔ with Qí,
then Chǔ will certainly go to Qín.
With a strong Qín having Jìn and Chǔ,
then Yān and Zhào will not dare not to follow,
and thus Qí will be isolated.
I request to speak to the King of Qín for you.”
The Hán clan expelled Xiàng Jìn to Zhōu.
Chéng Huī of Zhōu said to the King of Wèi on his behalf:
“Zhōu will surely be lenient and return him.
Why does Your Majesty not speak for him first?
Then Your Majesty will have the credit for Xiàng Jìn being in Zhōu.”
The King of Wèi said: “Very well.”
Chéng Huī then said to the King of Hán:
“The one who expelled Xiàng Jìn was Hán,
but the one who returned him was Wèi.
Would it not be better if Hán itself returned him!
Otherwise, Wèi will have the credit for Xiàng Jìn being in Zhōu,
while the King of Hán will have lost it.”
The King of Hán said: “Good.”
He also requested to restore him.
Zhāng Dēng spoke on behalf of Fèi Xiè:
“Please let Gōngzǐ Nián say to the King of Hán:
‘As for Fèi Xiè,
Western Zhōu considers him an enemy,
but Eastern Zhōu treasures him.
This man's family has ten thousand pieces of gold...’”
Why does the Wáng not summon him
to be the Yùshǐ of Sānchuān?
This will cause Xiè to use Sānchuān to be on guard against Xī Zhōu;
he will surely exhaust his household's resources to serve the Wáng.
Xī Zhōu will loathe this
and will surely offer the vessels of the former kings to stop the Wáng.
The Hán Wáng will certainly do this.
When Xī Zhōu hears of this,
they will surely absolve you of your crime
in order to stop your mission.
The Yùshǐ of Ānyì died,
and his deputy feared he would not obtain the position.
A person of Shū acted on his behalf and said to the Ān Lìng:
"Gōngsūn Qí is requesting the position of Yùshǐ from the Wáng for someone else.
The Wáng said:
'Does that man have a deputy?
It is difficult for me to violate the law.' "
Therefore, the deputy was immediately appointed.
The Wèi Wáng organized the Covenant of Jiǔlǐ
and intended to restore the Tiānzǐ.
Fáng Xǐ said to the Hán Wáng:
"Do not listen to him.
Great states loathe having a Tiānzǐ,
while small states find it advantageous.
If the Wáng and the great states do not listen,
how can Wèi establish him with only the small states?"
Jiànxìn Jūn slighted Hán Xī.
Zhào Áo spoke on his behalf to the Jiànxìn Hóu, saying:
"Regarding the geopolitical situation, the state that exists because it has Hán and would perish without it is Wèi.
The state that cannot be without an alliance is Hán.
The reason you slight Hán Xī now
is that your relations are good with Chǔ and Wèi.
When Qín sees that your relations have instead become good with Chǔ and Wèi,
its efforts to win over Hán will surely be increased.
If Hán joins the Zòng alliance, it is slighted;
if it joins the Héng alliance, it is treated with importance;
thus, it will not join an alliance where it is slighted.
If Qín sends troops to Sānchuān,
it will besiege Yān in the south,
and the roads of Cài and Shào will be cut off.
When Wèi is in urgent trouble,
its rescue of Zhào will surely be delayed.
If Qín raises troops and breaks Hándān,
Zhào will surely perish.
Therefore, if you win over Hán,
you can avoid conflict."
Duàn Chǎn said to the Xīnchéng Jūn:
"One who travels at night can avoid committing a crime,
but cannot stop dogs from barking at him.
Now, as I serve among the Lángzhōng,
I can refrain from criticizing you to the Wáng,
but I cannot stop others from criticizing me to you.
I hope the Jūn will consider this."
Duàngān Yuèrén said to the Xīnchéng Jūn:
"A disciple of Wáng Liáng was driving a carriage
and said he had obtained a thousand-li horse.
He met a disciple of Zào Fù.
The disciple of Zào Fù said:
'The horse cannot travel a thousand li.'
Wáng Liáng's disciple said:
'The horse is a thousand-li horse,
and the equipment
is thousand-li equipment.
Why then can it not travel a thousand li?'
The other replied:
'Your lead-rope is too long.
Although a lead-rope is only
one ten-thousandth of the equipment,
it can hinder a journey of a thousand li.'
Now, although I am unworthy,
I am also like one ten-thousandth part of Qín.
Yet the Xiàngguó sees me
and will not let me through the pass;
this is because my lead-rope is too long."
Sū Qín was about to form the Zòng alliance,
and went north to persuade the Yān Wén Hóu, saying:
"Yān has Cháoxiǎn and Liáodōng to the east,
Línhú and Lóufán to the north,
Yúnzhōng and Jiǔyuán to the west,
and the Hūtúo and Yì Shuǐ to the south.
The territory is over two thousand li square,
with hundreds of thousands of armored soldiers,
seven hundred chariots,
six thousand cavalry horses,
and grain to last ten years.
In the south, there is the abundance of Jiéshí and Yànmén;
in the north, the benefit of dates and chestnuts.
Even if the people do not labor in the fields,
the harvest of dates and chestnuts
is enough to feed the people.
This is what is called a Tiānfǔ.
For peacefulness and lack of trouble,
without the worry of armies being destroyed or generals being killed,
no state surpasses Yān.
Does the Wáng know why this is so?
The reason Yān is not invaded by bandits or subjected to war
is because Zhào serves as its shield to the south.
Qín and Zhào have fought five times;
Qín won twice and Zhào won three times.
Qín and Zhào exhaust each other,
while the Wáng uses a whole Yān to control their rear;
this is why Yān does not face difficulties.
Furthermore, for Qín to attack Yān,
it must cross Yúnzhōng and Jiǔyuán,
pass through Dài and Shànggǔ,
covering thousands of li of territory and roads.
Even if they captured a city in Yān,
Qín's strategy certainly could not hold it.
It is clear then that Qín cannot harm Yān.
Now, if Zhào were to attack Yān,
they would issue the orders,
and in less than ten days,
a force of hundreds of thousands
would be stationed at Dōngyuán.
They would cross the Hūtúo
and wade across the Yì Shuǐ;
in less than four or five days,
they would reach the capital.
Therefore, it is said:
when Qín attacks Yān,
the battle is fought more than a thousand li away;
when Zhào attacks Yān,
the battle is fought within a hundred li.
To not worry about a threat within a hundred li
while taking a threat from a thousand li away seriously—
no strategy is more erroneous than this.
For this reason, I hope the Wáng will form a Zòng alliance with Zhào
so the world becomes one;
then the state will surely be without trouble."
The Yān Wáng said: "My state is small,
pressed by powerful Qín to the west
and near Qí and Zhào to the south.
Qí and Zhào
are powerful states.
Now that you have fortunately come to instruct me
to join the Zòng alliance to secure Yān,
I respectfully offer my state to follow you."
Thereupon, he provided Sū Qín with carriages, horses, gold, and silk to go to Zhào.
Fèngyáng Jūn Lǐ Duì greatly disapproved of Sū Qín.
While Sū Qín was in Yān,
Lǐ Duì, on behalf of Sū Qín, said to the Fèngyáng Jūn:
"If Qí and Yān are estranged, then Zhào is important;
if Qí and Yān are united, then Zhào is slighted.
Now, your going to Qí
is not to Zhào's benefit.
I humbly believe this is not the right course for you."
Fèngyáng Jūn said:
"How have I united Yān with Qí?"
The reply was: "The one who controls Yān is Sū Zǐ.
But Yān is a weak state;
to the east, it is not the equal of Qí;
to the west, it is not the equal of Zhào.
How could it do without Qí to the east or Zhào to the west?
Yet you are very unkind to Sū Qín.
Can Sū Qín hold onto weak Yān while being isolated in the world?
This is driving Yān to unite with Qí.
Furthermore, Yān is the remnant of a fallen state;
it establishes itself through shifting power,
gains importance through external relations,
and serves those who are noble.
Therefore, in planning for you,
if you treat Sū Qín well, you win him over;
even if you do not like him, you should still win him over
in order to sow suspicion between Yān and Qí.
If Yān and Qí are suspicious,
then Zhào will be important.
If the Qí Wáng suspects Sū Qín,
then you will have many resources."
Fèngyáng Jūn said: "Excellent."
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to form an alliance with Sū Qín.
During the crisis of Quán,
Yān fought twice without victory,
and Zhào did not come to its rescue.
Kuài Zǐ said to the Wén Gōng:
"It is better to offer land to request an alliance with Qí;
then Zhào will surely rescue us.
If Zhào does not rescue us,
we will have no choice but to serve Qí."
Wén Gōng said: "Excellent."
He ordered Guō Rèn to use land to request peace talks with Qí.
When Zhào heard of this,
they finally sent troops to rescue Yān.
In the time of Yān Wén Gōng,
Qín Huì Wáng gave his daughter to be the wife of the Yān Tàizǐ.
When Wén Gōng died,
Yì Wáng ascended the throne.
Qí Xuān Wáng, taking advantage of the mourning in Yān, attacked them
and seized ten cities.
Lord Wǔ'ān Sū Qín was persuading the King of Qí on behalf of Yān.
He bowed twice to offer congratulations,
then looked up to offer condolences.
The King of Qí leaned on his halberd and stepped back,
saying:
"Why do these congratulations and condolences follow one another so quickly?"
Sū Qín replied:
"The reason a hungry person does not eat monkshood
is because although it temporarily fills the belly,
it brings the same disaster as death.
Although Yān is now weak and small,
its ruler is the young son-in-law of powerful Qín.
Your Majesty gains the profit of its ten cities,
but deeply makes an enemy of powerful Qín.
Now, making weak Yān the vanguard
while powerful Qín controls its rear
to summon the elite troops of the world
is like eating monkshood."
The King of Qí said:
"If that is so, then what should be done?"
Sū Qín replied: "When a sage manages affairs,
he turns disaster into fortune
and uses failure to create success.
Thus, Huán Gōng carried a woman on his back yet his reputation became more honored;
Hán Xiàn committed an offense yet his alliances became firmer.
These are all examples of turning disaster into fortune
and using failure to create success.
If Your Majesty can listen to your servant,
nothing would be better than returning the ten cities to Yān
and using humble words to apologize to Qín.
When Qín knows Your Majesty returned Yān's cities for its sake,
Qín will certainly feel indebted to Your Majesty.
When Yān recovers the ten cities for no reason,
Yān will also feel indebted to Your Majesty.
This is discarding a powerful enemy and establishing deep friendships.
Furthermore, if both Yān and Qín serve Qí,
then all under heaven will follow Your Majesty's commands.
Thus, Your Majesty attaches Qín with empty words
and takes the world with ten cities.
This is the enterprise of a Hegemon King.
This is what is called turning disaster into fortune
and using failure to create success."
The King of Qí was greatly pleased
and returned the cities of Yān.
He offered a thousand pounds of gold in apology afterward,
kowtowed in the middle of the road,
and wished to be brothers while asking for forgiveness from Qín.
Someone slandered Sū Qín to the King of Yān,
saying:
"Lord Wǔ'ān
is an untrustworthy person in the world.
Your Majesty humbles yourself before him with your state of ten thousand chariots,
honoring him at court;
this shows the world that you associate with a base person."
When Lord Wǔ'ān arrived from Qí,
the King of Yān did not provide him with lodging.
Sū Qín said to the King of Yān:
"I am a commoner from Dōng Zhōu.
I saw that you had no achievement even as small as an inch,
yet you welcomed me in the outskirts
and honored me at court.
Now I have acted as your envoy,
gained the profit of ten cities,
and performed the feat of saving Yān from danger.
Since Your Majesty does not listen to me,
it must be that someone has said I am untrustworthy
and has slandered me to the King.
My lack of trustworthiness
is actually Your Majesty's good fortune.
If I were as faithful as Wěi Shēng,
as incorruptible as Bó Yí,
and as filial as Zēng Shēn—
these three are noble conducts in the world—
but to serve Your Majesty with them,
would that be possible?"
The King of Yān said: "It would be possible."
Sū Qín said:
"If I were like these,
I would not be serving Your Majesty.
Furthermore, one as filial as Zēng Shēn
would out of duty not leave his parents to spend even one night outside.
How could Your Majesty send him to Qí?
One as incorruptible as Bó Yí
would not take a meal he had not earned,
considered King Wǔ's righteousness tainted and refused to be his minister,
declined to be the ruler of Gūzhú,
and died of hunger on Shǒuyáng Shān.
With such incorruptibility,
how would he be willing to walk thousands of miles
to serve the endangered lord of weak Yān?
One as faithful as Wěi Shēng
waited for a meeting but the other did not come,
so he embraced a bridge pillar and died.
His faithfulness reached such an extent.
How would he be willing to display the majesty of Yān and Qín in Qí to achieve great success?
Moreover, faithful conduct
is for one's own sake,
not for the sake of others.
These are all methods of self-preservation,
not the way of progressive achievement.
Furthermore, when the Sān Wáng arose in succession
and the Wǔ Bà flourished in turn,
none of them practiced self-preservation.
Does Your Majesty think self-preservation is appropriate?
If so, Qí would not have expanded beyond Yíngqiū,
Your Majesty would not have crossed the borders of Chǔ,
nor looked beyond the frontier cities.
Moreover, I have an old mother in Zhōu.
To leave my old mother to serve Your Majesty,
I abandoned the method of self-preservation
and planned for the way of progressive achievement.
My course of action is certainly not in accord with Your Majesty's.
Your Majesty desires self-preserving rulers,
while I am a minister of progressive achievement.
This is what is called being blamed by the lord despite loyalty and trustworthiness."
The King of Yān said: "As for loyalty and trustworthiness,
what crime can there be in them?"
Sū Qín replied: "Your Majesty does not know.
My neighbor had a husband who served as an official far away,
and his wife had a lover.
When the husband was about to return,
the lover was worried.
The wife said: 'Do not worry,
I have already prepared poisoned wine to wait for him.'
Two days later,
the husband arrived.
The wife had a concubine present the cup of wine to him.
The concubine knew it was poisoned wine;
if she presented it, she would kill the master of the house,
but if she spoke of it, she would cause the mistress to be expelled.
So she feigned a stumble and spilled the wine.
The master was furious and whipped her.
Thus, by the concubine's one stumble and spilling the wine,
she saved the master's life above
and preserved the mistress's place below.
Her loyalty reached such an extent,
yet she could not avoid being whipped.
This is an instance of being blamed despite loyalty and trustworthiness.
My service
unfortunately happens to be like the concubine's spilling the wine.
Moreover, in my service to Your Majesty,
I upheld righteousness and benefited the state,
yet now I am blamed.
I fear that in the future, those who serve Your Majesty
will not dare to commit themselves.
Furthermore, my persuasion of Qí
was never deceptive.
As for the method of persuading Qí,
nothing is better than my words;
even with the wisdom of Yáo or Shùn,
they would not dare to reject them."
Zhāng Yí, for the sake of Qín, broke the Vertical Alliance and formed the Horizontal Alliance.
He said to the King of Yān:
"Among those whom Your Majesty is close to,
none is like Zhào.
In the past, the King of Zhào gave his elder sister to be the wife of the King of Dài.
Wishing to annex Dài,
he arranged a meeting with the King of Dài at the Gùzhù Pass.
He ordered craftsmen to make a gold wine ladle
with a long handle,
making it capable of striking a person.
While drinking with the King of Dài,
he secretly told the cook:
'When the drinking is at its height and there is music,
bring in the hot soup,
then use the ladle to strike him.'
When the drinking reached its height and music played, the hot soup was brought in.
The cook came forward to pour the broth
and used the ladle to strike him,
such that the King of Dài's brains were scattered on the ground.
His sister, hearing of this,
sharpened her hairpin to stab herself.
Therefore, to this day there is a Mó Jī Shān,
which everyone in the world has heard of.
"The King of Zhào's cruelty and lack of regard for relatives
is clearly seen and known by Your Majesty.
Do you still think the King of Zhào can be trusted?
Zhào raised troops and attacked Yān,
twice besieged the capital of Yān and coerced Your Majesty,
and Your Majesty ceded ten cities before they withdrew in satisfaction.
Now the King of Zhào has already gone to court at Miǎnchí
and offered Héjiān to serve Qín.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qín,
Qín will send armored troops to Yúnzhōng and Jiǔyuán
and drive Zhào to attack Yān,
then the Yì Shuǐ and the Great Wall will no longer be Your Majesty's possession."
Moreover, at this time, Zhào's relationship with Qín
is like that of a commandery or county;
they do not dare to rashly raise an army to launch an invasion.
If Your Majesty now serves Qín,
the King of Qín will surely be pleased,
and Zhào will not dare to move rashly.
In this way, you will have the support of strong Qín to the west,
and will have no trouble from Qí or Zhào to the south.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully."
The King of Yān said: "I live in a remote place among the barbarians;
though I am a grown man,
I am merely like an infant.
My words are insufficient to seek the truth,
and my plans are insufficient to decide matters.
Now that an honored guest has fortunately come to instruct me,
I request to offer the state and turn westward to serve Qín,
presenting five cities at the foot of Chángshān."
Gōng Tuō went to Wèi as an envoy for Yān.
Wèi did not listen to him
and detained him for several months.
A guest said to the King of Wèi:
"Why do you not listen to the envoy from Yān?"
He said:
"Because of their internal disorder."
The guest replied: "When Tāng attacked Jié,
he desired his disorder.
Therefore, from one in great disorder, one can obtain their land;
from one in minor disorder, one can obtain their treasures.
Now the words of the envoy from Yān say:
'If the matter can be heard,
even if it exhausts all our treasures and land,
we would still do it.'
Why does Your Majesty not grant him an audience?"
The King of Wèi was pleased
and consequently granted the envoy of Yān an audience and sent him on his way.
Sū Qín died,
and his younger brother Sū Dài wished to succeed him.
He then went north to see King Kuài of Yān and said:
"I am a humble person from Dōngzhōu.
I have heard that Your Majesty's righteousness is very high and very compliant.
I am not clever,
yet I have set aside my hoe and spade to seek an audience with Your Majesty.
When I arrived at Hándān,
what I heard in Hándān
was even more impressive than what I had heard in Dōngzhōu.
Bearing my ambitions,
I have come to the court of Yān
and observed Your Majesty's ministers and officials;
Your Majesty is truly an enlightened ruler of the world."
The King said: "What you call an enlightened ruler of the world,
what kind of person is that?"
He replied: "I have heard that
an enlightened ruler strives to hear about his faults
and does not wish to hear about his virtues.
I beg to present Your Majesty's faults.
Now, Qí and Zhào
are Your Majesty's enemies;
Chǔ and Wèi
are Your Majesty's supporting states.
Now, for Your Majesty to serve your enemies in order to attack your supporting states
is not the way to benefit Yān.
If Your Majesty considers this yourself, then the plan is a mistake.
Those who have not remonstrated against this
are not loyal ministers."
The King said:
"Regarding Qí and Zhào,
I do not dare to wish to attack them."
Sū Dài said:
"Now, to have no intention of plotting against others
yet to cause others to suspect it
is dangerous;
to have the intention of plotting against others
yet to let others know of it
is clumsy;
if a plot is heard of outside before it is launched,
then it is perilous.
Now I have heard that Your Majesty's living is restless,
your food and drink are not sweet to you,
and you are constantly thinking of taking revenge on Qí;
you personally shave armor plates,
saying there is a great number of them;
your wife personally braids armor cords,
saying there is a great number of them.
Is this so?"
The King said: "Since you have heard this,
I do not dare to hide it.
I have deep resentment and accumulated anger toward Qí,
and I have wished to take revenge for two years.
Qí
is my enemy state;
therefore, it is the one I wish to attack.
I only worry that the state is exhausted
and its strength is insufficient.
If you can enable Yān to oppose Qí,
then I shall take my state and entrust it to you."
He replied: "Among the seven warring states of the world,
Yān is in a weak position.
It cannot fight alone,
but if it attaches itself to another, it becomes significant to all.
If it attaches to Chǔ in the south, then Chǔ becomes powerful;
if to Qín in the west, then Qín becomes powerful;
if to Hán or Wèi in the center, then Hán or Wèi becomes powerful.
Moreover, if the state it attaches to becomes powerful,
this will surely make Your Majesty powerful.
Now, the King of Qí
is a mature ruler
who is also self-willed.
He attacked Chǔ in the south for five years,
and his stored resources are scattered.
He troubled Qín in the west for three years;
his people are haggard and weary,
and his soldiers are exhausted.
He fought with Yān in the north,
overthrew three armies,
and captured two generals.
Then, using his remaining troops, he turned south to take on the powerful Sòng of five thousand chariots
and encompassed twelve feudal lords.
This is what the ruler desires to obtain,
but his people's strength is exhausted;
how can he still take anything?
Moreover, I have heard that frequent battles exhaust the people,
and keeping an army in the field for a long time wears out the soldiers."
The King said:
"I have heard that Qí has the Clear Jǐ and the Turbid River,
which can serve as strongholds;
they have the Long Wall and the Great Barrier, which are sufficient to serve as fortresses.
Is this truly so?"
He replied: "If the timing of Heaven is not granted,
even if they have the Clear Jǐ and the Turbid River,
how could they be sufficient as strongholds?
If the people's strength is depleted and exhausted,
even if they have the Long Wall and the Great Barrier,
how could they be sufficient as fortresses?
Furthermore, in former days,
the area west of the Jǐ was not conscripted,
as it was used to defend against Zhào;
the area north of the River was not garrisoned with troops,
as it was used to defend against Yān.
Now, the areas west of the Jǐ and north of the River
have all been conscripted,
and the interior of their borders is exhausted.
Now, an arrogant ruler will surely not be fond of planning,
and the ministers of a doomed state are greedy for wealth.
If Your Majesty can truly not begrudge sending a favored son or a younger brother of the same mother to be a hostage,
and using precious pearls, jade, and silks to serve those around him,
then he will be grateful to Yān and think lightly of destroying Sòng,
and thus Qí can be destroyed."
The King said: "I ultimately consider that through you I have received the mandate of Heaven!"
Sū Dài said:
"If internal troublemakers do not cooperate with the ruler, the external enemy cannot be resisted.
Your Majesty should manage things from the outside,
and I shall respond from the inside;
this is the situation for its destruction."
After King Kuài of Yān was enthroned,
Sū Qín died in Qí.
When Sū Qín was in Yān,
he had formed a marriage alliance with the Chancellor Zǐ Zhī;
Sū Dài was also a friend of Zǐ Zhī.
When Sū Qín died,
King Xuān of Qí again employed Sū Dài.
In the third year of King Kuài of Yān,
he attacked Qín together with Chǔ and the Sānjìn,
but they were not victorious and returned.
When Zǐ Zhī was Chancellor of Yān,
he was honored and respected and made the primary decisions.
Sū Dài went to Yān as an envoy for Qí,
and the King of Yān asked him:
"What kind of person is King Xuān of Qí?"
He replied: "He will surely not become a hegemon."
The King of Yān said: "Why?"
He replied: "Because he does not trust his ministers."
Sū Dài wished to use this to provoke the King of Yān to place heavy trust in Zǐ Zhī.
Thereupon, the King of Yān placed great trust in Zǐ Zhī.
Zǐ Zhī consequently sent Sū Dài a hundred pieces of gold
and followed his instructions.
Lùmáo Shòu said to the King of Yān:
"It would be better to abdicate the state to Zǐ Zhī.
People call Yáo worthy
because he offered the world to Xǔ Yóu;
Xǔ Yóu was certain not to accept it,
so Yáo gained the reputation of offering the world
without actually losing it.
If Your Majesty now abdicates the state to Chancellor Zǐ Zhī,
Zǐ Zhī will surely not dare to accept it,
and thus Your Majesty will be acting in the same manner as Yáo."
The King of Yān consequently entrusted the entire state to Zǐ Zhī,
and Zǐ Zhī became extremely powerful.
Or someone said: “Yǔ passed the world to Yì and appointed Qǐ as an official;
when he grew old,
he considered Qǐ insufficient to be entrusted with the world,
and passed it to Yì.
Qǐ and his faction attacked Yì and seized the world from him.
Thus, in name Yǔ passed the world to Yì,
but in reality he let Qǐ take it for himself.
Now the Wáng says he is entrusting the state to Zǐzhī,
but among the officials there are none who are not the Tàizǐ’s men;
this is in name entrusting it to Zǐzhī,
while the Tàizǐ manages affairs.”
The Wáng consequently collected the seals of all officials from the three-hundred dàn rank and above and handed them over to Zǐzhī.
Zǐzhī faced south and conducted the Wáng’s business,
while Kuài grew old and did not listen to government affairs,
turning instead to be a subject;
the affairs of the state were all decided by Zǐzhī.
In the third year of Zǐzhī, the state of Yān was in great chaos,
and the hundred surnames were grieved and resentful.
Jiāngjūn Shì Bèi and Tàizǐ Píng plotted
and were about to attack Zǐzhī.
Chǔzǐ said to Qí Xuān Wáng:
“If you take this opportunity to overthrow them,
the destruction of Yān is certain.”
The Wáng then sent someone to say to Tàizǐ Píng:
“I have heard of the Tàizǐ’s righteousness;
you are about to set aside private interest to establish the public good,
to rectify the duty of ruler and subject,
and to correct the positions of father and son.
My state is small
and insufficient to assist you.
Nevertheless,
I will simply follow whatever orders the Tàizǐ gives.”
The Tàizǐ then gathered a crowd from his faction;
Jiāngjūn Shì Bèi surrounded the public palace
and attacked Zǐzhī,
but was not successful.
Jiāngjūn Shì Bèi and the hundred surnames then turned to attack Tàizǐ Píng.
Jiāngjūn Shì Bèi died in the conflict; the state
suffered from internal strife for several months,
and the dead numbered several tens of thousands.
The people of Yān were grieved and resentful,
and the hundred surnames were alienated in their hearts.
Mèng Kè said to Qí Xuān Wáng:
“Attacking Yān now—
this is the time of Wén and Wǔ;
it must not be lost.”
The Wáng then ordered Zhāng Zǐ to command the troops of the Wǔ Dū,
using the forces of the Běidì to attack Yān.
The soldiers did not fight,
the city gates were not closed,
and Yān Wáng Kuài died.
Qí gained a great victory over Yān,
and Zǐzhī fled.
After two years,
the people of Yān established Gōngzǐ Píng,
who became Yān Zhāo Wáng.
Initially,
Sū Qín’s younger brother Lì, by means of the Yān hostage prince, sought an audience with the Qí Wáng.
The Qí Wáng resented Sū Qín,
and wanted to imprison Lì;
the Yān hostage apologized on his behalf and the matter ended, so he then presented himself as a subject.
The Yān Xiàng Zǐzhī had a marriage alliance with Sū Dài
and wished to obtain the power of Yān;
he then sent Sū Dài to accompany the hostage prince in Qí.
Qí sent Dài to report back to Yān.
Yān Wáng Kuài asked: “Will the Qí Wáng become a Bà?”
He said:
“He cannot.”
He asked:
“Why is that?”
He said:
“He does not trust his ministers.”
Thereupon the Yān Wáng solely entrusted Zǐzhī;
shortly after, he abdicated the throne, and Yān fell into great chaos.
Qí attacked Yān
and killed Wáng Kuài and Zǐzhī.
Yān established Zhāo Wáng.
And so Sū Dài and Lì did not dare enter Yān;
both eventually returned to Qí,
and Qí treated them well.
Sū Dài passed through Wèi,
and Wèi detained Dài on behalf of Yān.
Qí sent someone to say to Wèi Wáng:
“Qí requested to enfeoff Jìngyáng Jūn with Sòng,
but Qín did not accept.
It is not that it would not be advantageous for Qín to have Qí and obtain the lands of Sòng,
but they do not trust the Qí Wáng and Sū Zǐ.
Now Qí and Wèi are not in harmony,
and to such an extent,
then Qí will not deceive Qín.
Qín will trust Qí,
Qí and Qín will unite,
and Jìngyáng Jūn will have the lands of Sòng,
which is not to Wèi’s advantage.
Therefore, it would be better for the Wáng to send Sū Zǐ eastward;
Qín will surely be suspicious and not trust Sū Zǐ.
If Qí and Qín do not unite,
there will be no changes in the world,
and the conditions for attacking Qí will be established.”
Thereupon they released Sū Dài to go to Sòng,
and Sòng treated him well.
Yān Zhāo Wáng ascended the throne after the restoration of the broken Yān;
he humbled himself and offered thick gifts
to recruit the worthy, intending to use them to seek revenge.
Therefore he went to see Guō Kuí Xiānsheng and said:
“Qí took advantage of the chaos of my state
to launch a surprise attack and destroy Yān.
I well know that Yān is small and its strength is meager,
not enough to retaliate.
However, to obtain worthy men and share the state with them,
in order to wash away the disgrace of the former king,
is my wish.
I venture to ask, how does one seek revenge with a state?”
Guō Kuí Xiānsheng replied:
“One who would be an emperor dwells with teachers;
one who would be a king dwells with friends;
one who would be a hegemon dwells with ministers;
one whose state is destroyed dwells with servants.
If you humble yourself to serve them
and face north to receive instruction,
then those a hundred times better than yourself will arrive.
If you are first to hasten and last to rest,
first to ask and last to be silent,
then those ten times better than yourself will arrive.
If you hasten when others hasten,
then those equal to yourself will arrive.
If you lean on a table and grip a staff,
looking askance and giving orders with your fingers,
then servants and menials will arrive.
If you act with arrogance and strike out in anger,
shouting and scolding,
then only convicts and laborers will arrive.
This is the ancient method for submitting to the Way and attracting the worthy.
If the Wáng truly selects the worthy throughout the state
and pays court at their gates,
the world will hear that the Wáng is paying court to his worthy ministers,
and the scholars of the world will surely hasten toward Yān.”
Zhāo Wáng said: “To whom should I pay court?”
Guō Kuí Xiānsheng said:
“I have heard that among the rulers of old,
there was one who sought a thousand-lǐ horse with a thousand pieces of gold;
for three years he could not obtain one.
A Juānrén said to the ruler:
‘I beg to go seek it.’
The ruler sent him.
In three months he found a thousand-lǐ horse,
but the horse was already dead;
he bought its head for five hundred pieces of gold
and returned to report to the ruler.
The ruler was very angry and said:
‘What I sought was a living horse;
what use is a dead horse, yet you threw away five hundred pieces of gold?’
The Juānrén replied:
‘If even a dead horse was bought for five hundred pieces of gold,
how much more so a living one?
The world will surely believe that the Wáng is able to buy horses,
and horses will arrive now.’
Thereupon, before a full year had passed,
three thousand-lǐ horses arrived.
Now if the Wáng truly wishes to attract scholars,
begin first with Kuí;
if even Kuí is seen to be served,
how much more so those more worthy than Kuí?
Will they think a thousand lǐ too far?”
Thereupon Zhāo Wáng built a palace for Kuí and treated him as a teacher.
Lè Yì came from Wèi,
Zōu Yǎn came from Qí,
Jù Xīn came from Zhào;
scholars vied to flock to Yān.
The Yān Wáng mourned the dead and inquired after the living,
and shared his joys and sorrows with the hundred surnames.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the state of Yān was wealthy and prosperous,
and the soldiers were happy, rested, and made light of battle.
Thereupon he made Lè Yì the Shàng Jiāngjūn,
and conspired with Qín, Chǔ, and the Sān Jìn to attack Qí.
The Qí army was defeated,
and Mǐn Wáng fled abroad.
The Yān army alone pursued the defeated north and entered Línzī,
taking all the treasures of Qí,
and burning its palaces and ancestral temples.
Of the cities of Qí that did not submit,
only Jǔ and Jímò remained.
Qí attacked Sòng,
and Sòng was in a critical state.
Sū Dài then sent a letter to Yàn Zhāo Wáng, saying:
"To be ranked among the states of ten thousand chariots,
yet to send hostages to Qí,
makes your name lowly and your power light.
When Qín and Qí assist in the attack on Sòng,
the people are exhausted and resources are wasted.
To destroy Sòng,
damage Chǔ’s Huáiběi,
and enrich and enlarge Qí,
is to make your enemy strong while
your own state becomes weak.
These three things
are all major failures for a state,
yet you are carrying them out,
wishing to remove harm and gain trust from Qí.
But Qí has not increased its trust in you;
instead, its jealousy of Yàn has grown even more intense.
Thus, your service to Qí
has lost its purpose.
The people are exhausted and resources are wasted,
yet there is not an inch of achievement;
destroying Sòng enriches the enemy,
and generations will bear the burden of this disaster.
You consider Sòng added to Huáiběi
to be a strong state of ten thousand chariots,
but if Qí annexes it,
this adds one Qí.
The Northern Barbarian lands cover seven hundred lǐ;
add Lǔ and Wèi to this,
and this is what is called a strong state of ten thousand chariots;
if Qí annexes them,
this adds a second Qí.
Even with the strength of one Qí,
Yàn still cannot withstand it;
now, if three Qís press upon Yàn,
the disaster will surely be great.
Nevertheless,
I have heard that when a wise person initiates an undertaking,
they turn disaster into fortune
and achieve success through failure.
The people of Qí dye ruined silk purple,
and the price increases tenfold.
Yuè Wáng Gōu Jiàn took refuge at Huìjī,
yet later destroyed Wú and became hegemon of the world.
These are all cases of turning disaster into fortune
and making success out of failure.
Now, does the King wish to turn disaster into fortune
and make success out of failure?
Then nothing is better than acknowledging Qí as hegemon from afar and deeply honoring it,
sending envoys to form an alliance at the House of Zhōu,
burning all the Qín tallies in the world,
and making a pact saying:
'The best plan is to destroy Qín;
the next is to make Qín a permanent servant.'
With Qín being held as a servant while awaiting destruction,
the King of Qín will surely be troubled by it.
Qín for five generations has allied with the feudal lords,
but now it would be subordinate to Qí;
given the King of Qín’s ambition,
if he could exhaust Qí,
he would not hesitate to use his entire state and capital as the price for that achievement.
Therefore, why does the King not send a commoner
to persuade Qín with the strategy of exhausting Qí,
saying to the King of Qín:
'That Yàn and Zhào destroyed Sòng to enrich Qí and honored Qí by becoming its subordinates
was not to the benefit of Yàn and Zhào.
That they acted against their interests
was why?
It was because they did not trust the King of Qín.
Now, why does the King not send those who can be trusted to win over Yàn and Zhào?
If Jìngyáng Jūn or Gāolíng Jūn are sent first to Yàn and Zhào,
and if Qín should change its mind,
they can be held as hostages;
then Yàn and Zhào will trust Qín.
Qín shall be the Emperor of the West,
Zhào the Emperor of the Center,
Yàn the Emperor of the North;
establish the Three Emperors to command the feudal lords.
If Hán and Wèi do not obey,
then Qín shall attack them.
If Qí does not obey,
then Yàn and Zhào shall attack it.
Who in the world would dare not obey?
Once the world submits and obeys,
then drive Hán and Wèi to attack Qí,
saying that it must return the lands of Sòng
and restore Huáiběi to Chǔ.
Returning the lands of Sòng
and restoring Huáiběi to Chǔ
are in the common interest of Yàn and Zhào.
Establishing the Three Emperors together
is the common wish of Yàn and Zhào.
When the actual benefit is gained
and the desired reputation is achieved,
then Yàn and Zhào's abandonment of Qí
will be like casting off a worn-out straw sandal.
Now, if the King does not win over Yàn and Zhào,
then Qí's hegemony will surely be established.
If the feudal lords support Qí
and only the King does not follow,
the state will be attacked.
If the feudal lords support Qí
and the King follows them,
his name will be lowly.
If the King does not win over Yàn and Zhào,
his name will be lowly and his state in danger;
if the King wins over Yàn and Zhào,
his name will be honored and his state peaceful.
To abandon honor and peace and move toward lowliness and danger
is something a wise person does not do.'
When the King of Qín hears such a persuasion,
it will surely be like a pierce to his heart;
so why does the King not strive to send wise men to persuade Qín with these words?
Qín will certainly attack Qí.
To win over Qín is a superior alliance;
to attack Qí
is a direct benefit.
To honor a superior alliance
and strive for direct benefit
are the tasks of a sage king."
Yàn Zhāo Wáng approved of the letter,
saying:
"My ancestors once received kindness from the Sū clan;
during the rebellion of Zǐ Zhī,
the Sū clan left Yàn.
Yàn wishes to take revenge on Qí,
and it cannot be done without the Sū clan."
He then summoned the Sū clan
and treated them well once again.
He planned the attack on Qí with them,
and they eventually destroyed Qí,
and Mǐn Wáng fled.
Sū Dài said to Yàn Zhāo Wáng:
"Suppose there is a person here
as filial as Zēng Shēn and Xiào Jǐ,
as trustworthy as Wěi Shēng Gāo,
and as incorruptible as Bào Jiāo and Shǐ Qiú;
if they combined these three virtues to serve the King,
how would that be?"
The King said:
"That would be enough."
He replied:
"If you think that is enough,
then I cannot serve you.
I would rather reside in a state of non-action,
and return to plow the upper lands of Zhōu,
plowing to eat
and weaving to clothe myself."
The King asked: "What is the reason?"
He replied:
"One as filial as Zēng Shēn and Xiào Jǐ
would do no more than support their parents.
One as trustworthy as Wěi Shēng Gāo
would do no more than not deceive people.
One as incorruptible as Bào Jiāo and Shǐ Qiú
would do no more than not steal other people's property.
Now, I am one who seeks advancement.
I believe that incorruptibility does not lead to one's prominence,
and righteousness does not lead to one's success in life.
Benevolence and righteousness
are ways of perfecting oneself;
they are not methods for advancement."
The King asked: "Is caring for oneself not enough?"
He replied: "If caring for oneself were enough,
then Qín would not have come out of the Yáo Pass,
Qí would not have come out of Yíng Qiū,
and Chǔ would not have come out of Shū Zhāng.
That the Three Kings succeeded each other
and the Five Hegemons changed governance
was all because they did not just care for themselves.
If caring for oneself were enough,
then I would also just be in Zhōu carrying a basket;
why would I trouble the court of the Great King?
In the past, when Chǔ took Zhāng Wǔ,
the feudal lords turned north to pay homage.
When Qín took Xī Shān,
the feudal lords turned west to pay homage.
Previously, had Yàn not left the area of the House of Zhōu,
then the feudal lords would not have come to pay homage with their matched horses.
I have heard that
those who are good at handling affairs
first measure the size of their state
and evaluate the strength of their army;
thus success can be achieved
and fame can be established.
Those who are not good at handling affairs
do not first measure the size of their state
and do not evaluate the strength of their army;
thus success cannot be achieved and fame cannot be established.
Now the King has the intention to turn east and attack Qí,
and I, your humble servant, know it."
The King asked: "How do you know it?"
He replied: "By your fixing the halberds and sharpening the swords,
and by your climbing the hills to look east and sigh;
that is how I, your humble servant, know it."
Now, Wū Huò could lift weights of a thousand jūn;
yet having reached the age of eighty,
he must seek support to walk.
Therefore, although Qí is a powerful state,
it has been exhausted in the west by Sòng
and worn out in the south by Chǔ.
Thus, the army of Qí can be defeated,
and Héjiān can be captured."
The King of Yān said: "Excellent.
I wish to appoint you as Shàngqīng,
and grant you a hundred chariots.
Will you use these to travel east to Qí on my behalf?"
He replied: "Is it because Your Majesty loves me?
If so, why not give this to your beloved sons, your maternal uncles,
your paternal uncles, or your grandsons still in the cradle? They have not received it,
yet you give it to an incompetent minister. Why is that?
In Your Majesty's assessment of me,
what kind of person am I?
Now, the reason I serve Your Majesty
is out of loyalty and trustworthiness.
I fear that because of this loyalty and trustworthiness,
I shall be blamed by those around you."
The King said: "How could a minister who exerts all his strength
and exhausts his ability
ever be blamed?"
He replied: "Let me provide an analogy for Your Majesty.
Long ago, in Shàngdì of Zhōu, there was such a case.
A husband there had been away on official business for three years without returning.
His wife took a lover.
Her lover said:
'Your husband is returning;
what shall we do then?'
The wife said: 'Do not worry.
I have already prepared poisoned wine and await his arrival.'
Soon after, the husband did indeed return.
Thereupon, she ordered her concubine to pour the poisoned wine and present it to him.
The concubine knew the wine was poisoned.
She stopped halfway.
She reflected:
'If I give this to my master to drink,
then I will be killing my master;
if I inform my master of this matter,
then my mistress will be expelled.
Rather than killing my master or having my mistress expelled,
it is better that I pretend to stumble and spill it.'
Thereupon, she feigned a fall and spilled it.
The wife said: 'Because you have returned from a long journey,
I prepared some fine wine,
but the concubine has spilled it while presenting it.'
The husband, unaware of the truth,
bound the concubine and whipped her.
Thus, the reason the concubine was whipped
was due to her loyalty and trustworthiness.
Now, as I serve as Your Majesty’s envoy to Qí,
I fear that my loyalty and trustworthiness will not be understood by those around you.
I have heard it said:
'A ruler of ten thousand chariots
is not controlled by his ministers.
The head of a house of ten chariots
is not controlled by the multitude.
A commoner or a scholar traveling on foot
is not controlled by his wife or concubines.'
How much more should this be true for a worthy ruler of the present age?
I ask permission to depart now,
and I hope Your Majesty will not be controlled by your ministers."
The King of Yān said to Sū Dài:
"I very much dislike the speech of those who are persuasive."
Sū Dài replied: "In the land of Zhōu, matchmakers are held in low esteem
because they praise both sides.
To the man’s family, they say, 'The girl is beautiful.'
To the girl’s family, they say, 'The man is wealthy.'
Yet, according to the customs of Zhōu,
people do not take wives for themselves.
Moreover, an unmarried woman without a matchmaker
will grow old and never marry.
If she discards the matchmaker and promotes herself,
she will be disparaged and remain unmarried.
That which succeeds without failure,
and results in marriage without being disparaged,
is only the work of the matchmaker.
Furthermore, an affair cannot be established without strategic expediency,
nor can it be completed without favorable circumstances.
One who enables others to sit back and receive the fruits of success
is none other than the persuasive talker."
The King said: "Very well."
Qín summoned the King of Yān.
The King of Yān wished to go.
Sū Dài cautioned the King of Yān, saying:
"Chǔ obtained Zhǐ and its state perished.
Qí obtained Sòng and its state perished.
Why was it that Qí and Chǔ could not use Zhǐ and Sòng to serve Qín?
Why was this?
It is because those who achieve merit
are the deepest enemies of Qín.
In its attempt to take over the world, Qín
does not act with righteousness;
it acts with violence.
In exercising its violence against the world, Qín
formally warned Chǔ, saying:
'The troops of Shǔ
will board light boats on the Wèn River,
and ride the summer floodwaters down the river.
In five days they will reach Yǐng.
The troops of Hànzhōng
will board boats from Bā,
and ride the summer floodwaters down the Hàn River.
In four days they will reach Wǔzhǔ.
I shall mass my troops at Wǎn
and move east down to Suí.
The wise will not have time to devise a plan,
and the brave will not have time to rouse their anger.
I shall be like one shooting a falcon.
If Your Majesty waits for the states of the world to attack Hángǔ Pass,
is that not a far-fetched hope?'
For this reason, the King of Chǔ
served Qín for seventeen years.
Qín formally warned Hàn, saying:
'I shall set out from Shàoqū,
and in one day I shall cut off the Tàiháng Mountains.
I shall set out from Yíyáng and strike Píngyáng;
in two days, there will be nowhere I do not hold sway.
I shall leave the two Zhōu domains and strike Zhèng;
in five days, your state will be taken.'
The House of Hàn believed this to be true,
and so they served Qín.
Qín formally warned Wèi, saying:
'I shall take Ānyì,
block Nǚjǐ,
and the House of Hàn and Tàiyuán will be rolled up.
I shall go down to Zhǐ, pass through Nányáng, Fēng, and Jì,
envelop the two Zhōu domains,
ride the summer floodwaters,
and float light boats.
With strong crossbows in front
and sharp halberds behind,
I shall breach the Róng entrance;
then Wèi will no longer have Dàliáng.
I shall breach the Báimǎ entrance;
then Wèi will no longer have Jìyáng.
I shall breach the Sùxū entrance;
then Wèi will no longer have Xū or Dùnqiū.
If I attack by land, I shall strike Hénèi;
if I attack by water, I shall destroy Dàliáng.'
The House of Wèi believed this to be true,
and so they served Qín.
When Qín wished to attack Ānyì,
it feared that Qí would come to its rescue.
Therefore, it entrusted Sòng to Qí,
saying:
'The King of Sòng is unprincipled;
he has made a wooden effigy to resemble me
and shoots at its face.
My lands are remote and my troops are far away, so I cannot attack him.
If Your Majesty can destroy Sòng and take possession of it,
it would be as if I had obtained it myself.'
Once Qín had obtained Ānyì
and blocked Nǚjǐ,
it then used the destruction of Sòng as a pretext to charge Qí with a crime.
When Qín wished to attack Qí,
it feared that the states of the world would come to its rescue.
Therefore, it denounced Qí to the world, saying:
'The King of Qí has made four agreements with me
and has deceived me four times.
He has certainly led the world to attack me three times.
If there is a Qí, there can be no Qín;
if there is no Qí, then there can be a Qín.
We must attack them;
we must destroy them!'
Once Qín had obtained Yíyáng and Shàoqū,
and reached Lìn and Shí,
it then used the destruction of Qí as a pretext to charge the world with a crime.
When Qín wished to attack Wèi, it considered Chǔ of great importance.
Therefore, it entrusted Nányáng to Chǔ, saying:
'I am certainly about to break off relations with Hàn!
I shall devastate Jūnlíng
and block the Méng Pass.
If it is beneficial to Chǔ,
it would be as if I held it myself.'
When Wèi abandoned its allies and allied with Qín,
Qín then used the blocking of the Méng Pass as a pretext to charge Chǔ with a crime.
When the army is trapped in the forest,
he values Yàn and Zhào,
entrusting Jiǎodōng to Yàn
and Jìxī to Zhào.
Zhào obtained a peace agreement with Wèi;
when it reached Gōngzǐ Yán,
he followed Xīshǒu’s ranks to attack Zhào.
The army was wounded at Líshí
and met defeat at Mǎlíng,
and then he valued Wèi,
so he entrusted Shè and Cài to Wèi.
Having already obtained a peace agreement with Zhào,
he then threatened Wèi,
but Wèi would not cede land.
When trapped, he sends the Tàihòu and Rànghóu to make peace;
when strong, he deceives both his uncle and his mother.
To the one who goes to Yàn, he says:
“Give them Jiǎodōng.”
To the one who goes to Zhào, he says:
“Give them Jìxī.”
To the one who goes to Wèi, he says:
“Give them Shè and Cài.”
To the one who goes to Chǔ, he says:
“Give them the Mèng’ài Pass.”
To the one who goes to Qí, he says:
“Give them Sòng.”
This must make his words like a revolving cycle
and his use of troops like embroidering a cicada;
his mother cannot control him,
and his uncle cannot restrain him.
In the battle of Lóngjiǎ,
the battle of Ànmén,
the battle of Fēnglù,
the battle of Gāoshāng,
and the battle of Zhào Zhuāng,
