Qín has killed millions of the people of Sānjìn.
Those who are alive today
are all orphans of those killed by Qín.
The lands beyond Xīhé, the territory of Shàngluò, and Sānchuān
are the calamities of the Jìn state,
comprising half of the Sānjìn.
The calamity of Qín is as great as this,
yet those of Yàn and Zhào who go to Qín
all use the competition to serve Qín to persuade their lords;
this is what your servant greatly worries about.”
King Zhāo of Yàn did not follow Qín,
and Sū Dài again became highly valued in Yàn.
Yàn again renewed the Vertical Alliance of the feudal lords,
as in the time of Sū Qín;
some joined and some did not,
but the world thereafter revered the Sū family’s Vertical Alliance.
Dài and Lì both died of old age,
their names renowned among the feudal lords.
Sū Dài, on behalf of Fèngyáng Jūn, persuaded Yàn while in Zhào to attack Qí,
but Fèngyáng Jūn did not listen.
He then entered Qí and slandered Zhào,
causing Qí to break with Zhào.
Once Qí had broken with Zhào,
he went to Yàn
and said to King Zhāo:
“Hán Wéi said to me:
‘Someone told Fèngyáng Jūn:
The one who makes Qí distrust Zhào
is Sū Zǐ;
Now the King of Qí has summoned Shǔzǐ and ordered him not to attack Sòng,
it is Sū Zǐ;
The one who plots with the King of Qí to take a route through Qín to plot against Zhào
is Sū Zǐ;
The one who ordered Qí to guard the hostage prince of Zhào with armored soldiers
is also Sū Zǐ.
I request to tell you so that you may ask Qí;
if they indeed guard the hostage prince of Zhào with armored soldiers,
I will surely guard you with armored soldiers.’
His words were malicious.
Even so,
Your Majesty, do not worry.
I already knew that entering Qí would cause trouble with Zhào.
I went out to do this to achieve my desire;
if I die and Qí becomes a great enemy of Zhào,
it is as if I were still alive.
Making Qí and Zhào break off
can create a great disturbance.
In terms of character, I am not Zhāng Mèngtán;
but if I were like Zhāng Mèngtán, then Qí and Zhào would surely have someone like Zhì Bó.”
Fèngyáng Jūn told Zhū Huān and Zhào Zú:
“The King of Qí sent Gōngwáng Yuē and Mìngshuō to say
he would certainly not bring back Hán Mín,
yet now he has summoned him.
He would certainly not entrust Sū Zǐ with affairs,
yet now he has enfeoffed him and made him Prime Minister.
He ordered not to cooperate with Yàn,
yet now he takes Yàn as his primary ally.
What I relied on was Shùn;
now his words change more than his father’s.
Shùn was originally an enemy of Sū Zǐ.
Seeing him, I knew he was not a leper,
yet now he is esteemed and given two posts;
it is over,
I have lost Qí!”
Fèngyáng Jūn’s anger is extreme.
If the King of Qí does not trust Zhào,
and the petty man Fèngyáng Jūn
consequently betrays him,
if we do not take this moment to create a great disturbance
and they break apart only to reunite,
then later nothing can be done.
Therefore, if the alliance of Qí and Zhào can be broken,
death is not enough to be a concern for your servant;
fleeing is not enough to be a shame for your servant;
acting for the feudal lords is not enough to be a glory for your servant;
disheveling my hair and painting my body like a leper
is not enough to be a disgrace for your servant.
However, your servant has one concern:
If I die and Qí and Zhào do not break off,
and the enmity is attributed to me,
and afterward they cooperate with each other,
this is your servant’s concern.
If I die and they must attack each other,
I will surely strive for that and seek death therein.
Yáo and Shùn were virtuous yet they died;
Yǔ and Tāng were wise yet they died;
Mèng Bèn was brave yet he died;
Wū Huò was strong yet he died;
among all living things, is there anything that does not die?
Using an inevitable occurrence to achieve one’s desires,
why should Your Majesty doubt?
I think it is better for me to flee and leave.
I will cause Hán and Wèi to distance themselves from Qí
and for them I will take Qín,
deeply binding with Zhào to strengthen it.
In this way, they will be close to attacking each other.
Even if I cause trouble for Yàn because of this,
Fèngyáng Jūn told Zhū Huān:
‘Sū Zǐ is angry that the King of Yàn, because of me,
did not make him Prime Minister
nor did he make him a high minister;
there is likely no more Yàn.’
His suspicion has reached this point;
therefore, even if I do this, it will not trouble Yàn,
nor do I wish to be King.
Yī Yǐn twice fled from Tāng to go to Jié
and twice fled from Jié to go to Tāng,
finally resulting in the Battle of Míngtiáo
and making Tāng the Son of Heaven.
Wǔ Zǐxū fled Chǔ to go to Wú,
finally resulting in the Battle of Bójǔ
and avenging his father’s grievance.
Now I flee and throw Qí and Zhào into confusion;
only then can this be recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Moreover, of those who achieved great things,
who did not flee?
During the trouble of Huán Gōng,
Guǎn Zhòng fled to Lǔ;
during the trouble of Yáng Hǔ,
Kǒngzǐ fled to Wèi;
Zhāng Yí fled to Chǔ;
Bái Guī fled to Qín;
Wàng Zhū served as Prime Minister of Zhōngshān and went to Zhào,
where Zhào threatened him to demand land;
Wàng Zhū fought through the pass and fled.
During the trouble of Wàisūn,
the Lord of Xué changed clothes with Dài and escaped through the pass;
the Sānjìn praised him as a man of service.
Therefore, when performing great deeds,
fleeing is not enough to be a disgrace.”
In the end, he caused Qí to break with Zhào;
Zhào joined with Yàn to attack Qí
and defeated it.
Sū Dài, on behalf of Yàn, went to persuade Qí;
before he saw the King of Qí,
he first persuaded Chúnyú Kūn, saying:
“There was once a man selling a fine steed;
he stood in the market for three consecutive mornings,
but no one noticed it.
He went to see Bólè and said:
‘I have a fine steed
that I wish to sell;
I have stood in the market for three consecutive mornings,
but no one spoke with me.
I wish that you would walk around it and look at it
and then look back at it as you leave;
I beg to offer you the earnings of one morning.’
Bólè then walked around it and looked at it
and then looked back at it as he left;
in a single morning, the horse’s price increased tenfold.
Now I wish to present myself as a fine steed to the King,
but I have no one to introduce me.
Would you be willing to be my Bólè?
I beg to offer a pair of white jade discs
and a thousand gold yì
to pay for the horse’s fodder.”
Chúnyú Kūn said: “I respectfully hear your command.”
He went in to speak to the King and presented him;
the King of Qí was greatly pleased with Sū Zǐ.
Sū Dài went from Qí to send someone to say to Yàn Zhāowáng:
"I have heard that if Qí and Zhào are separated,
then Qí and Zhào will already be isolated.
Why does Your Majesty not dispatch troops to attack Qí?
I request to weaken them for Your Majesty."
Yàn then attacked Qí and struck Jìn.
He sent someone to say to King Mǐnwáng:
"The reason Yàn attacks Qí
is because they wish to reclaim their ancient lands.
Yàn's troops are at Jìn and do not advance;
this means their army is weak and their plans are hesitant.
Why does Your Majesty not order Sū Zǐ to lead the army and respond to Yàn?
With the worthiness of Sū Zǐ,
leading to respond to a weak Yàn,
Yàn's defeat is certain.
Once Yàn is defeated, then Zhào will not dare but to obey;
this would mean Your Majesty crushing Yàn and bringing Zhào to submission."
King Mǐnwáng said: "Good."
He then said to Sū Zǐ:
"Yàn's troops are at Jìn.
Now I will dispatch an army to respond to them.
I wish for you to act as my general for this."
He replied: "Regarding military matters,
how could I be adequate for the task?
I hope Your Majesty will choose someone else.
If Your Majesty employs me,
it will lead to the defeat of Your Majesty's army,
and I will be handed over to Yàn.
If the battle is not won,
there can be no recovery."
The King said: "Go, I know you."
Sū Zǐ then took command,
and fought the people of Yàn below Jìn.
The Qí army was defeated.
Yàn captured twenty thousand armored heads.
Sū Zǐ gathered the remaining troops
to defend Yángchéng,
and reported to King Mǐnwáng, saying:
"Your Majesty erred in your choice
by ordering me to respond to Yàn.
Now the army is defeated and twenty thousand men are lost.
I deserve the punishment of the axe and block;
I request to surrender myself to the officials to be executed."
King Mǐnwáng said: "This was my error;
you should not take the blame for it."
The next day, Yàn was again sent to attack Yángchéng and Lí.
Again, someone was sent to tell King Mǐnwáng:
"The other day Qí was not victorious below Jìn;
this was not the fault of the army.
Qí was unfortunate, while Yàn had heavenly luck.
Now Yàn attacks Yángchéng and Lí again;
they are using their heavenly luck to claim credit for themselves.
If Your Majesty again sends Sū Zǐ to respond to them,
Sū Zǐ, having first lost Your Majesty's army,
will surely strive to report victory to Your Majesty afterwards."
The King said: "Good."
He then employed Sū Zǐ again.
Sū Zǐ firmly declined,
but the King would not listen.
He then led the army to fight Yàn at Yángchéng.
The people of Yàn gained a great victory and took thirty thousand heads.
The ruler and ministers of Qí were no longer close,
and the common people became estranged.
Yàn then sent Lè Yì to raise a great army to attack Qí,
and crushed them.
Sū Dài presented a letter from Qí to the King of Yàn, saying:
"When I departed,
I surely knew there would be gossip;
therefore I presented a letter to the King before I left,
saying:
'If I am honored in Qí,
the Grand Officers of Yàn will not trust me;
if I am lowly,
they will slight me;
if I am employed,
they will have many expectations of me;
if Qí experiences misfortune,
they will blame me;
if the world does not attack Qí,
they will say I am good at plotting for Qí;
if the world attacks Qí,
they will want to execute me along with Qí.
My position is as precarious as stacked eggs.'
Your Majesty said to me:
'I will certainly not listen to the many mouths and slander.
My trust in you
is like the use of a weeding tool.
Above, you can be employed in Qí;
below, you can gain trust from me.
As long as you do not die,
there is nothing you should not do;
you may trust yourself.'
The conversation went:
'It is fine to leave Yàn for Qí;
just aim to accomplish the task.'
I received the order to be tasked with Qí
and it has been five years.
Qí has frequently dispatched troops
but has never plotted against Yàn.
The relations between Qí and Zhào
have united and separated repeatedly.
When the King of Yàn did not plot with Qí against Zhào,
then he plotted with Zhào against Qí.
Qí's trust in Yàn
went as far as emptying the northern lands to move its troops.
Now Your Majesty believes the words of Tián Fá, Cān, and Qùjí
and is about to attack Qí,
causing Qí to act like dogs and horses but say nothing of Yàn.
Now Your Majesty has again sent Qìng to tell me:
'I wish to employ those I favor.'
If Your Majesty truly wishes to employ them,
then I request to serve them for Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty wishes to release me and focus entirely on those you favor,
then I request to return and be released from my duties.
If I can but be granted an audience,
my wishes will be fulfilled."
Chén Cuì brought Qí and Yàn together
and was going to have the King of Yàn's younger brother serve as a hostage in Qí.
The King of Yàn agreed.
The Queen Dowager heard of this and was furious, saying:
"Lord Chén cannot manage the state for others,
and that would be one thing,
but how can he separate a mother and her child?
I want to have my way with him."
Chén Cuì wanted to see the Queen Dowager.
The King said:
"The Queen Dowager is currently angry with you;
you should wait."
Chén Cuì said: "There is no harm."
He then went in to see the Queen Dowager and said:
"Why have you become so thin?"
The Queen Dowager said:
"I rely on the leftover food of geese and ducks from the late King;
I should not be thin.
The reason I am thin
is that I worry the Prince will be a hostage in Qí."
Chén Cuì said: "A ruler's love for their children
is not as deep as that of a commoner.
Not only do they not love their children,
but they particularly lack love for their sons."
The Queen Dowager said:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"When the Queen Dowager marries off a daughter to a feudal lord,
you provide her with a thousand pieces of gold
and a dowry of a hundred lǐ of land
to be her support for life.
Now the King wishes to enfeoff the Prince;
the officials hold their posts
and the ministers show their loyalty, saying:
'The Prince has no merit and should not be enfeoffed.'
Now the King is sending the Prince as a hostage
precisely to establish merit for the Prince so that he may be enfeoffed.
If the Queen Dowager does not permit it,
this is how I know a ruler's love for their sons is particularly lacking.
Furthermore, while the Queen Dowager and the King are fortunately still here,
the Prince is noble.
After the Queen Dowager passes away and the King leaves the state,
and the Crown Prince ascends the throne,
the Prince will be lowlier than a commoner.
Therefore, if the Prince is not enfeoffed while the Queen Dowager and the King can do so,
then the Prince will never be enfeoffed in his life!"
The Queen Dowager said: "I did not understand the plan of an elder."
She then ordered the Prince to prepare the carriages and clothing for the journey.
Yàn Zhāowáng was about to join the rest of the world in attacking Qí.
There was a man of Qí serving in Yàn.
Zhāowáng summoned him and said:
"I am about to join the world in attacking Qí;
the order will be issued very soon.
You must argue against it.
If you argue and I do not listen,
you should then leave and go to Qí.
I may have a time when I seek reconciliation again,
and I will then use you to serve Qí."
At this time,
Yàn and Qí were irreconcilable,
yet the King still uniquely wished to have the intention of recovering relations like this.
Yàn was in famine,
and Zhào was about to attack it.
Chǔ sent a general to Yàn;
he passed through Wèi
and saw Zhào Huī.
Zhào Huī said:
"Ensuring that trouble never arrives
is easier than rescuing someone from trouble.
Wǔ Zǐxū and Gōngzhī Qí were not employed,
while Zhú Zhīwǔ and Zhāng Mèngtán received great rewards.
For this reason, strategists all apply themselves to the way of removing trouble,
but first ensure that the trouble never arrives."
Now I present you with a hundred catties of gold as a parting gift,
but it is better to provide you with words.
Listen to my words and say to the King of Zhào:
“In the past, Wú attacked Qí
because of its famine.
Attacking Qí did not necessarily guarantee victory,
yet the weak Yuè took advantage of their exhaustion to become the hegemon.
Now Your Majesty’s attack on Yān
is also because of its famine.
Attacking it may not necessarily result in victory,
while the powerful Qín will use its troops to press upon Your Majesty from the west.
This would cause the weak Zhào to occupy the position of the strong Wú,
and allow the powerful Qín to take the path by which the weak Yuè became the hegemon.
I hope Your Majesty considers this carefully.”
The messenger then used this to persuade the King of Zhào.
The King of Zhào was greatly pleased
and stopped.
King Zhāo of Yān heard of this
and granted him land as a fief.
Yuè Yì, the Lord of Chāngguó, assembled the troops of five nations for King Zhāo of Yān and attacked Qí,
capturing more than seventy cities,
all of which were turned into commanderies and counties belonging to Yān.
Three cities had not yet fallen
when King Zhāo of Yān died.
King Huì ascended the throne;
he employed the counter-espionage of a man from Qí,
doubted Yuè Yì,
and sent Qì Jié to replace him as general.
Yuè Yì fled to Zhào,
and Zhào enfeoffed him as the Lord of Wàngzhū.
Tián Dān of Qí deceived Qì Jié,
eventually defeated the Yān army,
and reclaimed the seventy cities to restore Qí.
The King of Yān regretted it
and feared that Zhào would use Yuè Yì to take advantage of Yān’s exhaustion to attack Yān.
The King of Yān then sent a messenger to reproach Yuè Yì,
and apologized saying:
“The late King entrusted the whole state to you, General.
You crushed Qí for Yān
and avenged the late King’s grievances.
There was no one in the world who was not shaken.
How could I dare to forget your achievements for even a single day!
It happened that the late King left his ministers,
and I had newly ascended the throne;
those around me misled me.
My reason for sending Qì Jié to replace you, General,
was because you had been exposed to the elements outside for a long time;
therefore, I summoned you to rest and deliberate on affairs.
You misunderstood
and believed there was a rift with me;
thus you abandoned Yān and returned to Zhào.
It is fine if you planned for yourself,
but how does that repay the intention with which the late King treated you?”
The Lord of Wàngzhū then sent a messenger to present a letter in reply to the King of Yān, saying:
“I am not talented;
I was unable to uphold the teachings of the late King
or harmonize with the hearts of your attendants.
Fearing the punishment of the axe and the block,
which would mar the wisdom of the late King
and harm Your Majesty’s righteousness,
I fled to Zhào.
Carrying the guilt of being unworthy,
I did not dare to offer excuses.
Now Your Majesty has sent a messenger to enumerate my crimes.
I fear that your attendants do not understand the principles by which the late King cherished and favored his servant,
and do not clarify the heart with which I served the late King;
thus I dare to respond with this letter.
I have heard that a wise and sagely ruler
does not grant stipends to favor his relatives
but bestows them upon those with great merit;
he does not grant offices to follow his affections
but places those who are capable in them.
Therefore, he who examines capability and bestows office
is a ruler who achieves success;
he who weighs conduct and forms associations
is a gentleman who establishes a reputation.
From what I have learned,
the actions of the late King
showed an ambition that transcended the world.
Thus, he borrowed the tallies from the King of Wèi,
and I was personally examined in Yān.
The late King mistakenly elevated me,
promoting me from among the guests
and placing me above the other ministers.
Without consulting his kinsmen,
he made me a Sub-Chancellor.
I thought that by following orders and receiving teachings,
I might fortunately remain free from blame;
thus, I accepted the command without decline.
The late King commanded me, saying:
‘I have accumulated resentment and deep anger toward Qí.
Without measuring our lightness or weakness,
I wish to make Qí my objective.’
I replied: ‘Qí is a state with the remaining teachings of a hegemon,
and its legacy of frequent victories persists.
They are skilled in arms and armor
and practiced in battle and siege.
If Your Majesty wishes to attack them,
you must mobilize the whole world to plan against them.
To mobilize the whole world to plan against them,
there is no more direct way than forming an alliance with Zhào.
Furthermore, the lands of Huáiběi and Sòng
are the shared desires of Chǔ and Wèi.
If Zhào grants permission
and we ally with Chǔ and Wèi,
and Sòng exerts its full effort,
with four nations attacking it,
Qí can be greatly defeated.’
The late King said: ‘Good.’
I then received the order in person,
prepared the tallies and credentials,
and was sent south as an envoy to Zhào.
Upon returning and reporting my mission,
troops were raised to follow and attack Qí.
By the Way of Heaven
and the spiritual power of the late King,
the lands north of the River
were taken by the late King at the Jì River.
The army at the Jì River followed orders to strike Qí
and won a great victory.
Light and elite troops
drove deep into their capital.
The King of Qí fled to Jǔ,
barely escaping with his life.
Pearls, jades, and treasures,
chariots, armor, and precious vessels
were all brought into Yān.
The Dàlǚ bell was displayed in the Yuányīng Hall,
the ancient tripods were returned to the Lìshì Room,
and the vessels of Qí were set upon the Níng Terrace.
The plants of Jìqiū
were planted at Wènhuáng.
Since the time of the Five Hegemons,
no merit has equaled that of the late King.
The late King felt his ambitions were satisfied
and considered that I had not failed his command;
thus, he partitioned land to enfeoff me,
allowing me to be ranked among the lords of small states.
I am not talented;
I thought that by following orders and receiving teachings,
I might fortunately remain free from blame;
thus, I accepted the command and did not decline.
I have heard that a wise and enlightened ruler
establishes achievements without letting them fall into ruin,
so they are recorded in the annals;
a scholar of early foresight
achieves fame without it being destroyed,
so he is praised by later generations.
As for the late King’s avenging of grievances and washing away of shame,
his overthrow of a powerful state of ten thousand chariots,
and his seizure of the accumulations of eight hundred years—
until the day he left his ministers,
the remaining orders and the legacy he bequeathed to his descendants,
as well as the ministers who held power and managed affairs,
the way they could follow the laws
and harmonize with the various branches of the family,
extending even to the common people and servants—
all these can serve as teachings for later generations.
I have heard that one who is good at beginning
is not necessarily good at completing;
one who is good at starting
is not necessarily good at finishing.
In the past, Wǔ Zǐxū’s advice was heard by Hélǘ,
so the King of Wú’s footprints reached as far as Yǐng.
Fūchāi did not agree with him,
gave him a chīyí leather sack and cast him into the river.
Thus King Fūchāi of Wú did not realize that previous counsel could establish merit,
and so he drowned Zǐxū without regret.
Zǐxū did not foresee early enough the difference in the caliber of his lords,
and so he entered the river without being able to change things.
To escape with one’s life and keep one’s achievements intact
so as to illuminate the tracks of the late King
was my best course of action.
To suffer the wrongs of slander and disgrace
and bring down the reputation of the late King
was my greatest fear.
To face an unfathomable crime
and hope for luck as a benefit
is something that righteousness does not dare to do.
I have heard that the gentlemen of old,
when severing a relationship, do not utter harsh words;
when a loyal minister leaves his state,
he does not try to clear his own name.
Although I am not talented,
I have many times received the teachings of gentlemen.
I fear that your attendants believe the words of those close to you
and do not examine the conduct of those who are distant.
Therefore, I dare to report with this letter;
may Your Majesty grant it your attention.”
Someone presented a letter to the Yān Wáng:
"If a Wáng cannot rely on himself,
and does not loathe a humble reputation to serve the strong,
serving the strong
can bring peace and stability to the state for a long time;
it is a beneficial plan for ten thousand generations.
If serving the strong cannot endure for ten thousand generations,
then it is better to unite the weak.
How can one deal with it if the weak unite but cannot act as one?
This is why I am distressed for Shāndōng.
The bìmùyú fish,
if they do not find each other, they cannot swim;
therefore the ancients praised them,
because they unite two into one.
Now Shāndōng unites the weak but cannot act as one;
this shows the wisdom of Shāndōng is inferior to that of a fish.
It is also like laborers pulling a cart;
if three people cannot move it,
they seek two more,
and with five people the cart then moves.
Now the three states of Shāndōng are weak and cannot oppose Qín;
if they seek two more states,
they will then be able to defeat Qín.
Yet Shāndōng does not know how to seek each other out;
their wisdom is certainly inferior to that of cart laborers.
The Hú and the Yuè people,
their languages are mutually unintelligible,
and their intentions do not communicate,
yet when they share a boat and ride the waves,
when it comes to it, they help each other as if one.
Now the relationship between the Shāndōng states
is like crossing in the same boat;
when the troops of Qín arrive,
they cannot help each other as one;
their wisdom is again inferior to that of the Hú and Yuè people.
These three things
are within human capability,
yet the lords of Shāndōng never realize this;
this is why I am distressed for Shāndōng.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
If Shāndōng unites,
its lords will not have a humble reputation,
its states can endure long,
and its soldiers can go out to guard the western borders of Hán and Liáng;
this is the best plan for Yān.
If this is not done urgently,
the state will surely be in danger,
and the lord will surely have great sorrow.
Now the three states of Hán, Liáng, and Zhào have already united;
when Qín sees the firmness of the Sānjìn,
it will surely attack Chǔ in the south.
When Zhào sees Qín attacking Chǔ,
it will surely attack Yān in the north.
In the nature of things, there are situations where the circumstances differ but the calamities are the same.
Qín long attacked Hán,
and therefore Zhōngshān perished;
now if it long attacks Chǔ,
Yān will surely perish.
I humbly plan for the Wáng: it is better to lead troops south to unite with the Sānjìn,
and agree to guard the western borders of Hán and Liáng.
If Shāndōng cannot firmly do this,
then they will all surely perish."
Yān indeed used its troops to go south and unite with the Sānjìn.
A guest said to the Yān Wáng:
"Qí has defeated Chǔ in the south,
and forced Qín to submit in the west;
using the troops of Hán and Wèi,
and the masses of Yān and Zhào,
is like using a whip or a lash.
If Qí were to face north and attack Yān,
then even five Yān states could not withstand it.
Why does Your Majesty not secretly send an envoy,
to scatter traveling scholars,
to exhaust Qí's troops,
and weary its people,
so that for generations there will be no trouble?"
The Yān Wáng said:
"Give me five years,
and I will achieve my ambition."
Sū Zǐ said: "I request that Your Majesty be given ten years."
The Yān Wáng was pleased,
and provided Sū Zǐ with fifty chariots,
sending him south as an envoy to Qí.
He said to the Qí Wáng:
"Qí has defeated Chǔ in the south,
and forced Qín to submit in the west;
using the troops of Hán and Wèi,
and the masses of Yān and Zhào,
is like using a whip or a lash.
I have heard that for a Wáng to arise in this age,
he must punish the tyrannical and correct the chaotic,
remove the wayless,
and attack the unrighteous.
Now the Sòng Wáng shoots at Heaven and whips the Earth,
casts statues of the zhūhóu,
and makes them attend to the screens and latrines,
stretching out their arms,
and flicking their noses;
this is the height of waylessness and unrighteousness in the world,
yet Your Majesty does not attack him;
Your Majesty's name will never be established.
Furthermore, Sòng
is the fertile land of the Zhōngguó,
where the neighbors dwell;
rather than gaining a hundred lǐ from Yān,
it is better to gain ten lǐ from Sòng.
If you attack it, the name is righteous,
and the reality is profitable;
why does Your Majesty not do it?"
The Qí Wáng said: "Good."
He then mobilized troops to attack Sòng,
defeated Sòng three times,
and Sòng was then taken.
When the Yān Wáng heard of this,
he broke off relations with Qí,
led the troops of the world to attack Qí,
with one major battle,
and two minor battles,
he exhausted the state of Qí,
and established his name.
Therefore it is said:
by following its strength and making it stronger,
it can then be broken;
by following its greatness and making it greater,
it can then be depleted.
Zhào was about to attack Yān;
Sū Dài, on behalf of Yān, said to Huì Wáng:
"Just now as I was coming,
passing the Yì Shuǐ,
a clam was out sunning itself,
and a snipe pecked at its flesh;
the clam closed up and nipped its beak.
The snipe said: 'If it does not rain today,
and it does not rain tomorrow,
then there will be a dead clam.'
The clam also said to the snipe: 'If you do not get out today,
and you do not get out tomorrow,
then there will be a dead snipe.'
Neither of the two was willing to let go,
and a fisherman came along and caught them both.
Now Zhào is about to attack Yān;
if Yān and Zhào sustain a conflict for a long time,
so as to weary the masses,
I fear that the powerful Qín will play the part of the fisherman.
Therefore I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully."
Huì Wáng said: "Good."
He then stopped.
Qí and Wèi were contending over Yān.
Qí said to the Yān Wáng:
"I have secured Zhào's support."
Wèi also said to the Yān Wáng:
"I have secured Zhào's support."
Yān had no way to decide,
and had not yet decided which to join.
Sū Zǐ said to the Yān Xiàng:
"I have heard that those whose words are humble but gifts are heavy
are those who lose the world;
those whose words are haughty but gifts are light
are those who gain the world.
Now Wèi's words are haughty and its gifts are light."
Yān therefore allied with Wèi,
secured Zhào,
and Qí then fled north.
Qí, Hán, and Wèi together attacked Yān;
Yān sent the Tài Zǐ to request help from Chǔ.
The Chǔ Wáng sent Jǐng Yáng to lead the rescue.
Stopping for the night,
he ordered the left and right Sīmǎ to each establish a camp;
when finished,
they planted markers.
Jǐng Yáng said angrily:
"The place where you have camped
will be reached by water so as to submerge the markers.
How can we stay here!"
He then ordered them to move.
The next day there was a heavy rain,
mountain waters flooded out,
and the place where they had camped
was entirely submerged past the markers.
The military officers then submitted.
Thereupon they did not rescue Yān,
but instead attacked Yōngqiū in Wèi,
taking it to give to Sòng.
The three states were afraid,
and so they withdrew their troops.
The Wèi army was to its west,
the Qí army was to its east,
and the Chǔ army wanted to return but could not.
Jǐng Yáng then opened the Xīhé Mén,
by day using chariots and cavalry,
by night using torches to be seen,
communicating with envoys to Wèi.
The Qí army found it strange,
and thinking that Yàn, Chǔ, and Wèi were conspiring against them,
they withdrew their troops and left.
Once the Qí troops had left,
Wèi lost its allies
and having no one with whom to join forces to attack Chǔ,
they fled under the cover of night.
The Chǔ army then returned.
Zhāng Chǒu was a hostage in Yàn.
The King of Yàn wanted to kill him.
As he was fleeing and about to cross the border,
a border official captured Chǒu.
Chǒu said: "The reason the King of Yàn is about to kill me
is that someone told him I have a precious pearl,
and the King wants to obtain it.
Now I have already lost it,
but the King of Yàn does not believe me.
Now, if you deliver me to him,
I shall say that you snatched my pearl and swallowed it.
The King of Yàn will certainly kill you,
ripping open your belly and searching through your intestines.
As for a ruler who desires to obtain something,
he cannot be persuaded by self-interest.
I will certainly die,
but your intestines will also be cut to pieces."
The border official was terrified and released him.
King Xǐ of Yàn sent Lì Fù with one hundred catties of gold to offer a toast for the longevity of King Xiàochéng of Zhào.
After three days of feasting,
he returned and reported:
"The robust men of Zhào all died at Chángpíng,
and their orphans have not yet grown up;
they can be attacked."
The King then summoned Yuè Jiàn, the Lord of Chāngguó, and asked:
"What do you think?"
He replied: "Zhào
is a state accessible from all sides,
and its people are all experienced in warfare;
you must not do battle with them."
The King said: "If I attack them with double the forces,
is it possible?"
He said:
"No."
He said:
"With triple the forces, is it possible?"
He said:
"No."
The King was greatly enraged.
All those around him thought that Zhào could be attacked,
so he hurriedly raised six hundred thousand troops to attack Zhào.
He ordered Lì Fù to attack
Hào with four hundred thousand men and sent Qìng Qín to attack Dài with two hundred thousand.
Zhào sent Lián Pō with eighty thousand men to meet Lì Fù at Hào
and sent Yuè Chéng with fifty thousand to meet Qìng Qín at Dài.
The people of Yàn were utterly defeated.
Yuè Jiàn entered Zhào.
The King of Yàn sent a letter to offer an apology,
saying:
"I am not talented
and was unable to follow your advice;
thus you abandoned the state and left,
and my unworthiness is clear.
I ventured to state my wishes,
but you were unwilling to listen;
therefore, I have sent a messenger to present my humble thoughts,
and I ask you to consider them.
A saying goes:
'The benevolent do not lightly break off relations;
the wise do not lightly harbor resentment.'
Your relationship with the former King
is something clearly known to the world.
I had hoped that if I were in the wrong, you would cover for me,
and I did not expect that you would publicly condemn me for it;
I had hoped that if I made a mistake, you would instruct and guide me,
and I did not expect that you would publicly condemn me for it.
Furthermore, regarding my sins,
there is no one in the state who does not know of them,
and no one in the world who has not heard of them;
but if you openly express resentment and abandon me,
then I must indeed be guilty.
Although this is so,
I fear that you have not been fully generous.
A proverb says:
'One who is generous does not disparage others to benefit himself;
one who is benevolent does not endanger others to seek fame.'
Therefore, covering up the wickedness of others
is the conduct of a generous person;
saving others from their mistakes
is the way of a benevolent person.
If there is someone in the world to cover up my wickedness
and save me from my mistakes,
is that not what I should expect from your heart?
Now, you received high office from the former King to achieve honor,
yet you lightly abandon me to satisfy your heart;
thus, covering up wickedness and saving me from mistakes
is something difficult to obtain from you.
Moreover, there are those in the world who are mean but for whom generous kindness is shown,
and those whose conduct is flawed but who are still graciously employed.
Now, if you make me bear the sin of unworthiness
while you yourself suffer the burden of having lost your generosity,
then in choosing this for yourself,
there is nothing to be gained from it.
A state having borders
is like a family having walls;
they are used to maintain good relations and conceal what is bad.
If those within a house cannot harmonize with each other
and go out to speak of it to the neighbors,
it is not a wise plan.
To openly abandon someone before any resentment or wickedness has been seen
is not fully generous.
Although I may be unworthy,
I am not as chaotic as Zhòu of Yīn;
although you may be frustrated,
you are not as burdened as Shāng Róng or Jīzǐ.
That being the case, not covering for me internally
but openly resenting me externally
will, I fear, only serve to damage your lofty status and cheapen your conduct;
this is not as it should be.
If it could manifest your righteousness
and perfect your lofty status,
even if I were to bear an evil name,
I would not find it difficult to accept.
If your original intention was to highlight my meanness,
you yourself will not achieve generosity;
if you publicize my disgrace,
you yourself will not achieve honor;
this is to fail in two ways with a single action.
One who is righteous does not diminish others to benefit himself,
much less does he harm others to damage himself!
I hope that you will not, because of my unworthiness,
tarnish the beauty of past events.
In the past,
Liǔxià Huì served as an official in Lǔ
and was dismissed three times yet did not leave.
Someone said to him:
"You should leave."
Liǔxià Huì replied:
"If I am to act differently from others,
where could I go and not be dismissed?
Since I would still be dismissed,
I would rather it be in my home state."
Liǔxià Huì did not let being thrice dismissed burden himself;
therefore, his former achievements were not forgotten.
He did not have the intention of leaving;
therefore, there was no criticism from near or far.
Now, regarding my sins,
while the people of my state do not yet know of them,
those who criticize me are found throughout the world.
A saying goes:
'Arguments do not cultivate the heart;
discussions do not burden external things;
the benevolent do not lightly break off relations;
the wise do not overlook merit.'
One who abandons great merit
is ceasing;
one who lightly breaks off great benefits
is resentful.
To cease and abandon them,
to be resentful and burden them,
might be appropriate for those far away,
but I did not expect this from you.
Now, if I am without guilt,
why should you resent me?
I wish that you would cast aside your resentment,
reflect on the former King,
and once again instruct me!
Perhaps you say:
'I shall harbor a wicked heart to bring your mistakes to completion
and disregard the former King to highlight your evil,'
causing me to be unable to advance and achieve merit
or to retreat and correct my mistakes.
This is what you have calculated;
I ask only that you consider it!
These are my humble thoughts.
I respectfully present them to you in this letter."
Yuè Jiàn and Yuè Chéng resented that their advice was not used; the two of them ultimately remained in Zhào
and did not reply.
Qín annexed Zhào
and turned northward toward Yàn.
When the King of Yàn heard of this,
he sent someone to congratulate the King of Qín.
As the messenger passed through Zhào,
the King of Zhào imprisoned him.
The messenger said: "If Qín and Zhào become one,
then the world will submit.
The reason I am receiving orders within Zhào
is for the sake of Qín.
Now I am serving as an envoy to Qín,
yet Zhào has imprisoned me;
this means there is a rift between Qín and Zhào.
If there is a rift between Qín and Zhào,
the world will certainly not submit,
and Yàn will not receive your commands.
Furthermore, my serving as an envoy to Qín
does not hinder Zhào from attacking Yàn."
The King of Zhào agreed
and sent him on his way.
The envoy saw the King of Qín and said:
"The King of Yàn has heard privately that Qín annexed Zhào,
and the King of Yàn has sent an envoy to offer congratulations with a thousand pieces of gold."
The King of Qín said: "Yàn is without the Way.
I have caused Zhào to possess it,
so why do you offer congratulations?"
The envoy said: "I have heard that when Zhào was whole,
its southern neighbor was Qín,
and to the north Xiàqǔyáng belonged to Yàn.
Zhào spanned three hundred lǐ
and resisted Qín for more than fifty years.
The reason it could not turn the tables and defeat Qín
was that the state was small and its territory had no place from which to expand.
Now Your Majesty makes Zhào annex Yàn in the north;
then Yàn and Zhào will combine their strength,
and they will surely never again submit to Qín.
I privately fear this for Your Majesty."
The King of Qín considered this to be so,
and he raised troops to rescue Yàn.
Crown Prince Dān of Yàn was a hostage in Qín,
but he fled and returned home.
Seeing that Qín was about to destroy the six states
and its troops had already reached the Yì Shǔi,
he feared that disaster was arriving.
Crown Prince Dān was troubled by this
and spoke to his Grand Tutor Jū Wǔ, saying:
"Yàn and Qín cannot both exist;
I wish the Grand Tutor would fortunately plan for this."
Wǔ replied: "Qín's territory encompasses all under Heaven,
and it threatens the Hán, Wèi, and Zhào families.
Thus, the area north of the Yì Shǔi
is not yet settled.
Why, because of the resentment of being mistreated,
do you wish to stroke its reverse scales?"
The Prince said: "If that is so, then by what means shall we act?"
The Grand Tutor said: "Please allow me to go in
and plan for it."
After a while had passed,
General Fán fled Qín for Yàn,
and the Prince sheltered him.
Grand Tutor Jū Wǔ remonstrated, saying: "This cannot be.
With the King of Qín's violence,
and his accumulated resentment toward Yàn,
it is enough to make one's heart go cold,
how much more so when he hears that General Fán is here!
This is like placing meat in the path of a hungry tiger;
the disaster will certainly be irremediable!
Even if we had Guǎn and Yàn,
they could not devise a plan.
I wish the Prince would quickly send General Fán into the Xiōngnú to eliminate the witness.
I ask that we ally with the Sānjìn to the west,
connect with Qí and Chǔ to the south,
and negotiate with the Chányú in the north;
only then can we make plans."
Crown Prince Dān said: "The Grand Tutor's plan
would take a very long time;
my mind is muddled,
and I fear I cannot wait even for a moment.
Moreover, it is not only because of this.
General Fán is destitute in the world
and has entrusted himself to me, Dān.
I, Dān, will never be pressured by powerful Qín
to abandon a friend whom I pity and place him among the Xiōngnú;
that would be the time when my life would surely end.
I wish the Grand Tutor would reconsider."
Jū Wǔ said: "In Yàn there is a Master Tián Guāng;
his wisdom is deep,
his courage is profound;
you may plan with him."
The Prince said:
"I wish, through the Grand Tutor, to make the acquaintance of Master Tián; is that possible?"
Jū Wǔ said: "I respectfully obey."
He went out to see Tián Guāng,
and spoke of the Prince, saying:
"The Prince wishes to plan state affairs with you, Master."
Tián Guāng said: "I respectfully receive your instruction."
Then he went there.
The Prince knelt and welcomed him,
walking backward to lead the way,
and kneeling to dust the mat.
When Master Tián was seated,
and no one else was around,
the Prince left his mat and requested, saying:
"Yàn and Qín cannot both exist;
I wish you, Master, would give this your attention."
Tián Guāng said: "I have heard that when a fine steed is in its prime,
it can gallop a thousand lǐ in one day.
But when it declines,
an inferior horse will lead it.
Now the Prince has heard of the time when I, Guāng, was in my prime,
but he does not know that my spirit has already vanished.
Nevertheless,
I do not dare to neglect state affairs.
My good friend Jīng Kē
can be employed."
The Prince said: "I wish, through you, Master, to make the acquaintance of Jīng Kē;
is that possible?"
Tián Guāng said: "I respectfully obey."
He immediately rose and hurried out.
The Prince saw him to the gate
and said:
"What I have reported
and what you have said, Master,
are great affairs of state;
I wish you, Master, would not leak them."
Tián Guāng bowed his head and smiled, saying:
"I obey."
Stooped, he went to see Jīng Kē
and said:
"I am close with you,
which everyone in the state of Yàn knows.
Now the Prince has heard of the time when I, Guāng, was in my prime,
not knowing that my physical form is no longer up to it.
Fortunately, he instructed me, saying:
'Yàn and Qín cannot both exist;
I wish you, Master, would give this your attention.'
I did not consider myself an outsider
and spoke of you to the Prince;
I wish you would visit the Prince at his palace."
Jīng Kē said: "I respectfully receive your instruction."
Tián Guāng said: "I have heard that the conduct of an elder
is not to make people doubt him.
Now the Prince cautioned me, saying:
'What we have spoken of
are great affairs of the state;
I wish you, Master, would not leak them.'
This means the Prince doubts me.
To act in a way that makes people doubt you
is not the way of a principled and heroic man."
He wished to kill himself to incite Jīng Kē,
and said:
"I wish you would quickly go to the Prince
and say that Guāng is already dead,
to prove that I will not speak."
Then he cut his own throat and died.
Kē saw the Prince
and told him that Tián Guāng was already dead,
to prove that he would not speak.
The Prince bowed twice and knelt,
crawling on his knees and shedding tears.
After a while, he spoke, saying:
"The reason I asked Master Tián not to speak
was that I wished to complete the plan for the great affair.
Now Master Tián has used his death to prove he would not leak the words;
how could this have been my intention?"
Jīng Kē sat down,
and the Prince left his mat, bowed his head to the ground, and said:
"Master Tián did not know that I, Dān, am unworthy,
yet he allowed you to come before me,
wishing that I might have something to say.
This is Heaven taking pity on Yàn and not abandoning its orphan.
Now Qín has a greedy heart,
and its desires cannot be satisfied.
Unless it takes all the land under Heaven
and makes all the kings within the four seas its subjects,
its mind will not be satiated.
Now Qín has already captured the King of Hán
and taken all his territory;
it has also raised troops to invade Chǔ in the south
and to press against Zhào in the north.
Wáng Jiǎn is leading several hundred thousand troops to approach Zhāng and Yè,
and Lǐ Xìn is coming out of Tàiyuán
and Yúnzhōng.
Zhào cannot withstand Qín
and will surely submit.
Once it submits,
then disaster will reach Yàn.
Yàn is small and weak,
and has been frequently distressed by wars;
currently, even mobilizing the whole state would not be enough to oppose Qín.
The feudal lords have submitted to Qín,
and none dare to form an alliance.
My private plan,
in my foolish opinion, is that if we could truly find a brave warrior of the world
to go as an envoy to Qín,
and tempt them with great profit,
the King of Qín would be greedy for the gifts,
and we would certainly get what we desire.
If we could truly kidnap the King of Qín
and make him return all the lands seized from the feudal lords,
like Cáo Mò did with Qí Huán Gōng,
then that would be excellent;
if that is not possible,
then we shall use the opportunity to assassinate him.
With their great generals commanding troops abroad
and great chaos within,
then the ruler and ministers will doubt each other.
By using that interval to influence the feudal lords,
the feudal lords will be able to form an alliance,
and they will certainly succeed in breaking Qín.
This is my ultimate wish,
but I do not know to whom I can entrust this task;
I only hope that you, Jīng Qīng, will give it your attention."
After a long time,
Jīng Kē said:
"This is a great matter of the state;
your servant is of mediocre ability
and I fear I am not worthy of the mission."
The Tàizǐ stepped forward and bowed his head,
firmly entreating him not to decline.
Only then did he give his promise.
Thereupon, he honored Jīng Kē as a Shàngqīng,
provided him with the finest residence,
and the Tàizǐ visited him every day to inquire after him,
providing him with the Tàiláo offerings and rare items,
occasionally presenting him with carriages, horses, and beautiful women,
indulging Jīng Kē's every desire
to satisfy his heart.
After a long time,
Jīng Qīng had not yet shown any intention of departing.
The Qín Jiàng Wáng Jiǎn crushed Zhào,
captured the Zhào Wáng,
seized all its land,
and advanced his troops north to conquer territory,
reaching the southern border of Yān.
Tàizǐ Dān was terrified
and thus pleaded with Jīng Qīng, saying:
"The Qín troops could cross the Yì Shuǐ at any moment;
then, though I might wish to serve you for a long time,
how could it be possible?"
Jīng Qīng said: "Even without the Tàizǐ’s words,
your servant would wish to seek an audience.
But if I go now without proof of trust,
then I cannot get close to Qín.
Now, regarding Jiāngjūn Fán,
the Qín Wáng has offered a reward of a thousand catties of gold
and a fief of ten thousand households for him.
If I could truly obtain Jiāngjūn Fán's head
and present it to the Qín Wáng along with the map of Dūkàng in Yān, the Qín Wáng will surely be pleased to see me,
and then I would have the means to repay the Tàizǐ."
The Tàizǐ said: "Jiāngjūn Fán came to return to Dān because of his desperate straits;
Dān cannot bear, for my own selfish reasons,
to harm the heart of a worthy man.
I hope you will reconsider."
Jīng Kē knew the Tàizǐ could not bear it,
so he privately went to see Fán Yúqī and said:
"The way Qín has treated you, Jiāngjūn,
can be called extreme.
Your parents and kinsmen
have all been executed or enslaved.
Now I hear there is a reward for the Jiāngjūn's head
of a thousand catties of gold
and a fief of ten thousand households.
What will you do?"
Jiāngjūn Fán looked up to heaven, sighed deeply, and wept, saying:
"Every time I think of it,
it pains me to my very marrow;
but I simply do not know what plan to follow."
Kē said: "Now I have a proposal
that can resolve the peril of the Yān Guó
and avenge the Jiāngjūn's grievances;
how does that sound?"
Fán Yúqī then stepped forward and said:
"How can it be done?"
Jīng Kē said:
"I wish to have the Jiāngjūn's head to present to Qín.
The Qín Wáng will surely be delighted and receive me well.
I will seize his sleeve with my left hand
and strike his chest with a dagger in my right hand.
If so, then the Jiāngjūn's vengeance will be achieved,
and the shame of the Yān Guó being bullied will be removed.
Does the Jiāngjūn have a mind for this?"
Fán Yúqī bared one shoulder, gripped his wrist, and stepped forward, saying:
"This is what I have ground my teeth and clutched my heart over day and night,
and only now do I receive your instruction."
He then cut his own throat.
The Tàizǐ heard of it, rushed there,
threw himself on the corpse and wailed,
in extreme grief.
When it was over,
as nothing could be done,
he finally collected and placed Fán Yúqī's head in a box
and sealed it.
Thereupon,
the Tàizǐ sought out the sharpest daggers in the world in advance.
He obtained the dagger of the Zhào person Xú Fūrén,
purchasing it for a hundred pieces of gold.
He had a craftsman temper it with poison
to test it on people.
If the blood wetted even a single thread,
there was no one who did not die instantly.
Then he prepared the equipment and sent off Jīng Kē.
In the Yān Guó there was a brave warrior named Qín Wǔyáng;
at the age of twelve,
he had killed a man,
and people did not dare to look him in the eye.
So he ordered Qín Wǔyáng to be the assistant.
Jīng Kē was waiting for someone
with whom he wished to go together;
that person lived far away and had not yet arrived,
so he stayed behind to wait for him.
A short while passed and he had not yet set out.
The Tàizǐ thought he was delaying
and suspected he had regrets;
he then pleaded with him again, saying:
"The days are running out;
does Jīng Qīng no longer have the intention?
Dān begs to send Qín Wǔyáng first." Jīng Kē grew angry
and shouted at the Tàizǐ, saying:
"One who goes today and does not return is a mere wretch!
To now take a single dagger into the unpredictable and powerful Qín—
the reason I stayed
was to wait for my guest to go together.
Now that the Tàizǐ thinks I am late,
I beg to take my final leave!"
Then he departed.
The Tàizǐ and those guests who knew of the matter
all wore white robes and caps to see him off.
Arriving at the bank of the Yì Shuǐ,
after performing the sacrifice to the road god,
they set out on the road.
Gāo Jiànlí struck the Zhù,
Jīng Kē sang in harmony,
producing the sound of the Biànzhǐ tone;
the men all shed tears and wept.
Then he stepped forward and sang a song, saying:
"The wind sighs, oh, the Yì Shuǐ is cold;
the brave man once gone, oh, never to return!"
Again he sang in the passionate Yǔ mode;
the men all glared with wide eyes,
and their hair all stood up, pointing at their caps.
Thereupon Jīng Kē mounted his carriage and left,
and in the end never looked back.
After arriving in Qín,
carrying gifts and goods worth a thousand pieces of gold,
he gave lavish presents to the Qín Wáng’s favorite official, the Zhōngshùzǐ Méng Jiā.
Jiā spoke first to the Qín Wáng, saying:
"The Yān Wáng is truly trembling with fear and in awe of Your Majesty's might;
he dares not raise troops to resist Your Majesty.
He wishes to offer his whole state to be an internal vassal,
ranking among the feudal lords,
and providing tribute and duties like a commandery or county,
so that he may maintain the ancestral temple of his former kings.
In fear, he did not dare to present himself,
so he has respectfully severed the head of Fán Yúqī
and presents the map of Dūkàng in Yān,
sealed in a box.
The Yān Wáng bowed as he saw them off from his court,
and sent envoys to inform Your Majesty.
We await only Your Majesty's command."
The Qín Wáng was greatly pleased to hear this.
He then put on his court robes,
arranged the Jiǔbīn ceremony,
and received the envoys of Yān at the Xiányáng Gōng.
Jīng Kē carried the box containing Fán Yúqī's head,
while Qín Wǔyáng carried the map case,
and they advanced in order to the steps of the throne.
Qín Wǔyáng's expression changed and he trembled with fear.
The courtiers found this strange.
Jīng Kē looked back and smiled at Wǔyáng,
then stepped forward to apologize, saying:
"He is a rustic man from the Běi Mán Yí
and has never seen the Tiānzǐ;
therefore he is trembling in awe.
I hope Your Majesty will be slightly indulgent with him
so that he may complete his mission before you."
The Qín Wáng said to Kē:
"Rise and take the map held by Wǔyáng."
Once Kē had taken the map and presented it,
he unrolled the map.
When the map was fully unrolled, the dagger appeared.
He then seized the Qín Wáng's sleeve with his left hand
and held the dagger with his right hand to strike him.
Before it reached his body,
the Qín Wáng was startled,
pulled himself back and stood up,
tearing off the sleeve.
He tried to draw his sword,
but the sword was long,
and he grasped its scabbard.
At that moment of distress and haste,
the sword was tight,
so it could not be drawn immediately.
Jīng Kē pursued the Qín Wáng,
and the Qín Wáng ran around a pillar.
The courtiers were stunned and horrified;
as the event happened so suddenly and unexpectedly,
they all lost their composure.
According to the law of Qín,
those of the officials attending in the palace hall
were not permitted to carry any weapon.
The various Lángzhōng who carried weapons
were all stationed below the hall,
and could not come up without a summons.
In the emergency,
there was no time to summon the guards from below;
for this reason, Jīng Kē pursued the Qín Wáng,
and in the sudden panic they had nothing with which to strike Kē,
so they fought him with their bare hands together.
At that time,
the attending physician Xià Wúqiě
used the medicine bag he was presenting to strike Jīng Kē.
As the King of Qín was running around the pillar,
in his sudden panic he did not know what to do.
The attendants then said:
"Your Majesty, carry the sword on your back!
Your Majesty, carry the sword on your back!"
He then drew it to strike Jīng Kē,
severing his left thigh.
Jīng Kē was incapacitated;
he then pulled out his dagger
to throw it at the King of Qín.
It did not hit him;
it hit the pillar.
The King of Qín struck Kē again,
and he received eight wounds.
Kē knew the matter would not succeed,
so he leaned against the pillar and laughed,
sitting with his legs spread out and cursing:
"The reason the matter did not succeed
was that I wanted to kidnap you alive,
to surely obtain a treaty to report to Tàizǐ Dān."
After the attendants stepped forward and cut down Jīng Kē,
the King of Qín's eyes were dazed for a long time.
Then he deliberated on the merits to reward the ministers and those who deserved punishment,
each with their respective differences.
He gave Xià Wúqiě two hundred yì of gold,
saying: "Xià Wúqiě loves me;
he used the medicine bag to strike Kē."
Thereupon, Qín was greatly enraged at Yān,
and sent more troops to Zhào,
decreeing that Wáng Jiǎn’s army should attack Yān.
In ten months, they captured the city of Jì in Yān.
King Xǐ of Yān, Tàizǐ Dān, and others
all led their elite troops east to take refuge in Liáodōng.
The Qín general Lǐ Xìn pursued and struck the King of Yān.
The King was in a desperate situation,
and used the plan of Jiā, the King of Dài,
to kill Tàizǐ Dān,
intending to present him to Qín.
Qín again advanced its troops to attack them.
After five years, they finally destroyed the state of Yān
and captured King Xǐ of Yān.
Qín unified the world.
Later, Jīng Kē's guest Gāo Jiànlí, by playing the zhù, had an audience with the Qín Emperor,
and he used the zhù to strike the Qín Emperor,
seeking revenge for Yān;
he missed and died.
Qí attacked Sòng,
and Sòng sent Zāngzǐ to seek help from Jīng.
The King of Jīng was greatly pleased,
and his promise of help was very encouraging.
Zāngzǐ was worried and returned.
His driver said: "You sought help and obtained it;
why do you have a worried look?"
Zāngzǐ said: "Sòng is small and Qí is large.
To seek help for small Sòng and incur the enmity of large Qí
is something the King should worry about;
yet the King of Jīng was very pleased,
so he must be doing it to strengthen our resolve.
If we are firm and Qí is exhausted,
it is to Jīng's advantage."
Zāngzǐ then returned.
The King of Qí indeed attacked,
capturing five cities of Sòng,
but the King of Jīng did not arrive.
Gōngshū Bān designed a machine for Chǔ,
intending to use it to attack Sòng.
Mòzǐ heard of this
and traveled a hundred shè until his feet were heavily calloused,
going to see Gōngshū Bān,
and said to him: "I have heard of you from Sòng.
I wish to borrow your help to kill a king."
Gōngshū Bān said: "My sense of righteousness certainly forbids me from killing a king."
Mòzǐ said:
"I heard that you have made cloud-ladders
to attack Sòng.
What crime has Sòng committed?
You say your righteousness forbids killing a king but you attack a state;
this is not killing the few but killing the many.
Dare I ask what righteousness there is in attacking Sòng?"
Gōngshū Bān was convinced
and requested him to see the King.
Mòzǐ saw the King of Chǔ and said:
"Suppose there is a person here
who abandons his decorated carriage
while his neighbor has a broken cart that he wishes to steal;
he abandons his fine silks
while his neighbor has a short coarse garment that he wishes to steal;
he abandons his fine meats
while his neighbor has dregs and husks that he wishes to steal.
What kind of person is this?"
The King said: "He must have a stealing sickness."
Mòzǐ said: "The territory of Jīng is five thousand lǐ square,
while Sòng is five hundred lǐ square;
this is like the decorated carriage compared to the broken cart.
Jīng has Yúnmèng,
where rhinoceroses, buffaloes, elks, and deer fill it,
and the fish, turtles, and alligators of the Jiāng and Hàn are the wealthiest in the world;
Sòng is what is called a place without pheasants, rabbits, or carp;
this is like the fine meats compared to the dregs and husks.
Jīng has tall pines, catalpas, camphor trees, and nanmu,
while Sòng has no tall timber;
this is like the fine silks compared to the short coarse garment.
I consider the King's officials' attack on Sòng
to be of the same category as this."
The King said: "Well said!
I request not to attack Sòng."
Xīshǒu attacked Huáng,
and passing through Wèi,
he sent a man to say to the Lord of Wèi:
"The army of my humble state is passing through the outskirts of your great state;
was there not even a single envoy to attend to us?
I venture to ask what our offense is.
Now the city of Huáng is about to fall;
when it is finished,
I will move my troops to the walls of your great state."
The Lord of Wèi was afraid
and gathered three hundred bundles of silk cord
and three hundred yì of gold
to follow the messenger.
Nán Wénzǐ stopped him, saying:
"If he conquers the city of Huáng,
he will certainly not dare to come;
if he does not conquer it,
he also will not dare to come.
If he conquers the city of Huáng,
his merit will be great and his reputation beautiful,
and internally he will oversee his peers.
Those in the court hate being overseen
and will criticize his affairs.
Bearing a great reputation
and holding successful achievement,
to sit and remain in control while awaiting the court's criticism—
even if Xīshǒu is foolish,
he will certainly not do this.
If he does not conquer the city of Huáng,
he will be disheartened and flee, returning home,
and fearing he will not escape punishment!
How would he dare to attack Wèi to aggravate the crime of his failure?"
He indeed conquered the city of Huáng,
led his army back,
and thus did not dare to pass through Wèi.
The King of Liáng attacked Hándān
and requested troops from Sòng.
The Lord of Sòng sent an envoy to request of the King of Zhào:
"The troops of Liáng are strong and their power is heavy;
now they request troops from my humble state.
If my humble state does not comply,
then I fear for the safety of our state;
if I help Liáng attack Zhào
and thereby harm the state of Zhào,
I cannot bear it.
I hope Your Majesty has some instruction for my humble state."
The King of Zhào said: "Indeed.
That Sòng is not a match for Liáng
is something I know.
To weaken Zhào and strengthen Liáng
would certainly not be advantageous for Sòng.
So what can I tell you that would be acceptable?"
The envoy said:
"I request to be given a border city;
we will slow our attack and prolong the days
just to wait until our officials have a city."
The King of Zhào said: "Excellent."
The people of Sòng accordingly raised troops and entered the border of Zhào
and besieged a city there.
The King of Liáng was very pleased,
and said:
"The people of Sòng are helping me in the attack."
The King of Zhào was also pleased and said:
"The people of Sòng have stopped at this."
Therefore, the troops withdrew and the difficulty was resolved;
kindness was bestowed upon Liáng while no resentment was held by Zhào.
Thus, the reputation was earned and the reality returned to its source.
Someone said to the Dàyǐn:
"The King is growing older every day;
when he personally manages the government,
you will have nothing to do.
You would be better off having Chǔ congratulate the King on his filial piety;
then the King will not take away the affairs of the Tàihòu,
and you will always be employed by Sòng."
Sòng and Chǔ were allies.
Qí attacked Sòng,
and the King of Chǔ declared he would rescue Sòng.
Sòng then used the influence of Chǔ as leverage to seek peace with Qí,
but Qí did not listen.
Sū Qín spoke to the Chancellor of Qí on behalf of Sòng, saying:
“It is better to grant them peace,
so as to make clear Sòng’s betrayal of Chǔ’s influence to Qí.
Chǔ will be enraged
and will certainly break with Sòng to serve Qí.
Once Qí and Chǔ are united,
then attacking Sòng will be easy.”
The Crown Prince of Wèi personally led an army
and passed through Wàihuáng in Sòng.
Xú Zǐ of Wàihuáng said:
“I have a tactic for winning a hundred victories in a hundred battles;
can the Prince listen to me?”
The Prince said: “I wish to hear it.”
The guest said: “I truly wish to offer it.
Now the Prince is personally leading an attack on Qí;
even if you win a great victory and annex Jǔ,
your wealth will not exceed what Wèi already possesses,
and your status will not increase beyond being a king.
If the battle is not won,
then for ten thousand generations there will be no Wèi.
This is my tactic for winning a hundred victories in a hundred battles.”
The Prince said: “Agreed.
I shall certainly follow your words and return.”
The guest said: “Although the Prince may wish to return,
he will not be able to.
Those who profit from the Prince’s warfare
and wish to satisfy their own desires are many;
although the Prince may wish to return,
I fear he will not be able to.”
The Prince boarded his carriage and requested to return.
His driver said: “To set out and then return
is the same as a defeat;
it is better to proceed.”
They then proceeded.
He fought with the people of Qí and died,
and in the end, he did not obtain Wèi.
During the time of Sòng Kāng Wáng,
a sparrow gave birth to a hawk in a corner of the city wall.
He ordered a historian to divine it,
who said:
“For the small to give birth to the large
means you will certainly hegemonize the world.”
Sòng Kāng Wáng was greatly pleased.
Thereupon he destroyed Téng and attacked Xuē,
taking the lands of Huáiběi.
He then became even more self-confident
and wished for his hegemony to be quickly achieved.
Therefore, he shot at the heavens and whipped the earth,
hacked at the altars of the soil and grain and burned them,
saying:
“My prestige subdues the ghosts and gods of the world.”
He cursed the state elders who remonstrated,
and wore a shameless cap
to display his courage.
He cut open the backs of hunchbacks
and chopped the shins of those crossing the river in the morning,
and the people of the state were greatly terrified.
Qí heard of this and attacked him;
the people dispersed,
and the city was not defended.
The King then fled to the lodge of the Ní Hóu,
where he was eventually caught and died.
To see an omen and not act with virtue
instead brings calamity.
Zhì Bó wished to attack Wèi.
He sent the Lord of Wèi four hundred wild horses
and one piece of white jade.
The Lord of Wèi was greatly pleased,
and all the ministers congratulated him,
but Nán Wénzǐ had a look of worry.
The Lord of Wèi said: “A great state shows such great joy,
so why do you have a look of worry?”
Nán Wénzǐ said: “A reward without merit
and a gift without effort
cannot go unexamined.
Four hundred wild horses
and one piece of white jade
are the gifts of a small state,
yet a great state offers them.
You, my Lord, should consider this.”
The Lord of Wèi reported these words to the borders.
Zhì Bó indeed raised troops to surprise Wèi,
but upon reaching the border, he turned back, saying:
“Wèi has a worthy man
who knew my plot in advance.”
Zhì Bó wished to surprise Wèi,
so he feigned the exile of his Crown Prince
and sent him to flee to Wèi.
Nán Wénzǐ said:
“Tàizǐ Yán is a gentleman,
greatly loved and favored.
If he has not committed a great crime and fled,
there must be a reason.”
He sent someone to meet him at the border,
saying:
“If his carriages exceed five,
be careful not to admit them.”
Zhì Bó heard of this
and so he stopped.
Qín attacked Pú of Wèi.
Hú Yǎn said to Chūlǐ Jí:
“In your lordship’s attack on Pú,
is it for Qín?
Or is it for Wèi?
If it is for Wèi, then it is good,
but if it is for Qín, then it is not beneficial.
The reason Wèi is what it is
is because it possesses Pú.
Now if Pú falls to Wèi,
Wèi will surely submit to Wèi.
Wèi lost the lands outside Xīhé
and was unable to retake them
because it was weak.
Now if Wèi annexes Wèi,
Wèi will certainly become strong.
On the day Wèi is strong,
the lands outside Xīhé will certainly be in danger.
Moreover, the King of Qín will also observe your lordship's actions.
If you harm Qín to benefit Wèi,
the King of Qín will certainly resent your lordship.”
Chūlǐ Jí said: “What should be done?”
Hú Yǎn said: “Your lordship should release Pú and not attack it.
I request to enter Pú on your lordship’s behalf to warn its defender,
so that you may show favor to the Lord of Wèi.”
Chūlǐ Jí said: “Good.”
Hú Yǎn then entered Pú
and said to its defender:
“Chūlǐ Zǐ knows the vulnerability of Pú.
He said,
‘I will certainly take Pú.’
Now I can make him release Pú and not attack.”
The defender of Pú bowed twice
and consequently offered three hundred yì of gold,
saying:
“If the Qín troops truly depart,
I request to speak highly of you to the Lord of Wèi.”
Hú Yǎn took the gold from Pú
to increase his own standing in Wèi.
Chūlǐ Zǐ also obtained three hundred jin of gold and returned,
and likewise showed favor to the Lord of Wèi.
Wèi sent a guest to serve Wèi,
but for three years he could not get an audience.
The guest of Wèi was troubled by this
and then went to see Wǔxià Xiānsheng,
promising him a hundred jin of gold.
Wǔxià Xiānsheng said: “Agreed.”
He then saw the King of Wèi and said:
“I hear Qín is sending out troops,
but it is not yet known where they are going.
It has been a long time since the relations between Qín and Wèi have been cultivated.
I wish for the King to serve Qín extensively
and have no other plan.”
The King of Wèi said: “Agreed.”
The guest hurried out,
reached the Lang Gate, and turned back, saying:
“I fear the King’s service to Qín is too late.”
The King said: “Why?”
The Mister said: “People are overly urgent in matters that serve themselves
and overly slow in matters of serving others.
Now the King is slow in matters that serve himself,
so how can he be urgent in serving others?”
“How do you know this?”
“The guest of Wèi said
that he has sought to serve the King for three years without an audience.
I know by this that the King is slow.”
The King of Wèi hurried to see the guest of Wèi.
Wèi Sì Jūn was ill.
Fù Shù said to Yīn Shùnqiě:
“If you listen to my words to persuade the Lord,
without adding or subtracting anything,
the Lord will certainly treat you well.
What a person does in life
is different from the state of mind when facing death.
Originally, what the Lord practiced in the world
was the favor of Gāolì;
those he employed
were Xiè Cuò and Ná Bó.
The ministers all believe the Lord treats the state lightly and loves Gāolì,
so there will certainly be none who talk to the Lord about state affairs.
You should say to the Lord:
‘What the Lord has practiced in the world is very erroneous.
Xiè Cuò makes decisions in the state
and Ná Bó assists him.
From now on, the Gōngsūn clan will surely not receive blood sacrifices.’”
The Lord said:
"Good."
He bestowed upon him the seal of prime minister
and said:
"When I die,
you shall manage the state."
When the Successor Lord died,
Yīn Shùn, using the Lord’s command, served as prime minister for a set term.
The clans of Xiè Cuò
and Ná Bó were all expelled.
During the time of Wèi Sì Jūn,
a convict escaped to the state of Wèi,
and Wèi offered a hundred pieces of gold to ransom him,
but they would not give him up.
Then he requested to trade the land of Zuǒshì for him.
The ministers remonstrated, saying:
"To use the land of Zuǒshì
to ransom a single convict,
is that not unacceptable?"
The Lord said: "In governing, no detail is small;
in disorder, no factor is large.
If moral transformation is clearly understood by the people,
a city of three hundred households
is sufficient to maintain order;
but if the people have no sense of honor or shame,
even if I had ten Zuǒshìs,
what use would they be?"
A man of Wèi was welcoming his new bride.
As the bride boarded the carriage,
she asked:
"The side horses,
whose horses are they?"
The driver said: "They are borrowed."
The bride said to the servant:
"Pat the side horses,
but do not whip the shaft horses."
When the carriage reached the gate,
she was supported as she entered, and she instructed her mother-in-law:
"Extinguish the stove,
or it will cause a fire."
Entering the room and seeing a mortar,
she said:
"Move it under the window;
it obstructs those coming and going."
The master of the house laughed at her.
These three statements
were all essential words,
yet the reason she did not escape being laughed at
was that her timing was either too early or too late.
Wèi Wén Hóu wished to destroy Zhōngshān.
Cháng Zhuāngtán said to Zhào Xiàngzǐ:
"If Wèi annexes Zhōngshān,
Zhào will surely be lost.
Why do you not ask for Gōngzǐ Qīng to be your primary wife,
and then enfeoff him in Zhōngshān,
so that Zhōngshān is restored?"
Xīshǒu established five kings,
but Zhōngshān was the last to hold the title.
Qí said to Zhào and Wèi:
"I am ashamed to be kings alongside Zhōngshān;
I wish to join your great states in attacking it
to abolish its kingship."
Zhōngshān heard of this
and was greatly afraid.
The Ruler summoned Zhāng Dēng and told him:
"I am about to become king,
but Qí told Zhào and Wèi
that it is ashamed to be kings alongside me,
and wishes to attack me.
I fear for the survival of the state
rather than just seeking the kingship.
None but you can save me."
Zhāng Dēng replied: "Prepare many carriages and heavy gifts for me,
and I request to see Tián Yīng."
The Ruler of Zhōngshān sent him to Qí.
He saw Yīng Zǐ and said:
"I have heard you wish to abolish Zhōngshān's kingship
and will join Zhào and Wèi to attack it;
this is an error.
With Zhōngshān's small size,
if three states attack it,
though Zhōngshān would be even more willing to abolish its kingship,
it would still submit.
Moreover, Zhōngshān is afraid
and will surely abolish its kingship for Zhào and Wèi and strive to attach itself to them.
This is like you driving sheep for Zhào and Wèi;
it is not to Qí's advantage.
Would it not be better if Zhōngshān abolished its kingship and served Qí instead?"
Tián Yīng said: "How can this be done?"
Zhāng Dēng said: "Now, if you summon Zhōngshān
to a meeting and grant it kingship,
Zhōngshān will surely be delighted and break with Zhào and Wèi.
Zhào and Wèi will be angry and attack Zhōngshān.
When Zhōngshān is in a crisis and finds it difficult to maintain its kingship because of you,
then Zhōngshān will surely be afraid
and will abolish its kingship to serve Qí.
Since they fear losing their state,
your abolishing their kingship and causing them to lose their state
would be superior to driving sheep for Zhào and Wèi."
Tián Yīng said: "Agreed."
Zhāng Chǒu said: "This is not possible.
I have heard
that those with the same desires hate each other,
while those with the same worries are close to each other.
Now the five states have recognized each other as kings,
but the coastal state of Qí is not among them.
Thus, their desire is all in being kings,
and their worry is the coastal state.
Now if you summon Zhōngshān
to a meeting and grant it kingship,
this is alienating the five states and benefiting the coastal state.
Bringing in Zhōngshān while blocking the four states
will make the four states lose heart.
They will surely recognize its kingship first to intentionally befriend it;
thus you will gain Zhōngshān but lose the four states.
Furthermore, as for Zhāng Dēng's character,
he has long been skilled at using subtle schemes to promote the Ruler of Zhōngshān;
it is difficult to trust him as beneficial."
Tián Yīng did not listen.
He indeed summoned the Ruler of Zhōngshān and granted him kingship.
Zhāng Dēng then said to Zhào and Wèi:
"Qí wishes to attack Hédōng.
How do I know this?
Qí was deeply ashamed to be kings with Zhōngshān,
yet now it summons Zhōngshān
to a meeting and grants it kingship;
this is because it wants to use its troops.
Would it not be better if your great states recognized its kingship first
to stop their meeting?"
Zhào and Wèi agreed
and indeed recognized the King of Zhōngshān and befriended him.
Zhōngshān indeed broke with Qí and followed Zhào and Wèi.
When Zhōngshān was recognized as king along with Yān and Zhào,
Qí closed its passes and would not allow Zhōngshān's envoys through.
Their words were:
"Ours is a state of ten thousand chariots,
while Zhōngshān is a state of one thousand chariots;
how can it equal my name?"
Qí wished to cede Píngyì to bribe Yān and Zhào
and dispatch troops to attack Zhōngshān.
Lán Zhū Jūn was worried about this.
Zhāng Dēng said to Lán Zhū Jūn:
"Why are you worried about Qí?"
Lán Zhū Jūn said: "Qí is strong,
a state of ten thousand chariots,
and it is ashamed to equal names with Zhōngshān.
It does not hesitate to cede land to bribe Yān and Zhào
and dispatch troops to attack Zhōngshān.
Yān and Zhào love status and are greedy for land;
I fear they will not stand by us.
In the worst case the state will be in danger, and in the next the kingship will be abolished;
how can I not worry?"
Zhāng Dēng said:
"I request to make Yān
and Zhào firmly support Zhōngshān and establish its kingship, so that the matter is settled.
Do you desire this?"
Lán Zhū Jūn said: "This is what I desire."
Zhāng Dēng said:
"I request that you act as the King of Qí while I try to persuade you.
If it works, then we shall proceed."
Lán Zhū Jūn said: "I wish to hear your argument."
Zhāng Dēng said:
"The reason the King does not hesitate to cede land to bribe Yān and Zhào
and dispatch troops to attack Zhōngshān
is that he actually wishes to abolish Zhōngshān's kingship.
The King will say: 'Indeed.'
However, the King's actions are costly and dangerous.
Ceding land to bribe Yān and Zhào
strengthens his enemies;
dispatching troops to attack Zhōngshān
initiates a conflict.
Even if the King does both,
what he seeks from Zhōngshān may not be obtained.
If the King uses my method,
land will not be diminished and troops will not be used,
yet Zhōngshān's kingship can be abolished.
The King will surely say: 'What is your method?'"
Lán Zhū Jūn said: "Then what is your method?"
Zhāng Dēng said: "The King should send a grand envoy
to tell the Ruler of Zhōngshān: 'The reason I closed the passes and did not allow envoys through
was that Zhōngshān uniquely became king with Yān and Zhào
and I was not consulted;
therefore I restricted it.
If the King will deign to meet with me,
I request to also support you.'
Zhōngshān fears that Yān and Zhào will not stand by it;
now that Qí's words say 'I will support the King,'
Zhōngshān will surely distance itself from Yān and Zhào
to meet with the King.
When Yān and Zhào hear of this,
they will be angry and break with it,"
The King will also cut them off,
and so Zhōngshān will be isolated.
If isolated, how could it avoid being abolished?
If you use this to persuade the King of Qí,
will the King of Qí listen?"
Lán Zhū Jūn said: "In that case, he will certainly listen.
This is the means to abolish it;
where is the means to preserve it?"
Zhāng Dēng said: "This is the very means by which the King can be preserved.
When Qí comes with this proposal,
use those words to inform Yān and Zhào and do not go to Qí,
thereby accumulating great favor with Yān and Zhào.
Yān and Zhào will surely say:
'Qí's desire to cede Píngyì to bribe us
is not because they wish to abolish the King of Zhōngshān,
but merely because they wish to alienate us from Zhōngshān
so that they may become close to it themselves.'
Even for a hundred Píngyìs,
Yān and Zhào will certainly not accept."
Lán Zhū Jūn said: "Good."
He sent Zhāng Dēng to go,
and indeed the proposal came with those words.
Zhōngshān then informed Yān
and Zhào and did not go.
Yān and Zhào indeed both assisted Zhōngshān and recognized its King.
The matter was thus settled.
Sīmǎ Xǐ was sent to Zhào
to seek the premiership of Zhōngshān for himself.
Gōngsūn Hóng secretly knew of this.
When the Lord of Zhōngshān went out,
Sīmǎ Xǐ drove the chariot
and Gōngsūn Hóng was the third passenger.
Hóng said:
"As a subject,
to summon the prestige of a great state
to seek the premiership for oneself—what do you think of that, my Lord?"
The Lord said: "I would eat his flesh
and not share it with anyone."
Sīmǎ Xǐ bowed his head against the carriage rail and said:
"Your servant knows that death has arrived!"
The Lord asked: "Why?"
"Your servant has committed a crime."
The Lord said: "Proceed,
I know of it."
After a short while,
an envoy from Zhào arrived
to request the premiership for Sīmǎ Xǐ.
The Lord of Zhōngshān greatly suspected Gōngsūn Hóng,
and Gōngsūn Hóng fled.
Sīmǎ Xǐ was Prime Minister of Zhōngshān three times,
and Yīn Jiǎn caused him difficulties.
Tián Jiǎn said to Sīmǎ Xǐ:
"The envoy from Zhào has just arrived;
could you not speak of the beauty of Yīn Jiǎn?
Zhào will surely request her.
If the Lord gives her to them,
then you will have no internal difficulties.
If the Lord does not give her to Zhào,
you should then urge the Lord to establish her as his legitimate wife.
Yīn Jiǎn's gratitude to you
will then be without end."
As expected, he caused Zhào to request her,
but the Lord did not give her.
Sīmǎ Xǐ said:
"If the Lord does not give her to Zhào,
the King of Zhào will surely be greatly enraged;
if he is greatly enraged, then the Lord will certainly be in danger.
However, if you establish her as your wife,
there is no precedent for someone requesting another's wife and, upon not getting her, bearing a grudge."
Tián Jiǎn believed himself successful in his mission,
as it served Sīmǎ Xǐ,
it served Yīn Jiǎn,
and it could make Zhào stop its request.
Yīn Jī and Jiāng Jī competed to be Queen.
Sīmǎ Xǐ said to Yīn Jī's father:
"If the matter succeeds,
then you will have land and people;
if it does not succeed, then I fear you will lose your life.
If you wish it to succeed,
why not see me?"
