Yīn Jī's father bowed his head and said: "It is truly as you say,
how can the matter be planned in advance?"
Sīmǎ Xǐ then submitted a memorial to the King of Zhōngshān, saying:
"Your servant has heard how to weaken Zhào and strengthen Zhōngshān."
The King of Zhōngshān was pleased and saw him, saying:
"I wish to hear the strategy to weaken Zhào and strengthen Zhōngshān."
Sīmǎ Xǐ said: "Your servant wishes to go to Zhào
to observe the strategic difficulty of its terrain,
the wealth or poverty of its people,
and the talent or incompetence of its ruler and ministers.
To use the enemy's situation as one's own resource
cannot be explained beforehand."
The King of Zhōngshān sent him.
He saw the King of Zhào and said:
"Your servant has heard that in Zhào,
people throughout the world are best at music,
and it is where beautiful women come from.
Now,
your servant has arrived at the border,
entered the capital and cities, and observed the people's songs and customs,
but their appearance and complexion
are by no means beautiful or fine.
Your servant has traveled to many places
and wandered everywhere without exception,
yet I have never seen anyone like Yīn Jī of Zhōngshān.
Those who do not know her
take her for a goddess;
description simply cannot do her justice.
Her appearance and complexion
far surpass all others.
As for her eyebrows, eyes, nose, and forehead,
and her noble features like the rhinoceros horn and crescent moon,
she is fit to be the Queen of an Emperor,
not the mere concubine of a feudal lord."
The King of Zhào's mind was swayed,
and greatly pleased, he said:
"I wish to request her,
what do you think?"
Sīmǎ Xǐ said: "Your servant privately saw her beauty
and could not help but speak of it.
If you wish to request her,
that is not something your servant dares to discuss.
I hope the King does not leak this."
Sīmǎ Xǐ took his leave,
returned, and reported to the King of Zhōngshān, saying:
"The King of Zhào is not a worthy king.
He does not love virtue,
but loves music and beauty;
he does not love benevolence and righteousness,
but loves bravery and strength.
Your servant heard that he even wishes to request the one called Yīn Jī."
The King of Zhōngshān's expression changed in displeasure.
Sīmǎ Xǐ said: "Zhào is a powerful state,
and they will certainly request her.
If the King does not give her to them,
then the state will be in danger; if you give her,
then you will be the laughingstock of the feudal lords."
The King of Zhōngshān said: "What should be done?"
Sīmǎ Xǐ said: "The King should establish her as Queen
to cut off the King of Zhào's intentions.
In this world, no one requests a Queen.
Even if he wanted to request her,
the neighboring states would not side with him."
The King of Zhōngshān then established her as Queen,
and the King of Zhào spoke no more of requesting her.
Zhǔfù wished to attack Zhōngshān
and sent Lǐ Cī to observe it.
Lǐ Cī said: "It can be attacked.
If you do not attack,
I fear you will fall behind the rest of the world."
Zhǔfù said: "Why?"
He replied: "The Lord of Zhōngshān
is one who tilts his canopy and carriage to pay court to scholars in poor alleys and narrow lanes,
numbering seventy families."
Zhǔfù said: "He is a worthy ruler;
how can he be attacked?"
Lǐ Cī said: "Not so.
By promoting scholars,
the people will strive for fame and ignore the foundation;
by paying court to the worthy,
the farmers will become lazy and the soldiers will become cowardly.
If a state like this does not perish,
it has never happened."
The Lord of Zhōngshān hosted a feast for the scholars of the capital,
and the Grandee Sīmǎ Zǐqī was among them.
The mutton soup did not reach everyone,
so Sīmǎ Zǐqī was enraged and fled to Chǔ, where he persuaded the King of Chǔ to attack Zhōngshān.
The Lord of Zhōngshān fled.
There were two men carrying spears following behind him.
The Lord of Zhōngshān looked back and said to the two men:
"Who are you?"
The two replied: "Our father
was once starving and about to die,
and you lowered a jar of food to feed him.
When our father was dying,
he said:
'If Zhōngshān has trouble,
you must die for it.'
Therefore we have come to die for you."
The Lord of Zhōngshān sighed deeply, looked up, and lamented:
"Giving does not depend on whether it is much or little,
but on meeting someone in distress;
resentment does not depend on whether it is deep or shallow,
but on hurting someone's heart.
I lost my state because of a bowl of mutton soup,
and gained two warriors because of a jar of food."
Yuè Yáng was a general for Wèi
who attacked Zhōngshān.
His son was in Zhōngshān at the time,
and the Zhōngshān Jūn boiled him
and made a soup to present to Yuè Yáng.
Yuè Yáng ate it.
From ancient times to the present, he has been praised:
Yuè Yáng ate his son to prove his own reliability,
and Míng harmed his father to seek adherence to the law.
After Zhāo Wáng had rested the people and repaired his armaments,
he again wished to attack Zhào.
Wǔ’ān Jūn said:
"It is not possible."
The King said: "The year before last, the state was depleted and the people were hungry;
you did not consider the strength of the common people
when you requested more military rations to destroy Zhào.
Now that I have rested the people to nourish the soldiers
and have accumulated grain and food,
and the pay of the three armies is double what it was before,
you yet say 'it is not possible.'
What is the explanation for this?"
Wǔ’ān Jūn said: "Regarding the affair of Chángpíng,
the Qín army won a great victory,
and the Zhào army was thoroughly crushed.
The people of Qín were joyful,
while the people of Zhào were terrified.
For the Qín people who died, there were lavish burials;
for the wounded, there was generous care;
for those who labored, there were mutual feasts
and provisions of food and drink,
thereby exhausting their wealth.
For the Zhào people who died, their bodies could not be collected;
for the wounded, there was no treatment.
They weep and mourn together,
uniting their efforts and sharing their sorrow.
They plow the fields and work diligently
to produce their wealth.
Now, although the army your Majesty sends out
is twice as large as before,
I estimate that the defensive preparations of Zhàoguó
have also increased tenfold. Since Chángpíng,
the Zhào ruler and his ministers have been anxious and fearful;
they go to court early and leave late.
They use humble words and heavy gifts;
they marry off their daughters in all directions
to form alliances with Yān and Wèi
and establish friendly relations with Qí and Chǔ.
They concentrate their thoughts and unite their hearts,
making preparations against Qín their primary task.
Internally, their state is substantial,
and externally, their diplomatic alliances are complete.
At this present time,
Zhào cannot yet be attacked."
The King said: "I have already raised the army."
He then sent the Grandee of Five Battalions, Wáng Líng, to lead the attack against Zhào.
Wáng Líng suffered a setback in battle
and lost five battalions.
The King wished to employ Wǔ’ān Jūn,
but Wǔ’ān Jūn claimed illness and would not go.
The King then sent Yìng Hóu to see Wǔ’ān Jūn
and rebuke him, saying: "Chǔ
has a territory of five thousand lǐ
and a million halberdiers.
Previously, you led a force of several tens of thousands into Chǔ,
captured Yān and Yǐng,
burned their ancestral temples,
and reached Jìnglíng in the east.
The people of Chǔ were struck with terror
and moved east, not daring to face west.
Hán and Wèi led one another
to raise a very large army,
of which those you led did not amount to half;
yet you fought them at Yīquē,
thoroughly crushed the armies of the two states,
where flowing blood floated shields
and two hundred and forty thousand heads were taken.
Because of this, Hán and Wèi are called the eastern vassals to this day.
These are your achievements,
which everyone in the world has heard of.
Now, seven or eight out of ten Zhào soldiers died at Chángpíng,
and their state is weak and exhausted.
Therefore, I have raised a great army
numbering twice the host of Zhàoguó.
I wish to have you lead them;
I certainly intend to destroy them.
You once struck the many with the few
and achieved victory like a god;
how much more so when striking the weak with the strong
and the few with the many?"
Wǔ’ān Jūn said:
"At that time, the Chǔ Wáng relied on the size of his state
and did not attend to its governance.
His ministers were jealous of one another’s achievements
and used flattery to manage affairs.
Good ministers were rejected and distanced,
the hearts of the common people were alienated,
and the city walls and moats were not repaired.
Having neither good ministers
nor defensive preparations,
this was how I, Qǐ, was able to lead troops deep into their territory,
taking many more cities and towns,
dismantling bridges and burning boats to make the people single-minded,
and plundering the countryside
to provide sufficient food for the army.
At that time,
the officers and soldiers of Qín
regarded the army as their home
and their generals as their parents.
Without any agreement, they were close;
without any consultation, they were trusting.
They were of one heart in their shared achievements
and would not turn their heels even in death.
The people of Chǔ were fighting on their own land;
all looked back toward their homes
and each had a mind to disperse;
none had the will to fight.
This was why I could achieve merit.
In the battle of Yīquē,
Hán was isolated and looked to Wèi,
not wishing to be the first to use its troops.
Wèi relied on the sharpness of Hán
and wished to push them forward as the vanguard.
The two armies did not apply their strength to the same advantage;
therefore, I was able to set up deceptive troops
to face the Hán battle lines
while concentrating the army and uniting our sharpest forces
to strike Wèi where they did not expect it.
Once the Wèi army was defeated,
the Hán army collapsed on its own.
We took advantage of the victory to pursue the fleeing enemies,
and for this reason, I was able to establish merit.
These were all matters of calculating the advantages of the situation
and following natural principles;
what was there of the 'divine'?
Now Qín has crushed the Zhào army at Chángpíng,
yet it did not immediately take advantage of their shock and terror to destroy them,
but instead released them out of fear,
allowing them to engage in farming to increase their stores,
care for the orphans, and raise the young
to increase their numbers,
repair their weapons and armor to increase their strength,
and heighten their walls and deepen their moats to increase their defenses.
Their ruler humbles himself to serve his ministers,
and the ministers put themselves second to serve the death-defying soldiers.
As for those like Píngyuán Jūn,
they even order their wives and concubines to do sewing among the ranks.
Ministers and people are of one heart, and high and low combine their strength,
just like when Gōujiàn was trapped at Kuàijī.
If we attack them now,
Zhào will surely defend firmly.
If we provoke their army to battle,
they will certainly refuse to come out.
If we besiege their capital,
it certainly cannot be overcome.
If we attack their various cities,
they certainly cannot be captured.
If we plunder their countryside,
we will surely gain nothing.
If the army goes out without success,
the feudal lords will harbor other intentions,
and external rescue will surely arrive.
I see the harm in it
but have not seen the benefit.
Furthermore, I am ill
and cannot go."
Yìng Hóu withdrew in shame,
and spoke of it to the Wáng.
The Wáng said:
"Without Bái Qǐ,
can I not destroy Zhào?"
He again dispatched more troops
and instead sent Wáng Hé to replace Wáng Líng in the attack on Zhào.
They besieged Hándān for eight or
nine months;
the dead and wounded were numerous,
but the city did not fall.
The Zhào Wáng sent out light and elite troops to raid their rear,
and Qín repeatedly faced setbacks.
Wǔ'ān Jūn said:
"Since my plan was not followed,
what is the situation now indeed?"
The Wáng was enraged upon hearing this,
and thereupon went to see Wǔ'ān Jūn,
forcing him to rise,
and said:
"Although you are ill,
force yourself for Guǎrén's sake to command the army even while lying in bed.
If there is success,
it is Guǎrén's wish
that I shall increase the honors bestowed upon you.
If you do not go,
Guǎrén will resent you."
Wǔ'ān Jūn kowtowed and said:
"I know that by going, though there may be no merit,
I might be spared from guilt.
Although not going is not a crime,
I will not escape execution.
However, I only wish that Dàwáng would look upon my humble plan:
release Zhào and nourish the people
to await changes among the Zhūhóu.
Soothe their fears,
attack their arrogance,
exterminate those who are without the Way,
and thereby command the Zhūhóu;
thus Tiānxià can be settled.
Why must Zhào be made the priority? This is what is called yielding to one official and conquering Tiānxià.
If Dàwáng does not examine my humble plan
but insists on satisfying your heart with Zhào
and thus brings punishment upon me,
this is also what is called conquering one official and yielding to Tiānxià.
Now, as for the sternness of conquering one official,
how can it compare to the greatness of the majesty of conquering Tiānxià?
I have heard that enlightened rulers love their state,
and loyal officials love their reputation.
A broken state cannot be made whole again,
and dead soldiers cannot be brought back to life.
I would rather prostrate myself and receive severe execution to die
than bear being the general of a disgraced army.
I hope Dàwáng will consider this."
The Wáng did not reply and left.
Qín raised an army to approach Zhōu and demand the Nine Tripods.
Qín attacked Yíyáng.
Dōngzhōu and Xīzhōu fought a war.
Dōngzhōu and Xīzhōu disputed.
Dōngzhōu wanted to plant rice.
Zhāoxiàn was in Yángdí.
Qín requested passage through Zhōu to attack Hán.
Chǔ attacked Yōngshì.
Zhōu Zuì spoke to Shí Lǐ.
The Chancellor of Zhōu, Lǚ Cāng, presented a guest to the Lord of Zhōu.
